News.title: Brit, 58, dies after being pulled from sea by lifeguards near popular Algarve holiday resort
News.content:
SEA TRAGEDY Brit, 58, dies after being pulled from sea by lifeguards near popular Algarve holiday resort







Next

A BRITISH man has been found dead in the sea at a popular Algarve holiday spot.

The 58-year-old was spotted floating in the water off Pintadinho Beach, near Portimão, on Wednesday morning before being pulled ashore.

Two lifeguards desperately performed CPR before emergency crews arrived and took over efforts to revive him.

But the man could not be saved and was pronounced dead at the scene.





It is not yet known whether he was holidaying in Portugal or lived in the area.

The circumstances surrounding his death remain unclear.

An autopsy is expected to establish whether he drowned or suffered a medical emergency while in the water.

Portugal’s National Maritime Authority said the alarm was raised at around 9.19am.



Psychologists were also sent to the scene to support the Brit’s devastated family.

A spokesman said: “The body of a 58-year-old English national man has been found floating at Pintadinho beach, in the municipality of Lagoa, with the causes of the incident unknown.

“Upon arrival at the scene, it was found that the victim had already been removed from the water by two lifeguards who began resuscitation efforts until the arrival of the emergency response teams.”

“The Maritime Police Psychology Office was activated and is providing support to the victim’s family.”



There is currently no suggestion the death is being treated as suspicious.

Pintadinho Beach is a small Blue Flag cove near the fishing village of Ferragudo, framed by the Algarve’s distinctive ochre-coloured cliffs.

The tragedy came shortly before another holidaymaker died in the sea just a short drive away.

A 64-year-old Irish man got into difficulties at Prainha Beach in Alvor on Thursday morning.

The alarm was raised shortly after 10.30am at the beach, around a 20-minute drive west of Pintadinho.



More to follow… For the latest news on this story keep checking back at The Sun Online

News.title: Homes evacuated near RAF base as major incident declared with bomb squad probing ‘number of vehicles’ & several arrested
News.content:
'BOMB' PROBE Homes evacuated near RAF base as major incident declared with bomb squad probing ‘number of vehicles’ & several arrested







Next

HOMES have been evacuated near an RAF base as a bomb squad is called in and several men are arrested under the Explosives Act, police say.

The Army’s specialist bomb disposal team is examining a number of vehicles in Whelford, Gloucestershire, near RAF Fairford.



Horrified locals are being evacuated to a nearby leisure centre with police declaring a major incident this morning.

A cordon is currently in place around the site with Gloucestershire Police saying it believes the incident is contained.



Police confirmed that several men had been taken into custody on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

Firearms officers were seen at the scene with roads leading to the nearby RAF base and the surrounding area blocked off by armed cops.

Fairford plays host to US Air Force Personnel and has ⁠been ​used by the US to launch operations ​against Iran.

The air base is home to the US 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron.



A spokesperson for Gloucestershire Police said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

“It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

“The Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles.

“The local residents are being evacuated to a nearby leisure centre.

“A cordon is currently in place but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained.



“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place.”

Security at the base has reportedly been significantly increased in recent days.

Roadblocks ‌and armed police prevented access and emergency vehicles remained parked nearby over the weekend, a witness claimed.



The UK said in July that its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack.

It followed Iran’s Revolutionary Guards warning the government not to allow US bombers to fly from England.

A US Air Force spokesperson said: “The 501st Combat Support ​Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the ​safety and security of our US service ​members, civilians, contractors, and their families.

“We ‌constantly ⁠assess a variety of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and ​their families.”

Villagers near the RAF base say they have been swamped with Iran war plane spotters who are reportedly causing traffic chaos and weeing everywhere.



The airbase, which is currently hosting US bombers amid the war in the Middle East, has been a focal point for national and foreign plane spotters.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Visitors camp outside the RAF base for days in their cars and caravans – using ladders to see over the screens that were installed to stop them from viewing the site.

But the constant influx of plane spotters is upsetting locals, who say they cause antisocial behaviour, “clog up the roads” and use fields surrounding the base as a “toilet.”

News.title: Horror moment huge wildfire erupts in Costa del Sol as firefighters race to battle flames & residents told stay indoors
News.content:
Next

THIS is the horrifying moment a huge wildfire erupts in the Costa del Sol – with residents urged to stay indoors as firefighters tackle the blaze.

The fierce inferno erupted shortly before midnight on Saturday, with shocking footage showing flames surrounding a mountain village near Marbella.



Towering plumes of smoke were seen rising into the night sky, creating an enormous orange glow.

Savage flames were filmed ripping into forested areas in the mountains as stunned bystanders watched the apocalyptic scenes unfold.



In one clip taken from inside a car, blazing trees were seen being swallowed up amid the hellish inferno.

At least 120 firefighters were deployed to tackle the terrifying fire near Igualeja in Malaga province – located halfway between Marbella and Ronda.



It is currently unclear if there are any injuries or whether anyone was evacuated.

Locals and tourists have been ordered to remain indoors during the sprawling wildfire.



Strong winds complicated efforts to battle the vicious flames, authorities confirmed.

They also said five fire engines and several emergency vehicles were deployed to help fight the blaze.

The region’s wildfire emergency was raised to operational level one in the early hours of Sunday.



Flames were reportedly visible from Ronda as the inferno grew larger overnight.

It is also unclear what the total area burned is.

Last night’s horror follows a spate of similar wildfires which have torn through Spain in recent weeks.

Earlier this month, another huge inferno broke out in the Costa del Sol – forcing residents to evacuate as over 100 firefighters battled the flames.

At least five helicopters and over 60 firefighters raced to the blaze in Benahavis, near Brit tourist hotspot Marbella.

News.title: How mystery poisoner who killed seven baffled cops for 40 years… as murder-obsessed chemist named as new suspect
News.content:
Next

It read like a mystery straight from the pages of an Agatha Christie novel.

Seven dead from cyanide poisoning, a prime suspect, ransom letters and talk of the perfect crime. Now investigators believe they have finally found the killer after more than four decades – but he will never face justice.



In late 1982, seven unsuspecting Chicagoans, including a 12-year-old girl, died after taking the painkiller Tylenol which had been intentionally laced with cyanide.

The FBI suspected for four decades that bookkeeper James Lewis was behind the murders after he sent letters to manufacturers Johnson & Johnson, demanding a million dollars to ‘stop the killing’.

Lewis was interviewed by FBI officers at least 34 times denying he had anything to do with the murders. Now cold case cops believe they have found the real culprit – who committed suicide three months after the killings.



They suspect chemist Dr Matthew Francis Betkouski, whose body was found beneath a church pew in Idaho city, was the actual poisoner. In a sick twist, he had killed himself using cyanide.

Betkouski’s body went unidentified for seven years after first being discovered in a Catholic church following a confessional service and became known as the ‘Unknown Wanderer’.

Detectives in Ada County Sheriff’s office this week named him as the potential mastermind behind the shocking deaths that struck fear into the hearts of Americans and forever changed the way medicines were packaged.

Last night America’s top forensic psychiatrist Dr Park Dietz, who helped the FBI with the initial case, told The Sun in an exclusive interview: “I never believed Lewis was guilty.

“These poisonings were the first case of its kind. I never thought that a man who had invented a new form of crime would be dumb enough to leave his fingerprints and DNA on ransom letters like Lewis did.”



Dietz, who has advised the FBI on high-profile cases such as Jeffrey Dahmer, the Unabomber Ted Kaczynski and the Boston Marathon attack, revealed that bosses who once sacked Betkouski from a chemical lab were so worried about retribution they hid cyanide supplies.

The Chicago poisonings began in September 1982 when 12-year-old Mary Kellerman collapsed after taking a Tylenol for cold symptoms.

The next victims were three members of the same family. Adam Janus, 27, took a pill for a headache and died, followed by his brother Stanley, 25, and his wife Theresa, 20, who ingested tablets from the same bottle during a subsequent family gathering of grief.



Mother-of-two Mary McFarland, 31, also died after taking a table to get rid of a sore head while 27-year-old Mary Reiner was trying to ease the pain from childbirth. Flight attendant Paula Prince, 35, was found dead in her flat after buying a bottle.

The idea that someone was lacing painkillers with deadly poison caused mass panic across America and manufacturers announced a huge recall.

Chicago cops put together a special 200-man unit to solve the crime.

Their first suspect came from a tip from a local bartender who said regular Roger Arnold, 48, boasted of possessing cyanide.

Detectives searched Arnold’s home and found several firearms, chemistry equipment and a book on making bombs. A bag of white powder found turned out not to be poison but, intriguingly, Arnold had visited bars near the Walgreens where Paula Prince bought her bottle of Tylenol.



He had also worked with victim Mary Reiner’s father at a warehouse – and Arnold’s wife had been treated at a hospital across the road from the shop where Mary bought the deadly tablets.

Angry that he was named as a suspect, Arnold started stalking the pubs and shot dead a man he believed had pointed the finger of suspicion. Tragically, victim Josh Stanisha, a 46-year-old computer consultant and dad-of-three, had no connection to the case at all.

Arnold was jailed for 30 years for murder in 1984 but served 15 and was freed on parole in the 90s.

By the time he got out of jail, the FBI had turned their attention to their main suspect.



They turned their sights on James Lewis, who also went by the name of Robert Richardson, after he sent a ransom note to pharmaceutical giant Johnson & Johnson demanding they hand over one million dollars to avoid a “bunch more” deaths.

A second letter in the same handwriting was addressed to President Ronald Reagan with the writer vowing to murder more if he raised taxes.



Lewis was convicted of extortion but always denied the murders.

He was repeatedly interviewed by FBI agents, almost goading them with theories on how the killer got away with murder.

Lewis suggested the culprit could have opened the capsule bottles with a paperclip while wearing gloves and, in a 2008 meeting with retired special agent Roy Lane, said: “Sounds to me like somebody did a pre-mix.”

As a teenager, Lewis reportedly chased his mother with an axe and spent time in a psychiatric hospital.

He lived under suspicion until his death in 2023 but it now turns out he could have been totally innocent after all.



Cold case Tim Cooper, of the Ada County police in Idaho, worked with Dr Dietz to prove his theory that Betkouski was behind the murder.

They have images that place the chemist in Chicago in December 1981 and they recovered the suspect’s hand-drawn maps of the city.

Betkouski worked for a fragrance firm in Jacksonville, Florida, from 1975 to 1979 before joining contractor Lockheed in New Mexico, working on a Nasa-related project at White Sands Test Facility.



Dr Dietz told The Sun: “People who knew Betkouski described him as being odd, a loner and paranoid.

“He had an interest in cyanide as a teenager and a very long standing interest in chemistry. In his childhood home he had a stack of recipes for making bombs.

“When he was a student, he created explosives and endangered the lives of others by throwing them under a bunkbed. It earned him the nickname of The Bomber.

“In 1978 he told a co-worker he was interested in working with cyanide.”

In March 1982, a year before the Tylenol killings, Betkouski caused a disturbance while trying to buy cyanide in bulk at a local chemist and lost his job.



Dr Dietz said: “When the company got ready to fire him they were worried about what he might do so got rid of all the cyanide from the lab.”

Betkouski also described to colleagues how the perfect murder could be committed using poison.

The organic chemist was also suffering from mental health issues – exacerbated, Dr Dietz, says by a fall in 1974, which left him in a coma.

Dietz said: “He had two spells in psychiatric units and wrote to friends saying that when he imagined killing people it made him feel euphoric.

“He also thought he would alleviate his mental health issues through poisoning and I suspect this is why he did what we believe he did.”



Dietz said the suspect also faced a series of stressors that could have contributed to Betkouski’s state of mind. He divorced his wife in 1981, then lost his job.

He was also humiliated when he invented a mobility device which was mocked in the local press for being a ‘flop’ in 1982 – on the same day his dad died.

Dietz believes the chemist committed suicide because of the publicity surrounding the death of his 12-year-old victim.

“I think he realised what he had done and couldn’t live with it,” he said.

The cyanide poisonings sparked copycat incidents throughout the 80s and 90s, including that of housewife Stella Nickell who, in 1986, laced migraine tablets with cyanide to murder her husband and killed an innocent woman in the process.



It changed the way medicines were packaged with the creation of tamper-proof lids.

Betkouski’s body was found in the Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise, Idaho less than a month after the Tylenol deaths.

He had no identification but carried a large sum of cash, nearly 30 keys and a suicide note typed with a fake name, Wm L.Toomey. It took police seven years to identify him because he had broken off contact with his family.



Detective Cooper and Dietz are now looking for evidence which places their suspect in Chicago just before the murders.

Cooper admits his evidence is all ‘circumstantial’ but he and Dietz have shared filed with Illinois police who are investigating.

The FBI warned against ‘premature conclusions’. It said past claims about suspects remain unsubstantiated and it will “release credible information” when the case is solved.

News.title: Cops hunt man, 38, over wrong-way crash on major motorway during police chase – as girl, 15, among 3 arrested
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

CRASH MANHUNT Cops hunt man, 38, over wrong-way crash on major motorway during police chase – as girl, 15, among 3 arrested







Next

COSP have launched a manhunt after a man in his 20s was seriously injured in a wrong-way motorway crash during a police chase.

Emergency services were scrambled to reports of a crash on the M1 near Wakefield, West Yorkshire, in the evening of September 11.

A blue Kia Proceed had been driven the wrong way on the northbound carriageway of the busy motorway after failing to stop for police.

The motor smashed into a red Dacia Sandero near Junction 41, leaving the driver of the Dacia, in his 20s, with potentially life changing injuries.





He was rushed to hospital for treatment, where he remains at this time.

An 18-year-old man, 15-year-old girl and a woman aged 30 were arrested at the scene.

All three have since been bailed as a probe into the incident continues.

West Yorkshire Police has now issued an appeal for information as the force launches a manhunt for David Nuttall, 38.

Police say Nuttall is wanted on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and theft of a motor vehicle.

Nuttall is described as a white male, about 5ft 10ins tall, of stocky build, with brown hair.

Anyone who knows his whereabouts or has any information that may assist officers in locating him is urged to contact the force immediately.

News.title: Boy, 14, is arrested months after four-year-old girl seriously injured when she was hit by e-scooter
News.content:
CRASH ARREST Boy, 14, is arrested months after four-year-old girl seriously injured when she was hit by e-scooter







Next

A 14-YEAR-OLD boy has been arrested months after a four-year-old girl was seriously injured by an e-scooter in a hit-and-run collision.

Police were called to reports that a young girl had been hit by a boy riding an e-scooter in a park in Fleet, Hampshire, on Saturday, June 20.

The little girl, identified as Ottilie Freeman, was rushed to hospital and received treatment for a serious head injury.

She reportedly suffered a fractured skull and a concussion in the collision.





Police said the boy on the scooter did not stop at the scene of the horror crash.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary has today confirmed that a 14-year-old boy has been taken into custody in connection with the incident.

The teen was arrested on suspicion of causing serious injury by dangerous driving, driving a motor vehicle otherwise than in accordance with a licence and using a motor vehicle on a road/public place without third party insurance.

He was also arrested on suspicion of being the driver of a vehicle involved in a road accident and failing to report that accident.

He remains in custody while an investigation into the hit-and-run continues.

The force said: “We want to thank everyone who got in touch with us with details. If you have any additional information which may help our enquiries, please contact 101 quoting reference 44260293398.”

Ottilie’s parents previously recounted the harrowing accident in an interview.

Speaking to ITV News her dad said: “Otts was sort of walking along the grassy verge by the tennis courts, tapping the wooden bars, and I was sort of walking in this service road, no traffic.



“Of course I feel terrible, I stepped forward, she steps into the road, and yeah before I knew it I heard this zipping noise and I sort of then turned fully and there was this young lad on his escooter.

“I shouted, you know, ‘Otts!’, she sort of ran in response to my shout and of course she changed direction , he moved with her and the next thing I know he’d knocked her flying.”

News.title: At least 17 killed after gunmen open fire at bar in South Africa as cops hunt suspects ‘armed with AK-47s & pistols’
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

GUN HORROR At least 17 killed after gunmen open fire at bar in South Africa as cops hunt suspects ‘armed with AK-47s & pistols’







Next

AT least 17 people have been killed after several gunmen armed with AK-47s and pistols opened fire at a bar in South Africa, local cops say.

An urgent manhunt has been launched for eight suspects following the deadly attack which also left 15 people injured.



Authorities say the assault unfolded at a bar in Wedela township, southwest of Johannesburg at 9.30pm local time on Saturday.

Emergency services rushed to the scene and pronounced 13 men and four women dead at the scene.



It is currently unclear what the motive behind the shooting is, South African police said on X.

Cops added: “Suspects were ​reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols.”

They also said the attackers allegedly searched some of the people inside and took their cellphones before fleeing in two vehicles.

The 15 injured victims have been rushed to hospital and are being treated for gunshot wounds.

No arrests have been made yet, authorities added.

The suspects allegedly targeted the tavern, opening fire on customers drinking outside.



The gunmen then entered the building before continuing to shoot bystanders, cops said.

It came just hours before another shooting broke out in Cape Town, South Africa’s second largest city.

At least 10 people were killed and 11 were injured after gunmen opened fire at an entertainment venue in Lwandle on Saturday night.

Local cops said five people were pronounced dead at the scene, while the other half succumbed to their injuries in hospital.

The deadly attack took place at around 11.45pm on the same night, just hours after the first shooting.

News.title: Chilling signs paranoid Putin is building huge doomsday nuclear bunker dubbed ‘Dead Hand’ hidden under remote mountain
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin looks to be building a doomsday nuclear bunker hidden under a mountain as the tyrant revives a Cold War programme.

Guarded by a machine gun turret, the underground command centre is one of Russia’s most top-secret facilities and could be used to hide a paranoid Putin should nuclear war break out.



The 24-room tunnel is at the centre of a strategy to guarantee retaliatory nuclear strikes against the West, a bombshell investigation has revealed.

Fitted with air filtration units to screen chemical, biological, and radioactive fallout, the bunker has been discovered beneath Kosvinsky Kamen mountain in the Urals region.



Codenamed Facility 1335, the cocoon was first built during the Cold War to ensure mutual destruction against the West in the event of a nuclear strike.

Dubbed the “Dead Hand project”, it would see back-up control channels activated if communication was lost with the Kremlin’s top brass.



These would transmit long-wave radio signals to mobilise missile launchers.

An investigation by The Sunday Times, Danish media group Danwatch and the Dossier Center has now revealed the site has been rebuilt.



The new, massive structure at the foothills of Kosvinsky Kamen is costing hundreds of millions of pounds.

Since 2018 Moscow has ferried heavy excavation and rock-drilling equipment, steel, piping and cabling into the mountain, procurement data shows.

The site has already used three million litres of fuel, 823,000 litres of gas and about 20,000 tonnes of steel – the weight of roughly three Eiffel Towers.

It is estimated that the concrete used would build at least 150,000 square meters of surface area, which is enough for a multi-storey building.

Mine ventilation systems and air filtration units capable of screening chemical, biological, and radioactive fallout have also been delivered to the site, the investigation found.



The bulk work was carried out between 2020 and 2021, records show.

A senior Russian military figure said “strategic missile forces will fulfil their historic mission of retaliation against any enemy” with Facility 1335.

The chilling findings come after Putin said publicly he would be ready to use a tactical nuclear weapon against Ukraine if the conflict escalated.



Clues of the project’s revival first appeared in 2020 when the Kremlin released transcripts of a meeting between Putin and his top brass.

During the meeting, Mad Vlad discussed the creation of a system to ensure Russia’s nuclear command and control infrastructure would survive an attack.

He said: “We are aware that a lot depends on the survivability of these systems and their ability to continue operating in a combat environment.

“They have told me that the creation of an absolutely secure facility for controlling strategic nuclear forces, among others, is nearing completion, and that it will have a very high safety margin.”

Putin has become increasingly paranoid about a US strike carried out with its bunker-buster bombs capable of hitting targets deep underground.



Norwegian Staff College and armed forces’ Russian security policy expert Tom Roseth told The Sunday Times: “It appears that the Russians are securing this facility against every type of attack.

“To protect 1335 and the command-and-control facilities of the nuclear forces, they therefore have to dig even deeper and reinforce the site even more.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The expansion of Facility 1335 follows a major upgrade of Russia’s nuclear forces, which has been given high priority within the Russian armed forces.

“The perimeter will once again be given priority now, in a more tense geopolitical situation in which Russia sees itself as being in conflict with the West.”

News.title: Men arrested and houses evacuated in major incident near RAF Fairford
News.content:
A "major incident" has been declared and homes have been evacuated in a village near an RAF base which hosts the United States Air Force.

Gloucestershire Police said residents in Whelford, near RAF Fairford, have been taken to a leisure centre while investigations continue.

Several men have been arrested on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act, police said.

The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team is currently examining a number of vehicles.

Police said a cordon was currently in place in the area and added officers believed the incident was contained.

A large emergency services presence was seen in the area, including a Hazardous Area Response Team.

Gloucestershire Police said: "A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

"It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act.

"We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place."

The base has been used to deploy US bombers since the conflict in Iran began on 28 February.

News.title: Ten NHS staff removed over Noah Woods data breach
News.content:
Ten NHS staff have been removed from duty or suspended after a data breach involving the medical records of three-year-old Noah Woods.

Launching an "urgent" investigation, Dr Martin Mansfield, deputy chief medical officer at East Suffolk and North Essex NHS Foundation Trust, said that any unauthorised access of patient data was "completely unacceptable".

The trust has apologised to Noah's family and said disciplinary action would be taken if needed.

A major search for Noah was carried out in the village of Brantham, Suffolk, after the child went missing on 15 September. His body was found the next day in nearby water by police divers.

A spokesperson for the trust said 10 employees had been "removed from active duty or suspended whilst investigations are concluded".

In the statement issued on Sunday,, external Mansfield said of the data breach: "Immediate steps were also taken to secure the records and prevent further access that was not for a legitimate, clinical reason.

"We have reported the matter to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO), and we will continue to keep Noah's family informed as our investigation progresses."

At least 1,300 people helped in the search for Noah in the 24 hours before he was found.

A tribute issued by his family called him a "happy, cheeky, playful" boy who loved to laugh. His mother urged other parents to "hold their children a little tighter and cherish every moment".

An inquest, which opened on Friday, heard that the three-year-old had left a play area "through a gap in the fence".

Assistant coroner Jyoti Gill said it was a "very sad and tragic death" as she opened and adjourned the inquest in Ipswich.

News.title: Faisal Islam: The two big calls the chancellor has to make ahead of the Budget
News.content:
"It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?

"Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted.

The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy.

But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October.

Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence.

In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%.

Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?
News.content:
If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around.

Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments.

It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths.

This time around, stand-up star Joe Lycett, 38, is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you".

Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling."

With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak.

"There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr.

If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyond James Acaster.

Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not.

A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar...

News.title: Can you eat ultra-processed foods and still be healthy? A dietitian analysed my weekly shop
News.content:
First things first, what is a UPF?

It depends who you ask. A basic rule of thumb is that to be ultra-processed a product needs more than five ingredients, with at least one not normally found in your kitchen - things like emulsifiers, additives and flavourings.

There is a large and growing body of evidence that shows UPFs are linked to obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders such as diabetes, as well as mental health problems and even premature death.

But scientists, doctors and dietitians can't agree on why. Is it purely down to the high fat, sugar, salt and calorie content? Or is the ultra-processing also a factor?

Studies show more than half the calories we consume in the UK come from ultra-processed food, external. Dr Chris van Tulleken has written books and made documentaries about how bad these foods can be, and he tells me they're "almost impossible to avoid" - even his own family's diet includes a few.

And my shopping list isn't UPF-free either.

Maeve Hanan, a member of the British Dietetic Association, pauses as she scans through some of my weekly shopping list (there was more fruit and veg, honest) and points to a box of bran flakes.

"This is ultra-processed, but I often buy this for my family. It's got so many health benefits."

Hanan says there's a "growing hysteria" about UPFs.

"Mainly because the messaging around them is so black and white," she says. "This food is good. This food is bad.

"It just fuels fear - and fear around food is never good."

News.title: Why families are being urged to look closer on autumn walks
News.content:
From fairytale toadstools to fungi that look like birds' nests, experts say some of Britain's most unusual mushrooms are beginning to emerge as autumn arrives.

Hidden in parks, woodlands and nature reserves, species ranging from the bright-red fly agaric to the rare red cage fungus can be found by anyone willing to slow down and take a closer look.

For James Benwell, of the Birmingham and Black Country Wildlife Trust, searching for fungi has become a way to explore the outdoors with his young son.

He said mushroom spotting can transform an ordinary walk into an adventure, revealing colourful and unusual species that many people pass by without noticing.

Across the West Midlands, fungi enthusiasts have recorded everything from tiny bird's nest fungi in Birmingham city centre, to fly agaric mushrooms growing beneath woodland birch trees and a rare red cage fungus discovered in Cannon Hill Park.

Many species can go unnoticed among fallen leaves, rotting wood and the bases of trees, but Benwell said taking the time to look more closely opens up a hidden world.

"Every walk becomes interesting and exciting if you're exploring and if you're looking for new things," he said.

News.title: England embrace the chaos - but control also needed to win big prizes
News.content:
England took advantage of those reprieves to somehow be ahead by the break, through star performer Anthony Gordon's composed finish and Harry Kane's deflected header.

Kane's penalty miss just after the break was a turning point, hitting the bar after slipping and touching the ball twice, before England once again paid the price for errors.

Nico O'Reilly coughed up possession in the build-up to Alex Baena's equaliser before another substitute in Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winner in the Euro 2024 final against England in Berlin, settled matters after 74 minutes.

If it was a bad night for Manchester City defensive duo Guehi and O'Reilly, it was not much better for Jarell Quansah, who was given the nod ahead of the recalled Trent Alexander-Arnold. He was uncertain throughout and does not look a natural right-back - perhaps because he is not a natural right-back.

Of course, it could have been different had Kane scored his penalty. He did not and it was not.

Kane said: "On another day we could have won." This was not another day and England did not win.

England's bolder approach after a shaky opening 25 minutes offered up the prospect of a landmark victory, but shambolic defending saw Guehi and O'Reilly present gifts Spain were happy to accept.

As against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta, England led by a Gordon goal and lost, but at least here they went down swinging and not by going into cowering retreat.

It was a small mercy appreciated by the home support, but the gulf in class when it mattered was still evident as Spain's smooth, unhurried style cut a sharp contrast to England's often frantic efforts.

Tuchel's defence looked horribly vulnerable and easy to slice through, although keeper Trafford â given two games before first-choice Jordan Pickford returns â was blameless and will have created a good impression as he tries to create greater competition in that department.

They have now shipped 13 goals in their last six matches in all competitions, after conceding only seven in their first 17 games under Tuchel.

Ironically, it was two players now plying their trade in Spain, Gordon at Barcelona and Jude Bellingham at Real Madrid, who were England's standout performers.

Gordon was in electrifying form, while Bellingham was relentless in driving England forward, even in a losing cause.

As for the chaos, Tuchel begged to differ.

He told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm not sure there was a lot of chaos. We had an incredible amount of high-ball recoveries in the opponent's half. I think 15 more than Spain. Overall, I think 15 in total in the first half. That only goes against a team like Spain if we play man to man, so we were very brave."

News.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
News.content:
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".

Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.

And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.

China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.

"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.

"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."

She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".

Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University â one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.

News.title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
News.content:
Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.

The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost Â£33bn, would open by 2035.

But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".

The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.

The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.

It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.

Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider Â£49bn modernisation of the airport.

The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.

The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.

News.title: Homes without water and roads closed after burst pipe
News.content:
Thousands of homes in parts of Crawley have water supply issues and a number of roads have flooded after what police are describing as a "significant" leak.

Roads around the Southgate Roundabout in Crawley have been closed on Sunday morning due to the burst water pipe, Sussex Police said.

Southern Water said around 9,000 customers were impacted and it was setting up bottled water stations.

A company spokesperson said: "Our teams are on site and working as quickly and safely as possible to repair the burst and restore supplies."

The company said customers were experiencing a loss of water supply or low pressure in the following areas - Woolborough Road, Holmcroft, Southgate, Tilgate and Furnace Green.

The Southern Water spokesperson added: "Restoring water to customers as quickly as possible remains our highest priority."

Southgate Avenue, Crawley Avenue and part of the A23 are currently closed, according to the company.

Sussex Police has asked that people avoid the area while emergency services manage the situation safely.

Martin Lawrence was making deliveries in the area at 05:00 BST.

He told BBC Radio Sussex: "I came across this massive flood going across the road.

"There was a large amount of water going from one side of the roundabout to the other and going into an underpass.

"I've never seen so much water in my life."

News.title: Traitors star burgled after sharing holiday photos
News.content:
Traitors star Paul Gorton did not think twice about sharing photographs on social media while enjoying a family holiday with his wife and two young children.

But when he returned home he discovered that his house in Cheshire had been burgled just days earlier.

"The eerie bit is at 21:10 BST I posted that me and Kate were by the side of the pool, we've got full bellies, the kids are in bed, we're actually having our little bit of the holiday," he said.

"About 20 minutes later, little did we know, our house has been broken into."

Paul's bike as well as several sentimental items including an irreplaceable ring from Kate's grandmother were stolen in the burglary on 28 August.

The perpetrators managed to break in through the bi-fold doors at the back of the house by using a technique known as lock snapping before cutting the broadband connection.

News.title: Man City chairman confident club will prove innocence
News.content:
Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.

On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website.

"Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said.

"Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

"But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.

Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine.

Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined".

"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added.

"There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."

News.title: 'No turning back' in independence journey, says first minister at rally
News.content:
Wales' first minister has said there is "no turning back" on the journey to independence for the country, as he attended a rally on Saturday.

In a speech addressing the crowd gathered in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, Rhun ap Iorwerth said the "next step" for Wales had to be "equality with Scotland, as a minimum".

Thousands were in attendance, with the event organisers, campaign group Yes Cymru, saying it estimated the march attracted between 8,000 and 9,000 people.

"[Wales is] on a journey, and there's no turning back," ap Iorwerth said.

Since 2019, thousands have taken part in independence marches across Wales, including in Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Merthyr Tydfil, Rhyl and Barry.

But this was the first time the first minister of Wales had attended a Yes Cymru march.

A Reform Cymru Member of the Senedd (MS) said he was "disappointed" by the first minister's decision to attend, while a Welsh Conservative MS said it would be "better for him to be behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems he said he would sort out".

News.title: Child's hidden letter found after 44 years
News.content:
A letter written by a 10-year-old girl in the 1980s and hidden in the cavity of the stairs at her home has been found 44 years later.

The house in Hockley, Essex, was undergoing renovation work when a worker found the scrap of paper and passed it to Michelle Harwood, who now lives there.

Filled with curiosity, the 36-year-old charity worker examined it - noting "really neat" handwriting for a child - and posted on her local Facebook community group on Thursday morning to track down the author.

Within an hour, multiple people had found and tagged Rachel Miles, now a 54-year- old teacher in Milton Keynes, Buckinghamshire. And she responded.

News.title: 'I was angry at my husband - I didn't know he had dementia'
News.content:
Since Clive's death in 1999, Helen has been working as a dementia researcher, raising awareness of his condition and continuing his legacy through her charity, The Clive Project.

She continues to tell her story because there is still "more to be done" to help dementia patients and their families, she said.

Helen described her late-husband as a calm, level-headed and "very active guy" who used to run marathons, even "before it was popular".

"Clive was unflappable," she said.

"He reckoned he failed if he lost his temper."

But as Clive approached his 40s things began to change.

"You can't really tell at what stage somebody's behaviour changes," she said.

"Younger people in particular are always going to be difficult to diagnose.

"And he covered up some things. He never admitted to me that he was having problems with reading and writing."

While Helen had never before heard of dementia in younger people, she said she "knew there was something wrong".

"I would make plans and he would forget he was looking after the children," she said.

"We had very many arguments about it.

"He said, 'I'm just growing old' - and he was early forties then."

News.title: Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said it feels "great" to be back in Britain after spending six years living in California.

He told Canadian network CTV: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to be able to really focus on the Invictus Games in Birmingham in July next year."

Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020, before returning to live in Britain last month.

It is thought the family are basing themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, had to be moved to a different school only days after they started over security concerns about the school run.

It is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had raised concerns about the distance and heavy traffic on the route to the school.

Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has been marked by tensions with the Royal Family.

A major incident has been declared and villagers have been evacuated from their homes near RAF Fairford following the arrest of several men on suspicion of explosives offences.

The Royal Air Force base in Gloucestershire also hosts the United States Air Force and has been used to launch operations against Iran during the Middle East conflict.

The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team is currently examining a number of vehicles.

Gloucestershire Police said: “A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident.

“It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act. The Army’s specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles.

“The local residents are being evacuated to a nearby leisure centre. A cordon is currently in place but we’d like to reassure people that we believe this incident is contained.

“We are working closely with our partners and are enacting the well-rehearsed plans we have in place.”

Security measures at the site in southwest England have significantly increased with roadblocks and armed police preventing access and emergency vehicles parked nearby, Reuters reported on Sunday.

A spokesperson for the US Air ⁠Force said they ​would not discuss specific force protection ⁠measures.

"The 501st Combat Support Wing and our fellow UK-based Wings remain vigilant and will take appropriate actions to ensure the safety and security of our US service members, civilians, contractors, and their families," the spokesperson said.

"We constantly assess a variety ⁠of factors that determine what measures we institute or modify to protect our installations, our people and their families."

More follows on this breaking news story...

A busy year of international action continues for Australia and South Africa as the two sides collide in an intriguing one-off Test in Perth.

The Springboks are heavily changed from the side that secured a 3-1 Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series success in their last outing two weeks ago, with Rassie Erasmus taking the opportunity to assess the depth of his squad. A trip to Western Australia is valuable preparation for next year’s World Cup, too, with the defending champions likely to play twice in Perth during the course of that tournament.

The Wallabies, meanwhile, will relish an opportunity to test themselves against the best having made an encouraging start to life under Les Kiss. Time is tight to find their groove before a World Cup on home soil but a statement win here could prove just the jolt they need with little more than 12 months to go.

British couples have lost tens of thousands of pounds after an IVF clinic in Portugal filed for insolvency – leaving many in limbo mid-treatment – in what has been described as the “biggest disaster globally in the sector”.

Ovom Care continued to take payments from its patients and administered treatments just days before they abruptly closed their business. Given that many of their patients had not paid via a credit card to avoid hefty exchange fees, they have been informed they are ineligible for refunds and have received no word about compensation.

Investors in Ovom said claims for prepaid treatment can be registered with the insolvency administrator.

One couple believe the ordeal has cost them upwards of £30,000, while another woman says she was left devastated to discover she had paid for three IVF rounds – despite her new doctor informing her she likely suffers from endometriosis.

At least 38 British patients are known to have been with the clinic at the time it became insolvent. However, The Independent has been told Ovom likely had around 200 clients and that around 60 per cent were UK nationals.

Ovom Care’s chief executive told The Independent the clinic was “deeply sorry” to patients for distress caused, but those who had paid for treatment they had not received would now need to contact insolvency administrators. She suggested a: “number of claims circulating publicly are factually not correct”, without specifying.

Pippa Hogg and her wife Jay Brown, both 39, had always known they wanted children. As a same-sex couple, they were aware of the financial pressures of undergoing IVF in the UK, which can spiral into the tens of thousands of pounds.

open image in gallery The Ovom clinic was backed by three venture capital firms ( Google Maps )

After researching various clinics and speaking with friends, they decided to pick Ovom Care as they felt protected by EU rules and were pleased that Portugal had almost identical laws to the UK on sperm donation. They travelled to the country and felt reassured by the staff and enjoyed a good relationship with their doctor – so decided to proceed with treatment.

After months of living on “the extreme frugal side”, they transferred £5,000 for a round in February which failed, and then made a second £10,000 payment on 15 August for three egg collections, as well as an additional £2,800 for their sperm donor vials.

Ms Hogg underwent her first scan on 21 August and began her simulation three days later. But the couple were left blindsided when they were informed on 28 August that Ovom were insolvent.

“It’s been really hard to be honest,” Ms Hogg told The Independent. “It was such a shock, I got really, really upset. As a queer person, you’ve already gone through other barriers and it felt like the final nail in the coffin. I also found it hard while also being treated for hormones and the procedure - I’ve not been back to work since. I’ve found it hard to be normal.”

Ms Hogg and Ms Brown are now undergoing treatment with Avenues. Given that they are now seeking another sperm donor and their bank has refused their fraud claim on the money paid to Ovom, they now believe the process has cost them in the region of £32,000.

A spokesperson for Ms Hogg and Ms Brown’s MP, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: “Miatta is very saddened and concerned to read about the experiences of those affected by the situation at Ovom Care.

“We would strongly encourage the constituents affected to get in touch with our office directly if they have not already done so. We will be looking out for their cases and will ensure that they are treated as a high-priority case by our office.”

Michelle, who does not wish to include her surname, 42, and her husband had been trying for a baby for years. They chose Ovom Care due to the high quality of doctors advertised but now feel their “one shot” of having a child has been taken from them.

Prior to beginning their treatment with Ovom, Ms Haworth says she went for a scan at a clinic in Harley Street, London, and was informed she may have endometriosis. Upon asking Ovom’s specialist doctors if she should investigate further, she said was reassured further scans were not necessary.

open image in gallery Pippa Hogg and Jay Brown paid £10,000 to Ovom just days before it was declared insolvent ( Supplied )

In December 2025, she underwent her first egg transfer. She discovered that the transfer had failed on Christmas Day, but claims to have felt pressured to continue with her second transfer in February, which also failed.

“I was in such a bad way mentally and thinking ‘what’s wrong with me physically, I’m killing these things. I’m the reason this isn’t working, I’m a bad person’,” she said.

Given her age, she asked if she should take part in another egg retrieval or undergo further testing, but says she was once again reassured by the clinic that all was well, and she should proceed with her third and final transfer in August.

She discovered this had also failed on 26 August, just one day after Ovom filed for insolvency and two days before they informed their patients.

An estimated 60 per cent of Ovom’s patients were British and London-based Avenues clinic, run by Ovom co-founder Dr Cristina Hickman, has offered to take over their care. Avenues subsequently informed Ms Haworth that her initial scans had shown endometriosis, endometrioma and adenomyosis.

She and her husband believe they are now £20,000 out of pocket, and are unsure how to raise the funds for a second opportunity. They have joined forces with other affected patients to launch a fundraiser, with the hope of using it to recuperate costs and pay for future treatment.

Dr Hickman, who said she left Ovom in 2024 over disagreements with the direction the clinic was taking, said there had been a “misalignment between healthcare and venture capital business”, which had failed to prioritise patients.

The clinic had been backed by venture capital firms Alpha Intelligence Capital, Ananda Impact Ventures and Merantix Capital, and received a €4.8m (£4.1m) investment in 2024.

“It’s hard to navigate the private equity and venture capital space as a healthcare provider as you want different things, there is a different target,” Dr Hickman said.

“Six months before your runway of money runs out you should do a transfer of care, stop further care from starting and transfer the embryos. There is a way to shut down clinics and there is no registered doctor I know that would have done this.

She added: “You don’t just announce an insolvency and walk away. People remortgage their households to do this treatment.

“This is the biggest disaster I have seen globally in the IVF sector, this is as bad as it gets.”

Ovom Care's German parent company is separately subject to its own insolvency proceedings. Restructuring measures are initiated and a mergers and acquisitions process is organised.

The insolvency administrator and Portugal's regulator for assisted reproduction, the CNPMA, approved a process for stored eggs, sperm and embryos to be transferred to the Ava Clinic in Lisbon. Ovom say this was safely carried out under the CNPMA’s authorisation and clinical data is also being securely transferred.

Rachael and Anthony Jones, 38 and 36, had been trying for a baby but had suffered three miscarriages. They were drawn to Ovom Care after continuously seeing their adverts “popping up online”, and after conducting their research and having a “no pressure” consultation, they felt that the clinic was a good fit.

In April, they made an up-front payment of more than £8,000 to cover three cycles of IVF and embryo transfers, and began the process in May. After travelling to Portugal for their egg retrieval, they felt encouraged by the “lovely” staff and nurses, and had no concerns about their treatment.

In July, they were informed that they could not undergo the embryo transfer as essential building work was taking place at the clinic, and on 21 August, they were disappointed when their transfer was delayed again due to a scan showing Rachael’s womb lining was not sufficiently optimal.

Just one week later, they received an email at 5:30pm on a Friday to inform them that the clinic had filed for insolvency.

“That weekend was just horrendous,” Rachael said. “I don’t think we slept properly. We were trying to contact Ava Clinic, where we were told the eggs would be transferred to, but they had also only found out on the Friday and were inundated with queries. They couldn’t get in touch with Ovom either. Ava only got our eggs a week ago and until then, it has been massively stressful.”

“We feel fleeced,” Anthony said. “The financial side has had to really dictate our choices. There’s the context of it as well - we’ve had three miscarriages which we haven’t really gotten over. You then take the scientific route and hope it will be a bit more in your control. We just feel like the unluckiest people in the world.”

Similar to Pippa and Jay, they are now also with Avenues, which has offered to retrieve their eggs for no additional cost. They are now hoping to embark on a new treatment plan in a few weeks, but the stress from the ordeal is believed to have triggered Rachael’s Graves’ disease, which means it is unlikely that they can go forwards with the embryo transfer for another six months.

Ovom Care chief executive, Felicia von Reden, said in a statement to The Independent: “I would like to start off by saying that we as management are deeply sorry for the distress and uncertainty caused by the insolvency proceedings.

“Stored eggs, sperm and embryos, together with patients' clinical records, have been transferred to AVA Clinic in Lisbon, with the authorisation of the Portuguese health authority (CNPMA). If you are currently undergoing treatment, or wish to continue your care, please contact AVA Clinic directly. They are able to advise on next steps.

“If you have paid for treatment that was not provided, this is a claim against the insolvent estate.

“We are currently in the process of finding a fair outcome for patients who paid for treatment that was not delivered, and I will communicate further as soon as there is something concrete to share.

“The circumstances surrounding the insolvency, including the operational decisions taken after the court appointed an independent administrator, are before courts in Portugal and Germany. It would not be appropriate for me to comment on matters under judicial review.

“I will say, however, that a number of claims circulating publicly are factually not correct.

“My focus, and the priority of everyone involved, is making sure patients get the support and answers they need - we are working on this with all the resources we have.”

A spokesperson for the Ava Clinic said: “Portugal has a long-standing reputation for safe, reliable and high-quality fertility treatment. Ava Clinic is proud to be part of that tradition, with more than 25 years of experience in assisted reproduction that patients can trust.

“The situation with Ovom Care is unfortunately an example of poor business practice which can impact any sector in any country; but should never be allowed to impact patients. For this reason, Ava Clinic had no hesitation in doing everything possible to ensure the safety of Ovom Care patients and their frozen reproductive material.

“When our support was requested by the court-appointed insolvency administrator and by Portugal’s assisted reproduction regulatory authority, our priority was immediately to protect patients and ensure continuity of care. Our team worked intensively to safeguard frozen reproductive material, preserve clinical records and support every patient who wished to continue treatment.”

A joint statement from Alpha Intelligence Capital, Merantix Capital and Ananda Impact Ventures said: “Our funds invested in Ovom Care between 2023 and 2024. Alpha Intelligence Capital and Merantix Capital had representatives on the board of its German parent company; Ananda Impact Ventures held an observer position on the board.

“The insolvency of the Portuguese clinic and its German parent company is the subject of court-supervised proceedings in Portugal and Germany. Management acted throughout on legal advice, and both entities cooperated, and continue to cooperate, fully with the insolvency administrators and the courts. As the proceedings are ongoing, it would not be appropriate for us to comment further on matters under judicial review.

“As Ovom has set out, patient safety measures were taken, including the transfer of biological material to an authorised backup facility, AVA Clinic in Lisbon, with the approval of the Portuguese health authority Claims for prepaid treatment can be registered with the Insolvency Administrator.

“Our sympathies are with everyone affected, particularly the patients whose treatment has been disrupted, and the clinic's staff.”

Thousands of grieving Nepalis are still struggling to come to terms with the scale of the losses caused by last month’s catastrophic floods, which tore through the Nepal-Tibet border and left widespread devastation in their wake.

The deadly floods in Nepal’s Bhote Koshi River on 26 August killed at least 1,453 people and left more than 6,000 others, including hundreds of foreign nationals, missing.

Those still missing include 33 Britons, 80 Americans, more than 50 Ukrainian nationals, as well as Australians and Indians, with most presumed to have been swept away by the tsunami-like waves that destroyed towns and villages in Rasuwa and Nuwakot.

Nepal's disaster management agency says only 112 bodies – of any nationality – have been handed over to their families following DNA tests. Despite technical assistance provided by China and India, identifying the dead amid such devastation has been a challenge.

The other 1,333 bodies founds so far have been temporarily buried pending identification. In neighbouring China, officials reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing.

open image in gallery A general view shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of the August 26 flash flood, at Betrawoti Bazaar in Nepal's Rasuwa district on September 26, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Pramod Poudel, 34, from Uckfield in East Sussex, said he does not believe his missing family members will be found. He travelled to Nepal to join the search after losing contact with his wife Sumitra, mother Tulisa, brother Pardip and uncle Madhav.

He told BBC News: "My heart is still saying that there might be something there, but I have to be realistic and accept that they are not there anymore.

"It was very hard to see all of the people in my community, and all of the houses that have been destroyed," he added.

Nepal's government is also struggling to re-home and provide support to an estimated 33,000 displaced people, many of whom have spent the past month in tents at rehabilitation shelters.

The UK Foreign Office said it was coordinating closely with the Nepali and Chinese authorities “as they lead the recovery and identification effort”.

“The scenes along the Nepal-China border are devastating and our thoughts remain with all those affected by this tragedy, and with those still waiting for news of loved ones,” a spokesperson told The Independent.

"Supporting British nationals and their families remains our highest priority, and our staff continues to provide consular support to those affected.”

Pasang Maya Tamang, 32, who lost her young son in the floods, said she still dreams of him pleading for help.

"The body of my son has been recovered, but I was not able to see him for the last time. I am very sad about that. I hear in my dreams him [asking] why I left him alone," Mr Tamang said at a shelter home in the flood-affected town of Nuwakot.

open image in gallery A general view shows damaged houses covered in sludge in the aftermath of the August 26 flash flood in Nepal's Nuwakot district on September 26, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Prime minister Balendra Shah used his first address to the UN General Assembly this week to highlight the flooding as a warning about the growing risks of the climate crisis, and to demand justice.

“The disaster was not just a local tragedy, but a warning to the world," Mr Shah said. "I ask you today: Have we really heard that warning?"

Mr Shah also called for greater international support for Nepal's recovery and stronger regional cooperation to prepare for climate-related disasters. "Climate change does not recognise borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with stamps and passports," he said.

The Nepal government estimates reconstruction and recovery will cost $4.77bn.

Mr Shah, 36, the youngest head of government to address the General Assembly this year, said Nepal contributed less than a tenth of one per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

Nepal is demanding $20m, the highest amount available for a single disaster, from the global fund for responding to loss and damage.

open image in gallery Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah addresses the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York City ( Reuters )

More than 800 people employed at 12 hydropower projects in Nepal are still unaccounted for, the country's energy minister told parliament.

Rescue teams were still continuing to comb through the ruins, with additional vehicles and helicopter deployed for mobilisation of explosives, fuel, equipment and specialised personnel.

"The government has accorded high priority to the search and rescue of people trapped inside underground hydropower structures or otherwise missing because of the disaster," said Biraj Bhakta Shrestha.

The rescue of a Chinese national from a tunnel on the 12th day after the floods, following the discovery of two hydropower plant employees alive on the 10th day, had raised fresh hopes of finding more survivors. But those hopes now appear to be fading.

Forty-seven bodies have been recovered from flood-hit project sites, according to reports.

open image in gallery Nepalese people perform religious rituals on the bank of Trishuli river at Dunge in Nuwakot, Nepal on Wednesday 23 September ( AP )

The floods severely damaged Nepal’s hydropower sector, a crucial driver of economic growth and an increasingly important source of export revenue.

Aid agencies have warned that further heavy rainfall forecast in the coming days could increase the threat of landslides, making it harder for help to reach areas where roads have already been damaged by the floods.

“The floodwaters may have receded, but for thousands of people, the crisis is far from over,” David Fisher, head of delegation for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal, said Friday.

“It is urgent to take the next steps in the recovery process to keep people healthy and avoid a spiral into poverty.”

Ishmita Shah, a roads engineer, said crews have been working with Nepal's army since the second day after the floods to reopen routes in affected areas.

Ms Shah said bridges were being built to improve access to the worst-affected areas and make it easier to transport relief supplies. But the work remains difficult, with more bad weather expected in the coming days, she said.

"The upcoming few days are going to be very challenging because of the weather, but we are fully prepared for that too," she said.
