World.title: ODM delegates reject Sakaja using the party for gubernatorial bid
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Nairobi ODM chairman George Aladwa addressing the media over the upcoming ODM nominations in Nairobi. [Collins Oduor, Standard]

Nairobi ODM delegates have resolved to reject and lobby against attempts by some people in President William Ruto's broad-based government to give Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja the ODM ticket in the 2027 gubernatorial race.

Party members, delegates and branch chairpersons met in Makadara, where they agreed that ODM be allowed to field their own candidates instead of the party allowing UDA leaders to vie on the party ticket.

They also resolved to back Makadara MP George Aladwa. With Tutam songs renting the air during the meeting, they also agreed to back President Ruto's re-election.

"Aladwa should be the party's candidate for Nairobi governor, and every candidate should seek the seat through their own political party," said an agitated delegate from Kasarani.

They insisted ODM should not allow an outsider to join the party and use its ticket to contest for the gubernatorial seat, arguing that the ODM ticket should be reserved for a candidate who enjoys the support of its members.

"We will not allow someone from another party to come and vie using ODM while we have our own members. As a party our only candidate is Aladwa," said delegate chairs.

They added that their position follows a series of meetings held across all 17 constituencies in Nairobi, with Makadara being the final constituency to hold its meeting.

They further argued that the Nairobi gubernatorial seat requires a leader with experience and leadership skills, warning ODM members against supporting candidates they believe lack the necessary political and leadership experience.

They also sustained their criticism towards former president Uhuru, alleging that he is undermining the party and dividing it, and they will not allow it.

George Aladwa backed the ODM members' position, saying every politician seeking elective office should do so through their own political party.

The delegates maintained that ODM should protect its identity and ticket, insisting that candidates from outside the party should not be allowed to use the ODM ticket to pursue elective positions when active and loyal members are sidelined.

The delegates are calling on ODM to ensure that the nomination process is free, fair and transparent, giving party members an opportunity to choose the candidate they want to represent them.

World.title: Oil rig arrives in Mombasa ahead of Kenya's first commercial drilling
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Oil rig arrives in Mombasa ahead of Kenya’s first commercial drilling. [Courtes]

Kenya has moved closer to commercial oil production after a 1,500 horsepower drilling rig arrived at the Port of Mombasa ahead of its deployment to the South Lokichar Basin in Turkana County.

The GW70 rig, leased by Gulf Energy E&P BV from Great Wall Drilling Company, docked at Kilindini Port on Friday aboard MV Transit Sedanka after sailing from Duqm Port in Oman.

It is expected to be transported to Turkana, where drilling is scheduled to begin on November 1.

“All workstreams at Gulf Energy E&P BV SEZ are running to a tight project management schedule, and the project remains on course for First Oil production in December 2026,” Gulf Energy Chief Executive Officer Paul Limoh said.

The arrival marks a step in the commercial development of the South Lokichar Basin, more than a decade after oil was first discovered in Turkana in 2012.

The first phase of the project is expected to produce about 20,000 barrels of crude oil per day, with output projected to rise to 50,000 barrels per day in the second phase.

The Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA) says Kenya is targeting first oil in December 2026, while the first crude exports through the Port of Mombasa are expected in the first quarter of 2027.

The GW70 will undergo commissioning and acceptance checks before drilling begins. Gulf Energy has contracted Baker Hughes for integrated well services and SLB to provide an early production facility for the first phase.

World.title: Two more suspects arrested over lawyer Kyalo Mbobu murder
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The two suspects are currently in custody undergoing processing as detectives pursue additional leads.

Detectives have arrested two more suspects in connection with the fatal shooting of lawyer Kyalo Mbobu, as an intelligence-led operation targeting people linked to the September 9, 2025 murder intensifies.

The two boda boda riders Nicholas Lemiso Naula and Noah Kipkirui Langat were arrested in Nairobi’s Central Business District, following sustained efforts by detectives to trace individuals suspected to have been involved in the killing.

According to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), Lemiso is a boda boda rider who allegedly ferried the main suspect, Police Constable Julius Cheruiyot, to and from the scene of the murder, while Langat was arrested over alleged surveillance on Mbobu before his killing.

"With three suspects now in custody, detectives are intensifying the hunt for other persons suspected to have played a role in the meticulously planned killing," DCI stated.

His arrest comes shortly after detectives arrested Cheruiyot in connection with the killing.

“The dragnet over the fatal shooting of lawyer Kyalo Mbobu has widened, with detectives arresting a second suspect as an intelligence-led operation targeting persons linked to the murder intensifies,” DCI said.

The two suspects are currently in custody undergoing processing as detectives pursue additional leads and seek to identify and arrest other people who may have been involved. The DCI said the operation remains active as investigators work to establish the circumstances surrounding Mbobu’s murder.

“The DCI is leaving no stone unturned in its efforts to unravel the full circumstances surrounding Lawyer Mbobu’s murder and bring all those responsible to justice,” the agency said.

World.title: KRA seizes 53,000 under-declared smartphones at Eldoret Airport
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

The consignment was intercepted by KRA enforcement teams following an intelligence report.

Kenya Revenue Authority (KRA) has seized a consignment containing 53,000 under-declared smartphones at Eldoret International Airport, averting a potential tax loss of Sh21.5 million.

KRA enforcement teams intercepted the consignment after an intelligence report indicated it contained undeclared mobile phones and other high-end electronic goods.

The cargo, which had been declared under five Customs entries, was part of consolidated shipments that also included shoes, clothing, automotive spare parts, household goods, electronic accessories and other assorted items.

KRA said an initial declaration listed only 3,000 smartphones. However, verification established 55,607 ordinary smartphones, alongside 309 undeclared high-end smartphones.

The high-end devices included Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, Samsung Galaxy Z Fold and Apple iPhone 17 Pro Max models.

“The consignment therefore reflects both under-declaration and non-declaration of dutiable goods,” KRA said in a statement issued on Wednesday.

The tax authority said the verification exercise was conducted to establish whether all mobile phones contained in the consignment had been properly declared.

KRA said the alleged tax evasion contravenes Section 203 of the East African Community Customs Management Act (EACCMA), 2004.

The law provides that a person who makes a false or incorrect Customs entry, or knowingly participates in the fraudulent evasion of duty, commits an offence.

“A person who, in any matter relating to Customs, makes any entry which is false or incorrect in any particular, or in any way is knowingly concerned in any fraudulent evasion of the payment of any duty, commits an offence,” KRA said, citing the law.

According to the authority, a person convicted under the provision is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years or a fine of up to US$10,000.

KRA said it was intensifying efforts to uncover tax evasion schemes to improve revenue compliance and ensure adherence to tax laws and procedures.

“KRA is actively engaged in unearthing tax evasion schemes to boost tax revenue compliance as well as adherence to tax laws and procedures, hence ensuring fair trade is maintained within the market,” the authority said.

The authority also appealed to members of the public, taxpayers and businesses with information on individuals, companies or networks involved in the generation, sale, purchase or use of fictitious VAT invoices to report them.

KRA said information provided would be treated confidentially and the identity of informants kept anonymous.

World.title: 'We know what happened': Uhuru claims Raila won 2022 polls
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Former President Uhuru Kenyatta. [File, Standard]

Former President Uhuru Kenyatta says he remains convinced that Raila Odinga won the 2022 presidential election.

Speaking during a Jubilee Party meeting in Nairobi on Tuesday, September 22, Uhuru questioned how the Azimio coalition could have lost the presidency despite performing strongly in other elective races.

“We did everything to help Baba become President of the Republic of Kenya. He got the votes, and to this day I know that he is the one who won those votes. We know how things happened, and we do not want it to happen that way again,” Uhuru said.

The late Odinga contested the August 9, 2022 election under the Azimio la Umoja-One Kenya Coalition Party, with Martha Karua as his running mate. Ruto ran under the United Democratic Alliance (UDA) as the presidential candidate of the Kenya Kwanza Alliance.

Ruto was declared president-elect after garnering 7,176,141 votes, 50.49 per cent, against Odinga's 6,942,930 votes, 48.85 per cent. Ruto's margin was 233,211 votes.

The Supreme Court later unanimously upheld his election after dismissing petitions challenging the results.

But Uhuru pointed to the coalition's performance in the parliamentary and county races to question how Azimio could have lost the presidency.

“How can you say we were defeated when we had most of the MPs, governors and senators? How were we defeated in the presidency?” he asked.

In the National Assembly, figures published after the election initially put Azimio ahead of Kenya Kwanza, with 165 seats against 160, while 12 seats were held by independent MPs.

Azimio also won 23 of the 47 governorships, while Kenya Kwanza secured 22. The remaining two were won by Taita Taveta Governor Andrew Mwadime and former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, who ran as independent candidates.

In the Senate, Kenya Kwanza had an advantage, winning 24 of the 47 directly elected seats against Azimio's 23.

The parliamentary balance later shifted in favour of Kenya Kwanza after several MPs changed their political allegiance.

In October 2022, National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula declared Kenya Kwanza the majority coalition with 179 MPs against Azimio's 157, after several MPs from parties including UDM, MDG, Maendeleo Chap Chap and PAA moved towards the Kenya Kwanza side.

Uhuru also rejected claims that he was responsible for Odinga's loss, saying he was not a candidate in the election.

“I am surprised when people say that we did not help Baba and that they defeated me. I was not on the ballot, and they are lying. I was only Raila's handyman,” he said.

He warned against what he described as divisive and dirty politics, saying Kenya should not repeat the events surrounding the 2022 election.

“Dirty politics and politics aimed at dividing Kenyans will take us nowhere. Let us not divide each other. What does it help us? Sell your manifesto,” Uhuru said.

He said he accepted the Supreme Court's decision after the 2022 presidential petitions and handed over power to Ruto without disputing the outcome, accusing Ruto of dragging his name in his failed leadership.

“When we finished and the court ruled, we did not dispute it. We went and handed over the presidency to them. And now, after four years, they are still talking about Uhuru. But when things are not working, people tend to look for excuses,” he said.

This is the clearest public assertion by the former president since the 2022 elections that Odinga won the presidential vote.

World.title: Ruto offers Kenya as test case on African risk
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto with Dangote Industries President and CEO Aliko Dangote and Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) CEO Samaila Zubairu on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, USA. [PCS]

President William Ruto has offered Kenya as a test case for how African risk is assessed, saying the country will open its default and recovery data to rating agencies and accept changes to the methodology if the evidence supports them.

Ruto said financial rules are steering African pension savings towards government securities rather than infrastructure, even where regulations allow greater investment in projects.

He made the proposal Monday, September 21, at the Africa We Build High-Level Roundtable on regulation, risk and reward in New York. The Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) convened the event on the margins of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Kenyan pension funds hold 46 per cent of their Sh3.2 trillion ($24.7 billion) in government securities but only 0.02 per cent in infrastructure debt, Ruto said. The rules allow pension funds to invest up to 10 per cent in infrastructure.

“Africa's problem is no longer the amount of capital available to it. Africa's problem is the set of rules that decide where that capital is allowed to go,” Ruto noted.

Ruto returned to an argument he made at the inaugural Africa We Build Summit in Nairobi in April, where he said African countries should use domestic capital to finance their own infrastructure.

At the New York roundtable, he revisited his earlier phrase, “he who pays the piper calls the tune”, using a teacher in Eldoret who has contributed to a pension fund for 20 years to illustrate his point.

“In Nairobi I said that he who pays the piper calls the tune. I meant it as a warning about depending on other people's money. This morning I mean it as an opportunity. The teacher in Eldoret is paying the piper. She has earned the right to call the tune,” Ruto explained.

He said the teacher's savings are more likely to sit in a US Treasury bill than in a nearby geothermal plant.

“Her fund manager is not being unpatriotic. He is being rational. The rules he works under tell him the Treasury bill is prudent and the power plant is adventurous. Capital follows incentives, and we wrote the incentives,” Ruto observed.

The Africa Finance Corporation's President and Chief Executive Samaila Zubairu framed the wider problem in similar terms at the Nairobi summit, saying Africa is “not capital-poor; it is capital-trapped.”

Ruto now wants African risk assessed using evidence from African markets rather than assumptions that he argues can make projects and countries appear more expensive to finance.

He said Kenya will make its pension and insurance regulators available to work with rating agencies, insurers and standard setters.

“If the evidence vindicates the current methodology, we will accept the finding and say so publicly. If it does not, we will expect the methodology to change,” Ruto added.

He proposed that the roundtable establish a working group based in Nairobi to continue the work and report to the next Africa We Build Summit in 12 months with findings backed by numbers.

President William Ruto on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, USA. [PCS]

Ruto made four requests to rating agencies, insurers, regulators and other institutions involved in financing: price African risk against African experience, make insurance on productive assets affordable, end penalties on long-term assets in prudential and liquidity rules and build bankable project pipelines.

He said African non-bank domestic capital pools have passed $2 trillion, while external concessional and commercial flows to Africa totalled $1.7 trillion between 2014 and 2024.

Official development assistance has also fallen every year since 2020, Ruto said, arguing that Africa can no longer rely on external financing to meet its infrastructure needs.

Kenya has begun putting some of the proposed financing mechanisms in place.

Ruto said the National Infrastructure Fund, signed into law in March, aims to mobilise up to $40 billion for roads, ports, power and water without new public debt.

In May, Kenya listed its first infrastructure fund on the Nairobi Securities Exchange and raised Sh3.4 billion with United Kingdom support. Kenya also increased its equity in the Africa Finance Corporation by Sh3.25 billion ($25 million), Ruto said.

The president said Kenya was willing to expose its own financing system to scrutiny as part of the test.

“If the evidence supports the current methodology, we will accept it. If it does not, we will expect the methodology to change,” Ruto told the roundtable.

The broader goal, he said, is to make it as easy for African institutional investors to finance productive assets as it is to buy government debt.

“The day a Kenyan pension trustee can buy a Kenyan power station as easily as she buys a Treasury bill, this argument will be over,” Ruto said.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro, Kinangop MP clash over alleged threatening message
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro arrives at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town for the service on September 20, 2026. [James Munyeki, Standard]

There was drama at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town during service on Sunday after Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro clashed with Kinangop MP Zachary Kwenya Thuku over an alleged threatening message.

Thuku, who is allied to the Kenya Kwanza government led by President William Ruto, is said to have warned Nyoro against attending the service.

"Yesterday, I received a message from the MP for Kinangop, Kwenya Thuku, warning me not to attend the church service. If I am lying, let him come here and read the message he sent me," Nyoro said.

He challenged the Kinangop MP to read the message aloud to the congregation.

"If anything happens to me today, Kenyans will judge whoever will be responsible," said Nyoro.

The Kiharu MP challenged Thuku to face him at a public rally at Engineer Trading Centre.

When he rose to speak, the Kinangop MP said he would not address the matter in church.

Instead, he said this was a political issue that the leaders would resolve.

"Let us solve this matter amicably. We are all brothers in this political journey," he said amid cheers from the congregation.

Recently, Nyoro added his voice to the growing political realignment in Mt Kenya, openly acknowledging the political tightrope he now walks as he distances himself from his former allies in the ruling party.

In a candid interview, he admitted that his previous close ties with President William Ruto and the Kenya Kwanza administration have left him vulnerable to suspicion from both sides of the political divide but insisted his decision to abandon the ruling party, United Democratic Alliance (UDA) was deliberate, difficult, and necessary.

World.title: Egyptian expats are key partners in development: Foreign Minister
World.content:
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty met with members of the Egyptian community in New York, reflecting a commitment to maintaining direct, continuous communication with Egyptian expatriates abroad.

Abdelatty hailed their active role in strengthening ties between Egypt and the US, as well as their contributions to raising awareness about Egypt within American society.

He noted that Egyptians abroad serve as a vital bridge connecting Egypt with the communities in which they live, acting as key partners in supporting national development efforts and advancing Egyptian interests internationally.

Abdelatty emphasized the state’s commitment to supporting talented Egyptians abroad, recognizing them as an integral part of Egypt’s soft power on the global stage.

A Foreign Ministry statement noted that, during the meeting, Abdelatty outlined the state’s efforts to look after Egyptians abroad and improve the services provided to them.

The Foreign Minister highlighted the ongoing enhancement of consular services through expanded digital transformation, the streamlining of procedures, and strengthened cooperation between Foreign Ministry and various state institutions to meet the needs of Egyptians abroad.

He also pointed to initiatives aimed at Egyptians abroad, as well as efforts to facilitate their access to investment opportunities in Egypt and leverage their international expertise in support of national development efforts.

Abdelatty also met with Egyptians working at the United Nations in New York, on the sidelines of his participation in the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

He expressed pride in the distinguished role played by Egyptian personnel across various UN bodies.

Abdelatty emphasized that their tangible contributions reflect their competence, expertise, and professional capabilities, and help strengthen Egypt’s presence in various fields of multilateral international work.

World.title: Warm weather weather across Egypt on Sunday: EMA
World.content:
The Egyptian Meteorological Authority (EMA) forecasts hot, humid weather during the day on Sunday across the north of the country—extending to Greater Cairo and northern Upper Egypt—and intensely hot weather in southern Upper Egypt.

Conditions are expected to be mild and humid at night and in the early morning across most regions.

Temperatures vary significantly across governorates: Greater Cairo and Lower Egypt will see 32C, the northern coasts 31C, and northern Upper Egypt 35C, while Southern Upper Egypt will see the highest temperatures, reaching 41C.

There is an intermittent chance of light rain in parts of the Northern Coast, the northern Lower Egypt, and areas of the Western Desert.

Wind activity is expected in most areas, helping to moderate the temperature in the shade and during the night in open areas.

Hot and humid daytime conditions are expected to persist until Thursday, October 1. There is a continued chance of light rain on Monday, September 28, along the northern coasts and in the Lower Egypt.

Greater Cairo is expected to reach 31C on Tuesday, September 29 – forecasts indicate a gradual drop in temperatures as October progresses.

Meteorologists advise wearing light cotton clothing during the day, exercising caution while driving in the early morning due to mist, and staying updated with the latest weather maps.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: War has returned to Ethiopia’s Tigray — and former enemies are now fighting together. What changed?
World.content:
Nearly four years ago, a peace deal ended the brutal war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 21st century. Now, the violence has returned — but the battle lines have changed.

Tigrayan rebels are again fighting the federal government, while forces that were once enemies are now fighting side by side.

On Wednesday, Tigrayan forces seized three airports controlled by the federal government, while fighting also broke out in the neighboring regions of Amhara and Afar.

The hostilities have shattered the 2022 peace agreement that ended a war estimated to have killed around 600,000 people. Relations between the federal government and Tigray’s leaders had been worsening for months.

It’s unclear what led to the recent fighting, with both sides offering conflicting accounts.

Tigray’s regional government said federal forces attacked first and that it ordered its forces to respond, calling it a “defensive war.” While Getachew Reda, an adviser to Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said the TPLF had launched an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Afar and Amhara and seized the three airports in Tigray, accusing it of taking “irresponsibility to new heights.”

The renewed violence this week follows almost two months of smaller clashes. The nongovernmental organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) says fighting between Tigrayan and federal forces began near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan on August 1. The two sides also accused each other of starting those clashes.

According to ACLED, federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments followed, with Tigrayan forces moving tanks and artillery south this month.

National carrier Ethiopian Airlines has suspended all flights to Tigray after the airport seizures.

How did Ethiopia get here?

Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) fighters prepare for battle at a camp in Mekele, the capital of Tigray region, Ethiopia, on June 30, 2021. Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images

The TPLF was once Ethiopia’s most powerful political force. It dominated the coalition that governed the country for nearly three decades, despite Tigrayans making up a relatively small share of Ethiopia’s population.

That changed after Abiy became prime minister in 2018 following years of anti-government protests. He introduced political reforms and made peace with neighboring Eritrea, which won him the Nobel Peace Prize a year later.

But relations with the TPLF deteriorated. Abiy replaced the old ruling coalition with his Prosperity Party in 2019; the TPLF refused to join.

After national elections were postponed during the Covid-19 pandemic, Tigray held its own regional vote despite objections from Addis Ababa.

In November 2020, Tigrayan forces attacked federal military bases in the region. Abiy sent troops in, and Eritrean forces and fighters from Amhara later fought alongside the federal army.

By the time the war ended two years later, millions of people had been displaced and parts of Tigray had been pushed into famine. Both sides faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.

Ethiopian soldiers pictured as children stand behind them at Mai Aini Refugee Camp, in Ethiopia, on January 30, 2021. Eduardo Soteras/AFP/Getty Images

Why did the peace deal fail?

Redwan Hussein (second left), Representative of the Ethiopian government, and Getachew Reda (second right), Representative of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), sign a peace agreement between the two parties at the Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) offices in Pretoria on November 2, 2022. Phill Magakoe/AFP/Getty Images

Hostilities came to an end when the federal government and TPLF signed an African Union-brokered agreement in Pretoria, South Africa, on November 2, 2022.

Under the deal, Tigrayan forces were to disarm and federal authority would return to the region. Humanitarian aid and basic services would resume, and an interim administration was later set up to govern Tigray until elections.

But major disputes remained, including over territory claimed by both Tigray and Amhara and the return of people displaced by the war. Meanwhile, Eritrea, whose soldiers had fought alongside federal forces, was not party to the agreement.

“The agreement didn’t collapse overnight — it was systematically hollowed out over three years,” Surafel Getahun, an Ethiopian geopolitics researcher, told CNN.

Getahun said both sides bore responsibility. He accused the federal government of failing to fulfill key parts of the agreement, including returning displaced people, and the TPLF of breaching it by retaking control of the regional administration and rebuilding its military forces.

The TPLF was also divided by an internal power struggle, which further weakened the peace process. Rival factions emerged around TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and Reda, the head of the Tigray interim administration who had been a senior TPLF figure. Reda was later expelled from the party by Gebremichael’s faction, and Abiy appointed a new interim leader in April 2025.

A month later, Gebremichael’s faction took back control of Tigray’s government. It restored the regional legislature that existed before the war and installed Gebremichael as regional president.

Chairman of Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) Debretsion Gebremichael speaks during the 38th African Union (AU) Summit, at the AU Headquarters in Addis Ababa on February 16, 2025. Amanuel Sileshi/AFP/Getty Images

On Sunday, the TPLF joined six other armed groups in a new alliance seeking to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The alliance includes former enemies who fought on opposite sides of the last war.

TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom told the Associated Press the groups would cooperate politically and militarily. Asked whether joining the alliance violated the Pretoria agreement, Asgedom said the accord was “no longer valid.”

The Amhara Fano National Movement fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF during the last war, then turned against it in 2023. The Oromo Liberation Army, which has long fought Abiy’s government in Oromia, is also a member.

Reuters reported Wednesday that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside the Fano group in Amhara and a local armed group in Afar.

But Getahun questioned how long the alliance would hold.

The TPLF and Fano remain divided over contested territory, particularly Western Tigray, and its members have different political and military goals.

“This is a temporary marriage of convenience against a mutual enemy rather than a lasting political agreement,” he said.

Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters on Monday that the groups had already been working together with financial backing from Eritrea. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated since their forces fought together in the last war, though the Eritrean government has repeatedly denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups.

The African Union (AU) said Wednesday that the airport seizures were inconsistent with the Pretoria deal and urged both parties to de-escalate. It also asked for help from former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 agreement.

Could the war spread further?

The charred remains of a tank from clashes between the Ethiopian National Defense Force (ENDF) and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) lie on a road near Gereb Agew, Southern Tigray, on March 3, 2026. Abel Gerezgiher/AFP/Getty Images

Tigray has yet to recover from the last war, with communities still rebuilding and many displaced people still unable to return home.

Ethiopia is already dealing with armed conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, and ACLED says the federal military was “stretched” before the renewed fighting with the TPLF. But the armed groups in the new alliance vary in their fighting capacity, with several lacking the organization or recruits for wider operations and others largely confined to local areas, according to the conflict monitor.

There is also the risk of Eritrea’s military becoming involved. Tensions have grown between the two countries over Ethiopia’s push for access to the Red Sea, including through Eritrea’s port of Assab. The AU urged Ethiopia’s neighbors to avoid actions that could fuel the conflict.

The region is already grappling with the war in Sudan and longstanding tensions between Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan over the Nile.

Getahun warned that the current fighting could become even more devastating than the previous conflict.

“A renewed war would likely end up far bloodier and more widespread than the 2020–2022 fighting,” he said.

“Immediate de-escalation and dialogue” are now essential, he added, arguing that negotiations remain “the only viable path forward.”

World.title: A good week for Iran at the UN – but latest offer to the US appears a non-starter
World.content:
Seven months after escaping with his life from a US-coordinated Israeli airstrike that killed Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran’s top diplomat walked the streets of Manhattan this week under the protection of the US Secret Service.

As leaders gathered in New York for the UN General Assembly, Abbas Araghchi and Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, have seized the opportunity to make their case to the world, casting the Islamic Republic as a country abiding by international law against “bullies” who are not.

Araghchi met with more than two dozen diplomats, including counterparts from more than ten European countries and even Jordan’s foreign minister, whose country Iran had attacked. More importantly, he held a rare direct meeting with US envoy Steve Witkoff and told western media that Iran had put a new offer on the table.

In his address to the UN gathering, Pezeshkian said the Islamic Republic would never “bow down” – a line that landed well with hardliners at home, some of whom had opposed the trip at a time when war-time sanctions and a US naval blockade are choking Iran’s economy.

On Thursday, Pezeshkian sat with Western journalists and think-tank analysts at a New York hotel to lay out his government’s thinking – a far cry from the morning of February 28, when he was feared dead after vanishing for hours amid waves of US-Israeli strikes.

In previous decades, Iran’s turns at the United Nations General Assembly have garnered attention, but under the shadow of war, this year’s visit became the main event. Tehran’s officials planned the visit strategically , mindful of both global and domestic attention.

Hardliners in Iran initially criticized Pezeshkian and Araghchi’s diplomatic overtures to Washington, deeming a decision to visit the country actively waging war against them as a sign of surrender. Araghchi, in particular, came under fire from Iran’s conservative lawmakers for meeting Witkoff.

“Foreign policy and national security are not arenas for recklessness,” a hardline lawmaker, Ebrahim Rezaei, wrote on X Wednesday. “The foreign minister must explain on which authorization his meeting with the representative of the enemy was conducted?”

Yet, despite the high risk of a political misstep, Iranian officials staged a visit that played well at home, revived a diplomatic track with their adversary, declared a message of survival to the world and delivered their thinking to the American public.

Pezeshkian declared Iran’s demands from the UN podium and held bilateral meetings with his counterparts. By contrast, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who co-launched the war on Iran, was met with protests on the streets of New York and a mass walkout of UN delegates as he delivered his speech from the floor.

Fresh proposal

Araghchi’s meeting with Witkoff to restart talks was an attempt to break three months of diplomatic deadlock.

Still, US officials were quick to caution that an agreement would take time.

NEW YORK, SEPTEMBER 23: President of Iran Masoud Pezeshkian speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations (U.N.) General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters on September 23, 2026 in New York City. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images

“If there’s going to be a deal with Iran…it’s going to involve a lot of hard work over a period of time, and it will engage and involve mediators as well,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week.

Iran said it had presented a proposal to the US that would swiftly re-open the Strait of Hormuz – in return for Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran – and restart the push towards a “final deal.”

Tehran’s fresh offer requires Washington to meet a set of conditions within seven days, Araghchi told reporters. He declined to elaborate on those conditions but said that they were “nothing more” than what was included in the Memorandum of Understanding – an ill-fated agreement signed between both parties in June that quickly collapsed.

There has been no official response. But the Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that US President Donald Trump has rejected Iran’s latest offer, telling staff that a renewed bombing campaign is likely after the upcoming midterm elections. The officials said Trump’s views could change over the coming weeks.

In response to Araghchi’s comments, a White House official told CNN they are having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators.”

“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush. Nearly 22 million barrels of oil left the strait last night,” the official said.

While a quick reopening of the strait and a resumption of talks over Tehran’s nuclear program could be tempting to Trump, obstacles remain.

Iran’s conditions include the US waiving sanctions on oil sales, lifting the naval blockade and ending other economic penalties imposed after the breakdown of the agreement back in June, a regional source familiar with the talks told CNN.

In further remarks, Araghchi said “the choice now rests with the United States.”

US, Iran locked in a showdown

“The offer now is essentially the same bargain, but with a very different sequence,” Sina Toossi, a senior fellow at the Center for International Policy in Washington, D.C told CNN. “The US takes concrete steps first, and only then does Iran ease its pressure over Hormuz.”

Under the June deal, which at the time was widely seen as favorable to Iran, the US agreed to lift a naval blockade, end sanctions on the regime, set up a $300 billion fund to reconstruct the country and accept the Islamic Republic’s role in managing a narrow waterway where a fifth of global oil crosses daily.

The agreement quickly collapsed after the Trump administration accused Tehran of firing on ships in the Hormuz. Iran, in turn, accused Washington of its own breaches by launching strikes on Iran and refusing to release cash frozen in banks abroad.

NEW YORK, SEPTEMBER 24: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi (L) meets with Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi (R) during the 81st United Nations General Assembly Iranian Foreign Ministry/Anadolu/Getty Images

“The central message from Pezeshkian’s New York trip is that Iran genuinely wants a deal,” Toossi added, “but it is no longer willing to strike a deal and de-escalate first and simply trust that Washington will follow through.”

Iran has also pursued a separate diplomatic track with Oman, the only other country that borders the Strait of Hormuz, on how to manage the waterway. Iran has in the past demanded future payment for managing the Strait, but it remains unclear if that demand is part of Tehran’s new offer. It’s also unclear if the new Iranian-Omani framework has been presented to the Trump administration. An attempt to bring neighboring Arab states on board failed last week.

One of the bigger lingering questions is whether Iran will accept a new negotiation that Washington could use to extract further concessions.

Both sides are currently locked in a showdown over who can live with the status quo the longest. Iran is advertising a high pain threshold while Trump insists that he will not be hurt in the midterm elections even as gas prices climb at the pump.

So, Tehran’s leaders might have had a good few days – but it is unclear how long the glow will last.

“They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election,” Trump said in his speech at the UN. “What they don’t realize is that I’m not running. I did that already and won in a landslide.”

World.title: Thai capital Bangkok declared disaster zone amid widespread flooding
World.content:
Bangkok Reuters — Bangkok’s governor on Saturday declared Thailand’s capital city a disaster-affected zone after torrential rain led to widespread flooding, while the weather agency forecast thunderstorms ​over the weekend.

Major roads were flooded with cars partly submerged and ​people were forced to wade through waist-height water after nearly ⁠300mm (12 inches) of rain fell within 48 hours.

Bangkok Governor Chadchart ​Sittipunt said the crisis “poses a risk to people’s lives” and could damage ​public and private property, and that the situation was most severe near canals.

The army said it is setting up shelters and field kitchens among other disaster relief efforts, ​while the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration has designated schools as temporary accommodation ​and asked residents to avoid unnecessary travel.

Supermarkets were crowded with people stocking up on ‌supplies.

“I’m ⁠worried too, because I haven’t stocked up on food beforehand, and I’ve never faced this kind of situation alone before, since my parents aren’t with me,” said 19-year-old Sansuk Laowatcharakul.

The government on Saturday issued an emergency ​advisory for people living ​near canals ⁠to move possessions to higher ground.

Before the warning, “I wasn’t aware enough to consider relocating,” said Bangkok resident Suppakarn ​Julavijitphong as he carried luggage from a condo surrounded ​by floodwater.

The ⁠city’s main airport, Suvarnabhumi, was operating normally though the tourism authority advised travellers to allow an extra two to three hours in their plans.

Thailand experienced ⁠its worst ​floods in decades in November when at ​least 145 people died and thousands of homes were damaged in the southern provinces.

World.title: The US wants the world to pick a side on AI. But for many countries, China’s pitch may be more compelling
World.content:
Hong Kong —

The rapid advances of Chinese artificial intelligence over the past year seem to have alerted Washington to the real possibility that the world’s second-largest economy could pull ahead of the United States in an increasingly tight technology race.

“We’re leading China in AI…and frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins,” US President Donald Trump said earlier this month.

Trump’s comments underscore the stakes of a US-China tech competition that is increasingly being framed in existential terms. The US has an obvious edge, with pioneering AI labs, the most advanced chips and deep-pocketed investors. Leveraging that dominance, Washington is also forcing countries around the world to pick a side.

But China has a vision that, for many, may be more compelling. Even as it trails the US in frontier AI models, it’s rapidly narrowing the technology gap while championing a more open ecosystem centered on accessibility and lower cost.

In July, Chinese leader Xi Jinping launched the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization – a rival grouping to the Pax Silica alliance that Trump formed last year to reduce reliance on China for AI supply chains.

While over two dozen countries and the European Union signed up to Trump’s Pax Silica, Xi has recruited 29 countries, including Russia, Indonesia and Pakistan, to his alternative vision of open models, which allow users to freely download, customize and run without paying hefty fees to American firms like Anthropic and OpenAI.

For developers in the Global South, an inexpensive Chinese model from DeepSeek or Moonshot may be more useful than a slightly more capable system requiring an expensive subscription and access to a foreign cloud provider, said Eric Olander, editor in chief of The China-Global South Project, a research agency.

Amid concerns about AI’s potential threat to humanity and growing calls for a global oversight body, the technology became a key focus of the Trump-Xi summit this week.

The right thing to do on AI, Xi said during talks with Trump, is to “draw on each other’s strengths, not guard against each other” – a reference to Beijing’s concern about US containment, from existing tech export controls to potential AI restrictions.

“The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” he added.

But the summit has yielded little progress on AI beyond a formal dialogue and a bilateral communication channel, proposals discussed before the two leaders’ summit – underscoring the entrenched mutual mistrust amid contrasting visions on AI.

Embrace of open systems

China’s embrace of open systems has not always been a top-down strategy by Beijing.

Restrictions on access to the most advanced chips because of US export controls, coupled with smaller capital markets, have pushed Chinese developers toward open models as a way to compete with leading US proprietary systems.

That shift has proved effective.

In a year, Chinese models’ global usage skyrocketed from less than 15% to over 54% last week, led by DeepSeek, according to AI leaderboard data by OpenRouter, a marketplace for models.

The “Canal Qiyuan DeepSeek Home” located in Changqing Street, Hangzhou, Zhejiang Province, China on June 16, 2026. CFOTO/Future Publishing/Getty Images

Even American firms, from Airbnb and DoorDash to Shopify, have embraced Chinese models, tapping into the advantages of open systems, including lower costs and greater flexibility for customization.

Rather than picking a side, companies – American or not – generally prefer to diversify their technology suppliers, Olander said. Chinese AI could spread through existing telecom, cloud and hardware networks, particularly in emerging markets where Chinese companies already have substantial distribution networks.

“It may not be that DeepSeek or Moonshot will make much money, but the companies surrounding them – Huawei, ZTE, the others providing support, providing technology, providing all the services around AI, may do very well,” Olander said.

The meaning of winning the AI race is also poorly defined. Different metrics, from profitability to market share, could yield a different result to the question.

“Is Apple winning the mobile phone race? Fewer people use Apple products, but Apple eats up 90% of the profits,” Olander said, adding that the likely outcome of the AI race may mirror Apple’s case, where the US holds the profits while China accumulates the users.

As AI capabilities continue to advance, the differences between the most advanced models and slightly less capable systems may become less noticeable to most people and businesses, experts said. Some companies may need frontier US models, while others may find Chinese models efficient enough for their needs.

New iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max smartphones are on display as the models go on sale at an Apple store in Beijing, China on September 18, 2026. Tingshu Wang/Reuters

“For most people around the world, the question will ultimately be about what kind of trade-off they want to make,” said Chucheng Feng, founding partner of advisory firm Hutong Research.

“Do I want a model that costs 10 times as much but is six months ahead, or one that costs one-tenth as much but is only six months behind?”

Limits to openness

Still, the appeal of Chinese models may hinge on the extent to which they remain accessible without restrictions, experts said.

At China’s signature AI conference in July, Xi called for greater openness and collaboration in AI, while stressing the need for regulation to keep it under human control.

The more capable Chinese models become, the less likely it is Beijing may leave them unrestricted, said Alex Colville, an analyst focusing on tech and security at the government-backed Australian Strategic Policy Institute.

“Beijing wants to export the country’s technology to bolster its international influence, but national security always comes first,” he said, explaining that restrictions could be placed around AI with Anthropic’s Mythos-like cyber capability, for example, that could pose a threat to China if misused.

“But it won’t be anything as black-and-white as total closure or total openness. What I think we will see going forward is a mixture of both open- and closed-source AI from China, as both serve the country’s national interests,” Colville said.

Chinese leader Xi Jinping speaks at the opening ceremony for the World AI Conference in Shanghai, China, July 17, 2026. Ng Han Guan/Pool/Reuters

Instead of a blanket ban, Beijing could use licensing rules to restrict where certain models could be used, he added.

Global developers and some governments have rushed to take advantage of Chinese open models to push for sovereign AI development and avoid picking a side. But they now have to worry about how long those models may stay open, as China may be compelled to limit the deployment of its most powerful open models to “avoid cyber anarchy,” said Reva Goujon, a director focusing on China at research and advisory firm Rhodium Group.

“China’s strategy is only more compelling to the world so long as the models remain available and open so that they can be adopted and fine-tuned for domestic and enterprise needs,” she said.

Deepening mistrust

As Chinese firms unveil increasingly capable models that near the performance of Anthropic and OpenAI’s most advanced systems, Washington has dialed up accusations that China is engaging in what it calls the “industrial-scale theft” of American trade secrets.

Both Anthropic and OpenAI have released reports claiming that leading Chinese AI labs trained their models on outputs from American systems, a process known as distillation. In a lengthy report earlier this month, Anthropic detailed how DeepSeek and Moonshot forwarded some customer requests to Claude to train and improve their own models, and in some of the processes, exposed sensitive information.

Anthropic’s Claude AI app is seen in the app store on a phone on February 16, 2026 in New York City. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Beijing has repeatedly rejected the distillation accusations. DeepSeek and Moonshot did not respond to CNN’s request for comment.

“Since the US has a very leaky export control regime, including a still gaping hole that allows Chinese access to US AI compute via overseas data centers, it’s very difficult to pinpoint just how much Chinese AI developers are relying on distillation to put out these incredibly advanced models,” Goujon said. “The question is what does this US administration actually do about it?”

Washington has floated possible sanctions and other restrictions on open Chinese models. But Nvidia, Meta, Microsoft and dozens of other companies warned against “sweeping restrictions” on open models in an open letter in July – revealing a rift between US tech companies and Washington.

Despite growing calls to prevent AI development from spiraling out of control, the Trump-Xi summit has produced little substance, as many experts expected.

Because of low levels of trust, cooperation between the two superpowers remains limited, said George Chen, chair of digital practice at The Asia Group consultancy.

“Beijing continues to believe Washington seeks to contain China’s rise in AI and other emerging technologies, a perception that will shape the pace and scope of future engagement for the two countries on AI,” he said.

World.title: Egypt’s water security is ‘existential issue’, stresses Madbouly to the UN
World.content:
Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly emphasized to the UN that Egypt’s water security is an existential matter that allows for no compromise.

Madbouly made the remarks on Saturday while delivering Egypt’s address at the General Debate of the High-Level Segment of the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly in New York, on behalf of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi.

He affirmed his country’s legitimate right to safeguard its water security and its rejection of any unilateral measures infringing upon its historical water shares, while noting this does not oppose the right of other nations to pursue development through cooperation.

Strengthening effective multilateralism.

He further called for restoring confidence in the international system and strengthening effective multilateralism.

Madbouly emphasized that the world requires a system that ensures every nation has a voice, respects the principle of sovereign equality, and commits to upholding international law and the peaceful settlement of disputes.

The world is changing at a pace that outstrips the capacity of governance institutions to respond, noting that the crisis lies not in a lack of principles but in the widening gap between what is proclaimed and what is implemented, and between those who make decisions and those affected by them.

The Prime Minister explained that the world does not need superficial multilateralism that merely gathers nations for discussions: rather it requires a system in which every state has a voice and all peoples can enjoy a fair share of decisions, opportunities, and resources.

He noted the declining confidence in the efficacy of collective action and the multilateral system, emphasizing the urgent need to restore adherence to international law and to avoid policies of polarization and double standards.

Restoring trust requires three interconnected pillars: fairness in representation and decision-making, fairness in the application of the law, and fairness in the distribution of opportunities for development and transformation.

This vision does not aim to rebuild the global system from scratch, but rather to fulfill its original promises and objectives, he emphasized.

Regional issues

Madbouly presented Egypt’s comprehensive vision regarding various regional and international issues, emphasizing that Palestine’s turmoil stands as the most prominent testament to the flaws within the international system and its credibility.

The Palestinian people must not be allowed to become a normalized reality, he stressed.

Madbouly called for consolidating the ceasefire in the Gaza Strip, halting violations, ensuring the sustainable delivery of humanitarian aid, and empowering the National Committee for the Management of Gaza.

He said that these steps are intended to pave the way for reconstruction and a transition to a serious political process that addresses the root causes of the conflict and leads to the establishment of an independent Palestinian state based on the June 4, 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

Madbouly reiterated Egypt’s categorical rejection of any attempts to displace Palestinians from their land.

He further declared Egypt’s rejection of the fragmentation of regional states or the creation of entities parallel to their national institutions, warning that support for armed groups and the undermining of state sovereignty fuel civil conflicts and threaten regional security as well as international navigation.

Comprehensive reform

The Prime Minister called for a comprehensive reform of the UN Security Council and the international financial system to ensure equitable representation and decision-making, and better support the emerging economies of the Global South without imposing additional burdens.

Madbouly emphasized the inextricable link between climate action, development, and poverty eradication.

On the topic of technology and military affairs, he stressed the importance of formulating comprehensive frameworks for artificial intelligence governance to protect privacy.

He reiterated Egypt’s rejection of arms races and its commitment to a disarmament regime free from double standards, noting that reforming the international system is closely tied to resolving the region’s crises.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: FM: Foreign policy anchored in ‘strategic commitment’, rejects military solutions
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Affairs Badr Abdelatty Saturday, September 26, 2026, said that Egypt’s foreign policy is based on the principle of “strategic commitment” established by President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, with de-escalation and political solutions among its key pillars, stressing that crises have no military solutions.

In a special interview with Al Qahera News Channel, where he is participating with the Egyptian delegation at the United Nations General Assembly, Abdelatty said Egypt’s stance consistently supports dialogue, negotiations, and the rejection of military solutions.

He cited lessons from the past showing that military escalation leads only to destruction and devastation, adding that Egypt is therefore acting intensively in line with the directives of the president.

Abdelatty said he had held contacts with the foreign ministers of Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia, as well as other contacts within the quartet comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, which, he added plays an important role in mediation efforts.

He also said he had been in contact with the Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister.

He explained that these moves are part of efforts to de-escalate tensions and promote political solutions.

The Foreign Minister stressed that Egypt is a major country with wise leadership represented by the president, and that no party can drag it into any conflicts.

“Egypt is a state that possesses its own positions and choices and acts according to its national interests,” Abdelatty said, adding that the political leadership sets the broad outlines of the country’s foreign policy moves to safeguard Egyptian interests and national security.

Abdelatty reiterated that there are no military solutions and that Egypt is pushing for de-escalation because it is bearing significant burdens from the continuing escalation in the region, particularly in terms of food security and rising prices of energy, gas, oil, wheat, and grains.

He noted that the impact extends beyond Egypt to countries across the region and the wider world.

Egypt is working intensively to find political solutions focusing on several issues, including the nuclear file, freedom of navigation and sanctions, Abdelatty said, adding that general principles governing these issues had been agreed upon and are being addressed within the framework of the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding.

He called for rebuilding the trust lost between the United States and Iran.

“We are working to encourage both sides to return to the negotiating table, leading to de-escalation and an integrated and final deal that serves the interests of both parties, as well as those of the region and the world, and supports stability and calm while avoiding escalation,” he said.

Regarding Egypt’s role in the Gaza Strip, Abdelatty highlighted several achievements resulting from intensive efforts by Egypt in cooperation with its regional partners, saying the efforts had contributed to a partial halt to the Israeli offensive on the Gaza Strip.

He said the situation remains dire and catastrophic, amid Israel’s failure to implement its obligations under U.S. President Donald Trump’s plan, particularly the removal of obstacles hindering the flow of humanitarian and medical aid into Gaza.

Israel has also failed to fulfill its commitments to rehabilitate hospitals, schools and medical clinics to allow the medical sector in the enclave to be rebuilt, Abdelatty said, adding that it had continued a policy of systematic assassinations carried out daily against the Palestinian people.

Abdelatty said the Palestinian side had fulfilled the obligations of the second phase of Trump’s plan, while Israel was, “unfortunately,” refusing to fulfill its commitments, particularly regarding withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and allowing an international stabilization force and the National Committee for the Administration of the Gaza Strip to enter.

Asked whether upcoming Israeli elections could help remove obstacles, Abdelatty stressed that Egypt does not interfere in the internal affairs of other countries, calling the vote an internal Israeli matter.

He nevertheless expressed hope that the elections would produce a partner willing to work with Egypt to establish a peace process.

As regards Sudan, Abdelatty said Egypt would spare no effort and would do everything within its capacity to help resolve the situation there and work toward a political settlement.

“Egypt supports Sudan’s unity and stability and the national institutions,” he said, adding that the continuation of the conflict serves neither the interests of the Sudanese people nor stability in Sudan and the region as a whole.

On Egyptian-American relations, Abdelatty said ties between the two countries are strong and solid and characterized by coordination.

He said Egypt’s strategy toward the United States is based on maintaining and strengthening bilateral relations, highlighting the strong ties between President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and US President Donald Trump.

Egypt and the United States are working together to restore stability in the Middle East, Abdelatty said, adding that Egyptian-American coordination continues to reduce escalation in the region and around the world.

World.title: Harrington Warns UPND Against Removing Presidential Term Limits
World.content:
Zambians Have Always Rejected Removing Presidential Term Limits, Says William Harrington

Former transport and communications minister William Harrington has said Zambians have consistently rejected proposals to remove presidential term limits, pointing to submissions made to the Chona, Mvunga, Mwanakatwe and Mung’omba constitutional review commissions. He spoke while the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) pushes for a constitutional amendment to remove the limit, which would allow President Hakainde Hichilema to continue ruling beyond 2031.

William Harrington’s insights on governance resonate strongly with the public’s sentiments regarding term limits.

The push has come from within the party’s own ranks in Parliament. UPND proportional representation MP Florence Chileshe Chama, one of 17 women the party nominated to the 20 seats reserved for women, said in a video shared on 20 September that women in Zambia “don’t want democracy but development”. She suggested this could be achieved by supporting Mr Hichilema beyond his final term, and other UPND members have made similar calls in recent days.

Civil society has pushed back hard. Civil rights activist Brebner Changala warned that “if there’s something Zambians will not tolerate even in their collective docility, it is a third term,” and said the UPND should not take the public’s silence after the disputed August elections for granted. Governance campaigner Mulenga Kapwepwe asked: “What is wrong with the Constitution for people to start pushing a narrative that the Constitution should be changed?”

Mr Harrington took the argument back to the historical record. In an interview, he said citizens who took part in successive constitutional reviews overwhelmingly supported limiting a president to two five-year terms, because they feared unlimited tenure would concentrate power and undermine democratic succession.

He said the Constitution guaranteed freedom of speech and conscience, but that citizens on either side of the amendment question had a duty to reach their positions through education and research rather than political expediency. Such research, Mr Harrington said, would point in only one direction.

“If citizens cared to take time to study the submissions made to various constitution review commissions such as the Chona, Mvunga, Mwanakatwe and Mung’omba commissions, they will discover that the overwhelming number of citizens consistently and persistently rejected unlimited or ‘freehold’ presidential terms, insisting that the presidential term of office must be limited to only two five-year terms,” he said.

The main case for term limits, he said, had always been the need to prevent dictatorship and the prolonged concentration of power in one individual. Mr Harrington recalled that the Council of Churches in Zambia (CCZ) and various political commentators had warned that removing the limit risked breeding a dictatorial leader or creating a life president, undermining the country’s democratic process.

Term limits also protect orderly change at the top, he said, allowing a country to experience regular and peaceful transfers of leadership. “Presidential term limits serve as a critical mechanism to ensure periodic, peaceful political succession,” Mr Harrington said.

He spoke directly to leaders who believe a decade in office is too short. Where a president felt that 10 years were not enough to achieve their objectives, Mr Harrington said, the answer lay in strengthening institutions and developing future leaders, not in changing the Constitution to extend tenure.

Zambians, he said, had rejected constitutional changes before when they saw them as driven by self-serving political interests. The country’s own history offered the clearest lesson, and he cited the failed third-term bid by former president Frederick Chiluba in 2001.

The amendment question is now open inside the ruling party. Mr Harrington says the answer has already been given four times, by citizens before four commissions: two terms of five years, and no more.

World.title: Mandevu, Lumezi North And Mbala Return To The Polls On 5 November
World.content:
Voters in Mandevu and Lumezi North will elect Members of Parliament on 5 November because the August general election produced no result in either constituency. Mbala will choose a new mayor after the mayor-elect died days after winning. The Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) announced the polls on Friday, together with by-elections in 11 wards, including the crucial Mandevu by-election.

Mandevu’s contest was lost in the days after polling. On 18 August, unknown individuals stormed the Mandevu totalling centre, attacked staff, destroyed result transmission kits and fled with election documents. Ballot papers were later found dumped in drainages and burnt, which left the returning officer unable to declare the National Assembly result for one of Lusaka Province’s key constituencies, leading to the upcoming Mandevu by-election.

Acting on a report from the Lusaka District Electoral Officer dated the same day, ECZ Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro announced at the end of August that the seat would be contested afresh. “In view of this, the Commission has resolved to hold a by-election for Mandevu Constituency, referred to as the Mandevu by-election, on a date to be communicated in due course,” he said.

The Foundation for Democratic Process (FODEP) and the Anti-Voter Apathy Project backed the decision as consistent with electoral standards where materials have been compromised. The Zambia Civil Liberties Union (ZCLU) challenged the commission’s authority, saying “there is no law that mandates the Electoral Commission of Zambia to cancel and conduct fresh parliamentary elections”. Politician Peter Sinkamba urged the ECZ to extend the fresh poll to Mandevu’s mayoral and councillor elections as well.

Lumezi North’s vacancy goes back to before polling day. Clement Mwale, the parliamentary candidate for the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) within the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance, died in the early hours of 16 July, after nominations had closed. He had been running against Anderson Banda of the UPND and Nebby Manda of the Leadership Movement.

Under Constitutional Amendment No. 13 of 2025, the death of a candidate after nominations obliges the commission to cancel the election in that constituency, and the sponsoring party then has 30 days to field a replacement. ECZ Commissioner McDonald Chipenzi said at the time that “once a sponsored candidate has died, the Commission is empowered to cancel that election and call for fresh nominations for that party.”

Mbala lost its new mayor within days of the vote. Steward Simutenda, elected on 13 August on the NRPUP ticket, died around midnight on 18 August following an illness, his brother Gabriel Simutenda said. A former Patriotic Front (PF) district chairperson for Mbala, he had been admitted to hospital about a week before polling.

The 11 ward vacancies arose from the deaths of nominated and elected candidates, from wards left uncontested at the general election, and from nominations nullified by the Local Government Elections Tribunal. The wards are Lungwishi in Mansa, Makaba and Nkonge in Chipili, Nachikufu in Mpika, Lubaleshi in Kanchibiya, Maako in Kasempa, Siluwe and Upangoma in Kalabo, Mbeta in Sioma, Mulimambango in Sesheke and Simanvwa in Choma.

Nominations open on Thursday 8 October, and campaigns run from 10 October until 18:00 hours on 4 November. Parliamentary and mayoral candidates will pay non-refundable fees of K17,000 for men, K14,000 for women, K10,500 for youths and K10,000 for persons with disabilities.

For the ruling party, the contests are a chance to renew its claim on voters. UPND deputy spokesperson Elvis Nkandu said the party would use the by-elections to make the case for the New Dawn Government. “This is another opportunity for us to appeal to the citizens and ask them to give us the mandate to continue delivering development,” he said.

Mr Nkandu said the party remained focused on service delivery and on the interests of ordinary Zambians. “We remain the voice of the voiceless, particularly when it comes to service delivery. Our focus is on ensuring that development reaches the people,” he said, adding that the UPND expected to take a strong share of the seats.

“We are going into these by-elections prepared, and we believe the people will have confidence in the UPND and its ability to deliver development,” Mr Nkandu said. He appealed to voters in the affected areas to back the party’s candidates.

Nominations open on 8 October. Mandevu, Lumezi North, Mbala and the 11 wards vote on 5 November.

World.title: Lusaka Catholics Called To Cathedral As Archbishop Banda Answers Fresh DEC Summons
World.content:
The Catholic Archdiocese of Lusaka has called its clergy and faithful to a solidarity Mass at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus on Monday morning. Archbishop Alick Banda reports to the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC) a few hours later on a renewed summons. The Church said it feared for his safety and well-being and urged Catholics to stand with him in prayer.

The Mass begins at 08:00 hours. From the cathedral, the Archbishop is expected to go on to the commission, where he is due at 10:00 hours.

“Mass will be celebrated at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus on Monday 28th September, 2026 at 08:00 hours in solidarity with the Archbishop, before he proceeds to the Drug Enforcement Commission at 10:00 hours,” the Archdiocese said.

The announcement came in a statement dated 25 September and signed by the Archdiocese’s Communications Office, which also published it on the Church’s official Facebook page. The statement calls the DEC call-out a “renewed” summons, which means the commission has called the Archbishop before.

The Church did not say what the commission wants to take up with him, or what happened with the earlier summons. The statement dealt only with the Archbishop himself and with the Church’s resolve to stand around him.

“The Archdiocese of Lusaka expresses its deep concern and unwavering solidarity with our Local Shepherd, His Grace Most Rev. Dr. Alick Banda, following renewed summons by the Drug Enforcement Commission (DEC),” the Church said.

Church leaders built their appeal around one line of Scripture, placed at the head of the statement. They chose Matthew 26:38, the words Christ spoke in the Garden of Gethsemane when he asked his disciples to keep vigil with him: “Stay here and keep watch with me.”

Concern for the Archbishop’s safety runs through the statement. The Church said more than once that it was deeply concerned for his safety and well-being, but it did not say what specific fear lay behind those words.

Even so, the Archdiocese made clear that the Archbishop would honour the summons. It asked the faithful to meet the moment with composure rather than alarm, and tied its call for calm directly to respect for the law.

“We therefore call upon the clergy, religious and lay faithful to remain united in prayer, calm in spirit and steadfast in faith as our Archbishop responds to the summons in accordance with the law,” the statement read.

With that emphasis on the law established, the Church turned to the Archbishop’s standing among his people. It presented him not as a lone figure going before a State agency, but as a pastor whose congregation would walk with him.

“Our Archbishop is not alone. He remains a shepherd surrounded by his flock, and the Church stands firmly with him in prayer, communion and solidarity,” the Archdiocese said.

The Church then cast the moment as a test for the faithful themselves. It told Catholics that fear had no place in their response.

“At this moment, we are called not to fear, but to remain vigilant in prayer and steadfast in our commitment to truth, justice and peace,” the statement said.

The Archdiocese invited Catholics across Lusaka to pray earnestly for the Archbishop’s safety, strength, wisdom and well-being. It also asked them to pray that justice, truth and peace would prevail “throughout this process”.

Everyone able to attend the cathedral service was encouraged to come. The Church asked the faithful to “stand together as one family” on Monday morning and closed its appeal with a four-part charge.

“Let us be united in prayer, steadfast in faith, peaceful in spirit and unwavering in our pursuit of truth,” the Archdiocese said.

The statement’s closing lines placed the matter in God’s hands. Church leaders said they trusted the Lord to carry the Archbishop through the days ahead.

“We place our trust in God, who is our refuge and strength. We entrust our Local Shepherd to God’s providence, confident that the Lord will sustain him and guide him through this moment,” the Church said.

The Archdiocese also entrusted itself, and what it called “the Archbishop’s cause”, to the intercession of Our Lady of Lusaka, the Mother of the Child Jesus.

Catholics will gather at the Cathedral of the Child Jesus from 08:00 hours on Monday. The Archbishop is due at the Drug Enforcement Commission two hours later.
