NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”

During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during Knicks’ NBA Finals games.

“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”

The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.

00:56 Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL' 00:00 00:00

“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”

Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.

“Can you foul out of ‘SNL?’” Towns asked.

In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson portrayed a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”

It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.

The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than the ones of Culhane’s character. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.

Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.

He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.

Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players, Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.

Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.

The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.

Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed season two of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”

“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

World.title: Trump says he has rejected Iranian proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian officials indicated that shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days if a deal was sealed.

“I rejected their deal. They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump told reporters as he boarded Marine One on the White House lawn, after indirect talks between the two countries were held on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York.

“What they wanted is to immediately open the Hormuz Strait. You know why? Because they’re dying. You know why they’re dying? Because they have no money coming in because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait,” he continued. “They outsmarted themselves. They said, ‘Let’s close it and cause a problem for the world.’ And I came along, and we put up the greatest blockade ever in military history.”

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected Iran’s offer to revive a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said Friday that the choice “rests with the United States.”

“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters.

He said a “concrete seven-day plan” that includes reopening the strait had been conveyed to the U.S. through mediator Qatar and was ready to start “as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”

00:48 Iran offers new proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz 00:00 00:00

Araghchi said the actions required of the U.S. in Iran’s proposal were commitments already agreed to in the June memorandum of understanding between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. That agreement, signed in June, collapsed within days after fresh strikes were exchanged.

One of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman, Araghchi had said Thursday.

A U.S. official said on Friday that the Trump administration was having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators but that it was not in any hurry to reach an agreement.

“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the U.S. official said. “Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the strait.”

Earlier this week, Trump said he was still considering whether to “annihilate” Iran or make a deal. Early Saturday, he posted an image to Truth Social of the Strait of Hormuz labeled the “Trump Strait.”

In an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that resolving the Hormuz issue “is possible through negotiations, not the use of force,” but warned that his country does not “trust” talks with Washington.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.

Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations, two days after Trump said he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the elections.

“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November midterms. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.

The U.S. this week announced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business ​with Iranian airlines, with the aim of grounding Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide.

Iraq said Saturday that it was engaging with the U.S. in an effort to restore humanitarian flights to and from Iran, after Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries in response to the sanctions.

Efforts were ongoing to “secure exemptions for certain Iraqi airports from these measures” in order to enable “the resumption of flights for humanitarian reasons, such as medical treatment, education, religious pilgrimages, and the interests of civilians,” the Iraqi prime minister’s office said.

Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan.

World.title: It’s cute. It’s cuddly. And it wants your data.
World.content:
Meta hopes its new AI agent will win people over by being cute.

Muse, the tech giant’s cuddly, doll-like AI agent, shot to the top of the Apple App Store charts after it was featured this week at the company’s Meta Connect conference.

The company is touting the tool, designed to help people with their everyday tasks, as an AI agent “built for everyone,” including those who lack experience with technology.

AI agents, which are systems that automatically execute tasks on a user’s behalf, are rapidly becoming ubiquitous in online workspaces, social apps and personal devices.

02:43 Meet Mark Zuckerberg's personal Muse AI agent 00:00 00:00

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the default Muse avatar, which is cream-colored and has beady black eyes and an upward smile, is named “Jolly,” for its “jolly and completely customizable character and personality.”

Muse is being launched as tech companies seek to make their AI-powered products more palatable to humans, often by giving them cute, almost petlike appearances, voices and personalities. Experts have said design choices that humanize technology may become more common as robot-human interaction grows more prevalent in everyday spaces, as cuteness evokes “deep-seated biological responses” in people.

“It was only about six months ago that having a personal agent running on your own computer was the sign of someone who is completely AI-pilled and thinking nonstop about agents,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, said Wednesday. “But for that small group of nerds ... it looked like the beginning of personal superintelligence. And today with Muse, we’ve brought that magic to everyone.”

Mark Zuckerberg's Muse AI Agent, Agrippa. Meta

Muse agents can take on a variety of appearances, with users able to customize everything from their names to their attire. Zuckerberg’s agent, which wears a toga and a wreath around its head, is named Agrippa, after the Roman general and statesman.

During the event, Zuckerberg also teased what he calls the “Muse charm,” a small handheld device that can activate the agent on the go. He raised the keychain charm onstage at Meta Connect in Menlo Park, California, showing off what looks like a blend of a Labubu and a Tamagotchi.

“Talking to your Muse is often the fastest way to get things done, and it is also just really fun and cute,” he said, saying he used Agrippa to come up with a baking recipe and order ingredients for him and his daughter.

Muse is also being integrated directly into Meta’s expanding lineup of AI-powered glasses, which have been criticized over fears of casual surveillance. Zuckerberg has told NBC News that Meta will continue to bolster privacy safeguards for its smart glasses.

Zuckerberg said every Muse agent has its own private and secure computer called Muse Secure VM, a dedicated secure computer that houses both the agent and the user’s personal data. Down the line, he said, Meta plans to release Muse Confidential VM “so that even Meta won’t be able to see that information.”

“In the coming years, I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives,” he said.

Online, the reaction has been mixed.

Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted a flurry of memes inserting Muse into moments from movies, shows and historical events.

Some followed his lead by making their own avatars and sharing screenshots on social media.

Others, however, expressed skepticism, citing security concerns.

“Am I the only one who doesn’t want to let meta have access to my whole life?” a user posted.

“We are going to need some tight defenses and 3rd party testing of these platforms... like all software products,” entrepreneur and angel investor Jason Calacanis wrote.

Zuckerberg has continued to be bullish on AI despite recent calls from tech executives and government officials to pump the brakes on AI development amid surging fears about the existential risk the technology poses.

He shared his thoughts recently on X, saying market forces should be enough to keep AI companies in line.

“My view is that trust and alignment are quickly becoming the most important capabilities that will differentiate agents and models. Any lab that doesn’t focus on alignment will fall behind,” he wrote, adding: “Meta delayed shipping Muse for several months to focus on safety and security. We didn’t call for everyone else to do this before we would.”

World.title: Should you bring iced coffee to a job interview? Question brews generational debate
World.content:
What started as a conversation about job interview tips online escalated into a generational debate over whether it’s taboo to show up with an iced coffee to talk to a potential employer.

The discourse over the caffeinated beverage gained momentum on TikTok this week after a creator, who goes by @caitlinrecruiter on the platform, shared a video in which she said she believes “when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day.”

“It looks a little too casual to me,” she said in the video, which she posted Sept. 16.

Caitlin Wehniainen, whose profile states she has 16 years of recruiting experience, has just over 1,000 followers on TikTok. But in the last week, her video has been clipped and recirculated by dozens of creators online, who engaged in a heated back-and-forth about whether she’s right.

The divide seemed to primarily be between younger and older users — with the former group suggesting Wehniainen’s tip “makes no sense at all” and that such a perspective is archaic.

Others, many who identified as Gen Xers in comments, agreed with Wehniainen, writing that “arguing against this is insane” and telling applicants that they should “save the iced coffee for when you actually get hired.”

By Monday, even the coffee giant Starbucks had taken a side, alluding to the debate in an Instagram post that featured an image of someone holding an iced coffee in one hand and sunglasses and their handbag in the other. “Pulling up to the interview like,” the caption read. Meanwhile, The Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf, another coffee chain, commented on Wehniainen’s video: “We’d hire them on spot...”

Outside Off-White, during New York Fashion Week, on September 12, 2025 in New York, New York Edward Berthelot / Getty Images file

When reached for comment on Friday, Wehniainen said in an email to NBC News that she was “shocked at how polarizing the topic is.”

“But I realize that the original message was taken out of context as the virality of the post grew,” she wrote. “As the topic spread, many decided to weigh in with their own general opinion on whether or not bringing an iced coffee into an interview is appropriate ... I also saw people reading into it too much, asking if coffee or water matters and what is appropriate. I will say, I think a bottled water is great to bring with you.”

The timing of the conversation coincides with a tough job market: Recent college graduates are facing higher unemployment rates than other age groups as it’s becoming more difficult to obtain entry-level jobs, NBC News reported last month. Employers are not looking to add talent, and employed people are not moving to new positions, as a rise in AI continues to threaten jobs.

For Los Angeles-based TikTok creator Esha, who preferred to be identified by only her first name, citing privacy concerns, Wehniainen’s words couldn’t be further from the truth. She was among the many weighing in online, telling her 81,000-plus TikTok followers that “the iced coffee controversy completely misunderstands interviews.”

“Thinking of a job interview as a stop in your day is very normal,” Esha, 22, added in an interview with NBC News, noting that she’s brought iced coffees to several interviews and hasn’t thought twice about it.

“Gen Z had this shift in recent years, where we can still have a life outside of work,” Esha said. “So, like, why am I changing who I am? Why am I missing my coffee for the day for this interview?”

In her video, she elaborated further on her take, saying that “the most easily relatable thing in corporate America is a coffee addiction.”

“Unless you’re like over the age of 30 and you can relate on having kids, and doing stuff with your kids, coffee is the main thing. Everyone’s like, ‘Gotta get that coffee’ ... and finding something personable about a person is so important,” she said. “Like, who is not starting their workday off with a coffee?”

Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications at LinkedIn, said she’s not surprised by the generational divisions when it comes to job etiquette.

“Gen Z is entering this workforce at such a challenging time, it’s such a competitive job market, and to then get judged by bringing an iced coffee just seems like, ‘Have we lost the plot here?’” she said.

That said, Fisher is among the cohort who believes it’s best to skip the iced coffee when headed to an interview.

“Even though I don’t like the answer, I think because everyone is so divided on it, I would be cautious and not bring one,” she said. “You just don’t know who’s on the other side of the interview, so why risk it over something so silly?”

Etiquette expert Thomas Farley, who is known as Mister Manners to his followers online, agreed with the more traditional point of view.

“I think it sends the wrong message in so many respects,” he said. “I think it shows you to be someone who didn’t plan your time accordingly, and you’re multitasking, and that’s not what you should be doing during the interview.”

Farley also warned of the physical pratfalls a coffee could bring.

“There are real practical considerations when you bring a liquid into someone’s office,” he said. “Where does it go? What happens if you spill it?”

While he doesn’t think it should be the deciding factor for any hiring manager, Farley argued candidates should be doing everything in their power to leave a positive impression.

“If it’s between you and three other people, and everyone’s qualifications are more or less equal, and that’s the one thing that potentially sinks your chance to get the job, I think that would be really unfortunate,” he said. “That would be a very expensive $7 cup of iced coffee.”

Still, Gen Zers like Esha are not convinced that bringing the beverage would make or break their job opportunity.

As another TikTok creator put it in their video: “It’s really, really not that serious most of the time.”

As for Wehniainen? Even after the online uproar, she said her “opinion still stands that you shouldn’t bring an iced coffee to your interview.”

“You want to leave outlying distractions like iced coffee behind,” she said, “and connect with your interviewer with full attention.”

World.title: San Francisco Giants’ ‘mom of the year’ defends husband after clip sparks online backlash
World.content:
A woman Giants announcers dubbed “mom of the year” after cameras caught her carrying a baby and an armful of food back to her seat while a man beside her began eating is saying the viral clip didn’t show the whole story.

“Before you decide what our marriage looks like, I would like you to hear from the woman you’re defending,” she wrote.

The woman, who identified herself as Erika, described what happened at Tuesday’s San Francisco Giants game in a Substack post Friday. She said she had taken their daughter to the restroom and offered to pick up food for her husband, Ramses, on the way back. He told her to get him whatever had the shortest line.

When she returned, Ramses asked whether she wanted to eat first, Erika wrote. She told him to go ahead because she had eaten before the game and knew he had not had a full meal that day. He also offered to take the food containers off her lap and share his sandwich, but she declined.

Giants announcers Mike Krukow and Duane Kuiper narrated the scene as the camera lingered on the family. They dubbed Erika “mom of the year” and jokingly imagined that Ramses had asked her for ketchup and that she wanted to smack him. Erika said neither exchange happened.

“I understand how it looked on television,” she wrote. “But we could hear each other. The announcers and audience couldn’t.”

The was another reason Erika wanted Ramses to enjoy the game, she said. He had recently lost a childhood friend who was a gifted baseball player, and she had suggested the outing as a way for her husband to remember him.

“The camera showed what I was carrying in my hands,” she wrote. “It couldn’t show what he was carrying that night.”

Erika said she and Ramses initially laughed at the broadcast. But as the clip spread online, strangers began criticizing him and making assumptions about their marriage. Some found the couple’s names and phone numbers, she wrote, and some sent Ramses messages telling him to kill himself.

Giants announcers Mike Krukow and Duane Kuiper narrated the scene as the camera lingered on the family. Suzanna Mitchell / San Francisco Giants via Getty Images

Erika said she believed that the announcers and Giants production team meant no harm. But she told them their jokes helped turn her husband into a source of ridicule.

“What was a few moments of amusement on your broadcast became days of real pain for our family,” she wrote.

A Giants spokesperson did not return a request for comment.

Erika said she appreciated being called “mom of the year” but asked people to listen when she described her own life.

“You can appreciate what I was doing that night without assuming I have to do everything alone,” she wrote. “Supporting me also means listening when I tell you about my own life.”

World.title: Nor'easter brings heavy flooding, major power outages to the East Coast
World.content:
A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the U.S. Northeast on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.

Tens of millions of people were in the path of the nor'easter, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. Around 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.

In Brooklyn, New York, a 56-year-old man was struck and killed by a falling tree, according to the New York City Police Department, the first confirmed fatality from the storm. The New York City Housing Authority later confirmed he was an employee of the agency. He was identified by Mayor Zohran Mamdani in a social media post as Leighton Brown.

And in Egg Harbor Township in eastern New Jersey, nine adults and a dog were rescued from flooded motel rooms.

The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There will be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Maryland.

A family carries their belongings through the water of a flooded road during a nor'easter storm on Sept. 26, 2026, in Point Pleasant, New Jersey, where a voluntary evacuation has been issued in the community. Ryan Murphy / Getty Images

Rainfall totals of 1 to 3 inches are expected from the Philadelphia region into eastern New Jersey, and portions of Long Island and southern New England could see 3 to 5 inches of rain.

The nor'easter is rapidly intensifying and is expected to make a sharp turn back toward the New Jersey coast Saturday night into Sunday. It may stall or meander nearby through Monday, prolonging the rain, wind and coastal impacts before finally departing on Tuesday.

A car is seen submerged in water on a flooded road during a nor'easter storm on September 26, 2026 in Point Pleasant, New Jersey. Ryan Murphy / Getty Images

Beach towns see severe flooding

In Long Island, New York, some people kayaked down flooded streets.

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, Kenny Formica sat at his home watching surveillance cameras showing water rising inside the marina he owns. Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.

Ahead of the storm, Formica said workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm's way and parked the marina's trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.

Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. One customer sent him a video around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot boat after it had blown off its lift.

"This is like an 8,000-pound boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.

In Ocean City, Maryland, heavy surf caused beach erosion, washed out fencing by the dunes and was leading to flooding.

"In all the canals, the water is up really high and coming into people's backyards," Jay Boyd said by telephone.

Further south, Ellie Hodge stood on her front stoop in Norfolk, Virginia, on Saturday and watched as passing vehicles left wakes. The coastal city has seen isolated flooding all week because of the nor'easter.

"We've seen cars get stuck on the road, going up the sidewalks," Hodge said. "It's been pretty bad this time around."

The storm forced a change of plans for many people. Hundreds of flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.

Forecasted rainfall totals from this weekend's nor'easter. Sept. 25, 2026. CBS News

Wind gusts may cause damage, increase flooding

The New Jersey and Delaware coasts could see wind gusts of about 60 miles per hour, though meteorologists have already seen reports of winds over 70 miles per hour. Inland, residents could see wind gusts of 40 to 50 mph.

Eastern Long Island and southeastern New England could see gusts of 45 to 65 mph.

Ted Friedli kayaks his way through a flooded section of Florence Avenue during a nor'easter in Long Branch, New Jersey, on Sept. 26, 2026. AP Photo/Noah K. Murray

Peak wind gusts for Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket could approach 60 to 65 miph on Friday night and Saturday, NWS meteorologist Matthew Belk said.

Inland residents will see wind gusts of about 50 to 55 mph, Belk said.

"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.



WBZ-TV weather graphic. CBS Boston

The early timing of the nor'easter in the season could lead to even more damaging effects. Because trees are still fully leafed, they will have more wind resistance, Belk said. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which, combined with the saturated ground caused by heavy rain, could cause power outages, leave debris on roads and lead to other property damage.

Strong winds could also push ocean waves over seawalls, creating flooding. Large waves and elevated water levels could also lead to beach erosion and sand dune breaches.

On Massachusetts' South Shore, the towns of Cohasset and Scituate were sitting right in the bullseye of the storm. While parts of the coastline are protected by seawalls, some of those seawalls are in the middle of repair projects or have seen those projects stall due to federal funding cuts.

"So the waves hit the seawall and they go straight up about 60, 70, 80 feet, and the wind hits it from the northeast and every wave ends up hitting the house," Kevin Gill, owner of an oceanfront Scituate home, told CBS News Boston on Thursday.

Waves pound the coast as the tide comes in during a Nor'Easter storm in Scituate, Massachusetts on September 26, 2026. Joseph Prezioso /AFP via Getty Images

Storm leads to event cancellations and travel disruptions

The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — both gearing up for the playoffs during the final weekend of the regular Major League Baseball season — had to shuffle the schedule for their three-game series. They played a double-header Friday in Boston to try to avoid the storm. Then MLB rescheduled their finale on Sunday to occur in Florida, at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays.

Ed Sheeran canceled his high-profile concerts Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Also canceled: an Ironman triathlon in New York and the three-day Oceans Calling Festival in Ocean City, Maryland, which had been promoted online as "a wave of music."

Farther south, a highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's Saturday wedding plans. The Virginia couple had made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported. A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music. Organizers invited anyone on the island to come celebrate with the couple Saturday afternoon.

In New York City, the Global Citizens Festival and All Things Go NYC were canceled ahead of the storm.

The nor'easter also caused hundreds of flight cancellations and delays. The flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 260 flight cancellations for Boston Logan International Airport as of early Saturday evening.

John Garrisi, left, and Gaige Graf move an outdoor table away from the shorefront during the early stages of a nor'easter storm, on Sept. 25, 2026, in Gloucester, Massachusetts. AP Photo/Robert F. Bukaty

State officials along the East Coast urged people to use caution. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but the storm will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as 20 feet.

"The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said early Saturday.

In Long Island, ferry owner Stephanie Sherman said she had paused operations between Patchogue and the barrier island of Fire Island.

"It's been a pretty wild storm," Sherman said. "But nothing that we haven't experienced in the past. These happen every so often."

World.title: Hurricane Polo is a strong Category 3 storm off Mexico. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Polo was downgraded to a Category 3 storm as its intensity fluctuated hundreds of miles off Mexico's southwestern coast on Saturday.

The storm still remains a major hurricane, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said in an update Saturday night, and it is expected to make landfall in Baja California on Monday. A hurricane warning is in effect for a stretch of northwestern Mexico and the southwestern U.S. from Punta Abreojos in Baja California Sur to Santa Fe, New Mexico.

The storm had maximum sustained winds of 120 mph. Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 40 mph from the center of the storm, while tropical storm force winds extended outward up to 160 mph. The storm was inching slowly northwest.

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Nolo strengthened into a hurricane as it moved past Hawaii's Big Island this weekend, bringing heavy rain to Hawaii's Big Island.

Maps show Hurricane Polo's projected path

Polo's core on Saturday was about 335 miles south-southwest of Cabo San Lucas at the tip of the Baja California peninsula. It was heading northwest at 10 mph.

The storm is expected to move north on Sunday. By Monday, Polo is forecast to turn northeast and make landfall in Baja California Sur and then move across northwestern mainland Mexico by Tuesday.

The State Department, citing forecast models, said the storm is expected to weaken to a Category 1 storm before making landfall. It will then continue northeast into southern Sonora, the State Department said. The hurricane center noted, however, that despite weakening, Polo is still expected to be a "strong hurricane" when it reaches Baja California Sur.

CBS News/Nikki Nolan

Polo could produce 4 to 8 inches of rain, and up to 10 inches in isolated areas, across parts of Baja California Sur, the hurricane center said, cautioning the rain "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain."

Along with the hurricane warning, both a hurricane watch and tropical storm warning were also in place for the west coast of Baja California Sur from Punta Eugenia to Punta Abreojos. A hurricane watch was in place for the east coast of Baja California Sur from Bahia San Juan Bautista to San Evaristo.

CBS News/Nikki Nolan

Polo-generated swells will affect the southwestern Mexican coast over the next couple of days, spreading north along the west-central coast and the Baja California peninsula through the weekend, the hurricane center said, warning that swells are "likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding."

Mexican leaders ordered evacuations, opened shelters and deployed military troops to areas that could be affected by the storm.

Classes were suspended at schools across the city of Acapulco, along the coast of Guerrero, its municipal government announced. Shelters across the state remained open, and officials said they were coordinating with local and national authorities to prepare for additional impacts of the hurricane.

Polo's extreme rapid intensification

Polo underwent what's called extreme rapid intensification, in which a storm's wind speeds increase by 58 mph or more over the course of 24 hours, between Sept. 21 and Sept. 22.

Its intensification was dramatic even by those standards, with winds that skyrocketed from 45 mph on the morning of Sept. 21 to 150 mph at around the same time the following day. The hurricane center described the storm's transformation as "truly remarkable."

Its maximum sustained winds climbed as high as 180 mph at one point, far exceeding the 157 mph threshold for Category 5, the strongest on the hurricane scale. By Saturday morning, the maximum sustained winds had lowered to near 160 miles per hour, with some higher gusts.

Polo's central pressure — an indicator of its strength and potential destructiveness — made it the second-strongest hurricane on record in the Eastern Pacific, behind 2015's Hurricane Patricia. The storm's wind speeds tied 2009's Hurricane Rick as the third-strongest on record for the region.

Unusually strong El Niño conditions this year have been amping up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific, with warmer waters, moist air and less wind shear enabling storm formation.

World.title: Hurricane Nolo weakens, but still brings heavy rain to Hawaii. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Nolo weakened slightly to a Category 1 storm Saturday as it began to move away from Hawaii, the National Hurricane Center said, but it was still expected to lash Hawaii's Big Island and Maui with heavy rains and winds through the weekend.

The storm was inching west late Saturday night local time at just 8 mph, the NHC said. It was forecast to remain well south of Hawaii's two big islands, although it was expected to strengthen into a major hurricane on Sunday and Monday before weakening next week. All watches and warnings for Hawaii had been canceled.

President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaii Gov. Josh Green said.

Map shows Hurricane Nolo's expected path

Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 90 mph, making it a Category 1 hurricane. This comes after it had strengthened Friday into a Category 2 storm with 105-mph winds. The hurricane center, however, said it would likely re-strengthen Sunday and become a major hurricane, which is defined as a Category 3 storm or stronger.

Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 35 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 150 miles.

The trajectory of Hurricane Nolo as it moves toward Hawaii. Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Nolo could bring up to 20 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island, forecasters said, and the island's western areas could see 1 to 2 inches of rain. For Maui, 4 to 8 inches is possible. The rest of Hawaii is likely to get 1 to 3 inches, with 5 at most, enough to trigger isolated flooding, forecasters said.

All state parks on the Big Island and on Maui will be closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.

The forecast wind speeds for Hurricane Nolo as it approaches Hawaii. Sept. 25, 2026. Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo, continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.

The Eastern Pacific tropical outlook as of Sept. 25, 2026. CBS News/Nikki Nolan

The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.

Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes, triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

World.title: FAA investigates software glitch in some Boeing 737 Max jets
World.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration is investigating a software glitch in some Boeing 737 Max jets that could prompt an automated flight guidance system to disengage during an aborted landing, commonly referred to as a go-around.

In rare circumstances where there is a missed approach — and where a pilot is using a precision approach with autopilot engaged and makes changes to their pre-programmed flight plan — an issue with the flight management computer could cause the plane's vertical navigation system, known as VNAV, to disengage and transition to a less sophisticated level of automated pitch control.

The VNAV is essentially designed to automatically maintain the pre-planned altitude at various waypoints along a flight path.

If this glitch occurs, however, pilots will need to take additional steps during their subsequent approach.

The scenario would typically occur in a low-altitude airport adjacent environment where pilots already have a high workload.

"How busy do you want your crew to be?" one airline source told CBS News about the glitch. "Are you introducing distractions at the worst possible moment?"

"Last month, we informed all 737 operators about a software issue where pilots may not have access to automated flight guidance during a specific landing scenario," a Boeing spokesperson told CBS News in a statement. "We shared information with operators that reinforced existing pilot procedures for safely handling such cases. Our engineers are working on a software update to permanently address the issue."

The Boeing spokesperson said that even if VNAV disengages, autopilot will continue to function, adding that all pilots are trained to safely land without VNAV.

In a bulletin sent to airlines late last month, Boeing told operators the glitch is not an immediate safety issue. It surfaced in versions 14 and 14.1 of the operating system for the Max's flight management computer.

"The FAA is aware of a potential issue in a software update for the flight computers on certain Boeing 737 MAX airplanes and is working closely with Boeing and the airlines," the FAA told CBS News in a statement. "The FAA will convene a Corrective Action Review Board (CARB) and will take immediate action if it identifies a safety concern."

Southwest Airlines and United Airlines have informed Boeing they will not accept delivery of new aircraft with that operating system, instead opting for a previous version.

Alaska Airlines, American Airlines, Southwest and United told CBS News none of their in-service 737 Max fleets use the software version in question.

CBS News has learned Boeing was first told of the issue by an airline in November 2024. The company reviewed it and determined in February 2025 that it was not a safety issue.

However, Boeing received what a source described as "additional information from operators" earlier this year that prompted the manufacturer to launch a formal safety review board. The board's findings were sent to the FAA this month and will be reviewed by CARB.

Boeing's initial bulletin told airlines a software fix would be ready sometime in 2028 and it would issue updated guidance about procedures for pilots to follow in November. The company is working to accelerate both of those efforts.

The FAA review could further delay the certification of the 737 Max 10, the fourth and largest variant of the Max. The Max 10 was thought to be days away from achieving FAA certification, but years behind schedule. The issue could also delay deliveries of the recently certified 737 Max 7. Nearly the entire order book for that aircraft is going to Southwest.

The Max is a cash cow for Boeing and is vital for its turnaround efforts. The plane has been the subject of two high-profile crashes in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people due to defective software, and it experienced a mid-flight door panel blowout on an Alaska Airlines flight in January 2024 that was blamed on manufacturing mistakes.

It is notable that several U.S. airlines appear to be taking a trust-but-verify approach to Boeing on the issue, having been stung by groundings and delays due to previous Boeing mistakes on the Max.

The Max 7 was certified with software version 14, while the Max 10 was using version 14.1 during its certification testing.

Southwest was set to start receiving Max 7 deliveries this fall. It is unclear if the airline will take delivery at this time, while Alaska Airlines is supposed to be the launch customer for the Max 10.

The software glitch was first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

CBS News has also reached out to Allegiant Air for comment, which also operates the 737 Max.

World.title: Russian foreign minister accuses Europe of blocking Ukraine peace talks
World.content:
Russia's foreign minister used his address at the United Nations General Assembly to accuse Europe of blocking efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine.

Both Moscow and Kyiv have stepped up attacks after the deadliest summer since 2022 — the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. On Saturday, Russian attacks killed four people across Ukraine, officials said, while Kyiv continued to target Russian oil refineries and industrial sites with long-range drones.

Efforts led by the U.S. have failed to produce a permanent ceasefire and peace deal, with President Trump saying on Saturday that he hoped Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy would "settle" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Europe of actively trying to block talks supported by the U.S. government.

Sergey Lavrov, Russia's foreign minister, speaks at a session of the U.N. General Assembly at the United Nations. Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images

"Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested," Lavrov said in a fiery speech to the U.N. General Assembly.

"The aims of the special military operation will be achieved, the threat to Russian security will be eliminated and peaceful life will come back. This will happen no matter the circumstances," he added, using Moscow's terminology for the conflict.

Before his speech, Lavrov met with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul – the first meeting between Moscow and Berlin's foreign ministers since before the war.

The talks took place as tensions between Berlin and Moscow intensified, Germany accusing Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport and each country ordering the closure of the other's consulate.

European countries, including Germany, have sounded the alarm in recent days over what they say are increased Russian sabotage activities on their soil.

"Russia's war targets the lives of millions of innocent people, the existence of the Ukrainian state and culture and the European peace order," Wadephul said in his own address to the assembly Saturday, urging Russia to negotiate toward ending the fighting.

Rescuers work at a site of a Russian drone strike on the central market of Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine, on Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. AP Photo/Kateryna Klochko

Mr. Trump commented on Saturday on his meeting with Zelenskyy at the U.N. General Assembly, saying that he hoped the Ukrainian leader would "settle" with Putin.

He said Saturday that Zelenskyy and Putin were "going along" and that "someday, hopefully in the not-too-distant future, maybe before the heavy winter, they'll make a deal."

"You know what I want him to do? Make a deal," Mr. Trump said, referring to Zelenskyy. "I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him."

Zelenskyy, who after the meeting on Tuesday said he trusted the White House could help end Russia's invasion of his country, said on Saturday that Russia is "escalating every single day."

"If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further," he wrote on social media.

World.title: Trump gave Xi Jinping a warm welcome. What did the talks accomplish?
World.content:
Trump gave Xi Jinping a warm welcome. What did the talks accomplish?

From the National Archives to the state dinner, President Trump and Xi Jinping looked comfortable together in Washington. Two former NPR China correspondents on what the visit did and didn't deliver.

Transcript

DEBBIE ELLIOTT, HOST:

President Xi of China loves to win. Donald Trump loves a winner. This week, the U.S. president hosted his Chinese counterpart for nearly two days of pageantry and ritual. But did either side make any real gains? China is arguably the most consequential and difficult geopolitical relationship that the U.S. has. So to unpack the visit, we have with us NPR White House correspondent Emily Feng and NPR's Rob Schmitz, both of whom have reported extensively on China.

And, Emily, before we get to the question of who got what, you were in the room with President Xi as he visited the National Archives here. What was that like?

EMILY FENG, BYLINE: What has struck me about the whole state visit is how congenial the nature of these events have been. They seemed very comfortable with one another. In public remarks in the past, they have emphasized their shared history between these two countries.

And for example, when the two leaders strolled around the National Archives, they looked at original copies of the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution. And Trump made this quip about China having 6,000 years of history, which, by the way, is longer even than the Chinese say they have. And Xi quipped back. He commended the U.S. on its, quote, "founding spirit" from 250 years ago.

ELLIOTT: And in terms of gains, Emily, the U.S. did extend a temporary trade truce. Why is that important?

FENG: So this trade truce that we're talking about is regarding rare earths, and this was a truce that was about to expire this November. And it had stopped China from cutting the U.S. off completely from rare earth elements, which China still dominates. Now, the U.S. and China have confirmed they've extended that by two months, so it expires in January, but this is far shorter than both sides were hoping for. And per my reporting, it was because mutual distrust has scuppered the possibility of a longer extension.

Now, despite the pageantry and the photo-ops in this Chinese state visit, the actual substance of what might come out of this visit is going to be about trade. We should see announcements soon on, say, joint tariff reductions on about $30 billion of goods on both sides. Trump also mentioned that Iran came up in talks with Xi Jinping, but he didn't give details.

And Iran matters in these talks because China is a big economic supporter of Iran, and it bought up most of Iran's oil exports in the past. There are still other issues that remain in this relationship that have not been resolved by this visit, where there's still a lot of daylight between the U.S. and China. And those involve, for example, artificial intelligence and Taiwan.

ELLIOTT: Now, Rob, you covered President Trump's first term from China. What's different now?

ROB SCHMITZ, BYLINE: Yeah, I remember, a month after Trump won the election in 2016, he was sort of getting congratulatory calls from world leaders. And one of those calls that he accepted was from Tsai Ing-wen, who was the president of Taiwan at that point. And at that time, this was sort of a very big deal because it broke with decades of diplomatic protocol. It broke with the One China policy. And China experts were sort of aghast at Trump's decision to take this call.

And at the time, Trump was quick to criticize China and Xi as well for taking part in America's economic decline at that point. Fast forward a decade, and now you've got Trump throwing this lavish welcome for Xi Jinping, showering him with praise. It's a very different world that we have now. China...

ELLIOTT: It's like a complete turnaround.

SCHMITZ: China is a much stronger country now, and it holds more cards when it comes to trade. You know, another interesting thing that I noticed as I've been watching coverage this week, both from here in the U.S. and Chinese coverage, is that, you know, typically when the U.S. president meets with the leader of China, the narrative coming from the media here in the U.S. is starkly different from that of China's state-run media. But this week, the images and video coming from both the U.S. media - and yes, we're getting less of it because of the White House ban on CNN and other outlets.

But the imagery from both the American media this week and the Chinese state-run media were, in many ways, very similar. Both sides showed an American president staging VIP treatment for his Chinese counterpart. And for people watching this in China, I think this is showing them that the world's biggest superpower and economy regards their country as an equal. And that's a powerful message to the people of China. And this comes despite a quite sluggish economy in China, where many people are beginning to really question whether their government is able to continue to promise real economic growth.

ELLIOTT: You know, part of - an important part of China's economy is artificial intelligence. There was a lot of expectation that somehow the leaders would talk about AI and come to some sort of agreement. Emily, what did the president say about this?

FENG: All Trump said was that AI came up in conversations, and AI is really important to the U.S. too. It's been a huge driver of American economic growth, not just in China. But there's differences in how Chinese and American leaders have been talking about AI and particularly regulation about AI.

So take Trump. He has said multiple times, including writing just hours before meeting with Xi Jinping, that he basically wants to leave AI the way it is, meaning no more regulation. Xi Jinping, by contrast, brought up AI first thing in his opening remarks in Washington, saying it should ultimately remain under human control. And the Chinese readout of the meeting with Trump urged the two countries to cooperate despite competition between their various companies in AI and to make sure AI, quote, "serves human progress."

And just to show how important AI and technology were - have become in the bilateral relationship, at the state dinner that Xi and Trump had on Thursday night, other than officials from both governments, many of the private citizens there were CEOs of major American AI and tech companies.

ELLIOTT: Oh, it was a who's who. Yeah.

FENG: Exactly. Meta, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI - and then sitting at the table with Xi Jinping and Trump - Nvidia's Jensen Huang, Elon Musk, the chipmaker AMD's Lisa Su and also Apple's Tim Cook.

ELLIOTT: Rob, to better understand Xi, I understand it's useful to listen to some of the terms that he loves to use - one of them, strategic stability. What is he trying to convey?

SCHMITZ: Yes, he uses a lot of these terms. He's fond of using a handful of phrases like this to promote the idea that China is rising and that the U.S. and the rest of the West is in a state of decline. He also likes to talk about Thucydides Trap, referring to the idea that when two big powers exist, they inevitably come to blows. And of course, Xi Jinping wants to avoid military conflict with the U.S., and he yearns for what he calls strategic stability, a state where the world's two superpowers can live in a type of harmony.

In essence, you know, the U.S. is both a rival but also an economic partner with China, and decoupling is virtually impossible at this stage. So perhaps it's in both countries' interest to acknowledge this and to move forward accordingly.

FENG: For Trump, he seemed to think that stepping out of the contours of superpower competition and taking a personal touch would impress Xi and influence the relationship. For example, the two leaders spent about 90 minutes in meetings on Thursday, but then they spent almost just as much time touring the White House South Lawn, where Trump showed Xi the new helipad he just built and the new Marine One helicopter.

And I'll note, Xi Jinping largely did not match Trump with this personal touch. He did wish people a happy mid-autumn festival at the state dinner. But in his public remarks, he chose to largely speak in sweeping historical terms and cast the U.S.-China relationship in terms of this grand historical context.

ELLIOTT: That's NPR's Emily Feng along with Rob Schmitz. Thank you both for bringing us your insights on the China-U.S. relationship.

SCHMITZ: Thanks, Debbie.

FENG: Thank you.

World.title: Trump calls Iranian plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz not 'acceptable'
World.content:
Trump calls Iranian plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz not 'acceptable'

toggle caption Aaron Schwartz/Getty Images North America

President Trump said on Saturday that he was rejecting an Iranian plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump said the deal "would not be acceptable," speaking to reporters as he was departing the White House, without giving further explanation.

"I like making a deal too," he said. "But, I'm not — that deal would not be acceptable."

"They want to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they're losing so badly," Trump added.

Iran made the proposal, which also called for resuming negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, at the United Nations General Assembly meetings in New York this week.

Sponsor Message

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters on Friday that Iran conveyed to the U.S. through Qatar a "concrete seven-day plan" to reopen the strait.

Iran initially closed the strait after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. The repeated closures have caused major disruptions to the world's oil supply.

"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi said on Friday. "The choice now rests with the United States."

The Iranian proposal is similar to a "memorandum of understanding" agreed upon by the U.S. and Iran back in June. It would have temporarily ended fighting and restarted ceasefire talks.

The MoU gave Iran relief from a U.S. naval blockade. The U.S. eased sanctions and freed up frozen Iranian assets. In return, Iran promised not to seek a nuclear weapon and said it would reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

The June agreement collapsed after disputes over the memo's vague wording, including language related to who would control the strait. The U.S. and Iran resumed strikes soon after.

"The actions that the United States should take are not new," Araghchi said. "They are all already in the MoU. They are already under the commitments of the United States. So we don't see any difficulty to implement them."

Sponsor Message

In a prerecorded interview with CBS set to air Sunday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will abide by its commitments and said the U.S. needs to show "that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration."

"If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before," Pezeshkian said to CBS. "Because right now, it's the United States that has blocked our way, and naturally, Iran has also blocked the way from its side. These are things that both sides need to open up first; then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand."

Pezeshkian said if the U.S. accepts the Iranian proposal on reopening the strait and resuming nuclear negotiations, Iran would allow U.N. nuclear inspectors to enter the country.

NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi and Emily Feng contributed reporting.

World.title: OpenAI says its models engaged with US government websites in misbehavior disclosure
World.content:
OpenAI says its models engaged with US government websites in misbehavior disclosure

toggle caption Michael Dwyer/AP

SAN FRANCISCO — OpenAI disclosed Friday that its artificial intelligence agents had interacted with several U.S. government websites in unexpected ways, discovered as part of an ongoing review into the company's models' unanticipated behavior.

The AI giant's models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as U.S. Census Bureau data, the company revealed Friday. OpenAI did not find any use of SEC credentials, access to accounts or nonpublic information, changes to SEC data or systems, or evidence of a compromise or vulnerability, the company said.

The disclosure comes at a time of heightened global concerns about AI systems escaping human control and hacking into external websites, as well as industry calls for a slowdown on AI development, which OpenAI has said it supports.

Sponsor Message

OpenAI spokesperson Liz Bourgeois said in a statement that the lab is continuing to conduct a review of "misaligned model activity" — meaning when AI systems behave in undesired ways — and is notifying organizations when it identifies potential impacts to their systems.

OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said on social media Friday that there is an "extensive and ongoing review related to our agents' use of internet access during training and evaluation."

AI evaluator and research lab Transluce said Friday that through an independent investigation it also found that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted a rudimentary hack on a Department of Education website for the department's civil rights office, which did not succeed.

The Department of Education's "system operations reviews" found "no evidence of any impact to our website or databases," a department spokesperson said Friday.

A Transluce spokesperson said as part of its investigation, it came across data on the open web that revealed fresh details about some previously identified OpenAI agents' activities on U.S. government websites and brought it to OpenAI's attention.

Transluce found "additional rogue activity, some of which is not clearly attributable to OpenAI," targeting other government agencies, including the Justice Department and the Commerce Department, as well as some state government websites in California, Maryland, Illinois, Texas and New York. The models were "using sites in unintended ways and sometimes violating explicit usage policies," Transluce said in a statement.

OpenAI said it is reviewing Transluce's report.

If OpenAI notifies organizations it identifies as being impacted by unexpected model behavior, that does not mean there was a security incident, the company said, and could identify a design issue or security weakness that impacted organizations want to address.

Sponsor Message

Most of the activity OpenAI said it has reviewed so far has involved routine research tasks where agents accessed public web content to answer questions, including government websites seen as authoritative sources of public information.

Several companies have disclosed incidents in recent months when they say their models have behaved unpredictably or hacked into other organizations' websites or systems. OpenAI disclosed in July that two of its most capable AI models were responsible for the cyberattack targeting AI startup Hugging Face.

Altman said in his social media post Friday that the Hugging Face incident "is still the most severe event we've seen."

That incident stirred widespread panic in the industry and beyond about AI models going rogue, and several competing AI labs made similar disclosures in the days and weeks that followed. OpenAI most recently shared six reports of "unexpected or concerning" behavior in AI models and introduced a framework for tracking, probing and disclosing instances of what it called misalignment.

World.title: OPINION: Trump's U.N. speech, a stark contrast with past presidents
World.content:
OPINION: Trump's U.N. speech, a stark contrast with past presidents

toggle caption Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

The world took note when President Trump told the United Nations General Assembly this week that he had asked himself whether to make a deal with Iran - or...

"Do I annihilate the Islamic Republic…

"Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?"

Those words seem especially forbidding from a leader who can command armies to march and missiles to fly.

On August 6, 1945, President Harry Truman told the world the United States had dropped the first atomic bomb, on Hiroshima, Japan. It instantly killed an estimated 70,000 people. Some 40,000 more died days later in Nagasaki, and tens of thousands more from radiation illnesses in the days, weeks, months and years thereafter.

Sponsor Message

In his speech announcing the nuclear attack on Hiroshima, President Truman called it "a harnessing of the basic power of the universe," and added cautions about "protecting the world from the danger of sudden destruction."

Nuclear weapons have not been used in war since. And Truman's successors have been pointedly measured when they talk about them. As President Ronald Reagan put it, "a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought."

When President John F. Kennedy ordered US ships to blockade Cuba to prevent the Soviet Union from installing nuclear missiles in 1962, he told Americans, "We will not prematurely or unnecessarily risk the costs of worldwide nuclear war in which even the fruits of victory would be ashes in our mouth."

In 1974, President Gerald Ford told the U.N. General Assembly, "A very stark reality has tempered America's actions for decades and must now temper the actions of all nations. Prevention of full-scale warfare in the nuclear age has become everybody's responsibility. Today's regional conflict must not become tomorrow's world disaster."

And in 2017, President Obama visited the Peace Park that now stands in Hiroshima and said, "Among those nations like my own that hold nuclear stockpiles, we must have the courage to escape the logic of fear and pursue a world without them."

Sponsor Message

All strong words from presidents sworn to protect the United States. So strong and measured, they might have felt it wasn't necessary to add threats of annihilation, and "no chance of survival…"

World.title: Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend
World.content:
Windy weddings and rocky cruises: How East Coasters are braving the nor'easter this weekend

toggle caption Robert F. Bukaty/AP

Talia Manno opened her door on Saturday morning to waves lapping halfway up the front steps to her Atlantic City, N.J., home.

"It got up to my fifth step," Manno said. "I was really freaking out."

Manno, a lifelong resident, said the last time water came that high was during Hurricane Sandy.

"Even if you live here and you see high tide and flooding, that was really scary and it happened so fast," she said.

Sponsor Message

Manno is among tens of millions of people from the mid-Atlantic through the coast of Maine who are in the path of a powerful and rare September nor'easter that is bringing coastal flooding, heavy rain and high winds this weekend.

Nearly 80,000 people were without power across New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and Massachusetts, as of Saturday evening, according to the PowerOutage.com map. The storm is expected to continue hitting the Jersey Shore, New York City, and Eastern Massachusetts into Sunday, according to NWS.

Videos posted on social media Saturday showed streets inundated with water in New Jersey, and massive waves hitting the coast. In New York City, people were seen kayaking in the streets. New Jersey and New York declared states of emergency in counties across the two states, including in New York City.

Francis Tarasiewicz, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Massachusetts, said wind gusts along the coast could reach up to 60 miles per hour this weekend. This nor'easter comes earlier than the typical October through May storm season, he said, and will last longer than normal.

toggle caption Robert F. Bukat/AP

"Many nor'easters affect the area over the course of about a day," he said. "It's a quick punch of strong winds, in many cases, heavy snow or rain." But, Tarasiewicz said, "with this one, we're looking at about a 48-hour period of winds greater than 35 to 40 miles per hour across the area."

Sponsor Message

The nor'easter is also making travel difficult. More than 1,000 flights were canceled Saturday with thousands more delayed, according to data from FlightAware. Ferry services on Cape Cod and in Rhode Island were disrupted, and Amtrak canceled several trains due to the weather and downed wires.

Off the coast of New York, the strong winds made for a rough cruise ride for Jessica Lisboa. She brought green apples, ginger ale and an acupressure anti-nausea bracelet to prepare for the Bermuda-bound cruise.

"Let me not sugarcoat it. Was it wild? Yeah, sure. It was a little wild," Lisboa said. "It felt honestly like a roller coaster." Still, she considered it a worthwhile adventure.

The nor'easter also took out a number of events planned for the weekend. Oceans Calling, one of Maryland's biggest music festivals, was canceled on Friday. An AC/DC concert in New Jersey was rescheduled. The Boston Red Sox announced they would move their game against the Chicago Cubs.

Some East Coasters found a way to adapt.

When Olga Ostrovetsky picked a date in September for her small outdoor wedding, she envisioned a beautiful, fall day.

But as she got ready to tie the knot in Wallkill, N.Y., she said, "It's very, very windy."

At first bummed, she's now finding the positives in the disruption.

"It's kind of fitting, to be honest, because my fiancé and I met and it was a torrential downpour," she said. "We met on a day like this, and we're also getting married on a day like this," she said.

As for Manno, the Atlantic City resident, is planning to spend Saturday night with family away from the coast. After this nor'easter, she said she doesn't know how much longer she'll live in the area.

"As the years pass, it seems like it's just getting more and more flooding," she said. "It's crazy."

World.title: Why this island paradise has the world's fastest-growing HIV epidemic
World.content:
Why this island paradise has the world's fastest-growing HIV epidemic

toggle caption Ian Cheibub for NPR

Best known as a tropical paradise and honeymoon destination, the island nation of Fiji now has the unfortunate distinction of facing two intertwined epidemics: HIV and addiction to crystal meth.

With HIV cases rising by 12-fold between 2010 and 2025, in mid-September, Fiji's government declared a national emergency. Estimates are that there are upward of 9,000 cases; the country's health minister has announced that 1 in 60 adults are now living with HIV.

At the July AIDS 2026 conference in Rio, Jason Mitchell, a public health specialist leading Fiji's HIV response, described it as the fastest-growing HIV epidemic in the world, noting that two-thirds of cases are in those ages 20-34. "Our young, active, productive population is currently being infected with HIV, and unless we find solutions quickly, this will continue to get worse," he says.

Sponsor Message

A key cause is another parallel epidemic — the rampant use of crystal meth among the nation's youth, who often inject it. That has led to transmission through shared needles.

"Two of my best friends passed away," says Mark Lal, a 25-year-old HIV activist from Fiji's capital of Suva. "The majority of my friends, they got HIV through crystal meth."

The meth factor

Crystal meth has long been available to some degree within Fiji — the islands are a known transit hub for the drug between South America and the eventual destinations of Australia and New Zealand. But since COVID, meth use has soared, something Fiji's HIV experts attribute to the lethal combination of rising unemployment and ever more accessible drugs.

"COVID was a difficult time for Fijians," says Sailosi Soqo, a doctor working on the national HIV response team. "Most lost their jobs, got less hours or were stuck at home. At the same time, we suspect that the travel restrictions, along with increased border security, decreased the movement of narcotics onto their target countries. Drugs that would otherwise have moved on stayed in Fiji, seeding this domestic market which didn't really exist before."

Soqo suggests that spiraling unemployment, combined with worsening mental health due to the impacts of lockdown, led to more young Fijians turning to meth, even preteens.

Sponsor Message

"The communities I work with report children as young as 9 using injectable drugs," he says.

According to Dashika Balak, a doctor who leads Fiji's national HIV treatment, care and support efforts, the risk of HIV transmission has also been exacerbated by a nationwide shift from smoking meth to injecting it. This includes the so-called "bluetoothing" or "hotspotting" practice where one person injects the drug and then another person injects their blood.

Bluetoothing is known to occur in settings of extreme poverty as a cheaper way of getting high. But Mitchell believes that its popularity in Fiji is partially because sharing all manner of things is a part of national culture — both alcohol and the ceremonial drink kava are consumed via a communal glass or bowl — and partially due to a scarcity of needles. Soqo says that law enforcement in Fiji has cracked down on needle availability in an attempt to curb meth use, something that he believes has inadvertently encouraged bluetoothing.

Unfortunately, bluetoothing has fueled the spread of HIV. Reports suggest that on average, one infected person in Fiji will pass the virus on to 10 others. "You add the existing culture in Fiji of sharing things, plus the limited access to clean injecting equipment, and you get the perfect storm for HIV transmission," says Soqo.

Fiji's HIV epidemic is also spreading in other ways, including risky sexual practices. "What we do know is that sexual intercourse, as a transmission route, made up roughly 50% of the new HIV cases for 2025," says Soqo.

Balak says that low condom use is encouraging the spread of HIV. A 2021 survey found that among 15- to 49-year-olds with multiple sexual partners in the past year, only 24% of men and 9% of women used a condom the last time they had sex. Lal can attest to this — having contracted HIV himself in the summer of 2024 through unprotected sex with a male partner. "You let your guard down once, and boom, it happens," he says.

Sponsor Message

Preventing a permanent epidemic

The surge in cases has led to an influx of foreign aid to support new HIV testing, prevention and treatment programs. Concerned about rising rates of infections and the potential for the epidemic to spread more widely through the Pacific, the Australian government announced a new $48 million funding package in August. According to a statement to NPR, the government is committed to supporting Fiji's HIV response to prevent new infections, improve early diagnosis and expand access to treatment.

One of the first priorities for Australian organizations working with Fiji is to make HIV testing available at all antenatal clinics. In 2025, 59 babies were born with HIV.

"We're trying to get a reliable rollout of these tests so that every single pregnant woman anywhere in the country will be tested for HIV," says Storm Holwill, a public health physician working at Melbourne's Peter Doherty Institute for Infection and Immunity.

Anyone who is HIV positive would then be placed on viral-suppressing medications known as antiretrovirals to limit the chances of HIV being passed on in utero.

Blocking new infections on a wider scale is far more challenging. Meth use is most prevalent in some of Fiji's poorest and most vulnerable populations, many of whom have no fixed address. This makes it difficult for medical professionals to test and prescribe treatments.

Balak explains that while anywhere between 9,100 and 12,000 people in Fiji are thought to have HIV, only 5,676 of these cases have been officially diagnosed. Even fewer are regularly taking antiretrovirals to keep their condition under control.

"Some stop treatment, and some cannot be reached because their contact details are incomplete," she says.

This means that while Australia's aid is providing Fiji with plentiful access to medications such as PrEP pills to block HIV infections, getting these drugs to the right people is not straightforward.

toggle caption Ian Cheibub for NPR

"We've just introduced PrEP about two months back," says Mitchell. "The uptake has been very slow, while at the same time, antiretroviral treatment is also freely available, but it's currently sitting on shelves."

Sponsor Message

Lal argues that one of the biggest problems is a lack of awareness. He says many people in Fiji have never heard of these medications. Even for those who have, obtaining them requires a lengthy journey to one of three dedicated clinical centers, either in the cities of Suva and Lautoka or the town of Labasa.

With Fiji's population spread across more than 100 islands, Lal says that such a journey likely deters many people from seeking care. "If they know the medications are far away, they won't even want to access them," he says. "In a country like ours where religion is big, people would — rather than go — pray and believe that God will heal them."

Mobile clinics and clean needles

To improve access to PrEP and antiretrovirals, Balak and her colleagues have started creating dedicated HIV response teams in 21 locations across the country. "They will soon be able to order their own antiretrovirals [and] dispense and fully manage their patients on their own," she says.

To track down more people living with HIV, the team is also recruiting and training peer support workers — including some existing meth users who are HIV positive. Balak says she hopes that this could be a way to connect more of the people at most risk of contracting HIV with medical teams.

Methamphetamine use remains a tense issue, and some of the proposed schemes to address the spread of HIV have clashed with law enforcement.

To break the chains of infections stemming from contaminated needles, Soqo has proposed supplying thousands of sterile needles and syringes to communities of methamphetamine users. However, Soqo says the government is blocking the plan. "The director prosecutor has told us, 'If you hand these out, we'll arrest you, and we'll charge you for aiding and abetting,'" he says. "As a result, I now have a warehouse full of needles and syringes, just collecting dust." Fiji's government did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

Sponsor Message

However, there is more optimism that other approaches could make a significant difference. Fiji is set to receive supplies of the drug lenacapavir, an injectable form of PrEP that provides those at risk of infection due to sexual behavior or drug use near 100% protection from HIV. Because this new preventive drug only needs to be administered twice yearly, Mitchell believes it will be easier to convince people to use it compared with daily pills.

To prevent women from contracting HIV from their partners while pregnant, antenatal clinics hope to start offering vaginal rings, which slowly release a protective antiretroviral drug over the course of a month.

Such innovations are badly needed. Projections suggest that if the epidemic continues at its current pace, 25,000 people in Fiji will be living with HIV by 2029, figures that Soqo says would push Fiji's fragile health system to the brink of collapse.

"Time is not on our side," says Soqo. "With the current numbers, we're already struggling. All our main hospitals are overcrowded and have chronic issues with staffing shortages. Our tuberculosis hospitals and primary healthcare facilities are telling us they're seeing an increase in advanced HIV cases and are overwhelmed. Imagine what things will be like in three years' time. There is an urgent need for more action now."

David Cox is a freelance health journalist who has written for publications around the world, including NPR, The New York Times, Wired and The Guardian. He has a Ph.D. in neuroscience.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions
World.content:
The AI safety debate is confusing. Here's our guide to the different factions

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images/Collage by Emily Bogle/NPR

The debate over the potential benefits and safety risks of accelerating artificial intelligence development reached a crescendo this month, as supporters and critics of the technology clashed over warnings that increasingly powerful AI could pose existential risks to humanity.

On September 8, Jacob Coxon, a researcher-turned-whistleblower, publicly resigned from major AI firm Anthropic after a previous stint at OpenAI, accusing the companies of "racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives."

Coxon's claims supercharged an ongoing debate over the potential damage AI could wreak on society and prompted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and other AI CEOs to call for a slowdown in AI development.

Over the past two months, companies including OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed multiple incidents in which their AI agents accessed the internet when they weren't supposed to and carried out unapproved activities. In OpenAI's case, swarms of agents worked together to hack the open-source software platform Hugging Face and OpenAI itself, without alerting humans.

Sponsor Message
