Limp Bizkit perform at FNB Stadium in Johannesburg on Sunday 13 December 2026, their first concert in South Africa. The American band was booked to tour the country in 2004, but those shows were cancelled.

Limp Bizkit Johannesburg 2026: FNB Stadium on Sunday 13 December

Limp Bizkit play FNB Stadium in Johannesburg on Sunday 13 December 2026, in what is their first South African concert. Big Concerts, the promoter, announced the date in June 2026 and opened general sales on 12 June.

The stadium sits in Nasrec, on the southern rim of Johannesburg and next to Soweto, and holds 94,736 people. Big Concerts gives doors at 4 p.m. Johannesburg time, with the show starting at 6.25 p.m.

Who Opens: Ecca Vandal and Jack Parow

Two support acts are billed for the evening, one Australian and one South African. Ecca Vandal was born in South Africa, lives in Melbourne, and mixes punk rock, hip hop and electronic music.

Jack Parow raps in Afrikaans and has shared stages with Eminem, Snoop Dogg and The Prodigy, The Citizen reported in June. Stage times for the two openers had not been published when this article was written.

What Tickets Cost at FNB Stadium

Seated tickets run from R1,095 to R2,426, about 67 to 149 US dollars at the exchange rate of 26 September 2026. The two middle tiers sit at R1,255 and R1,500, roughly 77 and 92 US dollars, according to the site Hypertext.

An aisle seat carries a surcharge of R100, about six US dollars, on top of the face price. The park and ride bus service costs R300 to R400 a person, between 18 and 25 US dollars.

The Calabash and Its Concert History

FNB Stadium opened in 1989, was rebuilt for the 2010 World Cup, and is known locally as the Calabash for its shape. It hosted the 2010 final, and it is where Nelson Mandela spoke first after leaving prison in 1990.

The City of Johannesburg owns the ground and Stadium Management South Africa runs it, including the concert calendar. U2, Coldplay and Ed Sheeran have all played there, so a rock booking of this size is familiar ground.

Soweto in Johannesburg, with FNB Stadium standing on the township’s northern edge (Photo: SuSanA Secretariat, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Twenty-Two Years After a Cancelled Tour

Limp Bizkit were booked to tour South Africa in 2004, but those shows were cancelled and never rescheduled. The business news site Bizcommunity noted that gap when the December date was announced in June.

South African stadium touring moves in long cycles, tied to the rand, to airfares and to what a promoter can carry. A band can be popular in the country for years before the arithmetic of a stadium booking works.

Two Stadium Nights in a Row at Nasrec

Big Concerts has also booked the rapper J Cole into FNB Stadium on Saturday 12 December 2026, the night before. Two stadium concerts on consecutive nights is unusual for Johannesburg, and it concentrates demand for hotels and transport.

Visitors travelling in for one show can reach the other without a second trip, which is part of the promoter’s logic. It also means the Nasrec area will be busy across the whole weekend, not only on the Sunday.

Practical Notes for Foreign Residents

The concert is in English, and no Afrikaans is needed to follow the evening, although Jack Parow raps in that language. Tickets are sold in rand through Ticketmaster South Africa and Big Concerts, which also ran a Mastercard presale.

Big Concerts sells a park and ride bus service, the simplest route to Nasrec for anyone without a car. Children aged three and over need their own ticket and ear protection, a rule the promoter states on the event page.

What Is Not Yet Published

Big Concerts does not print a price table for the standing zones, so the front zone and general admission figures stay unlisted. Stage times for Ecca Vandal and Jack Parow, and the length of the main set, have not been announced either.

The seated prices quoted here are the lowest figure in each block, and individual seats inside a block cost more. Any change to the timings or the entry rules before December would appear on the promoter’s own event page first.

The Festival Presidente de Música Latina returns to Santo Domingo, in the Dominican Republic, on Friday 11 and Saturday 12 December 2026. It is the first edition since 2017.

Festival Presidente Santo Domingo 2026: Two Nights at the Estadio Olímpico Félix Sánchez

The Festival Presidente de Música Latina runs on Friday 11 and Saturday 12 December 2026. Dominican newspapers place the event at the Estadio Olímpico Félix Sánchez, the athletics stadium inside the Centro Olímpico complex.

Cervecería Nacional Dominicana, the brewer behind Presidente beer, owns the festival, and SD Concerts produces it. This edition runs over two nights rather than the three the festival used in earlier years.

Who Plays on Friday 11 December

The official ticket site lists eleven acts for Friday 11 December. Juan Luis Guerra heads the night, with the Scottish producer Calvin Harris, the Colombian singer Beéle and the Venezuelan Danny Ocean.

Milly Quezada, called the queen of merengue in the Dominican press, also plays Friday, alongside the salsa band Chiquito Team Band. The rest of the Friday bill is Elena Rose, Fineta Records, Leo RD, La Mas Doll and Arlene MC.

Who Plays on Saturday 12 December

Saturday 12 December carries ten names on the official line-up. Don Omar, the Puerto Rican reggaeton singer, was the first artist the brewer confirmed, in July 2026.

Katy Perry plays the Dominican Republic for the first time on that night, according to her own announcement. The rest of Saturday is Omar Courtz, Aria Vega, Dalvin La Melodía, Yiyo Sarante, Karlo, Fineta Records, Lápiz Conciente and Donaty.

What the Tickets Cost

Tuboleta sells the tickets through festivalpresidente.tuboleta.com.do, the festival’s own page on the Dominican platform. One tier has already gone: the Grada D1, C1, A1 and B1 blocks at RD$3,900 a day, about 66 US dollars.

The cheapest tier still on sale is Gradas, the general stands, at RD$7,900 a day, about 133 US dollars. Field standing, called Terreno, costs RD$9,500 and Terreno VIP costs RD$12,500, about 160 and 210 US dollars.

The Zona Colonial in Santo Domingo, a taxi ride from the Centro Olímpico complex where the festival is staged (Photo: Максим Улитин, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Nine Years Between Editions

Cervecería Nacional Dominicana created the festival in 1995 to reward the buyers of its beer. It ran roughly every two years for two decades, then stopped after the 2017 edition.

The nine-year gap is the longest pause in the festival’s history, and the 2026 return is shorter than the old three-day format. A change in Dominican beer taxes also stopped the 2007 edition, so interruptions are not new here.

Where the Festival Sits on the Regional Map

The line-up mixes Dominican merengue and bachata with Puerto Rican reggaeton, Colombian and Venezuelan pop, and two acts from outside Latin music. Calvin Harris and Katy Perry are those two names, and the brewer announced Harris last.

Calvin Harris last played the Dominican Republic in 2012, and Katy Perry has never performed there before. Both festival dates fall on a weekend, which suits travellers coming in from Santiago, Punta Cana or abroad.

Practical Notes for Foreign Residents

The Estadio Olímpico Félix Sánchez stands inside the Centro Olímpico complex in the Distrito Nacional, the central district of Santo Domingo. That is a taxi or ride-app trip from the Zona Colonial, the old quarter where most short-term visitors stay.

Tickets arrive by email as a QR code, and the festival may ask for an identity document at the entrance. Tuboleta answers in Spanish on weekdays, and the listed ticket prices already include the service charge.

What Has Not Been Published

Several practical details were still missing when this article was filed. The festival’s own ticket pages do not name the venue, and neither gate nor stage times appear there.

The minimum age, the accessibility arrangements and the list of permitted items also remain unpublished. The organisers say those details will follow through their official channels, which usually happens in the final weeks before a show.

Omar Courtz Panama 2026: One Night at the Estadio Emilio Royo

Omar Courtz plays Panama City on Thursday 26 November 2026. The concert is a single night at the Estadio Emilio Royo, on the eastern side of the capital.

The date belongs to the singer’s Por Si Mañana No Estoy tour. Panatickets lists a 9 p.m. start in Panama City time and a scheduled end two and a half hours later.

What the Six Ticket Tiers Cost

Panatickets published six price tiers for the night, all of them quoted in US dollars. Standing on the field costs 25 US dollars, the back stand 40 US dollars and the side stands 65 US dollars.

The floor and premium places rise from there in even steps. Gold costs 100 US dollars, Platinum 125 US dollars and VIP 170 US dollars, a spread of 145 dollars.

Which Sections Have Already Gone

Four of the six tiers were marked sold out when the listing was checked on 26 September 2026. Those four are the standing field, the back stand, the side stands and the Platinum area.

Two tiers remained open on that date. Gold showed 102 places and VIP showed 320, which puts the cheapest remaining ticket at 100 US dollars, four times the standing price.

A 3,200-Seat Ground Built for American Football

The Estadio Emilio Royo seats about 3,200 people for sport. It opened in February 2020 as the first ground in Panama built for American football, at a reported cost near 7.5 million US dollars.

The stadium stands inside the Irving Saladino sports complex in Panama City and is run by the national sports institute. A concert that opens the field to standing holds more than the seated figure, though no capacity was published for this night.

Casco Viejo in Panama City; the Estadio Emilio Royo stands on the eastern side of the capital (Photo: Ivo Kruusamägi, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Panama’s Long Relationship With the Genre

Panama is not a side stop for this music. Spanish-language reggae took shape here in the late 1980s, carried by singers such as El General and Nando Boom, and it spread outward.

That history still shapes the touring map. Puerto Rican artists have treated Panama as a regular stop for decades, and Courtz played the Amador Convention Center in October 2025.

Paying in Panama: Balboas, Dollars and Cards

Panama uses the balboa, fixed at one balboa to one US dollar, and US notes circulate as the everyday cash. Prices are therefore quoted in dollars and no currency conversion is needed.

Panatickets takes Visa and Mastercard, the two networks most widely issued abroad. Cardholders of Caja de Ahorros, a state savings bank, can split purchases from 100 dollars into six instalments for a 10 dollar charge.

What Has Not Been Published

Several details were still missing from the listing on 26 September 2026. No support act was named, and no separate doors time was given ahead of the 9 p.m. start.

The promoter field on the vendor page was left empty. It is also unstated whether any sold-out tier will reopen if the stage layout changes.

How the Date Looks From Here

The picture two months out is a small ground with its cheaper tiers already gone. That pattern points to steady selling since the sale opened in late August, rather than a single rush.

Readers still choosing between Gold and VIP have time before the night itself. The stadium sits off Calle 116 Este in eastern Panama City, and a taxi or ride app reaches it most easily.

Karol G Costa Rica 2026: Two Nights at the Estadio Nacional

Karol G performs at the Estadio Nacional in San José on Friday 27 November and Saturday 28 November 2026. Both shows belong to her Viajando Por El Mundo Tropitour, the tour built around the album Tropicoqueta.

The promoter Move Concerts booked both dates, and the official seller is the Costa Rican platform eticket.cr. The venue sits in the La Sabana area of San José, west of the city centre.

The First Night Sold Out, the Second Did Not

Tickets for 27 November went on sale in May 2026 and sold out within days. Move Concerts responded by adding the Saturday date, 28 November, at the same venue.

As of 26 September 2026 the second night still had tickets listed on eticket.cr. The first night is listed as sold out, and no official resale channel had been announced at the time of writing.

What the Tickets Cost

Prices run from ₡33,400 for the Gradería Sur bleachers to ₡170,700 for the 200 Copas pits, about 74 to 376 US dollars. Both figures include service charges and tax, so the listed price is the price paid.

Between them sit the Gramilla standing area at ₡39,500 and the shaded side stands at ₡45,600, roughly 87 and 101 US dollars. The Tropicoqueta zone costs ₡73,500, about 162 US dollars.

Where Costa Rica Sits in the Tour

The Estadio Nacional holds about 35,000 people, which makes San José a modest stop by stadium standards. Two nights there doubles the capacity the country can offer a touring act.

Central America is usually skipped on Latin American stadium runs, which concentrate on Mexico, Colombia, Chile and Argentina. A two-night stand in San José is unusual for a stadium tour, and this run is the only Central American stop announced.

The Teatro Nacional in central San José, east of the La Sabana park where the Estadio Nacional stands (Photo: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada, CC BY-SA 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Venue and How to Reach It

The Estadio Nacional stands inside Parque La Sabana, on the western edge of central San José. Buses from the Paseo Colón run past the park, and ride apps reach the gates on ordinary nights.

Traffic around La Sabana is heavy before large events, so walking in from Paseo Colón is often faster. The stadium opened in 2011 and is the largest in Costa Rica, so the roads around it fill early.

Practical Notes for Foreign Residents

Tickets are sold in colones through eticket.cr, which also lists authorised physical sales points across the country. The checkout runs in Spanish, so readers still learning the language should allow extra time.

The vendor restricts the 200 Copas, Tropicoqueta and standing pitch zones to people aged 18 and over. Seated areas admit visitors from age 12 when a responsible adult comes with them.

What Is Not Yet Known

Neither the promoter nor the venue had published a doors-open time for the second night at the time of writing. Reports in May listed 8 p.m. San José time for 28 November, while the vendor lists 7 p.m. for both dates.

No support act has been named for either night, and no set list has been released. Whether any 27 November tickets return through an official channel had not been stated when this article was filed.

The Two Months Ahead

Just over two months separate this report from the first night at the Estadio Nacional. Availability for 28 November can change without an announcement, and the vendor page carries the current position.

Costa Rica rarely hosts two stadium concerts by the same artist in one weekend. The November dates will therefore give promoters a clearer reading of what the country can fill.

Martin Garrix Guatemala 2026: Explanada 5 on 13 November

Martin Garrix plays Guatemala City on Friday 13 November 2026, at the open-air venue Explanada 5. The ticket seller eticket gives the start as 8 p.m. Guatemala time, and lists the concert as scheduled.

The artist’s own website carries the date and points buyers to eticket, the Guatemalan seller handling the show. Show Business, a Guatemalan promoter, is named as the organiser on the vendor’s event page.

What the Tickets Cost

The vendor sells the show in three tiers, and all three were listed as available when this article was filed. Dancefloor costs Q790, about 103 US dollars, and the VIP tier costs Q1,110, roughly 145 US dollars.

The Lounge tier is the highest at Q1,740, about 228 US dollars at the exchange rate of late September. eticket states that its service charge is already included in each price, so the figure shown is the figure paid.

Who Martin Garrix Is

Martin Garrix is a Dutch DJ and producer who broke through in 2013 with the track Animals. His later songs include In the Name of Love with Bebe Rexha and Scared to Be Lonely with Dua Lipa.

The magazine DJ Mag has ranked him first in its annual readers poll five times, the Guatemalan site ConciertosGT notes. That standing explains why one date in Guatemala City draws attention beyond the country’s own dance scene.

Seven Years Since the Last Guatemala Date

Garrix last performed in Guatemala in April 2019, at the Forum Majadas in Guatemala City. Seven years separate that night from this one, a long gap for an artist who tours through most of the year.

In those seven years Explanada 5 became one of the capital’s main sites for large shows. The Guatemalan listings service Guatemala.com describes it as a leading destination for major musical performances.

Explanada 5 and Zona 5

Zona 5 lies close to the city centre, and most visitors reach it by taxi or by a ride-hailing app. Neither the venue nor the vendor has published a capacity figure or a parking plan for this date.

Central America draws fewer international touring dates than the larger South American markets, because its audiences are smaller. A Guatemala City booking therefore says something about how promoters now read demand in the country.

Touring moves in cycles, and a market skipped for several years can return once local promoters show steady sales. The gap since 2019 is the clearest measure of that cycle in the Guatemalan case.

Practical Notes for Foreign Residents

Tickets are sold in quetzales, and eticket also runs physical points of sale across Guatemala City. Readers without a Guatemalan card should check which payment methods the vendor accepts well before the date.

Photo identification is worth carrying, because door staff at large venues in the capital often check it. No Spanish is needed for a set without dialogue, although signage and staff at the venue work in Spanish.

What Is Still Open

Set lengths on tours of this kind are rarely announced in advance, and the vendor published no running order. All three tiers remained on sale in late September, which leaves buyers several weeks before the November date.

World.title: Healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago for Expats: Hospitals, Insurance and Costs
World.content:
GUIDES · TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

Key Facts — What it is A guide to hospitals, insurance and costs in a twin-island nation of about 1.37 million people.

— Who it’s for Expat workers in energy and finance, retirees, remote workers and long-stay visitors on either island.

— What it costs Public hospitals and the 811 ambulance are free at the point of use. Private hospitals want payment up front or proof of insurance.

— The rules Five Regional Health Authorities run public care. Free prescription drugs under the chronic disease programme are for citizens only.

— Why it matters About 45 percent of all health spending is paid out of pocket, four times the US share.

— The catch Public wards face long waits and short supplies, and serious cases can need an air evacuation abroad.

Healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago gives foreigners two worlds: free but crowded public hospitals, and well-equipped private ones that bill in advance. For an American or European moving to this Caribbean energy economy, insurance decides which world you use.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Analysis story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Trinidad and Tobago has roughly the population of New Hampshire, packed onto two islands just off the coast of Venezuela. Healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago handles most everyday needs. A serious emergency tests both the system and your policy.

How the public system works

The Ministry of Health sets policy, but it no longer runs hospitals directly. The Regional Health Authorities Act No. 5 of 1994 handed that job to Regional Health Authorities, known as RHAs.

RHAs are autonomous public bodies that own and operate the hospitals and health centres in their region. There are five of them, four on Trinidad and one on Tobago.

The North West RHA covers Port of Spain, the capital. The North Central RHA runs the Eric Williams Medical Sciences Complex, the Mt. Hope Women’s Hospital and the Caura Hospital.

The South-West RHA runs the San Fernando General Hospital and the Point Fortin Area Hospital. The Eastern RHA serves about 120,000 people on roughly a third of Trinidad. The Tobago RHA runs all public care on Tobago.

The Chancery Lane extension of San Fernando General Hospital in south Trinidad, in 2012 (Photo: Kalamazadkhan, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Can foreigners use public hospitals for free?

In practice, yes for emergencies. The US State Department states that “public medical care is free in Trinidad and Tobago.” Canada’s travel advice also says public hospitals offer free medical care.

The Ministry of Health’s Charter of Patient’s Rights says access to treatment should not depend on race, religion, gender or national origin. The same charter notes that this right is limited where a service is not reimbursable.

Some state programmes are explicitly for citizens. The Chronic Disease Assistance Programme, or CDAP, gives free drugs for conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure and asthma.

CDAP covers 47 drugs through more than 250 pharmacies, but only for citizens with a national ID card. The External Patient Programme, which funds procedures such as heart surgery and MRI scans, is also aimed at citizens.

The quality gap is the bigger issue. The State Department warns of long waits, overcrowding and limited staff and supplies, and Canada calls public hospitals under-resourced.

The main public hospitals

Port of Spain General Hospital stands on Upper Charlotte Street and is run by the North West RHA. It opened officially in 1858 and is a teaching hospital for the University of the West Indies.

The Eric Williams Medical Sciences Complex sits on the Uriah Butler Highway at Champ Fleurs, east of the capital. It is run by the North Central RHA, which also runs the nearby Mt. Hope Women’s Hospital.

In the south, the San Fernando General Hospital on Independence Avenue is the main public hospital for Trinidad’s second city. The Sangre Grande Hospital serves the rural east.

On Tobago, the Scarborough General Hospital sits at Signal Hill and is run by the Tobago RHA. It is open 24 hours and offers accident and emergency care, surgery, maternity, paediatrics, radiology and a laboratory.

Emergency departments see patients in order of urgency. With the long waits the State Department describes, a minor injury can take many hours.

Private hospitals most expats use

Most insured foreigners use the private sector, concentrated around Port of Spain and San Fernando. Three hospitals stand out for round-the-clock emergency care.

West Shore Medical Private Hospital, at 239 Western Main Road in Cocorite, has operated in north-west Trinidad since 2004. It lists a 24-hour accident and emergency department, intensive and cardiac care units, and open-heart surgery.

Port of Spain from the hills, with the Queen’s Park Savannah in the middle and the St. Clair and St. James districts in front (Photo: Grueslayer, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Medcorp St. Clair Medical, at 18 Elizabeth Street in St. Clair, describes itself as the oldest private hospital in the country. It says it opened the first 24-hour private emergency department and the first fully equipped private intensive care unit.

St. Clair Medical has 60 beds, three operating theatres, dialysis and a catheterisation laboratory for heart procedures. It is a short drive from the Queen’s Park Savannah.

Southern Medical Clinic, at 26–34 Dr. Rupert Indar Snr. Street in San Fernando, runs a 24-hour service. It offers cardiology and cardiac surgery, oncology, obstetrics, an intensive care unit and a desk for international patients.

What healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago costs

The local currency is the Trinidad and Tobago dollar, written TT$. On 26 September 2026 the rate was about TT$6.75 to the US dollar, according to open.er-api.com.

That matches the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago’s selling rate of about TT$6.77 per US dollar on 25 September 2026. A private bill of TT$1,000 is therefore about US$148.

World Bank data put total health spending at about US$1,276 per person in 2023, roughly TT$8,600. The United States spent about US$13,473 per person, more than ten times as much.

Health spending equals about 7.5 percent of Trinidad and Tobago’s economy, against about 16.7 percent in the US. The striking number is the private share.

Out-of-pocket payments made up about 45 percent of all health spending in 2023, according to the World Bank. In the United States the share was about 11 percent.

That gap shows how many residents skip public queues and pay private doctors directly. Private hospitals do not publish standard price lists online, so ask for a written estimate before any planned treatment.

Canada’s travel advice calls private hospital care expensive and says it requires immediate cash payment. The State Department says private hospitals often need payment up front or proof of good insurance before admitting a patient.

Local and international health insurance

Most US health plans do not pay for care abroad, the State Department warns. The US government does not pay medical bills either. Check any home-country plan from Canada or Europe in the same way.

Foreigners employed locally are often covered by a group health plan through their employer. Local insurers such as The Beacon Insurance Company sell group health and life plans to businesses of all sizes.

Guardian Life of the Caribbean, part of the Trinidad-based Guardian Group, also operates locally. Ask any local plan how much it pays for treatment outside the country.

An international expat policy costs more, but it can pay for treatment in the US or Europe. Check three things: direct billing with local private hospitals, evacuation cover, and exclusions for pre-existing conditions.

The State Department strongly recommends supplemental insurance for medical evacuation. The UK Foreign Office asks visitors to hold health insurance and accessible funds for treatment and repatriation.

Emergency numbers and the 811 ambulance

Dial 811 for an ambulance from any fixed or mobile phone. The service is free and is run by Global Medical Response of Trinidad and Tobago under contract with the Ministry of Health.

The 811 ambulance takes patients to the nearest public health institution, not to a private hospital of your choice. If you want private care, tell your insurer and the hospital as early as possible.

The Ministry of Health lists 999 for police, 990 for fire and 511 for the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Management. On Tobago, 211 reaches the Tobago Emergency Management Agency.

The State Department also lists 990 as an alternative ambulance number. Canada warns that emergency response times can be slow, especially in rural areas.

Tobago and medical evacuation

The port of Scarborough, the Tobago capital whose general hospital serves the whole island (Photo: Kalamazadkhan, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Tobago is the smaller of the two islands. Its public care rests on the Scarborough General Hospital and a network of health centres.

The UK Foreign Office notes that medical facilities can be limited in some areas. It says private clinics treat most ordinary problems, but serious cases may need medical evacuation.

An air ambulance to Miami covers about 2,600 kilometres, or roughly 1,600 miles, in a straight line. Canada warns that medical evacuation can be very expensive.

Buy a policy that names evacuation explicitly and states who decides when you fly. Keep the insurer’s 24-hour assistance number in your phone and your wallet.

What this means for foreigners

Use public hospitals as a free safety net, not as your plan. For planned care, choose a private hospital and an insurer before you need either.

Carry prescription medicines in their original packaging with a copy of the prescription, as the State Department advises. Since CDAP is closed to non-citizens, budget for the full cost of long-term drugs.

As of 26 September 2026, the US rates Trinidad and Tobago at Level 3, reconsider travel, citing crime, health and terrorism. That April 2026 advisory is one more reason to hold solid evacuation cover.

A crime-related state of emergency, in force for most of 2026, ended in mid-September when the government chose not to extend it. Al Jazeera reported the decision on 17 September 2026.

Healthcare in Trinidad and Tobago works well for foreigners who arrive insured and informed. The ones who struggle usually learned the rules at the emergency desk.

Sources: System, hospital, programme and emergency facts come from the Ministry of Health of Trinidad and Tobago, the hospitals’ own sites and the US, Canadian and UK governments; spending data from the World Bank; exchange rates from the Central Bank of Trinidad and Tobago and open.er-api.com. All accessed 26 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether public hospitals charge non-resident foreigners for planned, non-emergency treatment is not set out in any published fee schedule. The Ministry of Health describes public care as free but reserves limits where a service is not reimbursable. Practice may differ between the five RHAs.

Private hospital prices are not published in a standard form. The 45 percent out-of-pocket share shows how much residents pay privately, but not what a given visit or operation costs. A written estimate from the hospital is the only reliable figure.

What a medical evacuation costs depends on the aircraft, the destination and the patient’s condition. No official price exists, which is why the cover limit in your policy matters more than any quoted figure.

The latest World Bank health spending figures are for 2023. How spending, waiting times and staffing have changed since then is not captured in those numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is healthcare free for foreigners in Trinidad and Tobago?

Public medical care is free at the point of use, and the US State Department and Canada both describe public hospitals as free. Some programmes, such as free chronic disease drugs under CDAP, are for citizens only. Private hospitals charge and often want payment up front or proof of insurance.

What are the best private hospitals in Trinidad?

Three private hospitals run 24-hour emergency care: West Shore Medical Private Hospital in Cocorite, Medcorp St. Clair Medical in Port of Spain and Southern Medical Clinic in San Fernando. St. Clair Medical has 60 beds and calls itself the oldest private hospital in the country.

What is the emergency number for an ambulance in Trinidad and Tobago?

Dial 811 for a free ambulance run by Global Medical Response of Trinidad and Tobago. It takes patients to the nearest public hospital. Police are on 999, fire on 990, and the Tobago Emergency Management Agency on 211.

How much do people in Trinidad and Tobago spend on healthcare?

World Bank data put health spending at about US$1,276 per person in 2023, against about US$13,473 in the United States. About 45 percent of all health spending was paid out of pocket, compared with about 11 percent in the US.

Do I need medical evacuation insurance for Trinidad and Tobago?

The US State Department strongly recommends supplemental insurance for medical evacuation, and Canada warns evacuation can be very expensive. An air ambulance to Miami covers about 2,600 kilometres. Check that your policy names evacuation explicitly.

GUIDES · SURINAME

Key Facts — What it is A plain guide to how Suriname taxes people and companies in 2026, from wage tax to the 10% VAT.

— Who it’s for Foreign workers, remote earners, retirees and investors considering a move to Paramaribo.

— The rules A monthly tax-free sum of SRD 9,000 (about US$238), then rates of 8% to 38%. Companies pay 36%.

— Why it matters The 38% top rate starts at SRD 234,000 a year (about US$6,190), so almost any Western-level salary reaches it.

— The catch Treaty relief is thin: the 1975 treaty with the Netherlands has a patchy record, and a 2024 treaty with Curaçao has no confirmed start date.

— What is still open Proposals to raise the tax-free sum and to scrap dividend tax for individuals had not become law in the latest reports.

Suriname is a small, Dutch-speaking country on the north coast of South America, between Guyana and French Guiana. Its taxes are low at the bottom and steep at the top, and for anyone paid in dollars or euros the top rate arrives fast.

Taxes in Suriname rest on a wage and income tax with four brackets, a 36% company tax and a value-added tax that began on 1 January 2023. For a foreigner, the thresholds are the story: they are set in Surinamese dollars that have lost most of their value since 2020.

The exchange rate every figure depends on

The Central Bank of Suriname in Paramaribo (Photo: Sharmil2672, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Surinamese dollar, written SRD, floats against the US dollar. The Central Bank of Suriname (Centrale Bank van Suriname, CBvS) publishes weighted average exchange rates.

On 25 September 2026 the bank’s non-cash rate was 37.567 SRD to buy and 37.846 SRD to sell one US dollar. Open market data on 26 September 2026 showed about 37.9.

This guide converts at 37.8 SRD to the dollar. As a scale, SRD 1,000 is about US$26, and SRD 100,000 is about US$2,650.

The rate matters because the tax thresholds are fixed in SRD by law. In September 2020 the official rate was reset from 7.52 to about 14 SRD per dollar, so the same thresholds now buy far less.

Who counts as a tax resident in Suriname

Suriname’s income tax law dates from 1922 and has been amended many times. Its article 3 says residence is judged “by the circumstances”, not by a fixed day count.

In practice, that means the tax office, the Belastingdienst, looks at where your home, family, work and economic ties are. There is no simple 183-day rule written into that article.

Two special rules apply. Someone who leaves and returns to live in Suriname within a year, without living elsewhere meanwhile, is treated as resident for the whole absence.

Surinamese citizens working abroad for a Surinamese public body are also treated as resident, along with their spouse and minor children living with them.

Residents are taxed on their full annual income, after deductions. Non-residents are taxed only on income from Suriname, and the law gives them no tax-free sum.

A residence permit from immigration authorities is a separate matter. Holding one does not by itself settle your tax status, and lacking one does not exempt Surinamese income.

Wage tax and income tax: four brackets above a tax-free sum

Employees meet the wage tax, or loonbelasting, first. The employer calculates it, withholds it from gross pay and pays it to the Belastingdienst each month.

Wage tax is a prepayment on the annual income tax, the inkomstenbelasting. The self-employed and people with other income file income tax returns themselves.

Since 1 January 2024 the tax-free sum has been SRD 108,000 a year (about US$2,857), or SRD 9,000 (about US$238) a month. A state decree of 11 January 2024 set that figure.

Above the tax-free sum, the income tax law sets four bands. The next SRD 42,000 (about US$1,111) is taxed at 8%, and the following SRD 42,000 at 18%.

A third band of SRD 42,000 is taxed at 28%. Everything above SRD 234,000 a year (about US$6,190) is taxed at 38%.

Employees also get a fixed deduction for work expenses of SRD 4,800 a year (about US$127). Employers additionally withhold the premium for the state old-age pension, known as AOV.

What the brackets mean in US dollars

Take a salary of SRD 300,000 a year (about US$7,937). Before deductions, the tax comes to about SRD 47,760 (about US$1,263), an average rate near 16%.

Now take a foreign professional paid the SRD equivalent of US$5,000 a month, about SRD 2,268,000 a year. The same table gives tax of about SRD 795,600 (about US$21,048).

That is an average rate of about 35%, close to the 38% top rate. These are simple illustrations from the statutory table, not tax advice, and they ignore deductions and the AOV premium.

The lesson for foreigners is blunt. Taxes in Suriname feel light only on local wages; on a Western-level salary they approach rates seen in much of Europe.

VAT (BTW) since January 2023

The Centrale Markt market halls on the Suriname River, Paramaribo (Photo: Sn.fernandez, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Suriname introduced a value-added tax on 1 January 2023. It is called BTW, short for belasting over de toegevoegde waarde. Businesses collect it, and consumers bear it.

The general rate is 10% on most goods and services. A 5% rate covers water, electricity, cooking gas and domestic freight transport, according to the Belastingdienst and the specialist site btw.sr.

A 25% rate applies to goods on a separate list in the law’s third annex, and exports carry 0%. Another annex lists supplies that are exempt altogether.

Businesses must register once taxable turnover exceeds SRD 1,000,000 in a calendar year (about US$26,455). Returns and payments are due monthly, between the 1st and the 15th, for the previous month.

The rollout was contested. After union protests in late 2023, the government suspended VAT on utilities and cooking gas for six months. An official committee reviewed the law in 2024.

Companies and dividends

Companies based in Suriname pay a flat 36% tax on profits, under article 36 of the income tax law. That includes the naamloze vennootschap (NV), the local public limited company.

Any company set up under Surinamese law is always treated as based in Suriname. Foreign companies pay only on profits from Suriname.

Dividends face a separate withholding tax of 25% under article 5 of the Dividend Tax Act of 1973. Asiskumar Gajadien, parliamentary leader of the VHP party, cited that rate in January 2023 and said it raised less than SRD 2 million a year (about US$52,910).

Gajadien has proposed scrapping dividend tax for residents who receive dividends from Surinamese companies. He described it as a pending initiative in September 2026.

Oil contractors under the Petroleum Act of 1990 and miners with state agreements are exempt from dividend tax, Gajadien noted. Their special terms are no guide for ordinary investors.

Treaties: the Netherlands link and its limits

The Netherlands, the former colonial power, is the treaty partner that matters most to many foreigners. The two countries signed a double taxation agreement on 25 November 1975.

The Dutch treaty database records the agreement as in force since 13 April 1977. It aims to stop the same income being taxed twice and to curb tax evasion.

Its record is patchy. In 2018 then finance minister Gillmore Hoefdraad said he wanted to reactivate it, and Waterkant reported that it had never really worked.

Suriname signed a separate treaty with Curaçao in 2024. The Dutch treaty database lists it, but it records no date of entry into force.

Before relying on any treaty, get a written view from a Surinamese tax adviser and from your home tax authority. Treaty relief usually needs paperwork, not just residence.

The Guilder Question

The Central Bank’s Numismatic Museum in Paramaribo (Photo: Ymnes, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The Surinamese guilder was the national money until 1 January 2004. It was then replaced by the Surinamese dollar, with three zeros removed: 1,000 old guilders became SRD 1 (about US$0.03 today).

Existing coins and coin notes kept their face value in the new system. Any guilder amount in an old deed, lease or court record must be divided by 1,000.

The word still turns up in daily speech. In June 2026 a Paramaribo resident told Dagblad Suriname that cooking gas cost her “not even six guilders a day”, meaning SRD 5.60 (about US$0.15).

For a foreigner, that habit can confuse. A price quoted in “guilders” today may well mean Surinamese dollars, so ask which currency is meant before you sign.

Full dollarisation, meaning adopting the US dollar as legal money, was argued over in Surinamese media around 2016 and 2020. As of 26 September 2026, the SRD is still the official currency and floats.

The bigger practical risk is the SRD itself. It went from 7.52 to the US dollar before September 2020 to near 38 in 2026, eroding every threshold written in local money.

Filing, deadlines and the online portal

The Belastingdienst began digitising its processes in 2023. Employers file and pay wage tax and the AOV premium monthly, from the 26th until the 10th of the next month.

Income tax returns moved to the online portal from January 2025. The provisional return for 2025 had to be filed online, while returns for 2024 and earlier still used the old paper route.

Companies must file income tax returns digitally from tax year 2025. Registration in the portal runs through a tax identification number, known as the FIN.

A wider reform, a General Taxes Act covering returns, assessments, objections and penalties, was before parliament in August 2026. Its start date was still being debated.

Sources: Tax rules come from the Belastingdienst Suriname, the Income Tax Act 1922 and State Decree S.B. 2024 no. 2; rates from the Central Bank of Suriname; treaty data from the Dutch treaty database; plus Surinamese press. All accessed 26 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether the tax-free sum will rise is not known. In June 2026 MP Xiaobao Zheng proposed lifting it from SRD 9,000 to at least SRD 30,000 a month (about US$794). The outcome is not known.

The fate of the proposal to scrap dividend tax for resident individuals is open. So is the start date of the General Taxes Act, which MPs asked to phase in.

How the 1975 treaty with the Netherlands works in practice today is not clear from public sources. Whether the 2024 treaty with Curaçao is in force is also not confirmed.

Where the Surinamese dollar goes next cannot be known. Every threshold in this guide is fixed in SRD, so its dollar value moves with the exchange rate.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the income tax rates in Suriname in 2026?

After a tax-free sum of SRD 108,000 a year, about US$2,857, income is taxed at 8%, 18% and 28% in three bands of SRD 42,000 each. Everything above SRD 234,000 a year, about US$6,190, is taxed at 38%.

Who is a tax resident in Suriname?

Suriname judges residence by the circumstances, such as where your home, family and work are, rather than by a fixed day count. Residents are taxed on their full annual income. Non-residents pay only on income from Suriname and get no tax-free sum.

What is the VAT rate in Suriname?

Suriname introduced VAT, called BTW, on 1 January 2023. The general rate is 10%, with 5% for water, electricity, cooking gas and domestic freight, 25% for goods on a special list and 0% for exports. Businesses register once taxable turnover exceeds SRD 1,000,000 a year, about US$26,455.

How much tax do companies pay in Suriname?

Companies based in Suriname pay a flat 36% on taxable profit under the Income Tax Act 1922. Dividends face a separate 25% withholding tax under the Dividend Tax Act of 1973.

Does Suriname still use the guilder?

No. The Surinamese dollar replaced the guilder on 1 January 2004, and 1,000 old guilders became SRD 1. The word guilder still turns up in daily speech for Surinamese dollars, so check the currency on any quote or contract.

Is there a tax treaty between Suriname and the Netherlands?

Yes. The two countries signed a double taxation agreement on 25 November 1975, in force since 13 April 1977 according to the Dutch treaty database. A 2018 Waterkant report said it had never really worked, so take advice before relying on it.

World.title: Zimbabwe Visa and Residency: Permits, Costs and What Foreigners Need
World.content:
GUIDES · ZIMBABWE

Key Facts — What it is A standing guide to Zimbabwe’s visas, work permits, residence permits and permanent residence for foreigners.

— Who it’s for Tourists, safari visitors, contract workers, investors, spouses of Zimbabweans and would-be retirees from North America and Europe.

— What it costs US$30 for an ordinary single-entry visa, US$50 for the KAZA UniVisa, and US$300 to US$1,000 for most work and residence permits.

— The rules Americans and most Europeans can buy a visa on arrival or online; work or residence needs a permit from the Department of Immigration.

— Why it matters Zimbabwe prices its immigration fees in US dollars, so the swings of its local ZiG currency do not change what you pay.

— The catch There is no dedicated retirement permit, and time on a work permit does not count towards permanent residence.

Zimbabwe is a landlocked southern African country slightly larger than Germany, best known abroad for Victoria Falls. For foreigners, it runs a three-tier visa system, with every fee quoted in US dollars.

Zimbabwe visa and residency rules sort visitors by passport and residents by purpose. A US or British tourist can usually buy a visa at the airport. Anyone who wants to work, invest or settle needs a permit approved in Harare, the capital.

Who needs a visa: the three nationality categories

The Department of Immigration, part of the Ministry of Home Affairs, runs entry under the Immigration Act (Chapter 4:02). Its visa regime splits the world into three groups, called Category A, B and C.

Category A nationals need no visa at all. The list includes most neighbours, such as South Africa, Botswana and Zambia, plus Kenya, Singapore, Malaysia, Jamaica, Cyprus and Malta.

Category B nationals need a visa but may buy it at the port of entry. This group includes the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia and Japan.

Most European Union members also sit in Category B, among them Germany, Italy, Spain, the Netherlands, Ireland, Poland and Sweden. Switzerland and Norway are in the same group.

Category C nationals must apply and pay online before travelling. The list includes Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines, Vietnam, Colombia and Saudi Arabia.

The department encourages every traveller, visa-free or not, to complete the Zimbabwe Entry Declaration Form before the trip. Online visas are issued through evisa.gov.zw and sent by email for printing.

Visa fees in US dollars, and what the ZiG is

The department’s fee schedule lists an ordinary single-entry visa at US$30, whether bought online or at the border. A multiple-entry visa costs US$55, and an emergency online visa costs US$100.

British nationals pay a separate, higher rate: US$55 for a single entry and US$70 for a double entry, both online. That is almost double what an American pays for the same single entry.

Britain’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) says a visa on arrival is usually granted for 30 days. It advises carrying enough US dollars in small notes to pay the fee at the desk.

Under the Immigration Act, a visitor’s entry certificate cannot exceed six months in the first instance. The FCDO says extensions are made in person at the Immigration Department, and the embassy in London no longer issues visas.

Zimbabwe’s own currency is the ZiG, short for Zimbabwe Gold, which the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe (RBZ) introduced in April 2024. It is backed by gold and foreign-currency reserves, and it circulates alongside the US dollar.

The RBZ’s interbank average on 25 September 2026 was 26.63 ZiG to the US dollar. At that rate, a permit fee paid in local money would take about 13,315 ZiG (about US$500). That ZiG sum moves whenever the rate does.

The RBZ reported annual ZiG inflation of 3.70 percent for September 2026, against 3.46 percent for prices measured in US dollars. For a foreigner, the practical rule is simple: budget in dollars and carry clean, small notes.

The KAZA UniVisa for Victoria Falls

Victoria Falls sits on the Zambezi River, which forms the border between Zimbabwe and Zambia. The KAZA UniVisa lets eligible tourists cross between the two countries on one visa.

The Victoria Falls Bridge between Zimbabwe and Zambia (Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The UniVisa pilot began on 28 November 2014. It is named after the Kavango Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA), shared by Angola, Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. Permanent issuance started on 21 December 2016.

According to Zambia’s Department of Immigration, the UniVisa costs US$50 and is valid for up to 30 days in any 12-month period. It covers day trips into Botswana through the Kazungula border.

On the Zimbabwe side, Zambia lists Harare and Victoria Falls airports and the Victoria Falls and Kazungula land borders as issuing points. The FCDO adds Bulawayo airport, Zimbabwe’s second city.

The eligible list includes the United States, Britain, Canada, Australia and most EU countries, including France and Germany. It pays off only if you would otherwise need a visa for both countries.

Zambia has exempted nationals of 167 countries from visa requirements since 1 January 2025. If your passport is on Zambia’s exempt list, a Zimbabwe multiple-entry visa may serve you as well as the UniVisa.

Working in Zimbabwe: the temporary employment permit

Paid work needs a temporary employment permit, and the FCDO says volunteers and missionaries need one too. The application goes through the e-permits portal at epermits.zimimmigration.gov.zw and the head office in Harare.

The fee is US$500, plus US$300 for each dependant, and none of it is refundable. An extension costs another US$500, and a separate short-term permit is also priced at US$500.

The employer carries much of the paperwork. It must show a local newspaper  for the post and the CVs of shortlisted candidates. It must also name Zimbabweans who will understudy the foreign worker.

The worker supplies a contract, a CV and notarised degrees. A police clearance under six months old and a radiological (chest X-ray) certificate are also required. The company adds a licence from the Zimbabwe Investment and Development Agency (ZIDA). It also files tax clearance from the Zimbabwe Revenue Authority (ZIMRA).

For a worker bringing a spouse and two children, the first-year fees alone come to US$1,400. That is before notary, translation, medical and courier costs, which are not set by the state.

Investor, spouse and residence permits

A residence permit lets a foreigner live in Zimbabwe beyond the visitor period. The fee schedule prices both the non-investor and the investor residence permit at US$500, with US$300 per dependant.

Downtown Harare, where permit applications are decided (Photo: Suesen, CC BY-SA 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

The investor route is paperwork-heavy. It asks for a project proposal, banking history from the home country and proof of funds ready for transfer. Applicants also list the equipment they will import and the foreign and local staff they will hire.

The company behind the investment must file its registration papers, a ZIDA licence and ZIMRA tax clearance. The department’s permit pages do not publish a minimum investment amount.

Foreign spouses of Zimbabwean citizens have their own permit, backed by a guarantee form and proof of funds from the local spouse. The fee table prices it at US$300, while the requirements page states US$500 for a first application.

Students pay US$200 plus US$300 per dependant, and school pupils, called scholars, pay US$100. A separate temporary permit is listed at US$1,000, and a duplicate of a lost permit costs US$100.

Retiring in Zimbabwe: no dedicated permit

Zimbabwe does not list a retirement permit or visa. The department’s current permit pages cover scholars, students, investors, temporary employment and spouses only.

A retiree without a job, investment or Zimbabwean spouse would normally need the non-investor residence permit, priced at US$500. An archived version of the department’s site set out that ordinary residence permit in detail.

That archived page required a close-relative guarantee signed by a resident of Zimbabwe, with the guarantor’s bank statements and proof of accommodation. In plain terms, the ordinary route assumes family or a sponsor already in the country.

Foreign pensioners without those ties should expect the investor route or repeated visitor stays. Before any move, confirm the current route in writing with the department in Harare.

The path to permanent residence

Permanent residence is the settled status that removes the need to renew permits. The fee schedule lists it at US$500 for ordinary applicants and US$1,000 for investors.

Bulawayo City Hall in Zimbabwe’s second city (Photo: Scott.wheeler, CC BY 3.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Five years is the key number. The department’s archived rules allowed an application after five continuous years on a residence permit or a dependant’s residence permit. Holders of a temporary employment permit, NGO staff, government-to-government contract workers and diplomats did not qualify.

The Immigration Act adds a longer benchmark for domicile, the legal term for having Zimbabwe as your settled home. It requires ten years of lawful, continuous residence, and time spent on any permit other than a residence permit does not count.

That is the key trap for contract workers. Years on a temporary employment permit do not build towards domicile under the Act. A long career in Zimbabwe does not by itself lead to settlement.

Under the same Act, domicile is lost by settling abroad for good or by five years of continuous absence. The minister can extend that period on request.

How to apply without delays

Visas are handled online at evisa.gov.zw, and permits through the e-permits portal. Every permit file needs the residence permit application form, known as I.F.5, and a letter to the Chief Director of Immigration.

Documents from outside Zimbabwe must be notarised, and those issued inside the country certified by a Commissioner of Oaths. All translations must be in English, with originals available for inspection.

The head office is the Chingaira Building at the corner of L. Takawira and H. Chitepo streets in Harare. It is open from 07:45 to 16:45 Central Africa Time, Monday to Friday, except public holidays.

At the border, the US State Department asks travellers to carry two blank passport pages, or six if arriving via South Africa. A yellow fever certificate is required when arriving from or through countries where the disease is endemic.

Cash rules matter in a dollar-using country. The FCDO says cash of US$10,000 or more must be declared on arrival. It warns that leaving with more than US$2,000 is illegal. The US State Department says more may leave if it was declared and documented on entry.

The simplest sequence is to enter as a visitor, secure the job, investment or marriage papers, then file the permit. Keep receipts for every US dollar paid, because fees are non-refundable.

Sources: Visa categories, fees and permit requirements come from Zimbabwe’s Department of Immigration and the Immigration Act, with KAZA and travel rules from Zambia’s Department of Immigration, the UK FCDO and the US State Department, and exchange-rate and inflation data from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe. All accessed 26 September 2026.

What Is Not Known

Whether a minimum investment applies to the investor residence permit is not stated on the Department of Immigration’s permit pages. Any threshold would sit with ZIDA or with the department’s case-by-case review, and it should be confirmed before money is committed.

The spouse permit fee is not settled by the department’s own pages. The fee table says US$300, while the requirements page says US$500 for a first application.

The published visa-category lists do not show every country. France and Finland, for example, appear on none of the three lists, although both are on Zambia’s KAZA UniVisa list.

The five-year residence rule for permanent residence comes from an archived version of the department’s site. The current website does not restate it, and processing times for any permit are not published.

Where the ZiG goes next is not known. It traded at 26.63 to the US dollar on 25 September 2026, but fees stay in US dollars whatever the rate does.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do Americans need a visa for Zimbabwe?

Yes. The United States is in Category B, so Americans need a visa but can buy it on arrival or online at evisa.gov.zw. The Department of Immigration lists an ordinary single-entry visa at US$30 and a multiple-entry visa at US$55.

How much is a Zimbabwe visa for British citizens?

British nationals pay a separate rate: US$55 for a single-entry visa and US$70 for a double-entry visa, both online. The UK Foreign Office says a visa on arrival is usually granted for 30 days and advises carrying US dollars in small notes.

What is the KAZA UniVisa and how much does it cost?

The KAZA UniVisa is one visa for Zimbabwe and Zambia. It costs US$50, is valid for up to 30 days in any 12-month period, and covers day trips into Botswana through Kazungula. It is issued at Harare and Victoria Falls airports and at the Victoria Falls and Kazungula borders.

How much does a Zimbabwe work permit cost?

A temporary employment permit costs US$500, plus US$300 for each dependant, and the fees are non-refundable. An extension costs another US$500. The employer must show a local newspaper  and name Zimbabweans who will understudy the foreign worker.

Does Zimbabwe have a retirement visa?

No. The Department of Immigration lists no retirement permit or visa. Retirees without a job, investment or Zimbabwean spouse would normally have to fit the non-investor residence permit, priced at US$500, which has historically required a guarantor resident in Zimbabwe.

How do foreigners get permanent residence in Zimbabwe?

An archived checklist from the Department of Immigration required five years of continuous residence on a residence permit. The fee is US$500 for ordinary applicants and US$1,000 for investors. Time on a temporary employment permit does not count towards domicile under the Immigration Act.

World.title: Three Missing After Being Swept Away at Tarrazú Waterfall and Guanacaste Beach
World.content:
Three people remain missing after strong currents swept them away in two separate incidents today, one at a waterfall in the Los Santos region south of San José and the others at a beach in Guanacaste, according to the Costa Rican Red Cross. A fourth person, a woman, was rescued in Sarapiquí after floodwaters carried her off an overflowing bridge.

The first emergency was reported at 1:35 p.m. at the Los Reyes waterfall in San Lorenzo de Tarrazú, where an adult man was reportedly dragged away by the current. The Red Cross sent a first-response unit, a rescue team, basic life support ambulances and specialized divers to the site.

At 6:35 p.m., the Red Cross said it had suspended the search because of poor weather in the area and rescuers had not located the man. The search is set to resume early Sunday, depending on conditions at the site. At 5:43 p.m., a second alert came in from Playa Cabuyal in Liberia, Guanacaste, where two adults were pulled out by the curren and remain missing. The Red Cross said the weather prevented crews from searching overnight, and operations will restart at first light.

The last rescue took place around 6:15 p.m. in Puerto Viejo de Sarapiquí, Heredia when a woman tried to cross a flooded bridge on a motorcycle after heavy afternoon rain swelled the river, and the current swept her away. The Red Cross were able to get to her and bring her to safety, however, they have not released the identities or nationalities of the other three missing people.

The incidents came as Tropical Wave 47 crossed, bringing heavy downpours and thunderstorms to much of Costa Rica this afternoon. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) recorded up to 125 millimeters (4.9 inches) of rain at Laguna de Fraijanes. More storms are expected tomorrow and the IMN forecasts that instability left behind by the wave will produce isolated to scattered downpours and thunderstorms in the afternoon across the Pacific, the Central Valley, the Northern Zone and the Caribbean mountains.

Always keep in mind, fivers and waterfalls can rise within minutes when rain falls upstream, even where skies are clear. Swimming in rivers and pools below waterfalls is most dangerous during and after afternoon storms, and flooded roads and bridges should never be crossed on foot or by vehicle.

World.title: Dollar Rebounds From Record Low but Year-End Could Favor the Colón Again
World.content:
The U.S. dollar posted its strongest week against the Costa Rican colón in months, but the gain is small next to a slide that began in mid-2022, and at least one economist expects the colón to regain ground as the year closes. On the Foreign Currency Market (Monex), the dollar closed Friday, Sept. 25, at ₡454.70, up ₡6.92 from ₡447.78 a week earlier.

It was the highest close since June 29, when the dollar ended at ₡454.94, and it came just over a week after a record low of ₡446.80 on Sept. 17. Rates at the bank window are wider than Monex. As of late Friday afternoon, every bank was buying dollars at ₡436 or more, while Banco de Costa Rica, Banco Nacional and Banco Popular were selling at ₡462. Other private operators were selling between ₡460 and ₡463.

In practical terms, someone selling $1,000 at a bank on Friday would have received at least ₡436,000, while someone buying $1,000 at one of the three state banks would have paid about ₡462,000. The Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) reference rate for Saturday was ₡450.38 to buy and ₡455.60 to sell.

Trading was lighter during the rebound. A total of $161.06 million changed hands on Monex over five sessions, compared with $195.97 million in four sessions the previous week, when a holiday closed the market on Tuesday. The Central Bank bought $56.06 million on Monex this week to cover dollar demand from the non-bank public sector, down from $78.70 million the week before. It did not buy dollars to build its own reserves or carry out stabilization operations to smooth the price.

Dollar supply from the public remained strong. From Monday to Thursday, banks and other exchange intermediaries bought $622.08 million from customers and sold $541.95 million, leaving a surplus of $80.13 million, according to BCCR data. In other words, customers sold more dollars than they bought.

Whether the rebound lasts may depend on the calendar. Federico Quesada Chaves, director of the School of Administrative Sciences at the State Distance University (UNED), said the dollar could face renewed downward pressure in the final months of 2026. He pointed to the extra foreign currency that typically enters the market with aguinaldo payments, bonuses, holiday purchases and year-end business operations, beginning around late October and early November.

Quesada described that as a possible scenario rather than a certain decline. He also said that a new Eurobond placement, if the government raises dollars abroad and converts them into colones locally, could add to the supply of dollars. No such placement has been confirmed. UNED noted that the Central Bank holds more than $20 billion in reserve assets.

The Central Bank board recently kept its monetary policy rate at 3%, citing slower local growth and international tensions. Quesada has listed a lower policy rate and changes to banks’ reserve requirements among the tools that could ease pressure on the dollar. He noted that those decisions rest with the independent Central Bank.

The colón’s long run of strength has costs for businesses that earn in dollars but pay salaries, rent and services in colones. Shirley Calvo, executive director of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), has cited the currency’s appreciation as one factor weighing on small tourism businesses. Figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC) show that tourism-related employment fell by 20,137 jobs between the second quarter of 2024 and the same period of 2026.

For households, Quesada advised keeping debts in the same currency as income to limit exposure to swings in the exchange rate. Even after this week’s gain, the dollar sits only about ₡8 above its record low. The final quarter, when seasonal dollar inflows usually build, should show whether the rebound marks a turn or a pause.

World.title: Costa Rica Takes Growing Role in U.S. Deportation Program
World.content:
Costa Rica has quietly become an important destination in a growing U.S. deportation program that sends migrants to countries they are not from, leaving hundreds of people to decide whether to stay here, return home or try to move somewhere else. These are not Costa Ricans being deported back to Costa Rica but are people from countries including China, Mexico, Colombia, Brazil, Vietnam and several nations in Africa and Asia who were removed from the United States and flown here under an agreement between the two governments.

Between April 11 and September 3, Costa Rica received 424 people on 20 flights under the current program, according to figures from the Dirección General de Migración y Extranjería. They came from dozens of countries, making Costa Rica one of the more regular destinations being used by the United States for what are known as third-country deportations.

The term sounds complicated, but the idea is fairly simple. A third-country deportation happens when the United States removes someone but sends that person to a country other than his or her country of citizenship. Costa Rica agreed in March to accept proposed transfers of up to 25 people per week. Costa Rican authorities retain the right to accept or reject individual cases, while the United States provides funding for assistance coordinated through the International Organization for Migration, commonly known as the IOM.

The latest detailed government figures available through September 3 show that China accounted for the largest group, with 84 people, followed by Mexico with 68, Colombia with 52 and Brazil with 44. Of the 424 people received by that date, 187 were still in Costa Rica. Another 202 had already left the country, while 35 were in the process of arranging their departure.

What happens after they land is different from the detention system many experienced in the United States. Migrants are received by Costa Rican immigration officials and generally taken to hotels in the San José area. They are not being held as prisoners and are permitted to move around the country. They receive information about their options, which can include returning to their country of origin with assistance, seeking refugee protection in Costa Rica or looking at other legal ways to remain in the country.

That does not mean the process has been simple since some of those arriving speak languages that are uncommon in Costa Rica, including Mandarin, Russian and Arabic, creating challenges when officials try to explain immigration rules, work options and refugee procedures.

Costa Rican immigration authorities have said they receive information about incoming passengers ahead of the flights and arrange interpreters when necessary. Migrant advocates, however, have raised questions about whether everyone fully understands the choices available to them and whether they have enough access to independent legal advice.

International attention on Costa Rica’s role increased this week after reports examined the wider U.S. system of sending migrants to third countries. An international investigation coordinated by Forbidden Stories reported that at least 25,447 people had been deported by the United States to third countries through August 31, 2026. Most were sent to Mexico, but thousands of others have been transferred to countries in Latin America, Africa and the Pacific.

Costa Rica stands out partly because people sent here have more freedom than deportees placed in some other countries. They can leave their hotels, keep their documents and pursue immigration options in Costa Rica. An inspection by Costa Rica’s Defensoría de los Habitantes earlier in the program confirmed that the migrants it reviewed were not being held in custody and had been given regular immigration status, although the agency warned that providing adequate services could become more difficult as more people arrived.

There have also been disagreements over access to the migrants. Recent reporting noted that visits to the hotels by lawyers and migrant-rights organizations were temporarily suspended in August after authorities said some migrants were uncomfortable with the process. Advocates have argued that independent advice is particularly important for people deciding whether it is safe to return to their home countries.

For Costa Rica, the situation creates an unusual immigration challenge. Costa Rica has long received migrants and refugees from neighboring Nicaragua, Venezuela and other parts of Latin America. The U.S. agreement is different because Costa Rica is now receiving people who may have no previous connection to the country, may not speak Spanish and, in some cases, had originally hoped to seek protection in the United States.

Some leave Costa Rica quickly. Others are choosing to stay. As of September 3, nearly 44% of the people who had arrived under the current agreement were still in the country. Among them were 58 Chinese nationals, 33 Mexicans, 13 Vietnamese, 10 Brazilians and nine Colombians, along with smaller numbers from several other countries.

That means what began as a weekly arrangement involving relatively small flights is becoming a longer-term issue for Costa Rica’s immigration system. For the migrants themselves, landing at Juan Santamaría International Airport is not necessarily the end of their journey. For many, it is the beginning of another decision: go home, try another country or attempt to build a life in Costa Rica.

World.title: Tropical Wave 47 Brings Afternoon Storms to Costa Rica This Weekend
World.content:
If you have plans outdoors today, get them done before lunch. Tropical Wave 47 is crossing Costa Rica today, and afternoon downpours with thunderstorms are expected across the Central Valley, the Pacific and the Northern Zone, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN).

The morning is your window so expect mostly fair to partly cloudy skies early, with only isolated showers along the Pacific and Caribbean coasts. Clouds build toward late morning, and the storms start between late morning and early afternoon. The heaviest rain is forecast along the central mountain range and across the north. That puts the mountain roads around the Central Valley and the routes into San Carlos and the Arenal area squarely in the path.

The north already got a preview yesterday as heavy afternoon rain sent water into homes, businesses and the technical high school in Aguas Zarcas, according to local reports, and covered part of the road in La Marina de La Palmera. The National Emergency Commission (CNE) said yesterday afternoon it had no official reports of damage.

The storms won’t stop at sunset. Early tonight, downpours with possible thunderstorms are forecast for the Central and South Pacific and the Northern Zone, with scattered rain in the Central Valley and the North Pacific. Patches of fog are possible in the Central Valley overnight.

Temperatures stay warm ahead of the rain. San José ranges from 18.8°C (66°F) to 28.3°C (83°F). Liberia is the hot spot at up to 36.1°C (97°F), while Quepos tops out near 31.2°C (88°F) and Ciudad Quesada near 28°C (82°F).

The unsettled weather could carry into Sunday afternoon. Once the wave moves on, the IMN expects slightly less rain on the Pacific side from early next week. The Caribbean coast and plains should see less frequent rain than the rest of Costa Rica this weekend. If you’re driving, aim to be off mountain roads by early afternoon. Rain on ground that is already wet can swell streams and loosen slopes quickly, and visibility drops fast in a heavy downpour. Don’t try to cross a flooded road or river, because water that looks shallow can still sweep a car away.

If you’re hiking, rafting or at the beach, the same timing applies. Lightning is the main danger with these afternoon storms, so head for shelter as soon as you hear thunder and get out of the water. Rivers can also rise fast after rain upstream, even where the sky above you is still dry.

Tropical waves cross Costa Rica regularly during the rainy season, and this is the 47th of the year. Keep an eye on the IMN’s afternoon updates and call 911 to report an emergency.

World.title: Man calls police after brother in law steals his $35 ruda plant
World.content:
Man calls police after brother in law steals his $35 ruda plant

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 37 year old merchandiser of San Jose Palmar, Orange Walk District, has reported that his small ruda herbal plant was stolen.

The man told police that around 8:00pm on Friday, September 25, he noticed the plant, kept in a red container and valued at $35, was missing.

He suspected his brother in law, who lives in the same yard behind his house. When confronted, the relative allegedly denied it, but left the yard quickly after the man said he would contact police.

About an hour later, the relative allegedly returned with the plant.

Court action has been requested, and police are looking for the brother in law.

World.title: Man calls police after brother in law steals his $35 ruda plant
World.content:
Man calls police after brother in law steals his $35 ruda plant

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 15 year old boy has been arrested and charged with rape of a child following an investigation involving a five year old boy in Orange Walk Town.

According to the police report, the child was taken to the Orange Walk Police Station by his mother, where a report was made alleging that he had been sexually assaulted inside a residence while under the care of his stepfather.

Police say the alleged incident occurred inside the living room of the home.

A statement was recorded from the child in the presence of his mother, and court action was requested.

Investigators visited and photographed the reported scene.

The child was also taken to the Northern Regional Hospital accompanied by his mother and a social worker.

According to the police report, a pediatrician conducted a medical examination and documented injuries.

Police subsequently sought the teenage relative named in the complaint.

Investigators later located the teenager at a high school in Belize City and detained him before transporting him to the Orange Walk Police Station.

Police say the teenager was informed of his constitutional rights and chose to remain silent.

A social worker was contacted and an interview was subsequently conducted in the presence of the required adults.

The documents were then forwarded to the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions for advice.

According to police, the 15-year-old was formally arrested and charged, in the presents of his mother, with rape of a child on September 25, 2026.

Because both the complainant and accused are minors, their identities are being withheld.

World.title: 40 year old woman and 17 year old boy detained after crack and cannabis bust
World.content:
40 year old woman and 17 year old boy detained after crack and cannabis bust

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 40 year old woman and a 17 year old boy were taken into custody after police found suspected crack cocaine and cannabis at a home in San Jose Village, Orange Walk District.

Police say that on Friday, September 25, an anti drug team made up of Orange Walk Special Branch, GI3 and the Quick Response Team executed a search warrant at the residence.

A search of the teen’s front pants pocket allegedly turned up a clear plastic bag holding small foil parcels of suspected crack cocaine.

Officers then searched the house and reportedly found a plastic bag of suspected cannabis on the rooftop.

At the Orange Walk Police Station, the suspected crack was counted at 28 foil parcels weighing 3.99 grams.

World.title: Police stop man with groceries and find crack in cargo pocket
World.content:
Police stop man with groceries and find crack in cargo pocket

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 38 year old construction worker from San Jose Village, Orange Walk District, has been charged with possession of controlled drugs.

He is Oscar Alberto Rodriguez.

Police say that on Friday, September 25, officers conducting operations in Barrio Pobre Alley, Orange Walk Town, stopped Rodriguez, who was carrying a bag of groceries.

A search of his right cargo pocket allegedly turned up one piece of a white substance suspected to be crack cocaine, along with a piece of foil containing two more pieces.

The drugs weighed 0.4 grams. Rodriguez was arrested and charged with one count of possession of controlled drugs.

World.title: Boxer says neighbour threatened to kill him in Orange Walk Town
World.content:
Boxer says neighbour threatened to kill him in Orange Walk Town

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 23 year old Honduran boxer living on Temash Street in Orange Walk Town has reported that a fellow tenant threatened to kill him.

Police say that around 1:00am on Thursday, September 24, the man was asleep in his upstairs apartment with a friend when he was awakened by the sound of breaking bottles and a machete slamming against his front door and wall.

He recognized the voice of a man who rents in the same building. Police arrived and took that man away, but he returned about half an hour later.

Police were called again. As officers escorted the man and his son to the patrol vehicle, the man allegedly shouted in Spanish that he would come back and kill the boxer and that he would pay.

The boxer told police he feared for his life. Court action has been requested.

World.title: Mother and 17 year old son arrested after cannabis found on verandah roof
World.content:
Mother and 17 year old son arrested after cannabis found on verandah roof

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 40 year old woman and her 17 year old son of San Jose Village, Orange Walk District, were arrested after police allegedly found suspected cannabis on the roof of their verandah.

Police say that between 6:55pm and 7:30pm on Friday, September 25, the Quick Response Team and Special Branch officers executed a search warrant for illegal drugs at the family’s home.

When asked if she had anything illegal to declare, the woman reportedly said, “No sir.”

Nothing was found inside the house. But when officers checked on top of the zinc covering the verandah, they allegedly discovered a clear plastic bag containing suspected cannabis.

Both mother and son were arrested for possession of controlled drugs and taken to the Orange Walk Police Station.

World.title: PUP to mark 76 years, tracing Party’s Legacy from George Price to John Briceño
World.content:
PUP to mark 76 years, tracing Party’s Legacy from George Price to John Briceño
