World.title: Burnham’s AI agenda is already in disarray thanks to Trump
World.content:
Within the space of a week, however, Trump trashed any hopes that America will participate in global agreements on AI and POLITICO revealed that AISI’s usually privileged access to new AI models is now being delayed by the White House – which told leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their models with the U.K. until U.S. testers have finished ascertaining that they don’t pose a threat to American systems.

So if Burnham wants to stick to his plan of making U.K. the center for brokering international AI harmony he has to figure out how to bring the U.S. onside, or else press on without the U.K.’s closest ally.

When approached by POLITICO, a U.K. government spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a world leader in AI security, and the AI Security Institute continues to work closely with the U.S. government, international partners and leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.”

Special relationship problems

The U.K. already has a track record for convening global meetings on AI safety, but it has also tended to stick by the U.S. when deciding whether to sit out specific international agreements.

In 2023 the U.K. hosted the Bletchley Park Summit on AI safety, which produced an agreement on the opportunities and risks of AI signed by 28 countries, crucially including the U.S. and China.

However, at the Paris iteration of the summit in 2025 the U.K. declined to sign a new declaration on the ethical development of AI alongside the U.S.

World.title: Two mass shootings in South Africa leave at least 27 dead
World.content:
Two mass shootings in South Africa have left at least 27 people dead, police said on Sunday.

 

The SA Police Service reported that 17 people were fatally shot in an attack at a bar to the west of Johannesburg on Saturday night.

"It is alleged that patrons were drinking inside and outside the tavern when the suspects arrived and opened fire on those outside," the force said in a statement.

"The suspects then entered the tavern and continued shooting at patrons inside. The suspects were reportedly armed with AK-47 rifles and pistols. They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the statement continued. "Two vehicles were also set alight during the incident".

It added that 13 men and four women were killed in the shooting, which took place at around 9:30 pm.

Local police have launched an investigation into the incident, with detectives and specialised units deployed to track the suspects. No arrests have so far been made.

In a separate incident, 10 people were killed and 11 were injured in a shooting in Lwandle, just outside Cape Town, in the early hours of Sunday morning, according to the SA Police Service.

"Official police reports indicate that gunmen entered an entertainment place that also sells braaied meat (shisanyama) at approximately 01:46 and shot at patrons," the service said.

"As a consequence, five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained," its statement continued.

Local police have opened investigations into murder and attempted murder. The identities of the victims are to be released after their next of kin are informed.

World.title: Russian foreign minister rejects Berlin's call to abandon 'dangerous' escalation
World.content:
Russia's foreign minister has rejected calls from his German counterpart to pull back on "dangerous" escalatory steps as he accused Berlin of being Ukraine's "main sponsor."

 

Sergey Lavrov met with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Saturday, shortly before Lavrov delivered an address to world leaders.

During their talks, the German minister urged Moscow to abandon its "dangerous path of escalation" towards Europe while also suggesting Berlin was open to improving its relationship with Russia - provided the Kremlin showed it was genuinely willing to end its war in Ukraine, the Associated Press reported, citing a German delegation official.

Speaking at the General Assembly, Lavrov told the audience: "Chancellor Merz is stating that Germany must once again be a leading military power in Europe. Does Berlin understand what this could lead to? Did they not learn the lessons of World War II?"

In a press conference following his speech, the Russian diplomat was also asked about his meeting with Wadephul and Russian-German relations.

"Nothing new came from that initiative of the foreign minister," he told reporters.

"He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia. You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not?" he added later.

Tensions between Germany and Russia hit a flashpoint in early September after Berlin accused Russia of being behind a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport earlier this year.

Wadephul announced at the time new measures against Russia "as the perpetrator of the hybrid attack in Leipzig," with the Russian consulate in Bonn and Russia's Berlin cultural centre to be closed as part of the government's response.

He added that there would also be tighter border controls for Russian nationals moving forward and increased pressure on Russia's shadow fleet.

The Russian embassy in Germany issued a statement denying the claims and threatening "consequences" over the sanctions.

The Russian ambassador, Sergey Nechayev, "categorically rejected the accusations made by Berlin as unsubstantiated, absurd, and contrary to common sense," the statement read.

"He noted that the measures announced by the German side represent an unprecedented escalation in Russian-German relations and will not remain without consequences, for which the German government will bear full responsibility," it continued.

Lavrov on Saturday dismissed the incident as an "unclaimed drone" and said Germany had "immediately" claimed it was Russian.

Empty seats for Ukraine's delegation are seen as Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov speaks during the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Elsewhere in his speech, Lavrov said the US had "destroyed the European security system and created a Russophobic regime in Kyiv" while also accusing the West of aspiring "to inflict strategic defeat on Russia."

"These aspirations will result in the war mongers being led into a strategic dead end," the minister said.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that it was clear the Kremlin was not preparing to bring the war to an end any time soon.

"Putin always finds some lame excuse – not to meet, not to hold a trilateral, not to talk, not to end it, not to stop the killing," he said in a video address. "He is looking for excuses to keep waging the war".

World.title: Tomorrow's Infrastructure: AIIB Raises Its Development Ambitions for a Second Decade
World.content:
‘Partner Content’ is used to describe brand content that is paid for and controlled by the advertiser rather than the Euronews editorial team. This content is produced by commercial departments and does not involve Euronews editorial staff or news journalists. The funding partner has control of the topics, content and final approval in collaboration with Euronews’ commercial production department.

Asia needs an estimated $1.7 trillion a year in infrastructure investment through 2030, but no single bank can cover that. Instead, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank has built its strategy around a narrower question: how does public money pull in more money behind it? Working with governments, development banks and private investors, AIIB's focus is increasingly to turn infrastructure plans into projects that can actually attract capital.

 

That question sits at the heart of AIIB's 11th Annual Meeting of the Board of Governors, running in Doha, Qatar, on 28 and 29 September, under the theme "Tomorrow's Infrastructure: Impact and Innovation." It marks the start of the bank's second decade. Vice President and Corporate Secretary Sir Sherard Cowper-Coles sees the timing as a chance to sharpen what the bank's financing is actually for.

An Opportunity to Scale Impact

"It's a very important meeting because it's the first in our second decade," Cowper-Coles said in an interview at AIIB headquarters. "It's the first under the leadership of our new president, President Zou Jiayi. And it signals that we are concerned about maximising the impact of the money we raise, not only on our own account, but with our partners."

AIIB now has 111 approved members from six continents. Demand keeps rising with them. It also keeps changing shape. Renewable energy, clean water and resilient infrastructure remain the priorities, but Cowper-Coles pointed to health and digital infrastructure as growing fast alongside them. "We're looking beyond traditional infrastructure, not just ports and airports, roads and bridges, but also health infrastructure, digital infrastructure," he said. Infrastructure, in his description, has become "the operating system of a modern economy and a modern society."

Preparing projects for private capital

No single institution can finance demand at this scale, so AIIB has put more weight on what happens before a project ever reaches the market. That means working with clients early: preparing projects, structuring the risk, making them attractive enough that other investors follow. Sometimes it means AIIB taking on risk a private lender won't touch, or offering a guarantee that unlocks financing well beyond its own contribution.

"We are looking more and more at the way in which we can make projects bankable, prepare them for the market," Cowper-Coles said. "We can take on the risk, the guarantees that the private sector can't, and then draw in money from elsewhere."

A $200 million guarantee to Türk Eximbank shows how that plays out in practice, Cowper-Coles said. The deal covered 70% of the value of the bank's first green loan and brought in close to $300 million of financing from international banks. Local-currency financing and loan syndication are two more levers Cowper-Coles wants to pull harder as AIIB tries to grow the pool of capital it can deploy.

Climate at the centre

Climate financing already accounts for most of AIIB's lending. In 2025, 71% of the bank's financing was climate-related or green, a share the Bank is committed to hold above 50% for years to come. "It's absolutely central to what our members are asking for," he said. "It's also central to what we do."

The projects behind that figure look very different from one another. A $50 million water supply and sanitation project in Kyrgyzstan is bringing clean water to more than 100 towns and villages, reaching around 450,000 people. In Bangladesh, a $400 million programme with the Asian Development Bank is building climate resilience directly into how the government plans and budgets. And in Chile, Cowper-Coles pointed to a desalination plant and aqueduct the bank has financed, supplying clean water to "a region that has suffered from low rainfall for the past 10 years."

Infrastructure that connects

Some of AIIB's projects cross borders entirely. In Lao PDR, the bank is backing the Monsoon 600 MW wind project, which will let the country export electricity to Vietnam. Around a quarter of AIIB's financing currently supports cross-border connectivity, a share the bank wants to raise to 25–30% by 2030, Cowper-Coles said.

Closer to home for millions of people, AIIB's urban upgrading programme in Indonesia has reached an area where some 8.5 million people live. "We've delivered clean water, paved streets, safe areas for children to play, and we're very, very proud of it," Cowper-Coles said. "It's made a huge difference to a huge number of people." He pointed to other examples in the same breath: the Izmir Metro expansion in Türkiye, and a nationwide fibre network being rolled out across Oman, in both cases in partnership with others. Further afield, AIIB has backed the Zhanatas wind farm in Kazakhstan and solar power projects in Egypt, Oman and the Maldives.

A decade focused on delivery

AIIB is entering its second decade with a broader ambition. Guided by a focus on impact, innovation and integrity, the Bank aims to stretch its balance sheet further, and mobilise additional capital for sustainable infrastructure. For Cowper-Coles, the ultimate test is not the scale of commitments, but whether investments deliver tangible results for people and communities. "This isn't just about commitments and promises," he said. "It's about actually financing infrastructure for tomorrow, so that people get real benefits in terms of their quality of life."

World.title: Can solar power work underwater? Scientists test solar panels 10 metres beneath the sea
World.content:
Ten metres beneath the South China Sea, scientists have found an unlikely place to generate power from the sun.

 

Last week, researchers announced that they had successfully tested solar panels at underwater depths previously considered impractical for the technology.

Designed to capture the wavelengths of sunlight that can pass through seawater, the panels could eventually keep underwater equipment running for longer without relying just on batteries, they argue.

During a two-hour trial near the Weizhou Islands, off the southern coast of mainland China, the panels generated power from sunlight at a depth of 10 metres. Lab tests suggest that they could operate continuously for years, too.

The research, published in the science journal Joule, takes underwater solar well beyond previous studies, which have focused on depths of just two metres or less.

How can solar panels work 10 metres underwater?

One of the biggest obstacles to generating solar power underwater is that sunlight fades below the surface – and fast.

By a depth of 10 metres, much of the sun’s energy has already been absorbed or scattered by the water. But some types of light can reach deeper than others.

According to the researchers, enough blue and green light reaches these depths to generate electricity, so the team developed solar cells designed to make the most of it.

They used what are known as perovskites, an alternative to the silicon found in most solar panels, which can be adjusted to absorb different wavelengths of light.

In laboratory tests recreating conditions 10 metres underwater, the cells turned around 35 per cent of the sunlight that reached them into electricity.

The researchers then put bigger versions to the test in the South China Sea. At two metres deep, their 115 square centimetres of solar panels generated 1,416 milliwatt-hours over two hours, or about half the capacity of a rechargeable AA battery.

At 10 metres, they generated 324 milliwatt-hours over two hours – a small amount but still far beyond what the researchers expected.

Their panels also showed almost no loss in performance after 1,160 hours under simulated underwater conditions. Based on their tests, the researchers estimate they could operate continuously at 10 metres below the sea for around five and a half years.

“This work presents the first functional validation of submerged solar cells practically operating at a water depth of up to about 10 meters, greatly broadening their application scope,” says study author Wen-Hua Zhang, from China’s Yunnan University and Southwest United Graduate School in Kunming.

How solar is going off-grid

Once the sole domain of rooftops and wide open spaces, solar power continues to appear in places where electricity and fuel can be difficult to access.

Earlier this year, Dutch researchers unveiled the world’s first solar-powered ambulancein rural Kenya, designed to bring healthcare and medical equipment to hard-to-reach communities that lack reliable access to electricity or fuel.

In Norway’s Svalbard archipelago, solar has also begun to help power a remote former radio station, a site accessible only by boat or helicopter that previously relied on diesel-fuelled generators.

Other projects have found space for solar in existing infrastructure. In Switzerland, solar panels installed between railway tracks are generating electricity without taking up more land. The panels can also be removed for track maintenance, allowing railways to double as solar farms without disrupting services.

Underwater solar power could solve a different problem.

Ocean sensors, cameras and communication equipment can operate far from power supplies, but they must eventually be retrieved when their batteries run out.

The researchers believe the technology they studied could provide a lasting source of power for this kind of equipment.

First, however, they need to find out how well their solar panels work deeper undersea. They say their next step is to do just that and establish how far beneath the waves solar power can go.

World.title: Food prices vs minimum wages: Where in Europe has pay kept up?
World.content:
Food prices have risen sharply across Europe over the past five years, but minimum wages have risen even faster in most of the 26 countries examined by Euronews Business.

 

Malta is one exception. A worker on the minimum wage there can buy about 6% less food with their gross pay than they could five years ago, despite a rise in wages. Minimum-wage workers in Spain and France have also lost ground.

Food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 34% across the EU between August 2021 and August 2026, according to Eurostat. Hungary recorded the highest rise in the bloc, at 57%, followed by Bulgaria (54%) and Romania (53%). Cyprus had the lowest increase, at 21%.

Among the wider group of 35 European countries, Switzerland recorded the lowest increase, at 5%.

Turkey was an outlier: food and non-alcoholic beverage prices rose by 752% over the same period.

Turkey’s exceptional rise reflects years of high inflation, fuelled in part by a sharp fall in the lira, which pushed up the cost of imported goods and inputs. The lira’s decline was partly driven by a series of interest rate cuts that began in 2021, even as inflation rose. Lower rates made the currency less attractive to hold, adding to pressure on its value. Turkey reversed that policy in 2023 and raised rates sharply, but prices continued to rise.

Across the EU, food prices were already rising before Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The war added to the pressure by driving up energy, fertiliser and transport costs, as well as disrupting agricultural markets. Those costs fed through to supermarket prices.

Among the EU’s largest economies, food prices rose by 25% in France, 30% in Italy, 34% in Germany and 35% in Spain between August 2021 and August 2026.

How minimum wages compare

Monthly gross minimum wages also rose over the same period in many European countries with a statutory minimum wage.

Hungary recorded the largest increase in the EU, at 93%, while the minimum wage rose by 46% in Germany, 29% in Spain and 20% in France. These changes are measured in local currencies.

Turkey recorded the largest increase among the countries compared, at 823% over five years. Minimum wages also more than doubled in Serbia (103%) and Montenegro (102%).

But higher wages do not necessarily mean workers can afford more food. The comparison measures how much food a monthly gross minimum wage could buy in August 2021 and August 2026. It does not show how much money workers had left for groceries after tax, rent and other expenses.

Simply subtracting the food price increase from the minimum wage increase can be misleading, especially when inflation is high, as in Turkey. Comparing what the wage could buy at each point gives a clearer picture.

In three of the 26 countries compared, minimum-wage earners lost purchasing power when measured against food prices.

Malta recorded the biggest fall, at 6%. A minimum-wage earner who could buy 100 baskets of food in August 2021 could buy only 94 in August 2026. Spain and France followed, with falls of 5% and 4%, respectively.

Serbia and Montenegro recorded the largest increases in the amount of food a minimum wage could buy, at 37%. A minimum-wage earner who could buy 100 baskets of food in August 2021 could buy 137 in August 2026.

Croatia, Albania, Romania, Hungary, Bulgaria and Lithuania also saw increases of more than 20%.

Food purchasing power rose by 10% in Ireland, 9% in Germany, 7% in Greece, 6% in Belgium and the Netherlands, and 3% in Portugal.

The chart above, indexed at 100 in August 2021, shows how the amount of food a minimum-wage earner can buy changed over the five years.

In Turkey, the minimum wage rose by 823% and food prices by 752%. The difference is 71 percentage points, but the increase in food purchasing power was only 8%. Both wages and food prices rose steeply in lira, with wages rising slightly faster.

The chart above tracks Turkey’s minimum wage and food prices, both indexed at 100 in August 2021. It shows that minimum-wage earners lost ground at times in 2021 and 2022, when food prices rose faster than their wages. Since January 2024, the minimum wage has remained ahead of food prices, leaving workers able to buy more food than they could at the starting point.

World.title: Travelling with friends? These are the most popular cities for group holidays in 2026
World.content:
Revive the group chat, dust the cobwebs off the travel spreadsheet and get the posse to turn “let’s plan the trip” into “all flight tickets and stays are booked!”... Sometimes, this is easier said than done.

 

In Opodo’s “Solo Travel Trends 2026: The Year of Travelling Alone with Purpose” report released in August, as many as 30% of the 9,000 travellers surveyed said they opted to go the journey alone because their friends or family weren't available.

But when the group chat does finally deliver, travelling with friends can have its perks.

Dividing costs among friends for accommodation, rental cars, petrol and even food can “unlock significant savings”, according to Kayak, which added that renting a large villa overlooking an ocean view is a lot less expensive once the nightly rate is shared between five or more people. “The trick? Knowing where to go.”

Top searched destinations for groups

Kayak surveyed hotel and holiday rental searches for bookings made by parties of five or more between March and September for stays between July and December 2026.

In both cases, Europe took centre stage, with London ranking as the most searched hotel destination for groups. According to Kayak, the average price per night was €181 – 6% less than the previous year.

Second on the list is Paris, where the average hotel stay per night was found to be €144, a 3% decrease from last year. Meanwhile, the French capital was also the most searched for holiday rental destination for groups, with rental rates averaging €151 a night.

Other French destinations proved popular on the holiday rentals ranking, including Marseille and Nice, which took the second and eighth spots on Kayak’s list.

Steeped in more than 26 centuries of history, the port city of Marseille is typically less crowded from during October and November and the climate becomes cooler, too – making it ideal for exploring its oldest neighbourhood: the Panier District, dating back to 600BC.

Its streets are described by the official tourism board as open air museums in their own right, replete with murals, street art, and central venues with artisans and designers selling their wares.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV draws 800,000 faithful to Paris before emotional Lourdes pilgrimage
World.content:
France welcomed Pope Leo XIV to Paris on Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of people gathered along the Champs-Élysées to see the pontiff travel by popemobile to an outdoor Mass.

 

Waving flags and cheering, the crowds lined a 2-kilometre route from near the Arc de Triomphe towards Place de la Concorde. The Vatican estimated that about 800,000 people attended the Mass, exceeding the 600,000 who had registered in advance. Leo stopped repeatedly to wave to the crowd and bless children and babies before reaching the ceremony.

After the Paris Mass, Leo travelled to Lourdes, where he began his pilgrimage on Saturday evening with a silent prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions. The site is associated with the visions reported by Bernadette Soubirous, then aged 14, in 1858. On his first full day in Lourdes, the pope walked barefoot part of the way to the sanctuary, greeting pilgrims and pausing to speak with families who had travelled from across Europe. He spent several minutes in personal prayer inside the basilica before meeting privately with shrine rectors and chaplains.

On Sunday, Leo is due to meet French bishops and celebrate another outdoor Mass at the sanctuary. He is also scheduled to meet sick people and seven survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy and personnel, before concluding the visit with a Rosary and torchlight procession.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: Switzerland: Referendum to decide on stricter neutrality
World.content:
Swiss voters will decide whether a stricter application of neutrality is necessary. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

Voters in Switzerland on Sunday take part in a referendum to decide whether the longstanding policy of neutrality needs a stricter approach.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.

What is the Pro Schweiz Association seeking to achieve

The group wants:

Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"

Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense

Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties

Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked

UN approval of sanctions before Switzerland joins them

Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.

Nearly all major political parties reject the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."

Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'

Opponents of the initiative argue that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.

"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.

In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.

Another referendum on food security is also taking place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times. The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

World.title: China sends two giant pandas off to Atlanta zoo after Xi-Trump summit
World.content:
Ping Ping and Fu Shuang took off to Atlanta on a FedEx plane, with steamed corn buns, carrots and bamboo to snack on during the flight. Their trip is one of the few concrete things to come out the Xi-Trump summit.

Two giant pandas departed China's southwestern city of Chengdu for new home in Atlanta, as part of an agreement between Washington and Beijing.

Chinese President Xi Jinping announced that the pandas would be relocated to the capital of the US state of Georgia during his three-day summit with US President Donald Trump in Washington.

Xi said the panda loan program was an example of "friendship between the Chinese and Americans."

The loan was one of the few concrete things to come out of the summit.China has long used pandas as a key part of its global diplomatic outreach, turning such agreements into a well tested tool of soft power. On the flip side, Beijing has also let agreements lapse and pulled pandas back from countries when tensions arise.

Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Meet the pandas

Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, two adult pandas, will be on loan to Zoo Atlanta for 10 years, as part of the agreement. Both pandas were born in 2020 and have lived at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding.

A farewell ceremony was held before their departure.

Fans of Ping Ping and Fu Shuang gathered in Chengdu to wish them a good trip Image: Xu Bingjie/Xinhua/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ping Ping, who is male, Fu Shuang, female, departed from Chengdu Shuangliu International Airport on a chartered flight around 3:00 a.m. on Sunday (1900 GMT on Saturday).

The FedEx-operated Boeing 777 was equipped with steamed corn buns, bamboo shoots and carrots to keep the animals nourished during their journey, Chinese media reported. They are also being accompanied by experienced US zoo keepers who had traveled to China ahead of time.

In preparation of their arrival, Zoo Atlanta renovated its panda facilities and ensured a long and stable supply of locally grown bamboo. The zoo has decades of experience with pandas, hosting the animals between 1999 and 2024.

World.title: Gunmen kill 27 people in two mass shootings in South Africa
World.content:
South African police have launched a search for suspects after 17 people were found dead at a tavern southwest of Johannesburg. A separate tavern shooting near Cape Town left 10 dead.

At least 27 people have been killed in separate mass shooting incidents in South Africa's Gauteng and Western Cape provinces overnight.

In the first incident, gunmen armed with assault rifles killed 17 people and wounded 15 others at a bar in Wedela township, west of Johannesburg, police said on Sunday.

Manhunt underway for 8 suspects

Gauteng police said they have launched a manhunt for eight unidentified armed men following the deadly shooting.

"They allegedly searched some patrons and took their cellphones before fleeing the scene in two unidentified motor vehicles," the South African ​Police Service (SAPS) ‌said.

Emergency ‌services ‌declared all ​17 victims, 13 men and four women, dead at the scene. Authorities said the shooting occurred Saturday at around 9:30 p.m. local time (1930 UTC).

A motive for the shooting ⁠was ​not ​known, the SAPS said, adding that "suspects ​were reportedly ⁠armed with AK-47 rifles ⁠and ​pistols."

10 killed in Lwandle tavern shooting, Cape Town

In a separate shooting in the Western Cape, police said gunmen killed 10 people and wounded 11 more at an entertainment venue in Lwandle township at 1:46 a.m. (2346 Saturday GMT).

Authorities said five of the victims died at the scene while another five succumbed to their injuries after being taken to hospital.

Police said no arrests have been made and that a "multi-disciplinary team" led by serious and violent crime detectives had been established to track down those responsible.

More police resources have been sent to the area as the search for the perpetrators continues.

The latest incidents came just days after at least 11 people were gunned down at a home in KwaZulu-Natal Province.

That shooting occurred in KwaMakhutha, a township some 30 kilometers (19 miles) south of Durban, the eastern province's largest city.

SA deploys troops as organized crime grips communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

South Africa's high rate of violent crime

South Africa is grappling with violent crime and has one of the world's highest murder rates, with around 60 people dying violently in the country each day.

In one of the stories that has made international headlines in recent days, Johannesburg police are still trying to track down those responsible for a spate of killings in which the bodies of 10 women have been found in close proximity to one another.

Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found concrete evidence to suggest the same person or people were responsible.

In March, South Africa's leadership deployed troops to hotspots to support police dealing with rampant criminality that President Cyril Ramaphosa has described as one of the biggest challenges facing the country at present.

World.title: Powerful storm batters northeast US, hundreds of flights canceled
World.content:
Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed as a nor'easter brought flooding, power cuts and travel disruption to cities like New York, Boston and Philadelphia.

Heavy rain and strong winds pounded the northeastern United States on Saturday, forcing authorities to cancel hundreds of flights and leaving thousands without electricity.

New York, Boston and Philadelphia were in the firing line of the 'Nor'easter,' named after the northeasterly winds.

What is a nor'easter storm?

Nor'easters are large cyclones in the western North Atlantic Ocean, which typically form off the east coast of the US.

They can occur throughout the year but are more frequent between fall and early spring.

Nor'easters are almost always accompanied by heavy rainfall or snow, as well as strong winds.

What have authorities said about the nor'easter?

Residents in low-lying and coastal areas were warned of potential flooding and road closures, as the storm coincides with high tide.

"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the National Weather Service said in its latest forecast.

"Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses," it said.

Some 95,000 people in the states of New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island and Pennsylvania were facing a power outage as of 3 p.m. on Saturday (1900 GMT), as per poweroutage.com.

Local leaders urge caution

New York Governor Kathy Kochul said the storm was particularly impacting the coastal areas of New York City and Long Island.

"Conditions are extremely dangerous. Anyone who goes in or near the water this weekend is literally gambling with their life," she said in a press briefing.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani warned residents of the strong winds, saying "Don't travel if you don't have to."

Flights, events canceled

Hundreds of flights were cancelled due to the storm, with 253 at Boston's Logan airport alone, according to tracker FlightAware.

The unusually powerful autumn storm intensified, forcing the cancelation of hundreds of flights Image: Matthew Hatcher/AFP

Airlines including JetBlue, United and American have issued travel alerts, allowing passengers to change their flights without a fee.

As of 6:13 p.m. local time (2213 GMT), FlightAware said 439 flights involving US airports had been canceled and 2,459 flights were delayed.

Major cultural events have also been called off.

The Global Citizen and All Things Go Festivals in New York, and the Oceans Calling Festival in Maryland were canceled.

"Safety has to come first. This is the first time in 14 years we've had to cancel," said organizers of the Global Citizen event in Central Park, which was meant to feature Lenny Kravitz, Lauryn Hill, Alicia Keys and country stars Lainey Wilson and Shaboozey.

British Pop star Ed Sheeran's Weekend concerts near Boston were also canceled due to the storm.

About five inches (13 centimeters) of rain was forecast in areas of Massachusetts, including Boston. That's equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain.

'Nor'easter' are named so for its northeasterly winds Image: Joseph Prezioso/AFP

World.title: Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
World.content:
Tens of thousands rallied in the Spanish capital after an 87-year-old woman was dramatically evicted from her home this week. Protesters called for measures to curb rising costs and reduce evictions.

Tens of thousands of people protested in central Madrid on Saturday to denounce Spain's housing crisis.

The demonstrators called for better protection for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.

The march through the center of the Spanish capital was called after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted from her apartment where she had lived for seven decades.

Protesters carried signs reading 'we are all Maricarmen' Image: C. Carvajal/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent ahead of a general election next year.

Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth has put pressure on the already limited housing supply in the cities. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of 550,000 homes across the country last year.

Toxic tourism — Mallorca's housing crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters camp out in Puerta del Sol

Government authorities estimated that around 25,000 people had shown up to protest against Spain's growing housing crisis. The Madrid Tenants' Union, which organized the protest, said over 300,000 had taken part.

Once the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp in the city center's Puerta del Sol square with plans to stay put. Some even pitched up tents to stay the night, or until the police forcibly removed them.

Police officers looked on at about a dozen tents, surrounded by thousands of protesters, news agency AFP reported from the scene.

Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership Image: Tomas Calle/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Rallying around Abascal

The protest was triggered by Maricarmen Abascal's dramatic eviction on Wednesday from the house she had lived in for decades.

Abascal was greeted by supporters as she was removed from her home on a stretcher and loaded onto an ambulance.

"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. "And we can't keep maintaining this. Housing is a right, and we don't have it," she said.

According to Spanish media, Abascal's father first rented the home in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in 1956. After her parents died, she continued to live in the flat, which had a rent cap at the time.

Spain: Tourism boom worsens housing crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2018, the building changed ownership, and Urbagestion, an investment fund, bought the unit, raising the rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 ($3,018).

Abascal had been offered an opportunity to buy the apartment before this but could not afford it.

The fund later lowered her rent to €1,650, but Abascal could not afford that either. Courts had blocked her eviction three times previously and extensive media coverage turned her into a symbol of the crisis.

"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.

"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted," she added.

World.title: Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown
World.content:
09/26/2026 September 26, 2026 Mass protests against cuts to social services

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of cities across Germany on Saturday to voice their opposition to planned government spending cuts and call for a stronger welfare state.

Trade unions said a total of 175,000 took part in the protests, including in Nuremberg (over 20,000), Stuttgart (16,000), Frankfurt (15,000), Hanover (13,000), Essen (12,000), Berlin (5,500) and elsewhere under the slogan: "Hard-earned! Your work. Your health. Your pension."

Speaking in the western city of Essen, German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi criticized plans by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government to reform working hours and pensions, and warned against cuts to social security benefits.

"We will not simply allow what we have built up over many years in terms of social standards to be taken away from us," she said.

'Participation, self-determination, pension system, health system' - the blocks holding up 'democracy,' said protesters in Frankfurt Image: Bernd Kammerer/Presse- und Wirtschaftsdienst/picture alliance

Pension reform has been the focus of attention for months in Germany, while automobile giant Volkswagen has also announced sweeping job cuts.

The issues played a central role in the recent state elections in Berlin and the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which resulted in disastrous defeats for Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Nevertheless, the chancellor insisted earlier this month: "The reforms must go ahead."

Christiane Benner, leader of the trade union IG Metall, warned in Nuremberg against scaling back social security in times of restructuring and job cuts, for example in the automotive sector.

German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi spoke to crowds in Essen Image: Friedrich Stark/epd

"Economic change can only succeed with confidence in the future and with solidarity," she said.

German employers, however, accused the trade unions of a "ritual refusal to reform."

Steffen Kampeter, chief executive of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), told the DPA news agency that "the trade unions say 'no' to almost every change" and accused them of "dreaming of the world of yesterday."

World.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
World.content:
Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.

What happens when data centers lose power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

Several data centers are currently under construction in Europe Image: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

Hundreds protested against a Google data center saying that AI needed democracy Image: APA-Images/picture alliance

Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.

Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.

Data centers face backlash from US communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.

For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.

Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

World.title: China, US agree to set up channel for AI safety incidents
World.content:
Following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two superpowers pledged to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents and boost coordination on military matters.

Beijing and Washington promised to expand dialogue on AI safety and between the countries' militaries while also cutting tariffs on about $30 billion (€26.3 billion) of "non-sensitive goods."

The pledges follow the three-day summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in the US.

US President Trump described the summit in an online post as "one of Friendship, Strength, and Success" for both nations.

Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China's President Xi was more constrained, saying the two sides agree on "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."

Beijing and Washington to improve military communication

On Saturday, with Xi back in Beijing, China said the two sides agreed to a mutual tariff reduction on roughly $30 billion of "non-essential" goods. This applies to exports such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.

The Chinese statement also confirmed that the two side will be setting up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.

"Artificial intelligence technologies are continuously developing, all parties can strengthen exchanges, discuss in-depth and seek consensus in light of the latest situation," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

A new round of AI-focused dialogue is due to be held in November.

The two nations will also accelerate their work on military crisis communications, Beijing said, without providing details.

Xi to travel to the US again in December

The US had previously announced that Beijing and Washington agreed to extend their "trade truce" agreed by Trump and Xi in Busan last October. The agreement, which saw China suspending its controls on rare earths and the US cutting back on some of its tariffs, was due to expire on November 10. According to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the deal will remain in effect until January.

Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The White House also said the two sides addressed American concerns about rare earths supply "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the US in 2027 and 2028, according to the Trump administration.

While Donald Trump confirmed the Iran war was also on the agenda during the US talks, no major breakthroughs were reported on the issue. However, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said both sides agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons, and no country should impose transit tolls on international waterways, in reference to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump and Xi are due to meet twice more by the end of the year, with Trump expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ​summit in China in November and Xi expected back in the US for a G20 summit in December, which is due to be hosted in Trump's National Doral Miami golf club.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery
