World.title: Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019055/Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.content:
From preparing restaurant-worthy meals and repairing cars to programming robots and operating drones, young people from around the world will put their skills to the test in Shanghai this week at the largest WorldSkills Competition yet.

The event opens Tuesday with a record 1,385 competitors from 68 countries and regions, marking its first edition on the Chinese mainland. Often dubbed the “Skills Olympics,” the biennial competition will see participants vie for medals across 64 disciplines, ranging from traditional trades to advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies.

Unlike conventional sporting events, WorldSkills tests competitors on their ability to perform practical tasks drawn from the workplace. Participants generally must be under 22, although the age limit extends to 25 for some disciplines, and have between 15 and 22 hours to complete their assignments. They can compete only once in their lifetime.

In cooking, competitors must plan menus, prepare and plate dishes, and serve them on time while meeting food safety standards. Automobile technology contestants diagnose and repair vehicle faults, while robot systems integration contestants assemble and program industrial robots to perform automated tasks. This year’s debut unmanned aerial systems discipline tests skills in building, testing, and maintaining drones.

It’s one of seven disciplines added this year to reflect changing labor-market demands, with the others including dental prosthetics, digital media interactive design, intelligent security technology, rail vehicle technology, retail sales, and software testing.

Chen Yujie, deputy director and researcher at the Vocational and Skills Research Office of the Chinese Academy of Labour and Social Security, told state agency Xinhua that WorldSkills regularly adds, merges, or eliminates disciplines to keep pace with industry changes. Chen added that even established disciplines update their technical standards and competition content.

The inaugural competition, held in Madrid in 1950, featured just six disciplines — fitting, pattern making, turning, electrical installations, milling, and cabinetmaking — and 24 competitors from two countries.

This year’s opening ceremony will take place Tuesday evening at the Shanghai World Expo Cultural Center. The roughly 90-minute event centers on the mortise-and-tenon joint, a traditional Chinese woodworking technique.

Competition begins Wednesday and runs through Saturday at the National Exhibition and Convention Center, where roughly 300,000 square meters of space has been converted into workshops ranging from professional kitchens to drone-flight zones. Some 400,000 visitors are expected over the four days.

Admission is free, but visitors must reserve a time slot online. Once inside, they can watch competitors at work from just a meter away or try their hand at practical skills. Some events, including beauty therapy, hairdressing, and restaurant service, will also recruit members of the public to take part.

The event will also host the WorldSkills Conference, bringing together more than 2,000 delegates, including 50 government ministers, to discuss issues such as AI’s impact on labor and green development.

China joined WorldSkills International in 2010 and made its competitive debut the following year in London. From 2011 through 2024, Chinese competitors won 93 gold, 41 silver, and 28 bronze medals, along with 71 Medallions for Excellence. China topped both the gold-medal table and overall team rankings for four consecutive editions.

China will field competitors in all 64 disciplines this year, with vocational-school teachers and students making up more than 60% of its delegation, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security.

(Header image: South Korean mechatronics competitors prepare for the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, Sept. 21, 2026. Xinhua)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.title: China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.content:
China’s men’s basketball team has suffered its second-worst defeat in its history at the Asian Games, calling into question the coach’s abilities and the team’s training methods.

On Sunday, China lost 70-79 to Iran, two days after it lost 77-97 to Japan, host of this year’s Games, its second failure to reach the finals and its largest-margin loss in men’s basketball at the tournament. The country finished fourth, one place higher than at the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon — its worst result ever.

China has claimed eight Asian Games titles, with its most recent gold coming in 2018. Since then, China has failed to win the title.

Head coach Guo Shiqiang said the team fatigued toward the end of the tournament, noting that only nine players were available for rotation partway through the Games due to injuries. He also said the team’s younger players lacked major tournament experience and had struggled to play consistently, and that “the team had failed to execute its pregame tactical plans.”

China’s unusually long training and competition period this summer has been a focus of criticism. The team spent around 140 days in camp before the Games, domestic media reported. Internationally, teams typically spend only one to three weeks at training camps, widely considered to be intensive and demanding.

Criticism has also centered on Guo, 51, a former starting point guard for China’s national team who began coaching the team in 2006 and became head coach in 2009. After leaving the team to coach locally in 2010, he returned as head coach in 2024, and led China to a runner-up finish at the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.

Critics have questioned Guo’s tactical approach. Against Iran, China’s defense focused heavily on protecting the net rather than the court’s three-point line, leaving space for their opponents to take jump shots and make three-pointers. The team also struggled to secure rebounds in both its matches against Iran and Japan.

Others criticized Guo’s offensive strategy, arguing that he relied too heavily on the backcourt, that players became isolated at crucial moments, and that his in-game player selection was overly conservative.

The defeats have prompted broader discussion about whether China’s traditional approach of requiring athletes to spend a large portion of the year in training camps can keep pace with changes in the sport, particularly the increasing emphasis on spacing, perimeter shooting, and shooting efficiency.

“Everyone on our team has worked extremely hard this summer,” Guo said in a post-game interview with domestic media. “Every member of the Chinese men’s basketball team has put in a tremendous amount of effort.” His comments sparked widespread backlash online, with many arguing that the team’s prolonged exhaustion from training camp caused the poor results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Jiao Boqiao (left) of China blocks a shot by Mohammad Jamshidi of Iran during the men’s basketball bronze medal match between China and Iran at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. Andy Cheung/Getty Images/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.title: Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.content:
YUNNAN, Southwest China – Growing up in a remote mountain village in Yunnan province near China’s southwestern border with Vietnam, Zhou Lifang had only ever seen clouds from below. In late July, on her first flight, the 16-year-old saw them from above.

“I thought clouds were transparent because (my) textbook said clouds are made of water vapor,” she tells Sixth Tone. “But I didn’t expect them to be like a white wall. The clouds you see from the ground are in pieces, but from the sky they are one big mass.”

Lifang and her 14-year-old twin sisters, Zhou Lixin and Zhou Liyi, were among 145 students from Yunnan taking part in “Mountain-Sea Bond,” a four-day program in Shanghai that included reunions with parents working in the city.

The sisters are among China’s “left-behind children,” who remain in their home communities while their parents migrate for work, often placed in the care of grandparents or other relatives. China had 9 million such children in 2022, according to the 2023 Rural Education Development Report.

Born in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, the sisters have lived for more than a decade with their grandparents in a village in Malipo, a county in the Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture roughly 400 kilometers away by road. Their parents, Zhou Yuneng and Zhang Shunfen, now work in Shanghai, where Zhou drives for a ride-hailing service and Zhang sorts groceries at a supermarket warehouse.

Smartphones have long allowed Zhou and Zhang to remain involved in their daughters’ lives from afar. They check in, offer advice, and try to mediate fights between the sisters. But they can see and hear only what the girls choose to share, and cannot always persuade them to talk.

Asked how well she knows her daughters now, the mother says they all like drawing, then pauses. “Close to zero,” she admits. “I don’t really know what they like anymore.”

After more than a decade of parenting largely by phone, Zhou and Zhang would spend two weeks sharing a 20-square-meter room in Shanghai with their daughters, their longest stretch together since the girls went to live with their grandparents.

On her own

Before the sisters left early that morning, their grandmother, Kuang Tianzhen, 64, tucked 50 yuan ($7) into each girl’s pocket, twice their usual weekly allowance. Rumors of scams in their border village had made her uneasy about the journey.

“Where will you stay in Wenshan?” she asks, the prefecture’s seat. “This is all reliable, right?”

After the neighbor’s car carrying them disappeared from view, their grandfather, Zhou Shucheng, 72, sat brooding outside the house for at least half an hour, staring down the rain-soaked road and gently petting the tabby cat his granddaughters had adopted.

Four hours later, the sisters arrived at a hotel in Wenshan for a predeparture meeting with participants from surrounding villages and counties. They would spend the night there, then continue to Kunming the next day for the flight to Shanghai.

“Are you Zhou Lifang’s parents? Have your three children arrived yet?” a trip organizer asks over the phone.

“I am Zhou Lifang,” she replies. “We’re already here in the lobby.”

Lifang was the only child in the tour’s WeChat group; everyone else was a parent. She had followed instructions about when and where to meet and confirmed the arrangements for all three sisters.

Inside the hotel’s meeting hall, grandparents sit beside children waiting to register while organizers address the crowd from the stage.

Elders are heard asking “Where should I sign?” and “Do I fill this part in?” At the line marked “guardian,” some pause, unsure whether to write their own names or those of the children’s parents in Shanghai.

One grandmother checks her granddaughter’s schoolbag, rebraids her hair, and films her on her phone. When organizers ask the adults to leave, she goes downstairs, then turns back and slips inside again.

Lifang sat quietly on one side of a wide pillar, her twin sisters on the other. Unlike many of the children around them, the sisters had arrived without a grandparent.

The sisters began attending boarding school around age 6. When home, they helped with farm work and tended the family’s wood-burning stove. Before they had smartphones of their own, they called their parents using their grandmother’s phone or a public telephone at school.

At 12, Lifang went alone to a hospital near her school for a tuberculosis screening while her mother guided her through the process over a video call.

“Sometimes I felt pretty helpless,” she says. “I would ask adults passing by for help and follow their directions.” On other visits, her mother advised her to follow a classmate who knew the hospital better.

When the village prepared to allocate plots of collectively owned farmland, Lifang took the call and passed the information to her grandmother. During school vacations, she tidied the twins’ room and called her mother when she needed money or help handling her sisters.

Her grandfather divides farm work and allowances equally among the three girls. But when they argue, he tells Lifang, “You’re the older sister. You’re the eldest. You should give way to them.”

The twins usually side with each other against Lifang, and a stray remark can set off a fierce argument. From Shanghai, Zhang tells her, “If someone hits you, whether it’s your sisters or your schoolmates, you should hit them back.”

Lifang sometimes goes into a room and locks the door instead. “Then they can’t come in,” she says. “They’ll play a game, and after that, everything will be fine.”

She has repeatedly asked her parents for a room of her own. When she wants to be alone, she sometimes sits on a swing her father built on the rooftop. On a nearby window, smiling faces the sisters traced with their fingers years ago remain visible beneath layers of dust.

“Sometimes I wish I could be the younger sister, not the older one,” Lifang says.

Close to zero

When the twins moved to the village at 3, they sometimes cried for their mother. Their grandmother would carry one of them outside and point toward Kunming, along the road winding over the mountain.

“I’d hold her for a while and tell her that her mother was there,” Kuang recalls. “Then she’d stop crying. They’re good girls, easy to coax.”

Their father had tried to leave the twins in the village a year earlier. He drove them there when they were 2, but couldn’t bear to leave them and took them back to Kunming.

By 2015, private kindergarten in Kunming cost 1,800 yuan ($250) per child per month, meaning fees for all three would have consumed 5,400 yuan of the couple’s roughly 6,000-yuan monthly income.

The family was also hundreds of thousands of yuan in debt after rebuilding the village house and paying hospital bills for the grandfather and one of the twins, who had spent several weeks in neonatal intensive care with meningitis. Because the girls lacked local household registration, or hukou, enrolling them in Kunming’s public schools was difficult.

For the next decade, their parents remained in Kunming, making the six-hour drive to the village every month or two for a weekend or holiday.

Years of installing wood floors damaged both of Zhou’s knees. The work required him to squat and sometimes kneel. “After every shift, I would get off my scooter and walk stiff-legged,” he says. In 2025, chronic arthritis forced him out of construction, and the couple moved to Shanghai, approximately 2,500 kilometers away.

When the sisters missed their parents, Lifang says, they video-called them. “Mom and Dad would always say they only had a few more days of work and would be back to see us soon.”

Over time, however, the girls stopped asking when their parents would return for good. “They used to say, ‘Mom, I miss you,’” Zhang says. “Since I moved to Shanghai, I hardly ever hear that anymore.”

In 2023, the couple installed a camera at the gate of the village house, primarily for safety. It lets them check on the grandfather and see when the girls return from school. They chose not to install one in the girls’ bedroom.

“I just feel that girls, after all, need some privacy,” Zhang says.

The mother also bought her daughters smartphones with large screens to make video calls easier and placed few restrictions on how they used them.

“Kids today are different from us back then,” she says. “Digital devices aren’t just for studying anymore. They have access to so many things on their phones. I don’t restrict them too much.”

The twins often decline their parents’ calls or hang up after a few sentences. Sometimes, one answers while playing on the computer, points the phone’s camera at the ceiling, and keeps playing.

Asked why, one of the twins says, “Just because I don’t have the patience.”

Every time this happens, Zhang just smiles and rarely lets her temper show.

“I feel that if I push too hard, I lose the right to speak,” she says. “I’m afraid they’ll think, ‘You didn’t raise me. You weren’t there when I was small, and now you want to tell me what to do.’ So sometimes I can’t be too direct. I have to be careful how I put it.”

When Lifang and the twins argue, the parents try to settle their disputes by phone, usually scolding both sides. Each girl comes away believing that she alone has been blamed.

“That’s because of the distance and what a phone call can’t do,” the mother says. “If it were face to face, a few sentences would clear it up.”

Unlike the twins, Lifang video calls Zhang almost every day and has her saved in her phone as “Dear Mom.” But she seldom calls Zhou. “Dad is quite busy driving day and night, so I rarely call him,” Lifang says. “I’m afraid of interrupting his work. I feel like I’m not close to him because he’s too strict.”

Even with Zhang, much of Lifang’s life remains outside their conversations. At school, some classmates seek her out for tarot readings, calling her “Master Zhou.” Others mock the way she speaks, comparing it to barking, and give her insulting nicknames.

Lifang spends nearly every break between classes drawing. She draws when she feels happy, angry, or embarrassed, and says it helps her relax. She keeps one sketchbook, which she rarely shows others, for times when she feels low.

One drawing shows a figure with its arms crossed and an X over its mouth. In the background, Lifang has written, “What if speaking is also a fault?”

“All I can do is draw them as ugly monsters,” Lifang says.

She closes the sketchbook.

“There are some words I cannot show,” she says. “Cannot.”

In another sketchbook, Lifang has created Yumeng, a cheerful girl from the sea who grows increasingly troubled as she tries to save a city from destruction. “Why should I, who am already living such a miserable life, have to save others?” the character asks.

Lifang also has a circle of friends her parents know little about. She met them through a nonviolent multiplayer game she describes as “healing.” Unlike the competitive games her sisters prefer, it lets players explore different settings, build homes and farms together, and talk.

“Besides my best friend at school, they are the most important friends in my life,” Lifang says.

Before boarding the flight to Shanghai, Lifang sent them an update: “I’m boarding now, so I can’t reply to your messages. I’ll send you some amazing pictures later.”

Under one roof

Two days after reuniting privately with their parents, all three sisters stepped onto a stage in matching pale green T-shirts and brand-new canvas shoes their mother had prepared before their arrival. “Mountain-Sea Bond” organizers had chosen the family for a letter reading at the Aug. 1 reunion ceremony.

Standing between the twins, Lifang began reading, with Zhang beside her daughters and Zhou watching from the audience.

“Before, I never understood why you were always away and could not be with us,” she reads. “Only on this trip, after coming to Shanghai where you live and work, did I truly understand how hard you work and how much you have given.”

When Lifang finishes, the audience applauds, and Zhou begins to sob. As the sisters come down from the stage, he pulls the twins close and continues crying until his face turns red. The twins’ eyes fill with tears.

“You don’t see your children often,” he says after regaining his composure. “And then suddenly you realize they have grown up all at once.”

After the ceremony, the family go to Jing’an Joy City, a Shanghai mall the sisters had long wanted to visit for its anime shops. Lifang taught herself to draw manga and now takes commissions through an app from clients across China, earning several dozen yuan per drawing. She hopes to attend one of China’s leading art academies, though she usually tells adults she wants to become a civil servant like her older cousin.

The program ended that day, but the sisters remained in Shanghai for the rest of their two-week stay. All five shared a one-room, 20-square-meter unit with a private bathroom and an induction cooker in one corner.

Zhou and Zhang had moved there at the beginning of the year, hoping the girls might eventually join them in Shanghai. Before the trip, Lifang had assumed the move had made her parents’ lives easier.

“Now that Mom and Dad work in Shanghai, the conditions are better, and the work is a little easier,” she says.

Zhou no longer installs floors, but his ride-hailing shifts often last at least 12 hours. “If you work less, you can’t make enough,” he says. “You drive for 11 or 12 hours, come back, charge the car, make something to eat, then sleep. The next day, you get up and repeat it. That’s the job.”

Zhang works similar hours sorting groceries at a supermarket warehouse and has no regular weekends. Sometimes they go an entire day without seeing each other awake; one leaves breakfast behind before the other gets up.

During the visit, Zhou took another week off from driving, while Zhang continued working. The parents would not allow the girls to go out alone in an unfamiliar city.

Before leaving Yunnan, Lifang says, “I want to help my mom sort groceries at the supermarket warehouse.” In Shanghai, she often accompanied Zhang to work, while the twins remained in the apartment.

One night, Zhang returned late from work and began tidying the room. One of the twins ran over and hugged her.

“Mom, I feel like you’ve worked so hard,” Zhang recalls her saying. The girl then began to cry.

“I feel like she’s really growing up,” Zhang says.

Despite all five sharing one room, the sisters argued less during the visit. Disputes that had been difficult to settle over the phone rarely became as heated in person, Zhang says.

Even before his daughters arrived, Zhou had been considering returning to Yunnan after another year in Shanghai.

“Whatever happens, I should go back and do whatever work I can, as long as we are by their side,” he says.

But Zhou has taken no steps toward moving and cannot say what work he might find near the village. Its karst terrain leaves little room to expand farmland, and 796 of its 2,172 residents work elsewhere, according to a village official.

Zhou and Zhang each earn about 8,000 yuan ($1,120) a month in Shanghai, though Zhou can make more by taking fewer days off. Returning would mean giving up the income that had drawn them farther from their daughters.

During their stay in Shanghai, the sisters called their grandmother about once a week. One day at a café, a blue parrot perched on Lifang’s shoulder. She has long wanted one like it, and blue is her favorite color. Lifang immediately called Kuang on video.

“Grandma, look what’s on my shoulder,” Lifang says. “Isn’t it impressive?”

“Behave yourself,” Kuang replies. “Where are the twins?”

“They went with Mom to work.”

“When will you come back?” Kuang asks. “How are you getting home?”

“Dad says he’ll drive us back next weekend,” Lifang says. “My school starts early.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Zhou Lifang (left) and her 14-year-old twin sisters, Zhou Lixin (middle) and Zhou Liyi (right), attend the “Mountain-Sea Bond” reunion ceremony in Shanghai, Aug. 1, 2026. The Shanghai Small and Medium-sized Enterprises Technology Talent Introduction Service Center has organized six such reunions since 2024. Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.title: ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ and Bicol’s unwavering fight for human rights
World.content:
DESAPARECIDOS. Scarecrows erected in the fields of the fictional town of Sinibaan symbolize the many farmers and activists who remain missing in the Philippines.

Weaving Bicol folk dance and music, the film 'An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’ shows the enduring hope of the families of the desaparecidos

ALBAY, Philippines – Drawing inspiration from the lives of Bicol farmers, An Sayaw nin mga Salampati (Dance of the Pigeons) transforms the grief and longing of the families of desaparecidos (victims of enforced disappearances) into a sharp look at the region’s long-standing fight against systemic human rights violations.

Through the haunting cadences of “Sarung Banggi” (One Evening), playful beats of “Salampating Guminaro” (The Little Pigeon That Has Grown Tame), the melancholic rhythm of “Kudot-kudotan” (The Pinching Game), and other Bicol folk music and dances, the film not only puts the spotlight on regional traditions, but also the people’s collective courage and resistance.

“Beyond being an agricultural nation, the Philippines suffers among the highest recorded cases of disappearances and extrajudicial killings targeting farmer-activists fighting for their ancestral land rights — a reality we aim to shed light on in this film,” said multi-awarded Bicolano filmmaker Arjanmar Rebeta.

Since the 1970s, at least 2,300 desaparecidos have remained missing in the Philippines. Among the latest recorded cases in Bicol are human rights defenders James Jazmines and Felix Salaveria Jr., who were both abducted by alleged state forces in Tabaco City, Albay.

Jazmines was taken on August 23, 2024, and Salaveria suffered the same fate five days later on August 28. Two years on, their families continue to search tirelessly and demand the safe resurfacing of both activists.

Defiance movement

“In the fictional town of Sinibaan, women dress scarecrows in the last-worn clothes of the disappeared to stand across the fields as a symbol of their families’ longing for their return. The women left behind by their desaparecido husbands dance the pantomina,” shared Rebeta.

Pantomina is a traditional Bicolano courtship dance, typically performed by newlyweds during weddings to mimic the movements of doves or pigeons.

For Rebeta, the characters performing the dance serve as “a stark reminder for the government and a courtship for justice — a movement that will continue as an act of remembrance and resistance.”

PROTEST. Reimagining the pantomina as an act of defiance, the women of ‘An Sayaw nin Mga Salampati’ channel collective grief into a movement that courts justice.

In the film, Ramona Yusay portrays Maura, a folk dance instructor whose husband, Lando (played by Jhong Hilario), has been forcibly disappeared.

Maura and the women of Sinibaan — including Gunda, played by Marietta “Pokwang” Subon — danced pantomina to “express their grief into the streets and fields, turning the dance into a challenge against a system that silences their voices and leaves their loved ones unaccounted for.”

The cast is also joined by local Bicolano artists and the region’s top creative talents in music, dance, and production, including performers Mildred Estella and Kyle Adrian Paga, alongside renowned composer and arranger Ruben Federizon.

Grassroots cinema

As a full-scale musical film, the production faced significant resource hurdles, especially for Giya Studios. Seeing the challenge, the local community stepped up — everyone from thrift shop vendors and farmers to even pigeon owners donated goods and services to drive the project forward.

“During our six-day first shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur, the community truly adopted us and helped us in so many ways — from small gestures to large contributions,” said Khaye Medina, managing director of Giya Studios.

“They helped us save on costs and sustain this advocacy project, doing everything from building production sets to joining us as talents.”

SOLIDARITY. Jhong Hilario, local talents, and volunteers help complete the first six-day shooting leg in Cabusao and Libmanan, Camarines Sur.

Medina shared that the local community members who joined as talents did not just help on set; they even organized a “Zumba for a Cause” event to raise funds for the film’s upcoming second shooting leg.

With most of the production crew working as volunteers, Medina and Rebeta emphasized that their top priority for the upcoming second leg is providing proper meals, accommodations, and transportation allowances for the team.

As of September 17, the film’s online crowdfunding campaign has raised P130,000 in cash donations, alongside production support and meal sponsorships provided by local communities.

“Of course, we provide honoraria to our talents, but we never expected them to take the initiative to give back and help us raise funds for production,” said Medina. “That is the real beauty of making this film — it is not just about the community; it is supported and embraced by them.”

FILMMAKERS. Filming across rural villages, production volunteers bring to life the 1990s landscape of the fictional town of Sinibaan.

– Rappler.com

The production team is preparing for its next shooting schedule and continues to seek partnerships, major sponsorships, collaborations, and other forms of support.

Those interested in helping can message ‘An Sayaw nin mga Salampati’s (Dance of the Pigeons)’ official Facebook page or contribute through its crowdfunding campaign.

World.title: Asian Games organizer says sorry for logistical headaches
World.content:
STAY. A man walks near Italian cruise ship Costa Serena, which will serve as a floating temporary athletes' village for 4,000 to 5,000 participants during the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games, after it docked at the port of Nagoya, Japan, September 15, 2026.

The unexpected surge of late entries has strained accommodation and transport networks in the Asian Games, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays

NAGOYA, Japan – The chief organizer of the Asian Games apologized on Saturday, September 26, for the logistical headaches plaguing the event, saying a late influx of athletes and officials had made it difficult to extend smooth service.

The number of participants at the continental showpiece ballooned to 17,000 following a flurry of late entries — around 2,000 more than the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games Organising Committee had initially projected.

The unexpected surge strained accommodation and transport networks, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms, small beds, and travel delays.

“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport, for various reasons,” AINAGOC Secretary General Satoshi Murate told a press conference.

“Whatever the cause, AINAGOC is responsible for providing the service, and I frankly apologzse for the mistakes.

“Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and make sure they don’t happen again. I think you can see that accommodation and transport have improved greatly compared with the early days.”

Murate added that maintaining consistent service standards had proved challenging following the “significant” increase in delegation sizes.

“Our top priority is making sure the athletes can compete at their best. We are fully committed to making the necessary improvements to ensure that they can do so,” he said.

“We are already working on a number of improvements, and in the second half of the Games, we want to make sure those efforts produce results and that we can manage things more smoothly and effectively.”

Mongolian women’s basketball coach Javier Garcia Alvarez criticized the transport system after a training session had to be scrapped when the team bus failed to arrive.

“I played in many FIBA Asia basketball cups and even Asian Games in Incheon some years ago. I never had this kind of issue that the bus is not coming for practice,” he told Reuters.

“It was kind of disappointing because we were planning some practice, some shooting for the girls and the mind was prepared for that, and then at the end we had to cancel.”

Filipino squash player Yvonne Alyssa Dalida had to endure a lengthy wait before checking into her room aboard a chartered cruise ship, though she found a silver lining in the unconventional setup.

“I think Japan or AINAGOC could have prepared better for this event, but I find it cool as well because it’s very unique.”

“I’ve never been on a cruise, so I think that’s also the upside of them using this.” – Rappler.com

World.title: [Tech Thoughts] How bad actors weaponize copyright to silence journalism online
World.content:
As a journalist whose primary world is being online, I didn’t really think much about how social media impacted the reach of stories. My concerns were mostly about writing stories, leaving much of the amplification of my work to others in Rappler.

It wasn’t until I attended an online webinar this week that I learned more about how bad actors use copyright and weaponize social media moderation and website takedown mechanisms to silence journalists and weaken — or negate — the reach of investigative journalism.

Wait, bad actors can do that?

The webinar, hosted by the Global Investigative Journalist Network (GIJN), had experts speaking out about instances journalists from around the world had experienced being silenced.

This isn’t a physical access issue, like what would happen if a president barred a reporter or a group of reporters within a press pool from being able to be in the same room with the president.

Instead, the webinar shared experiences and case studies showing how rampant and far-reaching the effects of bad actors are when they undertake the process of copyright-striking legitimate pages to get them taken down or to otherwise negate the ability of an investigative journalism piece to be shared or read.

How does this happen?

There are a number of ways in which this takes shape, but in broad strokes, it’s basically stealing and backdating content or faking evidence to make it appear as if the bad actors are the originators of the content seeking to be taken down.

There is apparently a thriving industry of “reputation management groups,” whether legitimate businesses or just smaller unofficial outfits willing to do dirty work for money, that advertise specific services. like content removal, webpage removal, mass reporting, astroturfing, or similar tasks.

To silence journalists, these bad actors make false reports to social media companies and fake evidence against legitimate groups or posts to get the social media companies’ automated systems to do the work of taking down a page for them.

For instance, Bangladeshi-based networks were operating to take down content in Central Asia and Africa.

To get takedowns done on social media, they would clone videos or steal the text of reports — say from an African investigative report. The bad actors would then, in the case of videos, add Bengali voiceovers on top of videos to make it seem from their region.

For videos or text pieces, they would then falsify further by backdating the content on social media or on a legitimate-seeming website so that they could say the content came from them and request the takedown of posts from the automated systems handling moderation on social media platforms like Facebook or X.

In some other instances, bad actors abuse the memorialization feature of Facebook — the feature that creates a static memorial page for dead Facebook users — to disable the posting capabiltiies of specific journalists.

The memorialization trick is more involved, as it requires falsifying death certificates and submitting the fake death certificate and possibly other documents to Facebook so the page can be memorialized.

In other parts of the world, where investigative journalists or teams work together and have a website for their investigations, copyright abuse is the trick used to get legitimate sites taken down.

Similar to social media takedowns, copyright abuse see bad actors cloning content and making a false website that backdates the content.

They then make bogus copyright requests so legitimate sites can be taken down and their search results scrubbed from search engines through the US Digital Millennium Copyright Act, even if the sites aren’t based in the United States.

What can be done?

While journalists are fighting the good fight of doing research and investigating anomalies, there are ways in which things could change to make this industry die out.

For victims of such actions, they can reach out to Access Now, a global nonprofit organization that helps get people back online by defending digital rights, or seek help from their local digital rights helpline, if a country has one.

Journalists may also want to investigate these malign actors, while digital advocacy groups can hold platforms — especially social media platforms frightened by intellectual property claims — accountable for offloading takedown requests to machines rather than humans. – Rappler.com

World.title: Valid visas, baseless claims: The aggressive deportation of Filipino seafarers
World.content:
Hundreds of seafarers — mostly Filipinos — were detained at US ports and shackled for deportation following interrogations 'full of torment and terror’

September 27 is National Seafarers’ Day. But this year’s theme, “Marinong Filipino: Matatag sa Alon, Matibay sa Hamon!” holds special irony for Filipino seafarers caught in the US immigration crackdown known as “Operation Tidal Wave.”

Operation Tidal Wave mandates Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) to arrest and deport cruise ship workers who allegedly consume child pornography.

According to US immigration lawyer Ian Seruelo, contrary to how US immigration has operated in the past, CBP is allowed to act solely on suspicion and is not required to produce evidence to support its allegations.

This has disproportionately impacted Filipino cruise ship workers.

Approximately 278 cruise ship workers — 270 of whom are Filipinos — have been deported from US ports since April 2025. Many were longtime cruise ship workers who had experienced no issues prior to 2025.

Source: Pilipino Workers Center

Aqui Soriano, executive director of Pilipino Workers Center (PWC), situated these deportations within the context of a changed US immigration system.

“Now there are less guardrails,” said Aqui. “In the push to fulfill Trump’s quota of 1 million deportations, they say they are targeting criminal aliens when the vast majority have no criminal records at all.”

Deported Filipino seafarers are part of this larger trend.

‘All Filipinos are suspect’

On cruise ships worldwide, almost 1 out of 3 workers is Filipino.

“So is there specific targeting or is it proportional?” asks Ellene Sana, executive director of the Quezon City-based Center for Migrant Advocacy. “We don’t know. But we know the impact of the deportations is far and wide.”

Deported seafarers attest to the severe impacts. Many are the primary breadwinners for intergenerational families. Many are still in debt from the cost of trainings and certifications required to land cruise ship employment. Many of them also believe that Filipinos are being specifically targeted for deportation.

“There was one Filipino who was caught in 2024,” said Reynaldo, a deported seafarer who worked as a galley attendant. “Since then I think that’s been an excuse to randomly target other Filipinos like us.”

Seruelo agrees that deported Filipino seafarers could be the victims of collective punishment.

“This administration has the propensity to do that,” he said. “Since one or two Filipino workers have been charged, now all Filipinos are suspects.”

No evidence to support accusations

At a September 21st public forum in Quezon City organized by PWC, the Center for Migrant Advocacy, and the Save Our Seafarers Coalition, seafarers shared their stories of being targeted, arrested, and deported by Customs and Border Patrol. A pattern emerges from these, as well as the stories of nine other seafarers interviewed by Rappler.

The seafarers were forcibly taken from ships docked at ports throughout the US, where they were legally and diligently working as cooks, casino dealers, galley attendants, motormen, security officers, and more.

Customs and Border Patrol agents interrogated them on their ships, searched their cabins — sometimes violently — seized their phones and confiscated many of their possessions. The seafarers were then taken off the ship for further interrogation at the port, with only the uniform on their backs, then shackled and transported by third-party private drivers to the nearest airport.

At the airport, many were subjected to further interrogation for hours, in freezing temperatures with no food and little water, and were not allowed to make phone calls or even talk to their fellow detainees.

All of the deported seafarers had valid C1/D visas that allowed them to work on their ships. None was attempting to enter the US by leaving their ships. All of the seafarers were subject to erratic accusations ranging from clicking on email links to affiliating with African child trafficking rings to possessing photos of naked children.

None of the seafarers interviewed by Rappler were ever presented with evidence to support CBP’s accusations. One seafarer, however, was shown a video he had taken of a seal swimming in the ocean as supposed “evidence” of child pornography.

‘Likely to jump ship’

Alex, a manager who has worked on cruise ships for more than 23 years, was accused of possessing child pornography, and also of terrorist activity through alleged involvement with Mexican drug cartels.

“I had no idea where this was coming from,” Alex said. “I just said no, of course I’ve never been involved in either of those things!”

Mark, a cook, said he was accused of clicking a link in a child pornography email, but when he asked to see the email, CBP never complied. CBP then pressured him to sign a form and threatened him with a US$100,000 fine.

Feeling he had no other choice, Mark signed, only to discover that the form had no mention of child pornography. All it said was he was “likely to jump ship” and that he was working illegally, even though he had a valid working visa.

Jordan, an assistant cook, was never even accused of a crime. He was just told there was a problem with his visa and then deported. He is now facing the same discrimination as the other seafarers for having a revoked US visa.

James, a motorman with more than 20 years experience working on cruise ships, believes that Filipinos are being deported using any reason that CBP can get away with, and not exactly for the sake of collective punishment.

“Filipinos are the main targets because they know that our government is weak,” said James. “The US has a quota to fill and they know the Philippine government is not going to do anything to protest.”

James was able to obtain a new contract on a Chinese ship, but only because he happened to have a contact in China. “The government didn’t help me at all,” he said.

Ellene Sana, executive director of the Center for Migrant Advocacy

Last year, approximately 90 deported seafarers were able to avail of monetary support from a newly created government Aksyon Fund. But according to Myrla Baldonado of PWC, this fund dried up and left the majority of deported seafarers without assistance.

Reynaldo, who is now working in Europe thanks to support from his manning agency, also expressed disappointment in the Philippine government.

“The DMW’s promises never came to fruition,” he said. “They excel at making promises and putting on appearances when the harsh reality is, it felt like a complete show just to make it look like they were doing their jobs.”

Advocates from the Save Our Seafarers coalition are hoping this will change.

At the September 21st forum, representatives from the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) and the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration (OWWA) both pledged a renewed commitment to helping deported seafarers.

“This situation is mas maingay, mas delikado (louder, more dangerous) because of our Middle East crisis. But this forum has triggered interest to let the government hear you again,” said DMW Assistant Secretary Ogie San Diego.

“We have to dwell on your innocence. The DMW wants to add personal welfare officers in every port, but we have to be careful about encroaching on the sovereignty of the US.”

OWWA lawyer Jasmine Ann Gapatan echoed the need to respect US sovereignty, but committed to individual case management for affected seafarers. She also announced new skills training for land-based employment including virtual assistant, barista, and digital content training.

Later that same afternoon, Senator Risa Hontiveros delivered a privilege speech on deported seafarers that urged the DMW and the Department of Foreign Affairs to account for every deported seafarers’ needs.

“A person should not lose an entire career simply because an allegation followed him home,” said Hontiveros. “The fight against child sexual abuse and the protection of due process are not opposing principles. We can, and must, do both.”

No new contracts

Ellene of CMA praised the senator’s speech saying it was a message of “assurance that the Philippine government heard [the seafarers’] cry for justice loud and clear.”

Hontiveros also called for stronger mechanisms for consular intervention, and pressing for compliance with mandatory consular notification.

This is a practice that could have helped James. At the time of his removal, CBP was also removing a Norwegian worker from the ship. But an HR representative from Viking Ocean Cruises called the Norwegian embassy, and as a result the Norwegian worker was allowed to stay. James did not receive the same treatment.

But James is one of the lucky ones who was able to find new work. A few others were helped by E-GMP International and North Seas, rare manning agencies who have actually stood up for their kababayan (compatriot). But the majority of deported seafarers are still searching for new contracts and facing discrimination along the way.

Carl and his wife Mica, who met while working in cruise ship casinos, have been unable to secure new contracts since April 2025. Carl was deported due to false accusations, and Mica was later forced to resign.

“The ordeal we went through was full of torment and terror,” said Carl. “More than a year has passed and it’s still a struggle. All we ask is for the chance to rebuild what was taken from us.”

Royal Caribbean regularly awarded Carl and Mica Employees of the Month while they worked on the ship. Given their skills and how popular they were with passengers and managers alike, Carl feels strongly that they are now being discriminated against given the false accusations of possessing child pornography. He appealed to both the government and manning agencies to do more for all deported seafarers.

“You call us OFWs the modern day heroes, but even heroes need help,” said Carl. “We are not asking for special treatment. We are asking for fairness, due process, and protection.”

There is foreign precedent for the protection Filipino seafarers are demanding. In September 2025, 300 South Koreans with valid B-1 visas were swept up in an immigration raid at a US auto plant. They were similarly placed in shackles, held in detention, and forced to sign documents they didn’t understand.

The South Korean government took swift action, with the president condemning the raid and the foreign minister flying to Washington within days. This diplomatic action led to a reversal from Trump, changes to the US visa system, and an offer to return to work for all Koreans affected by the raid.

Will the Philippine government follow South Korea’s example and step up its defense of Filipino seafarers? Or will more Filipino heroes have to suffer the consequences of what lawyer Ian Seruelo calls US immigration enforcement’s “groundless assaults on people’s rights”?

According to US Customs and Border Patrol, there is no deadline for Operation Tidal Wave, and it may even be extended to other ships, including cargo ships, in the future. – Rappler.com

Seafarers’ names have been changed to protect their privacy and prevent potential discrimination by government or manning agencies.

World.title: Stephen Curry, Warriors agree on 2-year extension – report
World.content:
Stephen Curry reportedly takes a deal $20 million below the max to give the Warriors more salary-cap flexibility next offseason

The Golden State Warriors and Stephen Curry agreed to a two-year, $116 million extension, ESPN reported.

The deal, according to the report, includes a player option for the 2028-29 season.

ESPN also reported that Curry will receive $20 million less than what he could have maxed out at to give the Warriors more salary-cap space for next offseason. According to the report, Curry and the team had been working on several contract ideas once he became eligible for a two-year, $136.7 million max deal in August.

If Curry plays through the 2028-29 campaign, it would be his 20th season, all with the Warriors.

The 38-year-old was limited to 43 games last season, with much of the time missed because of a lingering knee injury. Nonetheless, Curry averaged 26.6 points, 4.4 made three-pointers, and 11.3 attempted 3-pointers per game — all above his career averages.

A 12-time All-Star drafted seventh overall out of Davidson in 2009, Curry has two scoring titles, two MVP awards, and a Finals MVP award to go with four NBA championships. However, the Warriors are coming off a 37-45 season, their worst in a non-shortened season since going 36-46 in 2010-11.

Earlier this week, Curry said he wanted “no drama” with the contract talks, particularly with camp opening on Tuesday, September 29.

“The idea of getting back to work is exciting,” Curry said Wednesday, September 23. “I feel like I’ve taken advantage of the offseason. I feel like there’s no hesitation about where I’m at physically going in. … But I’m excited about getting back to work.”

Curry has career averages of 24.8 points, 4.0 made three-pointers, and 9.4 attempted per game. The latter two marks are NBA records, as is his career .912 free throw percentage.

He also holds the NBA career marks for three-pointers made (4,248) and attempted (10,073). – Rappler.com

World.title: When the lepa lights up, Tawi-Tawi tells its story
World.content:
LIGHTS ON THE WATER. Decorated lepa glow along the Bongao waterfront after nightfall during the Lepa Festival.

At the Philippines’ southern edge, a festival of boats, dance, music, and light offers a glimpse of a maritime culture deeply rooted in community

BONGAO, Philippines — From the plane, Tawi-Tawi first appears in blue.

As the aircraft descends toward Sanga-Sanga Airport, the Sulu Sea fills the window, broken by islands, reefs, and strips of green. For someone coming from the mountains of Northern Luzon, the landscape feels almost like another country.

But what strikes you first is not distance. It is how much of Tawi-Tawi still feels untouched by the kind of tourism that can reshape a place before visitors have learned to understand it.

The sea is everywhere. Boats are everywhere. Communities remain closely tied to the water. You see the beauty, and you hope it stays that way.

On my first evening in the province, I was told there was an event at the port. I went. The masts were the first things I saw.

They rose above the crowd in the fading light, ornate wooden forms visible from a distance before the boats themselves came into view. Up close, the waterfront was a burst of color.

Red, yellow, green, pink, blue, and gold streamed from the boats. Cloth stretched from tall masts toward the bows. Flags fluttered above carved hulls. Decorative panels, umbrellas, lights, and patterns made each vessel distinct.

This was the Lepa Festival, part of the Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi, the province’s founding anniversary celebration. Then the music started.

LEPA ON DISPLAY. A brightly decorated lepa joins the Lepa Festival in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi, on September 24, 2026, as part of the 53rd Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi. All photos by Mia Magdalena Fokno/Rappler

Almost every boat seemed to have its own sound system. Songs overlapped across the water as dancers moved on narrow decks, surrounded by musicians, children, and performers waiting their turn.

The noise was immense. So was the energy. Amid it all, the dancers held your attention.

Their movements were controlled and fluid, especially in the hands and wrists. Some of the women wore long silver fingernail extensions that gave every gesture more shape and drama. Men and children danced alongside them.

The performances drew from igal, a traditional dance associated with Sama communities, known for expressive movements of the hands, arms, and body.

Even in the din, the dancers moved with remarkable composure. The boats themselves carried another story.

IGAL. Dancers perform igal during the Lepa Festival in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi.

The lepa is more than a festival vessel. Traditionally, it served as home, transport, and livelihood for Sama Dilaut communities whose lives were closely connected to the sea.

Many families later moved into stilt houses along the coast, but the lepa remains one of the strongest symbols of that maritime heritage.

Beneath the lights and decorations were carved hulls, elaborate wooden forms, long sweeps of cloth, and craftsmanship passed down over generations.

There were LED lights and generators, too. This was not an attempt to freeze culture in the past. It was culture being carried into the present.

Nothing about the festival felt like heritage placed neatly on display for outsiders.

People were dancing on the boats. Children were performing. Musicians were playing. Crews checked ropes and lights. Families watched from the shore. Spectators took photos and videos, but the boats still felt like community spaces rather than props.

The pride was unmistakable.

HERITAGE UNDER THE MOON. An ornate masthead rises above a lepa during the 53rd Kamahardikaan sin Tawi-Tawi celebration in Bongao, with the evening moon visible in the background.

Entries came from different municipalities across Tawi-Tawi, with some supported by local officials.

As darkness settled over Bongao, the crowd thickened along the waterfront, and the tall masts formed a colorful skyline over the port.

Then came the countdown. Generators were switched on. One by one, the lepa lit up!

Green, purple, blue, red, and white lights traced the hulls, masts, carvings, and cloth. Their reflections shimmered across the dark water.

Phones went up. Children pressed closer to the front. The dancers kept moving. For a few minutes, the entire waterfront seemed to glow.

Governor Yshmael “Mang” Sali and Vice Governor Al-Syed Sali were among the provincial officials present, along with mayors, members of the Bangsamoro Parliament, and other local leaders who also served as judges.

But the officials were not the center of the night. The boats were. More importantly, the people who built, decorated, sailed, danced on, and gathered around them were.

Hja. Elmasia Madjilon, Tawi-Tawi commissioner of the Bangsamoro Commission for the Preservation of Cultural Heritage, described the lighting of the lepa as something larger than spectacle.

“We are not just simply lighting a traditional vessel,” she told the crowd. “We are bringing life to a story that has traveled across generations.”

She spoke of the lepa as a vessel carrying knowledge of boatmaking, navigation, art, and a way of life shaped by the waters surrounding the islands.

“Every form, every design, and every meter carries the memory and wisdom of our ancestors,” she said.

YOUNG DANCERS. Children perform traditional dance movements aboard and beside decorated lepa during the festival in Bongao, showing how cultural traditions continue to be passed on to younger generations.

Standing beside the boats, that was easy to understand. Heritage here was not confined to a museum. It was in the carved wood, the dancers’ hands, the children learning the movements, and the people who still knew how to build, decorate, and explain the vessels.

Festivals can sometimes reduce culture to spectacle.

There was certainly spectacle in Bongao that night: bright lights, competing sound systems, prizes, judges, and hundreds of phones pointed toward the water. But the celebration never felt hollow.

It felt communal, joyful, and rooted in place. Coming from the Cordillera, I found something familiar in that.

The landscapes could not be more different, but communities in the North also carry traditions while negotiating a rapidly changing world.

In the mountains, identity is often tied to land, ritual, weaving, memory, and place.

In Tawi-Tawi, much of that story is carried by the sea.

And on my first night in the Philippines’ southernmost province, those stories glowed on the water, one lepa after another. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Two Pronged] Our undergraduate interns are a nightmare
World.content:
'This year, I decided to expand our internship program to include AB (undergraduate) seniors in our internship. It is a nightmare and we will never do it again.'

Rappler’s People section runs an advice column by couple Jeremy Baer and clinical psychologist Dr. Margarita Holmes.

Jeremy has a master’s degree in law from Oxford University. A banker of 37 years who worked in three continents, he has been training with Dr. Holmes for the last 10 years as co-lecturer and, occasionally, as co-therapist, especially with clients whose financial concerns intrude into their daily lives.

Together, they have written two books: Love Triangles: Understanding the Macho-Mistress Mentality and Imported Love: Filipino-Foreign Liaisons.

Dear Dr. Holmes and Mr. Baer,

I am the head of an HR dept in a mid size hospital in Metro Manila. As part of my position and for the past 15 years, I have been in charge of internship programs for graduate students enrolled in the allied medical fields (OT, MT, etc).

This year, I decided to expand our internship program to include AB (undergraduate) seniors in our internship.

It is a nightmare and we will never do it again. At first the undergrad interns showed such promise: not as scared as the older graduates to speak up their minds. But then they started expecting their opinions to be “respected” which really means to be accepted as truth, even if they have no research or past clinical experience to back these up.

Worse, they do not have the amor propio (self respect) to apologize or even be embarrassed when they are caught inventing their test results.

They even complain that they are “triggered” when our staff scold them for things that graduate students accept, apologize for, and try to do better.

We want to stop this internship program for undergraduates but the owner of the hospital does not. The kudos he receives for this is so much that I think that (and not the program) is what he resists losing.

Please help.

– Aimee

Dear Aimee,

You are clearly unhappy with the quality of the current batch of undergraduate interns that your company has hired. However, if it is in fact the case that the owner of the company is determined to maintain the program, then there is presumably little or nothing that you can do to cancel future intakes.

That said, there are other avenues you can explore. I imagine there is a selection process which you can use to weed out those applicants who demonstrate the qualities above that you find unacceptable, always supposing that the interns are unwilling to change their ways.

In addition, when individual interns reach the end of their internships, the company can simply decide not to employ them further.

A problem may develop if the company owner relies on some of these interns becoming full time employees. The fact that none successfully graduates will give you the opportunity to discuss the unsuitability of the present intake and the sustainability of an AB senior intern program, at least as it is structured now, and support your view that AB seniors do not align with your corporate requirements.

An additional argument in your favor must be that no company should be keen to employ people who are willing to invent test results and not take responsibility when caught out.

At the end of the day, your owner may come round to the view that an internship program that ultimately does not benefit his company is a luxury he can ill afford, whatever the supposed kudos involved.

Best wishes,

– JAF Baer

Dear Aimee,

Thank you very much for your letter. Thank you too, Mr Baer, for adding the perspective needed about how companies really work for those of us who have never worked in one.

When I first read your letter, I thought it might mean simply underscoring the differences between Gen Z and Gen Y (millennials). These would include what research backs up as “typically gen Z” and “typically Gen Y.”

Usually, a Gen Z person is anyone born between 2012 and 1996 (ages 14 to 29 in 2026).

This would then include most of both the BA and MA graduates; most MA students are usually Gen Z-ers themselves. So any differences between your MA graduates (older Gen Z-er’s) and your BA graduates may just be differences between the oldest among the Gen Z-ers and the not-so-old.

An alternative explanation is that your perception of the differences may also be a function of your expectations. This anticipation of expanding your program to include undergraduate seniors in your internship must have garnered some attention at least among other hospitals. Hence, the kudos given the owner of yours. Kudos he may be reluctant to lose — especially after so short a time.

It is tempting to “demonize” a group because their characteristics are so different from previous interns and much more difficult to adjust to.

Perhaps, the excitement of the new expansion encouraged you to focus solely on the good that could come from it, and minimize the possible problems.

It would be understandable to assure oneself that: “Nothing major could possibly go wrong! These (already) senior undergrads are just a year younger than most of the interns we already have in our program.”

But I think problems arose, thus things did go wrong and having such high expectations made them seem worse than they really were.

It is easy to look for a scapegoat when plans go awry and much easier when problems that arise are so closely connected (at least in time) to the new group that just came in. But it could only mean that new procedures are always difficult to adjust to. It could even be that this particular group of AB seniors have quirks much more difficult to take.

Mr Baer’s suggestion to improve your selection process might be most important. It might not necessarily mean the next bunch of interns you decide to bring in will be perfect, but I think they will be far better than those you already have.

At the risk of sounding naïve, I doubt your ending this expansion immediately will be well received either by your boss, but also by your cohorts.

Another way of dealing with this problem is to concentrate on yourself.

The most important is to try and shift your nervous system from one that is, at present, on high alert and thus reactive, and take slow, deep breaths that will calm you.

Another calming possibility is acknowledging your feelings: Is it frustration? Shock? Extreme disappointment? Or merely confusion? If you can do this without judging or berating yourself, (after all, we cannot be responsible for our feelings, just for what we do with them) you will be in a better state to decide what the best next step might be.

Finally, avoid immediate assumptions: Remind yourself that an unexpected difference is not automatically a catastrophe or a personal threat.

These three suggestions will not solve all your problems, but I hope will ease some of the worry that block us from choosing the most rational decision. It takes a lot of courage to try and improve a system that was already running smoothly. It takes even more courage to recognize and admit that, in the beginning at least, it seemed not the best decision to make.

And yet, you did both of that! Kudos to you!

With every best wish!

– MG Holmes

– Rappler.com

Life got complicated? Write to our Two Pronged duo at twopronged@rappler.com.

World.title: [Tambay] Eggie Apostol, Recah Trinidad: Pagpupugay sa mga alamat ng peryodismo
World.content:
Noong nakaraang linggo sinakluban ng pagluluksâ ng mga Filipinong peryodista sa magkasunod na pagpanaw ng dalawang haligi ng industriya. Pahintulutan po ninyo ang abang tambay na ito na saluduhan sila — si Eugenia “Eggie” Apostol at Recah Trinidad.

* * *

May urban legend noong early ’80s sa mga estudyanteng manginginom ng UST AB tulad ng tambay na ito. Sa Piso-piso kami nagpapalipas ng oras kapag may break sa pagitan ng mga klase. Kaniya-kaniyang dukot sa allowance para ambag sa pambilí ng pangpawi ng uhaw. Malamig na San Miguel Beer ang paboritong serbesa. Pero ang mga babae kong kaklase Red Horse ang tinutungga. Mas malakas pa sila uminom kaysa sa aming mga lalaki.

Doon sa Piso-piso sa kalye Asturias halos katapat ng UST Dapitan gate ko unang nadinig ang pangalang Recah Trinidad. Yung henerasyon daw nila kasi ng mga taga-UST AB noong ’70s ang nagbansag sa Piso-piso. Mga literati ang pagkakakilanlan sa grupo nila Recah.

Yari lang ng kahoy ang estrukturang puwesto ng Piso-piso, tulad ng mga tipikal na aksesorya o bahay-paupahan sa Maynila nung panahong ito. Lumalangitngit ang nilalakarang sahig. Kahoy na walang tapete ang mesa. Kahoy din ang mga upuan. Malapad at bukas na bukas ang kupas na bintanang capiz para makapasok ang preskong hangin Maynila.

Mga dormitoryo, karinderya, sari-sari store at shop ng sastre’t modista ang makikita paglabas ng Dapitan gate. Walang pa yung mga mamahaling coffee shop at burger joints. Noong panahon iyon, dalawang restoran ang de-aircon ang malapit sa Dapitan gate, yung Janet’s at Food Pan. Parehong hindi ako nakakain sa dalawang iyan dahil hindi afford ng allowance ko.

Dahil tinapos na ni Marcos Sr. ang Martial Law noong dulo ng 1980 pinayagang mag-organisa muli ang mga student council. Ipinagbawal kasi noong Batas Militar ang mga student council, tulad ng pagsupil sa malayang pamamahayag. Pero ang totoo, sa papel lang nawala ang Batas Militar — pakitang-tao ng rehimeng Marcos dahil iyan ang kasama sa mga kondisyon para paunlakan ni Pope John Paul II ang imbitasyon na dumalaw sa Pinas.

Namulat ako sa pakikibaka noong panahon iyon dahil sa pagbabasa ng mosquito press, kasama na dito yung Mr. & Ms. magazine. Dahil yung mga malalaking mainstream media (TV, radyo, telebisyon) ay pag-aari ng mga crony ni Marcos, panay puri sa diktador ang mababasa, mapapakinggan, mapapanood dito. Ang nag-uulat o nagbibigay ng opinyon sa mga kabuktutan ng diktadurya ay yung mga maliliit na media na binansagang mosquito press. Doon sa Mr. & Ms. ko binabasa ang mga kolum nila Rene Saguisag, SP Lopez, Max Soliven. Yung nanay ko, palibhasa single parent ng tatlong growing boys, ginugupit ang pahina ng magasin para sa mga suggested ulam for the week.

Ang editor at may-ari ng Mr. & Ms. ay si Eugenia D. Apostol.

Kung tutuusin, mapanganib ang sumulat at magbasa ng mga anti-Marcos na artikulo noon. Maaari kang makulong. Kung susuwertihin, mawawalan ka lang ng trabaho. Kahit ganoon ang sitwasyon, tuloy pa rin ang paninindigan ni Ms Apostol sa Mr. & Ms. Si Recah naman naging unang editor ng Tempo, ang tabloid ng pro-Marcos na grupo ng pahayagang Bulletin Today. Panay din ang sundot ni Recah sa gobyerno sa mga editorial ng Tempo. Di nagtagal, sinibak sa trabaho si Recah. Sumunod sa kanya ang iba pang mga editor ng Tempo, kasama ang kanyang “sparring partner” na si Al S. Mendoza.

* * *

Nag-umpisa ako sa Philippine Daily Inquirer noong 1986, katatapos lang noon ng EDSA People Power at sinipa na ng taumbayan ang pamilya Marcos. Si Cory Aquino na ang pangulo.

Maliit na pahayagan lang ang Inquirer noon. Ang opisína nito ay nasa 13th corner Railroad Street, Port Area. Building iyon ng Star publications ng pamilya ni Betty Go-Belmonte.

Para sa isang uhúging sportswriter tulad ko, mind-blowing ang maging bahagi ng Inquirer at makasama ang mga idol mong manunulat. (Ang isa pang bigatin na naabutan ko sa Inquirer, bagaman hindi ko nakadaupang-palad ay ang National Artist na si Nick Joaquin. Ang kolum niyang “Small Beer” ay nasa page 1 ng PDI. Kaibigan ni Recah at Al si Ginoong Joaquin.)

Tatlong grupo ang nag-ambagan para mabuo ang Philippine Daily Inquirer. Pangunahing layunin nila ang mabigyan ng boses ang oposisyon para sa pinatawag ni Marcos sa snap elections. Ang building at ang printing press (na nasa loob ng gusaling iyon) ang ambag ng grupo nila Betty Go. Yung grupong civil society na nakilala naming mga reporter noon ay pinamumunuan nila Dr. Florangel Braid, Danilo Venida, at Anicia Mejia, bitbit ang financial backing at administrative know-how. Si Eggie Apostol ang nagdala ng office equipment, at editorial staff. Doon sa pioneering PDI group kasama ang Big 3 na mga kolumnísta na sila Max Soliven, Art Borjal, at Louie Beltran, na siyang naging unang editor in chief.

Maliit lang na kumpanya nag-umpisa ang PDI. Masikip na opisina, maingay, kulang sa gamit. Parang pamilya ang pagpapatakbo. Kaya’t yung mga reporter, Tita Eggie at Tita Betty ang tawag kay Mrs. Apostol at Mrs. Belmonte.

Ang pangarap sana ng mga orihinal na bumuo ng PDI ay maging isa itong kooperatibang mga peryodísta ang magpapatakbo. Yun nga lang, medyo nalihis ito. Ikanga sa Ingles: “life happened.”

Bandang July 1986 lumipat ang Inquirer sa bagong opisina, ang dating Madrid Restaurant sa EDSA, Mandaluyong (katabi ng noo’y Polymedic Hospital at ngayo’y VRP Medical Center). Noong araw na lumipat ang PDI sa Madrid ang araw din na pinaalam ni Tita Betty na aalis na siya ng Inquirer. (Sa ibang araw na yung kuwento ko tungkol diyan.) Kasama niyang umalis yung Big 3 na mga kolumnista.

Si Tita Eggie at ang grupo ng civil society ang namuno muna kaya tuloy pa din yung pangarap na maging kooperatiba. Noong 1987, sa bisperas ng sana’y unang company-sponsored Valentine’s Party na gaganapin sa bagong opisina sa Madrid, inanúnsiyó ng mga reporter na binuo nila ang PDI Employees’ Union. Kasabay nito sinabi sa management ng bagong silang na union na nais nilang bumuo ng collective bargaining agreement.

Bagaman nginingitian pa rin niya kami, tumamlay ang pakikiharap sa amin ni Tita Eggie. Noong unang CBA ng PDI, nakumpirma namin na kahit may tampo sa amin si Tita Eggie, ang puso niya ay nasa kapakanan ng mga peryodista. Halos patapos na ang negosasyon sa CBA, nung may dalawang probisyon na pinadagdag sa kasunduan sila Tita Eggie at yung grupo nila Dr. Braid. Una, ang magkaroon ng health insurance ang mga empleyado na tutustusan ng kumpanya. Ikalawa, ang magkaroon ng profit-sharing.

Noon at magpa-hanggang ngayon, bihira ang kumpanyang kusang nagbibigay ng bahagi ng kinita sa mga manggagawa. Hindi ito hiningi ng PDIEU. Management sa ilalim ni Tita Eggie at nung grupong civil society ang nagdagdag nito sa CBA.

Natural, wala kaming tutol. Kahit alam namin na noong panahon iyon, halos walang kinikita ang PDI.

* * *

Taga-sambot ako nung araw ng kolum ni Ka Recah. Dinidikta niya ito sa telepono (landline, dahil hindi pa naimbento noon ang cellphone), at agad ko naman tinitipa sa typewriter. Dito ko unang nakasalamuhà ang alamat.

Bukod sa sports kolum niyang “Bare Eye,” minsan idinidikta rin sa akin ni Ka Recah ang kanyang sinusumiteng mga artikulo. Sa aking pagbabalík-tanáw, proud ako na napagdaanan ko ito. Naiisip ko din na ang suwerte ko.

Malapitan kong namalas kung gaano kagaling na manunulat si Recah. Nasa hanay siya ng mga bukod-tanging journalist na — baga sa Ingles “among the rarefied group worthy of the title ‘auteurs’.” Minsan pinayuhan niya akong magbasa ng mga akda ng Amerikanong nobelistang si Ernest Hemingway. Ang sabi ko kay Ka Recah nakabasa nako ng ilang nobela ni Hemingway, at napansin kong magkahawig sila ng estílo.

Mapili at mabusisi siya sa mga salitang ginagamit niya. Minsan tapos na ang aming diktahan at naibaba na ang telepono. Tatawag pa ulit si Ka Recah at may papalitang salita o paragraph. Kailan ko lang nalaman na akma pala ang bansag namin sa kanya na “wordsmith.” Ginawaran pala si Recah noong 1978 ng Carlos Palanca Award for English poetry.

Gayunman, tumatak sa akin ang kababaang-loob ni Recah. Nilalarawan niya sa sarili niya na isa lamang “typist who is racing the rat.” Pinong-pino siya tumuligsa sa kanyang kolum sa mga isyu o personalidad na hindi niya sinasang-ayunan. Ika nga, punyal ang kanyang pangtarak sa kanyang kolum, hindi siya gumagamit ng maso.

Dahil sa kanyang kakaibang pangalan (kasi nga Recah, na tila babaeng Rico), madalas ay makatanggap siya tuwing Valentine’s Day ng mga bouquet ng rosas at kahon ng tsokolate. Nagpapasalamat siya sa nagbigay, sabay sabi na may ireregalo na siya sa “resident China doll” nila — ang kanyang maybahay na si Fe Lacsamana.

Sumilip ang pagiging literati ni Ka Recah nung binyagang niyang “Point Laureate” ang PBA player na si Ronnie Magsanoc. Malapit din niyang kaibigan ang kilalang pintor na si Danny Dalena ng Pakil, Laguna. Madalas dumalaw si Dalena kanila Ka Recah at Al Mendoza sa opisina ng Inquirer. Unang tingin mo pa lang kay Dalena, alam mo agad na artist siya dahil sa trademark niyang suot na sombrero at kahoy na bakya.

Isa pang malapit na kaibigan ni Recah ay si Ramon Tulfo. Magkasama na sila nung araw sa Bulletin Today at maging sa Inquirer.

Taong 2024, huli kong nakita si Ka Recah. Lamay iyon ng panganay niyang si Chino na nasawi sa atake sa puso. Napasakit sa isang magulang ang mamatayan ng anak. Niyakap ako ni boss, at bumulong sa tenga ko ng may makirot na tinig: “Hindi ko na naabutang buhay, Tochi.”

* * *

Nung nagretiro ako sa Inquirer matapos ang mahigit tatlong dekadang paninilbihan, sinulat ko sa isang social media post na ang highlight sa mahabang listahan ko ng good memories ay ang makapaglakad sa lilim ng mga anino ng mga higante ng Philippine journalism. Si Recah at Tita Eggie ang mga nangunguna sa listahan kong iyon.

Dahil sa kanilang mga ambag sa pagsulong ng malayang pamamahayag, nababagay kay Tita Eggie at Recah ang nasabi ng bida sa pelikulang halaw sa Greek epic ni Homer — “sasambitin ang kanilang pangalan habang panahon.” – Rappler.com

Si Chito de la Vega ay Tambay ng Rappler dalawang beses kada buwan. Kasama rin siya sa mga anchor-host ng programang Balita Kwento Serbisyo ng DZME 1530.

World.title: From Tiny Corals to Caspian Seals: Exhibition in Astana Traces Nature’s Connections
World.content:
ASTANA – From coral reefs and the microscopic organisms that sustain them to marine mammals inhabiting the Caspian Sea, every species is part of a larger natural system. A photo exhibition that explores this interconnected world opened in Astana on Sept. 23, bringing together stories of biodiversity from Kazakhstan and around the world.

An exhibition, titled “Invisible World: A City Underwater” will run through Nov. 1.

One biodiversity story comes from a small laboratory in London, where marine biologist Jamie Craggs, a co-founder of Coral Spawning International, managed to recreate the natural conditions required for coral spawning. The work has opened new possibilities for producing young corals in controlled conditions while maintaining greater genetic diversity.

The project later expanded to the Seychelles, where Nature Seychelles established another laboratory as part of the Assisted Recovery of Coral (ARC) Programme. Unlike traditional coral gardening methods, the project uses sexual reproduction to produce genetically diverse corals. Early results recorded the settlement and growth of around 65,000 young corals.

As Maral Rakhimzhanova, corporate communications manager at Canon’s representative office in Kazakhstan, explained, the importance of coral reefs extends far beyond their colourful appearance.

“Corals are very colorful, but in fact their color is given by algae that live in symbiosis with them. It is a relationship between two living organisms,” she said.

When water temperatures rise, corals can become stressed and expel the algae living within their tissues, causing coral bleaching. If the stress continues, the corals may eventually die. Reefs also provide food and shelter for a wide range of marine species, linking corals to the wider food chain.

Rakhimzhanova noted that these connections are relevant for a landlocked country such as Kazakhstan, as changes in one part of the natural world can have consequences far beyond it.

The same idea takes a different form in Kazakhstan’s waters, where the Caspian seal is among the species facing a changing environment. The animal, which is found only in the Caspian Sea, is included in Kazakhstan’s Red Book and has been the subject of long-term research by scientist Assel Baimukanova.

“Field research shows that these animals have their own character and social interactions that we are still learning to understand. The Caspian Sea is their home, and protecting the Caspian seal has become my main goal. These animals are affected by a range of factors, including shipping, fishing, environmental pollution and climate change. As the sea changes, seals are also forced to adapt and change their usual resting sites,” Baimukanova explained.

“The health of the Caspian seal is closely connected to the health of the Caspian Sea itself. By observing how the animals are doing, we can learn a great deal about the condition of the ecosystem they depend on. Exhibitions like this help bring scientific research closer to the public, make science more accessible and encourage more people to take an interest in these issues,” Baimukanova told The Astana Times.

Her photographs are featured alongside works by Mirgaliy Baimukanov, a director of the Institute of Hydrobiology and Ecology, Dmitry Malakhov, a researcher at the Institute of Zoology of Kazakhstan, wildlife photographer Vladislav Yakushkin and birdwatcher Gennady Dyakin. Illustrations of rare fish by designers Vladimir Timokhanov and Timofei Bannikov add another perspective to the collection.

The story extends beyond photography through virtual reality technology, allowing visitors to virtually explore coral reefs and experience the underwater environment.

World.title: Murder? Ancient Burial in Southern Kazakhstan Reveals Woman With Fatal Skull Injury
World.content:
ASTANA – Archaeologists excavating ancient burial sites in southern Kazakhstan have uncovered the remains of a woman with a fatal skull injury, among findings dating to the Late Bronze Age and the Kangju period.

Researchers are now examining whether the injury was linked to violence or to a burial practice previously undocumented in the region, according to Otyrar.kz news website.

The excavation was led by Alexander Podushkin, a doctor of historical sciences and professor at the South Kazakhstan Pedagogical University named after Ozbekali Zhanibekov, with specialists from the Ordabasy state historical-cultural reserve. Podushkin has led excavations of Kangju period burial grounds in the region before, including inscribed bricks and funerary artifacts unearthed this July.
