World.title: Azerbaijan's ombudsman issues statement on September 27 - Remembrance Day
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 27. Azerbaijani Ombudsman Sabina Aliyeva has issued a statement on September 27 - Remembrance Day.

The letter reads:

"Six years have passed since the Patriotic War that began on September 27, 2020. That day is not only a significant milestone in the history of the Azerbaijani people, but also holds great importance in addressing the severe humanitarian consequences of the conflict, bringing to justice those who committed war crimes resulting in loss of life, and restoring rights violated for many years.

The Patriotic War became a new phase in the restoration of Azerbaijan's territorial integrity and violated fundamental rights of people who had been forcibly displaced from their native lands for many years.

Harm to the lives and health of the civilian population, and the destruction of settlements and social infrastructure during the war resulted in serious humanitarian consequences. These events demonstrate once again that the civilian population bears the heaviest burden of armed conflicts, and that the protection of civilians under the international humanitarian law, as well as the safeguarding of their right to life, must remain a constant priority.

During the Patriotic War, the armed forces of Armenia shelled densely populated Azerbaijani settlements, particularly Ganja, Barda, Naftalan, and Tartar, and other cities and districts, using heavy artillery and internationally prohibited long-range missile systems. These attacks resulted in civilian casualties and injuries and caused serious damage to residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure, including social, educational, healthcare, religious, and other facilities. These facts were documented in reports prepared by the Azerbaijani Ombudsman during the fact-finding missions carried out at that time.

It is essential to conduct an objective and comprehensive investigation into violations of international law regarding the attacks against the civilian population and civilian objects, and to identify those responsible and hold them accountable in accordance with national legislation and applicable international law. Preventing impunity for those responsible for such acts is crucial for the protection of human rights and the prevention of the recurrence of similar incidents in the future.

As the Commissioner for Human Rights (Ombudsman) of the Republic of Azerbaijan, I believe that restoring human rights violated as a result of war and conflict, determining the fate of missing persons, clearing areas contaminated with mines and unexploded remnants of war, and ensuring the safe and dignified return of formerly displaced persons to their native lands are among the key humanitarian priorities of the post-conflict period.

From this standpoint, large-scale restoration and reconstruction works in the liberated territories, the return of people to their native lands, and the reliable guarantee of all their fundamental rights make a significant contribution to strengthening peace and sustainable development.

The significant results achieved in advancing the peace agenda, also in finalizing the peace treaty between Azerbaijan and Armenia are of particular importance for the future of the region as a whole. This process creates new opportunities for strengthening sustainable and long-term peace, stability, security, and cooperation.

In this regard, sustaining the gains made towards peace and transforming them into lasting peace places a significant responsibility on international organizations, the global community, States, national human rights institutions, and civil society.

September 27 is not merely the day that marked the beginning of large-scale counter-offensive operations that put an end to the policy of aggression, occupation, and provocation pursued against our republic and people for many years. Today has also been etched in memory as a day demonstrating the power of our state, our army, which achieved victory under the leadership of the country’s President and Commander-in-Chief, Mr. Ilham Aliyev, and our people, who displayed a true example of patriotism even in the most difficult times.

Respectfully honoring the cherished memory of our compatriots who have fallen for the territorial integrity and sovereignty of our Motherland, I wish patience for their families and a healthy, prosperous future for war participants and all those affected by the war.

I truly believe that the greatest tribute to the memory of our martyrs is to ensure that future generations live in peace, security, and prosperity, free from war and violence. I wish the legacy and cherished memory left to us by Remembrance Day - a day etched in our history with solemn and honorable memories will bring tranquility to our country and people, solid and lasting peace to our region, a secure life free from war, and progressive development."

World.title: Wallaroos 'got some work to do' despite snapping losing streak
World.content:
Snapping a six-match losing streak was not enough to leave the Wallaroos satisfied with their 30-10 win over Scotland in Edinburgh this morning.

The Wallaroos were outplayed in the first half, with Scotland entering the break with a 10-5 lead in the WXV Global Series Test.

But following a blunt half-time address from their coaching staff and with the wind behind them in the second term, the Wallaroos regrouped to score 25 unanswered points and secure their first victory since March.

Desiree Miller provided the only points for the Wallaroos in the first half with a try.

Samantha Wood, Brianna Hoy and player-of-the-match Faitala Moleka crossed the stripe in the second half.

The three second-half tries were scored during seven minutes, with Hoy and Moleka's efforts coming while Scotland was reduced to 14 players following Evie Gallagher's yellow card.

Wood added two conversions and as many penalty goals to finish with a 15-point haul.

"Credit to Scotland, they found opportunities, and you could see where they exploited those areas," Wallaroos captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona said after the match.

"Overall, we know we have a lot of things to improve on, but we'll take the positives out of that."

Palu Sekona said the Wallaroos were taught some harsh lessons in the previous week's 29-26 loss to France in Aix-en-Provence.

The Wallaroos had led 19-0 during the match, while France had only 11 players on the field at one stage due to red and yellow cards.

"We learned from last week's game," Palu Sekona said.

"We have to be relentless. When you get opportunities like that [Gallagher's yellow card], you've got to capitalise."

The Wallaroos celebrate Desiree Miller's (right) first-half try. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Rugby Australia's director of women's high performance Tim Walsh is essentially the Wallaroos' caretaker head coach until Sione Fukofuka assumes the role next year.

Walsh was unimpressed with the Wallaroos' display in the opening half, admitting he did not hide his feelings when he spoke to the players at the break.

"It wasn't a pleasant message," Walsh said.

"I thought if we didn't have two or three individuals that really took the game to Scotland, I reckon it would have been a draw, or we would have lost.

"So I wasn't happy with our performance. Glad we got the win and came home with it, but the advantage was the wind and a few key players who I thought had tremendous games."

The Wallaroos are heading back to Australia, with two WXV Global Series Tests against Scotland coming up next month.

They play each other in Sydney on October 17, ahead of the Wallabies' Bledisloe Cup clash against the All Blacks.

The final Test will be staged in Canberra on October 23.

As far as Walsh is concerned, the Wallaroos will not be taking the easy route on the training paddock over the next three weeks.

"We've got some work to do," he said.

World.title: Pressure grows to import experimental sea lion vaccine as bird flu campaign launches
World.content:
The Federal Government has launched a national education campaign on the H5N1 bird flu to provide "practical advice" to Australians on what to do if they come across sick or dead birds.

It comes as 652 bird flu events have been recorded across the country, with 319 in SA, 67 in NSW, two in QLD, 45 in Tasmania, 208 in Victoria and 10 in WA.

Speaking in Hobart on Sunday, Federal Minister for Agriculture Julie Collins said the new 'Bird flu - Know what to do' campaign will run across television, radio, social media and other channels for six weeks.

"What it does is encourages Australians to take simple steps to know what to do if they encounter a suspected bird flu event," Ms Collins said.

Federal Minister for Agriculture Julie Collins launched the campaign on Sunday. (ABC News)

"I remind Australians to avoid touching sick or dead birds... and to report suspected cases to the emergency animal disease hotline through birdflu.gov.au."

Ms Collins said the campaign provided information to the public who may have questions about bird flu.

"If you have backyard chickens and you have localised bird flu in your area, it will give you practical advice about what to do," Ms Collins said.

The Australian Government launched the 'Bird Flu - Know what to do' campaign on Sunday. (Supplied: Australian Government)

"If you are taking your dog out for a walk and you come across dead birds, it will give you practical advice about what to do."

Adelaide University professor and epidemiologist Adrian Esterman said the campaign had consistent messaging.

"I think they've got all the right things, not to touch dead birds, notify the hotline if they find any," Prof Esterman said.

Calls to protect endangered sea lions

On the same day as the national campaign was launched, SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke reiterated the state's willingness to support a trial vaccine from America to help protect Australian Sea Lions against bird flu.

The experimental vaccine would need to be approved by the Federal Government.

So far five Australian sea lions have tested positive to the virus in South Australia.

All five cases were located on important breeding colonies for the endangered species on Kangaroo Island and the Pages Islands.

"We're very focused on our sea lions and that's why we're trying to pull every lever possible and make it very, very clear as a state that we want it to progress and we want to make sure that it can be done safely," Ms Bourke said.

SA Environment Minister Emily Bourke has called for the Federal Government to approve an experimental vaccine to help protect sea lions against bird flu. (ABC News: Ashlin Blieschke)

"We have made, if not daily, very regular communication available to the Federal Government to say that we want this into the country as quickly as possible, but obviously this is an experimental vaccine and it needs to be done in the appropriate way."

Ms Collins previously said there was no commercially available vaccine for mammals available.

"We are working very closely in terms of some of the trials that are occurring overseas, particularly in the USA, in relation to some monk seals that are being tested for a vaccine in Hawaii and California, and we continue to have those discussions."

Prof Esterman said the experimental vaccine being trialled in America was "definitely worth trying".

"I will emphasise it's very experimental, it's actually based on a cattle vaccine for Avian Flu, because Avian Flu has got into the dairy herds across America," he said.

Epidemiologist Professor Adrian Esterman said it was worth importing the US trial vaccine for sea lions to Australia. (Supplied)

"And it's actually not H5N1 it's H5N2, so slighty different virus but very similar.

"They've tried it out in some seals and sea lions... and they've shown that it does produce an immune response.

"[Australia] would have to try and import it, we would have to go through all our regulatory authorities.. even if it did happen, it's still incredibly experimental.

"It's shown to give an immune response, but there's no guarantee it would actually protect the sea mammals, but if we can get hold of that it's definitely worth trying."

The epidemiologist said there would have to be a lot of red tape to cut if Australia were to import the experimental vaccine.

"This is an animal vaccine, it still has animal ethics committees it has to go through. I think you're definitely talking months."

World.title: One-year-old dies in car crash in central Queensland
World.content:
A young child has died and another infant and a woman have sustained injuries after a single vehicle car crash in central Queensland on Sunday morning.

Emergency services were called to Golden Mile Road near Dysart, about 250 kilometres south-west of Mackay, about 9am after a vehicle left the road and rolled.

A one-year-old girl died at the scene.

The incident occurred near Dysart, 180 kilometres south-east of Mackay.

The driver, a 22-year-old Moranbah woman, sustained minor injuries and a five-month-old boy suffered serious injuries.

Queensland Ambulance Service transported the pair to Dysart Hospital before they were flown to Mackay by helicopter.

The forensic crash unit is investigating and police are appealing to anyone with information to come forward.

World.title: Broncos into fifth NRLW grand final after toppling Titans
World.content:
Defending premier Brisbane is through to another NRLW grand final showdown with the Sydney Roosters after ending the dream run of Gold Coast in the preliminary final.

The Broncos won 20-8 away at Robina to secure their fifth win in a row to qualify for their fifth grand final. They have won all four that they have contested.

The showdown next Sunday will be Broncos legend Ali Brigginshaw's final match before retiring.

Last year the Broncos beat the Roosters 22-18.

The Broncos romped to a 20-4 lead in a four-try opening half on Sunday where they dominated in every area.

Titans lock Sienna Lofipo was ruled out of the match with a suspected broken jaw late in the half in a huge blow.

The big game experience of in-form Broncos trio Tamika Upton, Jesse Southwell and Romy Teitzel came to the fore as the hosts wilted under the pressure.

Upton, from full-back, was too elusive and strong to score the opening try when she beat three Titans with a step and a surge.

The discipline of the hosts, who had won their previous 10 matches in a row, let them down early with three penalties and they paid the price.

Half-back Southwell turned second-rower Romy Teitzel back on the inside and she raced through a giant hole.

A stunning cutout pass by Titans second-rower and standout player Evania Isa'ako close to the line got the hosts on the board with winger Destiny Mino-Sinapati diving over in the corner.

Gold Coast's numbering in defence inside their quarter line was all at sea in the first half and it was too easy for Upton to put back-rower Lauren Dam over.

Sienna Lofipo copped a nasty blow to the jaw. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Teitzel turned creator and powerhouse winger Julia Robinson, who had a blinder, was on the end of it and the Titans were on the rack.

Isa'ako collected her own ricocheted grubber kick to give the Titans a sniff after the break but Brisbane's defence on its line was too good.

Titans full-back Lily Patston also had an early finish when she went off with a category one HIA in the second half.

The Titans had a great season under coach Karyn Murphy but will be disappointed after failing to hit their straps in the biggest game of the season.

AAP

World.title: Double the height, 160 times the voltage. The latest ugly side effect of the AI revolution
World.content:
When Cameron Botterill left home one morning, he didn't expect to return to 15-metre power poles soaring above his residential street in Melbourne's inner west.

"They're absolute monstrosities," Mr Botterill said.

"They're ginormous. They tower above anything else in the suburb and they look very industrial. We're in a residential area here and we definitely did not ask for them to be installed."

The power poles went up within a day. (ABC News)

The new poles are more than twice the height of the 7-metre wooden poles they replaced, and can carry up to 66,000 volts of electricity, roughly 160 times the voltage that previously ran through his street.

In July, Mr Botterill was notified by his electricity distributor, Jemena, that the power would be shut off to allow workers to replace the poles on his street.

He didn't find out why until the day the new poles appeared.

"I asked them why they had installed this. They told me it was to run power to a data centre. That data centre is at least over a kilometre [away]," he said.

"I was shocked that this could be installed in a residential area."

The site of the NextDC data centre in West Footscray. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

The NextDC data centre in nearby West Footscray is already operating, and it's being expanded. One more data centre is proposed for the suburb with another in Spotswood.

Jemena says the new power poles are part of its local network upgrade "to help support Melbourne's growing energy needs".

"These taller power poles are required mainly for safety reasons," said Michael Brear, a mechanical engineering professor at the University of Melbourne.

"When you have a large electrical load like a data centre, you supply it most economically at a higher voltage than typically you would in your home.

" In order to deliver that electricity economically and safely to those loads, you need to build these taller power poles. "

On streets where the poles have been installed in Melbourne's inner west, there is a strikingly consistent complaint: residents didn't know the change was happening.

The power levels required for data centres mean old 7-metre wooden poles have to be replaced. (ABC News)

In response to questions from 7.30, Jemena said: "We have heard feedback from residents and other stakeholders that our communication and engagement could have been better, and we are taking that feedback seriously."

The company told 7.30 it has "paused works and [is] taking the time to listen to the community to understand their concerns".

Paul Tyndale was one of those caught by surprise when Jemena crews disconnected his power in the inner west suburb of Spotswood to install a new taller pole.

It was only then his family found out a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away.

Paul Tyndale found out from a tradie that a new data centre was being proposed less than half a kilometre away from his home. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

"We found out about the data centre when the tradie who was disconnecting our house told my partner, 'This is for the new data centre,'" he said.

" That was how we found out about it. That's how everyone around here found out about it. "

Car and bin blockade

On Sanderson Street in Yarraville, residents decided to fight back. After neighbours saw 15-metre poles go up a few blocks over, they knew their block was next.

Residents on Sanderson Street saw the 15-metre poles going up nearby. (Supplied)

On the day Jemena crews showed up in August, residents left cars and bins out to block equipment needed to install the poles. Some taped notes on car windows explaining the protest action.

Residents on Sanderson Street left cars out to block the equipment needed to install the poles. (Supplied)

"We were all just really caught off guard and just felt like it was really unfair that we weren't told about what was happening," resident Katrina Dardha said.

" So we said, 'No, enough's enough.' "

Eventually, unable to get their equipment in position, the crews filled in the holes they had prepared for upgraded power poles and left.

They have not returned.

Milco Bogoevski (second from the right) and his neighbours staged a protest to stop the power poles from going up in their street. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

"Everyone decided this is not happening on our watch," resident Milco Bogoevski said.

"If you stay quiet, it's at your own peril. I guess sometimes it takes something to make you really angry, to make you stand up."

State Labor MP Katie Hall's seat includes West Footscray, home to a large NextDC data centre. She says she understands why residents are angry about the tall 15-metre poles that have appeared on their streets.

Katie Hall is the Labor MP for Footscray. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

"I think there's a frustration there. I think there's a lack of understanding around why this needs to go down a residential street. Why can't it go down a bigger street?" she said.

" [What] I would like to see is for these powerlines to be rerouted. I've asked about whether they could be underground infrastructure. "

But placing powerlines underground is more expensive and can be more complex, according to Jemena.

Katie Hall says powerlines should be placed underground, but that would be more expensive for Jemena's network upgrade. (ABC News)

"[The company] determined that augmenting the existing overhead network was the most efficient and practical way to deliver the required electricity outcomes," a Jemena spokesperson said.

Jemena also provided some clarity as to who was paying for the installation of new power poles as part of its network upgrade.

According to Data Centres Australia: "Under the National Electricity Rules, large load users including data centres are required to pay 100 per cent up-front for their connection costs, including any augmentations required to connect their site to the network."

Jemena told 7.30 upgraded power poles would be within scope of those augmentations.

As the controversy over the power poles has grown, Ms Hall has increased calls for stricter guardrails to regulate data centre development.

On September 22, Victoria's government announced new regulations that would ban data centres in residential areas, enact a 150-metre buffer zone from homes and require data centres to use renewable power.

But some residents believe the new rules are too little, too late.

This protest was held outside a federal Senate committee public hearing on AI and data centres. (ABC News: Norman Hermant)

"These will not apply to any of the existing or planned data centres," said Ella Sjodin, who was at a protest against AI and data centre development in inner western Yarraville.

"They're only going to apply to future data centres that aren't yet planned.

" There's dozens and dozens that are already up and already planned. So, I think it's just absolutely not good enough. "

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: ACT's top cop backs controversial laws in battle against bikies
World.content:
ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee has no doubt about the damage outlaw bikie gangs are causing in Canberra.

"Outlaw motorcycle gangs exist for one reason, and that's in relation to organised crime" he said.

While raw numbers in the Canberra region do not match those in Sydney and Melbourne, there has been a notable increase in the past few years.

Deputy Commissioner Lee said there were currently five outlaw motorcycle gangs (OMCGs) in the ACT, with about 45 members and approximately 20 associates.

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee says the growing number of OMCG members is concerning. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"So that number has grown, which is a concern for us," he said.

ACT Policing is stepping up its fight against this growing threat in a bid to disrupt the gangs' criminal activities.

Land of opportunity?

For decades the ACT had one established bikie gang that ruled the roost — the Rebels.

But since the early 2010s, most Rebels have "patched over" to other groups, including the Bandidos, the Hells Angels, the Finks, and the Comancheros.

Several now have established "chapters" or bases in the ACT, rather than using Canberra solely as a transit corridor.

Do you know more? Contact Adam Shirley on encrypted email. Please note end-to-end encryption is only possible with your own encrypted email system like Protonmail.

Deputy Commissioner Lee thinks the primary reason is that Canberra is a growing city, and market.

"Where you have those prosperous communities, they're attractive propositions for investment, but they're also attractive propositions for crime," he said.

The Bandidos are one of five outlaw motorcycle gangs in the ACT. (ABC News: Henry Zwartz)

Associate Professor Mark Lauchs has been researching OMCG activities in Australia for decades.

"They're increasing in Canberra, because it's much harder for them to operate elsewhere in the country," he said.

Anti-consorting laws

One measure Deputy Commissioner Lee advocates for is anti-consorting laws, which have been a controversial debate in the ACT.

"We support that legislation," he said.

"We've seen the benefits of it in other jurisdictions where it has an ability to disrupt associations, or certainly overt associations, and the ability for these people to gather."

Deputy Commissioner Lee emphasised that anti-consorting laws preventing outlaw motorcycle gangs from meeting in public were not a magical cure-all.

"OMCGs continue to exist in every jurisdiction," he said.

"But where you have those real overt showings of OMCGs, what we have with the national runs, it would disrupt that type of activity."

ACT Chief Police Officer Scott Lee is advocating for anti-consorting laws, but says they are not a cure-all to OMCGs. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The ACT has repeatedly resisted introducing these laws, with previous Labor-led governments arguing they conflict with the ACT Human Rights Act.

Associate Professor Lauchs agreed that "good, strong, well-targeted" anti-consorting laws were needed, but he said it was reasonable the ACT had resisted until now.

"The arguments [against anti-consorting laws] aren't wrong. There are human rights issues there that have to be addressed," he said.

"However, being right is not enough in this case, because everybody else did it.

" So, you became the eventual inevitable victim of everybody else's laws. "

An attractive market

Sergeant Mark Alexander leads the specialist ongoing Task Force Invidia, which investigates, infiltrates and disrupts the gangs.

He said the groups were "really sophisticated, and their operational security is quite a challenge for us to try and monitor".

"They are an undercurrent and a really strong presence in the ACT in illicit commodities," he said.

Associate Professor Mark Lauchs is an expert in outlaw motorcycle gangs. (LinkedIn: Mark Lauchs)

Those commodities include the usual suspects — drugs, guns, weapons and extortion.

Associate Professor Lauchs argued that the illicit drug trade was the big draw for outlaw gangs.

"Is Canberra the greatest per capita usage in Australia? No, but it's a sufficiently high usage rate that there's a marketplace," he said.

" And when there's a marketplace for cocaine, there's going to be a marketplace for bikies to be involved. "

'Billions and billions'

This illicit economy is substantial; earlier this month, police arrested several ACT gang members alleged to have trafficked 70kg of cocaine with a street value of approximately $10 million.

"When you extrapolate that out to the [national] illicit drug market, we're talking billions and billions of dollars in terms of the illicit commodities that are moved into our country," Deputy Commissioner Lee said.

He explained the gangs had established transnational connections to overseas chapters in Europe, South America and other source regions.

ACT Policing Sergeant Mark Alexander says aside from top brass in OMCGs, most members do not make very much money. (ABC News: Adam Shirley)

Chapters are also constantly trying to recruit new members, particularly vulnerable young men seeking "status".

"They see outlaw motorcycle gangs as money and power," Sergeant Alexander said.

But police say except for OMCG top brass, most gang members take extreme risks for little reward.

"They are not making a lot of money. They are very poor. Sometimes they will struggle to pay the rent," Sergeant Alexander said.

Disrupting the cycle

New proposed laws may see a ban on OMCG members wearing the colours or patches of the gang. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

New laws announced by the ACT government in February will give police more power to search for illegal firearms without needing a warrant.

Another change announced by the ACT government in March this year — just prior to a national Bandidos meeting in Canberra — was a ban on 'colours' or 'patches'.

"Colours are obviously worn to intimidate the community. They bring with it a connection to that OMCG," CPO Lee said.

"It is something I've been supportive of with government, and I've advocated with government for the banning of colours here in the ACT."

Both proposals are yet to be debated in the ACT Legislative Assembly.

Constantly evolving

Officers rely on anonymous tips from the public to police outlaw motorcycle gangs. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

Whatever laws change, police say bikie gangs will adapt, adopting new tactics and strategies to keep business going.

"We are seeing a more underground meeting[s]… or it's in public areas, bars, clubs, restaurants, but they're not wearing their colours," Sergeant Mark Alexander said.

So, in the police's evolving fight against the gangs, they are clear one thing will never change: the need for public assistance.

"We can't be on every street corner keeping an eye on these people," Sergeant Alexander said.

"We rely on anonymous tips."

And Deputy Commissioner Lee urged the public to come forward.

"We need your help."

World.title: 'Open your eyes': Why China's sixth Antarctic base is raising concerns
World.content:
China is preparing to build its sixth research station in Antarctica, expanding into Marie Byrd Land — a remote, little-studied stretch of the continent's west.

It has some experts and politicians worried.

Independent senator Jacqui Lambie is among those concerned about Australia's defence priorities.

"Five bases have already been built, and China claims there is no geopolitical motive," she said.

" Open your eyes, [Department of] Defence. "

Whether that alarm is warranted depends on who you ask.

A new radio telescope installed by China's Antarctica team. (Xinhua via AFP)

China says the new base, which it plans to build next year, will support research into climate change, ice sheets and marine systems.

And it is far from the only country with a significant presence.

The US operates three permanent year-round bases. So does Australia, which claims 42 per cent of the continent, while Russia has five year-round stations.

But experts warn what matters most is not the station itself.

It is what the project might signal about China's deepening influence inside the institutions that govern Antarctica.

China's proposed new station is in Marie Byrd Land. (ABC News: Cordelia Brown)

Military use or just science?

Jiliang Chen, a lecturer in Antarctic law and governance at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania, sees the new station mainly as a matter of prestige.

"Building a station is China capitalising on its strength in this strategic game," Mr Chen said.

China's new station is being developed as per the Antarctic Treaty System's environmental assessment procedures.

Under the Antarctic Treaty, member states cannot veto a proposed new station.

The treaty was originally signed by 12 countries in 1959 and designed to ensure the use of the area for peaceful purposes only and the protection of the environment.

China's scientific expedition team constructing Qinling Station two years ago. (Zhou Yuan/Xinhua via AFP)

Mr Chen said a stronger physical presence helped consolidate China's role in future decisions on the continent.

"It gives people one more thing to be proud of, scientists more facilities to do research, and more projects to plan," he said.

One complication is that equipment such as satellite systems, communications hardware, aircraft and drones serve civilian research and can easily be adapted for military use.

That dual-use capability is why Mr Chen believes inspection and transparency matter most.

Other experts are more suspicious.

Elizabeth Buchanan, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), points to China's existing satellite ground stations and its Military-Civil Fusion policy, which enables civilian companies to develop or supply technologies for military use.

Her deeper worry is that China's spread of stations could eventually let it operate across Antarctica without depending on other countries.

"Polar power with serious polar independence means we have very little leverage left," she said.

West Antarctica has not been heavily researched. (Supplied: Matt Burke)

Some say that framing is overblown.

The Antarctic Treaty prohibits military bases, weapons and new territorial claims, while permitting military personnel and equipment for peaceful purposes.

China's embassy in Canberra told the ABC it was "fully committed to ensuring its activities in the region strictly align with the Antarctic Treaty System".

Tony Press, the former head of the Australian Antarctic Division, said he believed mining and military fears were exaggerated, citing the cost and difficulty of moving people and equipment across such a hostile environment.

"Antarctica is a terrible place to fight a war from," Mr Press said.

Unlike China's year-round Quinling station, the new base would run only in summer, hardly the profile of a strategic outpost, Mr Press said.

Instead, he said China was making a geopolitical statement.

"China is obviously doing the old strategic thing of making sure they've got stations around Antarctica that demonstrate quite clearly that they are a big player in, and have an interest in, all parts of Antarctica," he said.

China opened its fifth station, Qinling, in 2024. (YouTube: China News Service)

Working the system, not breaking it

Analysts say China is finding ways to become increasingly influential without breaking the rules.

China joined the treaty later than other countries, in 1983.

"China has always been nervous about natural resources and probably more hungry for economic growth," Mr Chen said.

Fishing is where this showed most clearly, he said.

China joined the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR), largely because of its interest in Antarctic fishing, Mr Chen said.

China has invested in icebreakers alongside building new bases. (Huang Taoming/Xinhua via AFP)

Ms Buchanan pointed to the broader growth of China's fishing fleet and domestically built fleet of icebreakers as part of its "Polar Silk Road" strategy.

She said China was also preparing to unveil a nuclear-powered icebreaker, which she said would reduce its reliance on gateway ports such as Hobart.

China is limiting the size of its high sea fishing fleet, except for the polar regions, Mr Chen said.

Antarctic krill fishing is an exception in China's plan for high sea fishing.

Many of Antarctica's emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure. (Supplied: Klein & Hubert/WWF)

Emperor penguins caught in the middle of geopolitics

China has generally opposed new marine protected areas in Antarctica.

Nearly half of Antarctica's 60 emperor penguin colonies have suffered increased or total breeding failure since 2016 as sea ice they depend on has retreated, according to researchers from the British Antarctic Survey.

Efforts to list them as a Special Protected Species have stalled at CCAMLR, blocked by China and Russia.

The stated objections cite insufficient scientific evidence, or argue that such a listing would address a symptom (habitat loss) rather than its underlying cause of climate change, which sits outside the treaty's scope.

Lyn Goldsworthy, an adjunct researcher at the University of Tasmania's Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies, said China was operating from a strategic perspective, and wanted to avoid restricting access to certain areas in case it had "certain aspirations" in the future.

Ms Goldsworthy added China appeared to join the conservation body CCAMLR for the purpose of fishing first, not marine biology or conservation.

Krill is another source of tension.

The tiny crustaceans are a primary food source for penguins and whales.

Next month's CCAMLR meeting, known as the "Krill Convention", will debate fishing limits.

China has a particular interest in Antarctic krill, which is increasingly valuable as an ingredient in aquaculture feed and nutritional supplements.

Emperor penguins have suffered after record-low Antarctic sea ice. (Supplied: Bryan and Cherry Alexander/WWF)

Krill products were pulled from shelves in Australian supermarkets after environmental campaigns, but China and Norway are pushing to raise the current catch limit much higher.

Ms Goldsworthy described years of stalemate.

"You have China saying, 'We don't believe in marine protected areas, you should give us our krill fishery'. Other countries are saying, 'No, we won't discuss krill fishery expansion until we've progressed marine protected areas,'" she said.

"There is now a deep distrust."

The underlying ecological concern that over-concentration of fishing in certain areas damages predator populations and habitats has become inseparable from the geopolitics around it, Ms Goldsworthy said.

One flashpoint was an area where heavy Chinese fishing activity overlapped with an Argentine-Chilean proposal for a marine protected area, she said.

Experts say Russia has also played a "disruptive" role, objecting alongside China to new marine protection sites.

China has been increasing its number of bases for scientific research. (Xinhua via AFP)

'Treaty not about to topple over'

Indi Hodgson-Johnston, a senior lecturer in marine and Antarctic law and policy, describes a pattern of "quiet disruption" by China, but technically no broken rules.

"The treaty is not about to topple over. I can't see that happening," said Ms Hodgson-Johnston, who works at the Institute for Marine and Antarctic Studies at the University of Tasmania.

"There's disruption everywhere at the moment. I would say Antarctica is just not a special case," she said.

However, ASPI's Ms Buchanan warned consensus-based governance could just as easily mask a "holding pattern" while one party's capacity and presence grows.

"We can't continue to assume, blindly, it's all happening in good faith," she said.

"We need a dual-track approach that has some optimism in continued adherence to the treaty while crafting a mighty stick or plan B to balance China's expansive ambition in Antarctica."

The ABC has approached the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade for comment.

World.title: Why strangulation has become part of the sexual 'playbook'
World.content:
Warning: this story contains details readers may find distressing.

Laura Crozier can't believe the conversations she used to have in high school about sex.

Specifically, sexual strangulation, commonly referred to as choking.

"I would talk with my friends and be like, oh yeah, he put his hands up my neck, and it was really cool," she said.

"It was just kinky."

The now 25-year-old runs the Yeah, Nah: Affirmative consent education project with the Youth Affairs Council of Victoria.

A proud bisexual woman, Ms Crozier said strangulation had become "just a part of the playbook of a sexual encounter".

"It's so normalised it's barely kinky anymore. It's just vanilla, which is terrifying because nobody understands it."

Elaquare Spencer is a 21-year-old university student in Sydney. (Supplied: Elaquare Spencer)

University student Elaquare Spencer, who is in her early 20s, said that for her and her friends, strangulation was framed as a sexual preference.

For Talon, a heterosexual man in his early 20s, strangulation was a way to play with power dynamics.

"Like that balance between subjugation and domination."

These young people candidly shared their experiences of sexual strangulation in a Radio National panel discussion this week, alongside violence prevention educator Maree Crabbe.

They did this to give context to staggering statistics about the rates of sexual strangulation among young people, and in the wake of the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney's northern beaches last month, which the ABC understands is related to a suspected choking act.

Loading...

Why is sexual strangulation so common?

According to Ms Crabbe, a violence prevention educator and co-founder of the Breathless campaign, there has been an enormous increase in depictions of sexual strangulation in television, films and popular culture.

Maree Crabbe worries people don't understand the health consequences of strangulation. (Supplied: Maree Crabbe)

But Ms Crabbe said research indicated pornography was the most significant influence shaping the increase in rates of sexual strangulation.

"A study that looked at depictions of strangulation in pornography from the early 2000s through to 2024 found that it went from being in basically zero per cent of scenes to being in 15 per cent of scenes in popular pornography," she said.

Ms Crabbe said strangulation had become such a pervasive part of sexual culture that even without watching porn, the expectation to engage with it was emerging in the bedroom.

Laura Crozier says it's common for women and gender diverse people to "go along" with sexual scenarios to protect their safety. (Supplied: Laura Crozier)

When Ms Crozier first began exploring her sexuality, she said there was a gap between her idea of pleasure and the sex she agreed to have.

"Sex wasn't really based on what I thought was good. It was based on what society thought was good," she said.

As a young man who has consensually strangled partners during sex, Talon said he felt like he was following a script expected of him.

"I see within my peers … myself, this sense of, well, I feel like I have to do this. I feel like I should do this," he said.

"Why do I as a man feel obliged to take part of this normalised culture?

"When I think about how I experience this play of power … why is it coming up as strangulation? Why do I want to cause this physical harm?"

The gendered nature of sexual strangulation

Ms Spencer said that while she had never asked someone to strangle her, she has had to ask not to be strangled.

Elaquare Spencer says the best approach is to ask a partner what they want and what makes them comfortable. (Supplied: Elaquare Spencer)

"In my own personal sexual encounters, I have had situations quite a lot of times where a man's hand has just sort of crept up on my throat," the politics and international relations student said.

In those moments, Ms Spencer said she even apologised for asking not to be strangled.

"How damning that is, that people feel uncomfortable to ask to not be strangled," she said.

Ms Crabbe said it was most common for men and boys to strangle, and for women, girls and sexual and gender diverse people to be strangled.

She said the power imbalance in sexual strangulation was highly gendered.

"Inequality is not edgy or sexy. It's not new, it's old. It's the patterns that we've tried to reject."

Ms Spencer thinks the historical context of strangulation is important.

"Harm towards and dominance over women has often been portrayed as sexy," she said.

"And what better way to assert dominance than to literally strip the air from their lungs?"

The health risks of strangulation

Ms Crabbe is concerned the wide range of health consequences of strangulation are misunderstood.

"Anybody could harm someone if they put pressure on their neck, because you only need the level of pressure of opening a can of soft drink to kill someone," she said.

"It's not just that someone can die in the moment, but the possibility of it impacting on your memory and migraines and eyesight and hearing and miscarriage and strokes and all sorts of things.

"A deprivation of oxygen to the brain impacts our capacity to make decisions and also to act.

"That can mean that even if someone consents at the time that they commence engaging in sexual strangulation, that they are likely not to be in a good position to make decisions in an ongoing way."

Tanya Plibersek has called for depictions of strangulation in porn to be banned. (ABC: Matt Roberts)

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said there was no safe way of strangling someone.

"It can cause death immediately, it can cause death weeks down the track through blood clots, it can cause dementia years and years after the practice has been used," she said.

The minister has called for depictions of strangulation in porn to be banned.

What do the statistics say? Read more Read more A 2024 study of 4,702 young people aged 18-35 published in the Archives of Sexual Behaviour from the University of Queensland and the Melbourne University Law School found that 57 per cent had been strangled during sex at least once and 51 per cent had strangled a partner at least once.

Of those young people who had experienced sexual strangulation, one third were between 19 and 21 when they were strangled by a partner for the first time.

On average, people reported they had been strangled five times by three partners.

People said they found out about sexual strangulation through various sources, most commonly pornography (61 per cent), but also through movies (40 per cent), friends (32 per cent), social media (31 per cent) and discussions with current or potential partners (29 per cent).

There is nothing hotter than consent

Ms Crozier encouraged sexual partners to listen to each other.

"Find pleasure in hearing each other and bonding and connecting rather than doing what society thinks is the best thing for you to do," she said.

Laura Crozier says when she first started having sex, it wasn't based on what she thought was good but what society thought was good. (Supplied: Laura Crozier)

Talon agreed.

"There is genuinely nothing wrong with just having plain old vanilla sex.

"I don't even want to use that language … but honestly, look your partner in the eyes and just be with them and be present and don't rush and take your time.

"Strangulation, it's not necessary."

Talon encouraged men and boys to self-reflect.

"What are you actually looking for?

"What do you actually want? Figure your own shit out before you go engaging with anyone else."

"I think consent is sexy," Ms Spencer said.

"The best, the sexiest and the nicest practice is to ask that person what they want, what makes them comfortable: what do they enjoy?"

World.title: NRL finals 2026 LIVE updates: Newcastle to face Roosters in NRL grand final after 12-man second half following Crossland send off
World.content:
Newcastle are through to the 2026 grand final after defeating the Panthers 22-14.

Where to begin? This is sensational.

They’ve gone from the wooden spoon in 2025 to a grand final appearance in 2026. And they did it a man down for the entire second half after Phoenix Crossland was sent off for a hip-drop tackle on Nathan Cleary.

Sandon Smith, who scored the intercept pass to seal victory, will face the Roosters in the grand final. The Tricolours didn’t want him – he was let go by the club in favour of Daly Cherry-Evans and Hugo Savala. And now he has led Newcastle to the decider against them.

This is Newcastle’s first grand final appearance since 2001. That is a 25-year drought broken.

Let’s not forget the drama and devastation of this match, though. Cleary left the field with a compound fracture, and Blaize Talagi was also taken off after suffering an achilles injury.

But still, Newcastle were gutsy and impressive, as Dominic Young and then Smith scored two tries in challenging conditions to keep Newcastle’s dream alive.

Defend the kingdom. The Knights march on.

Full-time: Knights 22, Panthers 14

World.title: Is ‘Wharfie Time’ dead? Dockers footy boss weighs in after capitulation
World.content:
SportAFLAFL grand final Is ‘Wharfie Time’ dead? Dockers footy boss weighs in after capitulation Peter Ryan Updated September 27, 2026 — 5:52pm ,first published 12:56pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fremantle’s football boss has backed the club using “Wharfie Time” in the future despite the capitulation that followed its activation with just four minutes and 18 seconds remaining in the grand final. At that point, the Dockers had established a game high 17-point lead and had one hand on their first premiership cup. Loading But the Lions kicked the final four goals of the match to snatch an incredible victory to become just the second premier this century to win after being behind at three-quarter time. Speaking at Melbourne Airport before the team returned to Fremantle, football boss Joe Brierty backed the fan activation, which Lions players said spurred them on to an unlikely victory.



“I’m sure it will [live on],” Brierty said. “It’s a fan activation for our club. Obviously, Brisbane have their songs. There’s obviously a lot of theatre behind it, but whatever’s talked about it doesn’t impact the result of the game from a football perspective. Patrick Voss looked to have sealed the match when he kicked his third goal to put the Dockers 17 points up with 4 minutes 18 seconds remaining Eddie Jim “That’s my role to oversee our footy program. We reflect on the things that we control in game and the way that we can review those things.” It was only the third occasion Wharfie Time has been activated this season and the first time outside of Perth.



Dockers’ supporters went crazy as the bells rang around the ground and the atmosphere inside the MCG lifted. Unfortunately, it lifted the Lions players rather than its intended target with Lions veteran Dayne Zorko explaining on Sunday how the team had plotted to turn the Dockers rallying cry against them. Back-line coach Dale Morris had played the audio during coach Chris Fagan’s team meeting on Friday after the AFL agreed to allow each club to whip up their fans after goals. The future of Wharfie Time is uncertain. AFL Photos via Getty Images “We spoke about it on Friday in Fages’ last meeting, they’re going to play this at some point, why don’t we change the mentality around about them coming for us, why don’t we go back at them. That’s exactly what we did,” Zorko said. “It honestly felt like out on the ground once those bells went there was a real calmness over the group, [we thought] we need to go for it now, this might be our last chance... It didn’t last very long. I think it was only allowed to play after goals so it happened pretty quickly but it was almost like a flick switched in our head and off we went.”



Fagan appeared on stage at Brunswick Street Oval on Sunday morning to thank Melbourne-based Lions fans for their devotion. “I’m sure you’re really proud of the way the team played yesterday. It wasn’t the prettiest of grand finals and for a large part we looked like we probably weren’t going to win the game,” he said. “But we have got amazing heart and amazing resilience. When they got 17 points up and they played that wharfie thing, our boys fired up and were able to play the best five minutes you’ll ever see in a grand final. As their coach I am ever so grateful for their efforts.” Lions’ star Will Ashcroft also reflected post-game after his heroic performance during that final period. “I think ‘Wharfie Time’ spurred us on a bit there,” Ashcroft said. “We knew it was coming at some point. We just wanted to harness it and turn it into energy for us.”



Related Article Live

AFL grand final AFL grand final wash up LIVE: Why all parents need this footy mum’s advice The Dockers were without skipper Alex Pearce in the final quarter after he injured his Achilles and his opponent Logan Morris bobbed up to kick three goals to win the game for the Lions. “We reflect on what we control as a footy program,” Brierty said. “There were aspects of the game that we didn’t get quite right, and a quality side in Brisbane took their moments, and that’s why they’ve just done a three-peat. “That’s what we want to get to. That’s what we reflect on. They lost four years ago in a grand final. We take some solace out of that.

World.title: ‘We have nothing but gratitude:’ Lions give Collingwood-bound Neale their blessing
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘We have nothing but gratitude:’ Lions give Collingwood-bound Neale their blessing Peter Ryan September 27, 2026 — 5:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Lions’ champion Lachie Neale is expected to officially inform Brisbane he has decided to join Collingwood ahead of the free agency period opening on Friday and the Lions say he will go with their blessing. Essendon, West Coast and the Magpies approached the triple premiership Lion in 2026 after he became available following his marriage break-up at the end of last season. Lachie Neale signs autographs at Brunswick Street Oval on Sunday. Getty Images He also met with St Kilda’s Ross Lyon – his former coach at Fremantle – during the season. Multiple industry sources have confirmed the dual Brownlow medallist has settled on joining Collingwood on a three-year deal after the Lions did not offer him a contract to continue with them in 2027.



Lions president Andrew Wellington said the Lions would be forever grateful for Neale’s decision to join the club when they were battling to win matches. “It was a really important platform for turning the club around, and if you look at his performances in grand finals and big games, he has been incredible, so we have got nothing but gratitude for what he has done for our club,” Wellington said. Neale had 20 disposals in the grand final. His ball-handling was clean, and he used the ball well throughout. His seven last-quarter touches, including a vital kick to Hugh McCluggage in the dying minutes which led to Logan Morris’ go-ahead goal, were crucial to the result. He did so while being booed each time he gathered the ball after the AFL appeals board made a shock call to overturn the one-match ban that was imposed on him for striking Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the preliminary final a week earlier. The success of his appeal relied on his record of 320 matches without a suspension.



On Sunday Neale joined his Lions teammates at Brunswick Street Oval after posting a cheeky reply to Ginnivan on Instagram. Neale had shared a photo of himself holding all three Lions premiership cups, captioned: “What now...” After Ginnivan replied to his post with an emoji, Neale responded: “hope your tummy okay my guy x”. Later on Sunday he posted a “court sketch” of himself to his Instagram story in reference to the tribunal case.



The 33-year-old Neale admitted after the grand final he had played his last game for the Lions and that he expected the finer details of his move south to be completed in the week ahead, which will include exit meetings as the club celebrates its third consecutive flag. “We’ve still got some things to work out, but I can’t thank the [Lions] enough for the last eight years. It has been the best eight years of my life,” Neale said. “It still doesn’t really feel real that this is probably the end of my time here.” Lachie Neale leaves Brisbane with two Brownlow Medals and three premierships. via Getty Images Fellow Lions midfielder Lions Will Ashcroft said Neale had been a huge influence on his career since he was drafted to the club for 2022. “I love him. He has helped me so much. When I came in, he won the Brownlow in my first year. He has been a great role model for me on the field and a great mate for me off the field,” Ashcroft said.

World.title: AFL grand final wash up LIVE: Why all parents need this footy mum’s advice
World.content:
In the wake of Will Ashcroft winning another premiership and, almost, claiming a third Norm Smith Medal, it’s worth reading this Good Weekend profile on him from earlier in the season.

It didn’t look too bad on the telly. There was young Will Ashcroft, chasing the ball into a pack, as he is prone to do, surrounded by players much bigger than his 182-centimetre, 82-kilogram self. Suddenly he was on the ground, sandwiched between two Geelong Cats players, his right leg planted in one direction as the ball bounced off in another. So par-for-the-course did it seem for Aussie rules that the camera moved on, following the ball down the field. It took a few beats for the cameraman to realise something was happening behind play and to pan back. There, lying on the ground, holding his knee, was the Brisbane Lions midfielder. Moments later the physios swooped in, and a few moments after that Ashcroft hobbled off the ground, pain etched across his face. It was July 22, 2023, midway through the fourth quarter of a round-19 AFL match at the Gabba, the Lions’ home turf. The day Will Ashcroft ruptured his anterior cruciate ligament. The worst day of his then-19-year life.

Will Ashcroft has pedigree on his side. But his path to success involved other factors, too – plenty of children of star athletes don’t ever achieve great heights. Paul Harris

You might say this means Will Ashcroft has had a pretty blessed life, and you wouldn’t be wrong. Eldest child of former Lions triple premiership player Marcus Ashcroft and PE teacher Bekky, Ashcroft has been marinated in sport his whole life. Indeed, been a star his whole life: winning at school swimming and athletics, captaining his Gold Coast school’s rugby union team, moving south in year 10 to Melbourne’s Brighton Grammar, where two years later he was footy co-captain and best-and-fairest. Leading the U18s Aussie rules team, the Sandringham Dragons, to grand final victory in 2022, captaining the U18 All-Australian team that year.

Drafted to his father’s old club, the Brisbane Lions, for a hotly anticipated 2023 debut, playing every match in the first half of that season, gunning for the 2023 Rising Star award. Then: a fleeting moment of bad luck, one necessitating a knee reconstruction and the best part of a year off footy.
