World.title: Cut off for $750: Victorian man left in the dark after power company refused payment plan
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBills Cut off for $750: Victorian man left in the dark after power company refused payment plan Annika Smethurst September 27, 2026 — 5:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When a Victorian man contacted his energy provider over an outstanding utility bill of $750, he expected to discuss payment plans or hardship assistance with an operator – options that have become increasingly common as the cost-of-living crisis continues to bite. Instead, the man’s energy provider disconnected his service and told him that the entire outstanding amount would have to be paid in full before it could be switched back on. It was only after he contacted the state’s energy and water watchdog that his power was reconnected. That same day, not only was his service returned, but he was offered a cheaper plan and given up to two years to pay off his outstanding debt. The number of Victorians having utilities disconnected has steadily increased over the past 12 months. Getty Images/iStockphoto His case comes as new figures from the state’s Energy and Water Ombudsman reveal complaints from Victorians facing gas or electricity disconnections have doubled between April and June, compared with the same quarter last year, prompting consumer advocates to warn that cutting off struggling households must be a “last resort” or outlawed.



The latest data also shows complaints involving debt collection have jumped 58 per cent in 12 months, while cases involving customers struggling to pay their utility bills had also increased by 28 per cent compared with the same quarter last year. Consumer Action Law Centre assistant director, Eleanor Doran, said she was “deeply concerned” about the increase in complaints about disconnections and warned that retailers had an obligation to help customers struggling to pay. “We say disconnecting people from energy in a cost-of-living crisis is not fair, and must be an absolute last resort for retailers,” she told The Age. “Retailers have obligations to work with customers if they are experiencing energy debt.”



Victorian Council of Social Service (VCOSS) said it wanted gas and electricity retailers barred from cutting off customers altogether, bringing them into line with longstanding protections against households. “Disconnections do nothing to help people pay off their debt,” VCOSS chief executive Juanita Pope said. “Research shows that disconnection – or even the threat of it – can harm people’s health. It causes distress, anxiety, isolation and shame. It can also push people into harmful behaviour such as rationing energy or other essentials like food. “Victorian households can’t be disconnected from water if they can’t pay – with good reason because water is essential. And like water, access to energy is something that everyone needs to live healthy and dignified lives.” The most recent data from the Essential Services Commission shows electricity disconnections for unpaid bills jumped 37 per cent in a single year, with 13,776 residential customers cut off in the 12 months to March, up from 10,055.



Household gas disconnections rose even more sharply, surging 64 per cent, from 3682 residential customers to 6050 in the 12 months to March. In July, the Commission issued a warning to Victorians that energy retailers cannot force customers to completely pay off debts before reconnecting essential energy services. In total, EWOV recorded 23,957 complaints last financial year – up 23 per cent. The state watchdog also found repeat examples of energy companies demanding struggling customers pay large sums of money upfront before their power or gas was switched back on, which it said was creating “a significant barrier to restoring an essential service”.



Ombudsman Catherine Wolthuizen said some energy and water companies were required to provide assistance. “Customers experiencing payment difficulty should be met with practical support from providers, not unnecessary barriers,” she said. “We ask providers to act fairly, give full consideration to a consumer’s circumstances and support them to access the right assistance.” The ombudsman also highlighted the financial impact of billing system failures, with the watchdog intervening in one case involving a small business owner who went almost two years without receiving an energy bill before being hit with a bill of more than $21,000. The business owner said a fault in his energy provider’s billing system meant he had been unable to monitor his usage during the 22-month period. After the watchdog intervened, the provider backdated the bills at a cheaper rate, wiping about $900 from his bill and offering a further $5000 discount if he paid the remaining amount upfront.



The surge in complaints about utility providers comes as households continue to grapple with cost-of-living pressures. Prices rose 3.8 per cent in the year to June, with electricity remaining one of the biggest contributors to inflation, rising by more than 20 per cent in 12 months following the end of government subsidies. Data from the National Debt Helpline, provided to The Age, shows demand for financial counselling has also jumped in the past year, with call and chat inquiries up 12 per cent in the 12 months to the end of August. Working-age households accounted for the bulk of demand, with 70 per cent of callers aged between 25 and 54. Financial counselling Victoria chief executive Zyl Hovenga-Wauchope said households often prioritised rent and mortgage repayments over bills. “Around one third of Australian households report difficulty paying home electricity or gas bills, showing that energy affordability and access to hardship support are systemic problems,” he said.



“Energy retailers must ensure they are offering genuine and realistic hardship provisions.” National Debt helpline: 1800 007 007

World.title: Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails
World.content:
BusinessWorkplaceGender equality Informed of a job interview at 4am, but female garbo’s discrimination claim still fails Millie Muroi September 27, 2026 — 4:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A woman who was knocked back for a job as a garbage collector has failed in a gender discrimination claim, despite several men getting more notice of the interview than she did for the role in the male-dominated industry. The female casual garbage truck driver was applying for a permanent role with Sydney’s Inner West Council, but was only told at 4am that she would be interviewed at 10.30am the same day, with a shift in between, preventing her from preparing or changing out of her work clothes. A Sydney garbage truck driver who claimed she received different treatment because of her gender has lost her case. Kate Geraghty Recycling and waste collection is classed as an “almost completely male-dominated” field, with 95 per cent male workers, according to the federal government’s Jobs and Skills Australia agency. The case, heard in the NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal, involved one of the few women working as a garbage truck driver at Sydney’s Inner West Council, and highlighted how hard it can be to show an employer has breached anti-discrimination laws.



The woman, who this masthead has chosen not to name, began working with the Inner West Council in 2023 as a casual garbage truck driver via an external company, and applied for a full-time job in March the next year. She was told she lacked enough experience, which she then obtained. When permanent loader and driver positions opened up later that year, she applied and was interviewed for them. However, she said that in July 2024, she became aware that a number of her male colleagues had been notified that they would be interviewed for the position. Approximately two weeks later, she had not yet been notified. She said she was only told by one of her superiors at about 4am on August 7, while starting one of her ordinary shifts, that she was required to return to the depot by 10.30am that morning because she had an interview. She said she was therefore required to do her ordinary work before attending the interview, and had no meaningful opportunity to prepare or change into what she suggested was more appropriate clothing.



She also complained the male candidates had been notified by text, rather than verbally. There was no dispute that the male candidates had been informed of their interviews at least a few days earlier than her. Related Article Unfair dismissal ‘Crack pipe and two meth bags’: Coles worker fails to regain job after alleged drug use While the interview panel convenor accepted that having more notice of an interview would give an advantage to a candidate, the tribunal ruled there was no evidence that suggested her performance at the interview was compromised by short notice or what she wore. She also said she was verbally informed she had a medical assessment for the job shortly after returning from leave, and that she was briefly shown the appointment details on a mobile phone which she hurriedly tried to photograph before the phone was put away. She argued the successful male candidates had been notified by email, and not merely by being shown details on a phone. The female driver argued this all formed a “broader pattern of differential treatment” during the recruitment process on the ground of her sex.



The council said while the female driver performed well in the interviews, she was “not among the most meritorious candidates”, with her supervisor noting she had been in “quite a few accidents”, more than most other employees. The supervisor also said the woman was included in the interview process for the driver position despite not initially progressing to the interview stage, after he realised interviews for the loader position would probably occur while she was on leave. She had not initially been selected because she did not have as much driving experience as the other candidates, but scored third- or fourth-highest in the interview. The full-time positions were offered to male candidates who the female garbage truck driver claimed had equal or lesser relevant experience than she did. The tribunal ruled there was no evidence showing that any of the council’s conduct was on the basis of her sex. “There is, as it is sometimes called, no smoking gun to which [she] can point,” the tribunal said.



Peter Roney, KC, who oversaw the case, said the female driver’s supervisor had no issue working alongside women in the workplace. “That is, in our view, significant because absent that, there is little to explain why he may have engaged in the conduct [she] accused him of,” Roney said. Related Article Workplace You’ve been put on a performance management plan. Are you on the way out? The tribunal, which described the woman as “an ambitious and articulate woman who had great confidence in herself”, said she was not materially disadvantaged by the recruitment process, and that the different treatment she faced was not on the ground of sex. “Clumsy, disorganised or less than optimal management practices they may have been, but none was shown to have occurred consciously or unconsciously on the ground that she was female.” Inner West Council General Manager Peter Gainsford said the council respected the tribunal’s finding which dismissed the complaint and found there was no basis to conclude that the recruitment decisions were made based on gender.



“The tribunal also identified improvements needed in the council recruitment processes,” he said. “As a result, we are reviewing these processes. Council is committed to the highest standards of employment conditions. The applicant continues to be employed by council.” Get workplace news, advice and perspectives to help make your job work for you.

World.title: ‘Something’s changed’: Why Socceroos’ confidence has gone through the roof
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerAustralian soccer ‘Something’s changed’: Why Socceroos’ confidence has gone through the roof Vince Rugari September 27, 2026 — 4:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you watched the Socceroos play Brazil on Friday night, you probably noticed it. Tony Popovic can see it in the way his players now carry themselves. Alessandro Circati can feel it coursing through his veins. “For sure, something’s changed,” he said. Loading There is a swagger about this team that wasn’t there before, an intangible growth spurt that can only be triggered by experience: of knowing what it feels like to play at a World Cup, realising that you belong on that grand stage, climbing the ladder at club level and realising it again. Circati is one of the 11 players who parlayed their World Cup campaign into career advancement at club level, transferring from Parma to Portuguese giants Benfica for $33 million.



He remembers being on holiday and driving back from the beach when he got the call to tell him that he might have to start thinking about moving his life to Lisbon. Now at one of the world’s biggest clubs, he broke through for his starting debut last month in a 2-0 UEFA Europa League victory away to AC Milan. His family all support the Rossoneri, and his uncle wore a Milan scarf and a Benfica jersey to the match. Socceroo Alessandro Circati. Getty Images It was a “dream come true”, Circati said - but dreams like these have quickly become part of a new reality for Circati and many of his Socceroos teammates. “When you make a move, the positive or the negative, you always change. You grow,” he said.



“Personally, for Nestor [Irankunda], Lucas [Herrington], Patty [Beach] … we’ve all gone to bigger clubs. You’re a bit more confident, you’re playing at a higher level, you’re training at a higher level, so it’s normal that you develop.” What Popovic now wants to see when these players gather to represent their country every few months is for that confidence to manifest on the pitch. Socceroos boss Tony Popovic. Getty Images That is what happened in Townsville. Instead of sitting deep and deferring to their glamorous opponents, they seized the initiative. They played through Brazil’s press, they showed bravery in their pass selection, and but for a last-minute header they conceded with the final play of the match, they would have had a famous result to show for it. Many have pigeonholed Popovic as a conservative, bus-parking tactician, but this is the kind of direction he wants to take the Socceroos - and perhaps only now do they have the belief in themselves to execute.



“In the days leading up to the game, the boss did specify what he wanted from us, and we had to put that on show,” Circati said. Related Article Australian soccer ‘That’s just Nestor’: The ridiculous thing about Irankunda’s Brazil wondergoal “It all starts from him, and then we’ve got to sort of be able to showcase that we can do what he asks. He wanted us to play out a little bit more, be a bit more brave, break in their press, and maybe risking a pass more … essentially it’s maybe risking the few per cent, not playing the pass that you know 100 per cent is going to arrive to your teammate. “Maybe that’s the horizontal or back one, maybe risking the pass forward where your team-mate’s got the man behind him or to the side of him, or simply going one-v-one with an attacker or just simple things like this, which from the outside doesn’t seem like a big risk, but from the inside, it’s the difference between keeping the ball or losing the ball, which essentially can lead to scoring or conceding.” Ideally, that experience against Brazil will have a compounding effect. Having just measured up against the five-time world champions, and left knowing they were good enough to beat them, they should feel even more emboldened about who they are, and where they can go as a team.



And so, when they face Brazil again on Tuesday night at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane, there will be no reason why they should think about backing down. “I feel like I’m built for these situations,” said striker Tete Yengi, whose hold-up play was an underappreciated highlight of the 1-1 draw. “We have a lot of confidence in ourselves as a group. We have a lot of players playing at top levels now … week in, week out, you’re going against top players. That naturally builds confidence and belief in yourself that you can go out there and do any game. “We’re physically one of the best, I feel like. And technically also, we’re getting so much better. So if we compete on both of those levels, then yeah: why not?”

World.title: Labor senator’s extra staffer told to pay back $12,000 hire car bill
World.content:
Parliament’s expenses watchdog found Senator Tammy Tyrrell’s senior adviser had inappropriately charged the taxpayer almost $12,000 in hire car fees just days before Prime Minister Anthony Albanese allowed her to retain him as an employee. Veteran political staffer Cameron Amos, who previously worked for the Labor Party, is yet to repay the bill he racked up while working for then-crossbench Senator Tyrrell and Senator Jacqui Lambie. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with Senator Tammy Tyrrell. Dominic Lorrimer This masthead last week revealed that Albanese allowed Tyrrell to keep two well-paid adviser-level staff when she defected to the Labor Party, infuriating some of her new colleagues who believed she didn’t have the workload to warrant the additional staffing. Tyrrell’s allocation of two additional well-paid senior advisers – on top of the five electorate office staff allocated to every MP – means she has the same number of senior staff and extra resources as 13 Labor colleagues who hold assistant minister positions, or who have special envoy duties.



Amos has worked across the parliament since 2015 in the offices of Tyrrell, Lambie, former Labor MP Gai Brodtmann and Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young. He played a role in bringing Tyrrell over to the Labor Party earlier this year. Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese’s staffing double standard props up Lambie defector after joining Labor Amos was based in Canberra during the period that was investigated, and would regularly travel to northern Tasmania where senators Tyrrell and Lambie were based. He believed his use of hire cars was approved and that he was saving the taxpayer money by not charging taxis for the 110km return trip between Devonport Airport and Burnie, where Lambie’s office is located. Lambie asked the Independent Parliamentary Expenses Authority on February 12, 2024 to audit Amos’ use of hire cars and ensure it was within the rules. In an audit report published in May of this year, the watchdog found it was appropriate for Amos to hire cars for transport between Devonport airport and Burnie; however, 27 hire car bookings were found to contravene the rules. In one instance, Amos hired a car for 29 days while in Tasmania.



Another Tasmania trip in 2022 lasted 12 days and taxpayers were charged more than $1300. Amos often retained use of his hire car over weekends. On another occasion, in July 2020, Amos hired a car while in Canberra for two days, racking up almost 600km of travel. The total cost to taxpayers for the 27 trips came to $11,694.49 and Amos is yet to pay this sum back, but is negotiating with the watchdog over a payment plan. The maximum allowable hire period under expenses rules is 10 days, and hire cars can only be used for work-related purposes. Each instance of hiring must be approved by either the MP or a designated employee within their office. In a formal response to the watchdog’s audit, Amos said it would have been “enormously self-destructive and irresponsible” of him to bring Lambie into disrepute. He added that “unequivocally, without exception” he has never made inappropriate expense claims, and to the contrary had “frequently not claimed expenses” to which he was entitled because doing so was not “a good look”.



“It is not within my character to [make unapproved claims]. I am by no means a saint, but I am also by no means a thief. I do not rip off taxpayers by claiming unreasonable expenses or living large off their chequebook,” Amos wrote. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership Albanese once criticised rivals for abusing this power. Just look at him now James Massola Chief political commentator “To believe this account of events is to believe that some prolonged bout of insanity overcame me, for four years, but only to such a narrow and specific extent that it limited itself only to the use of parliamentary travel expenses.” In the audit, the watchdog found no evidence “of approval for Mr Amos to keep the hire car for extended periods, or to use it for travel around Tasmania, other than travelling between the airport and his accommodation”. In an interview at the commencement of the audit, and in later correspondence, Lambie stated to the watchdog she was intent on ensuring her staff followed travel rules. She said staff used taxis for official business and no other staff in her office used hire cars in the way Amos did.



Comment was sought from Amos, Lambie and the prime minister’s office. Labor MPs who spoke to this masthead on the condition of anonymity said it was unfair for Tyrrell to retain staff who could have better supported more senior colleagues with higher duties such as committee chairs. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: 'A lot more activity' - significant rise in people trafficking investigations
World.content:
The Government has pointed to a lack of resources and blurred roles hampering its battle against human trafficking.

It has launched a five-year action plan, saying horticulture, beauty services, construction and hospitality are problems areas.

Associate Immigration Minister Casey Costello, whose previous work included fighting migrant exploitation, said there had been a significant recent increase in people trafficking investigations.

"Trafficking is a difficult prosecution because it was always relating to bringing across the border, and it really didn't recognise that we have domestic trafficking as well, and that was where the differential needs to be looked at, and that's why fit for purpose legislation is so critically important. But yes, there has been a lot more activity, and I think there's a lot more we can do."

Thirteen people were granted victims of people trafficking work visas last year.

Trafficking involves coercion, deception or abuse of power to use people for forced labour or criminality, servitude, slavery or prostitution.

Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) identified several deficiencies in the cross-government trafficking response, including fragmented reporting pathways, unclear agency roles and data-sharing barriers

Variation existed between agencies in the identification of potential victims, and in their frontline capability, with "constrained investigative capacity" and limited public awareness.

Police, Immigration New Zealand compliance, the Labour Inspectorate and Internal Affairs could be involved in cross-border work, and the ministries of education, justice and children among other departments whose staff dealt with trafficking issues

The action plan's first steps were mapping the existing trafficking systems, and creating a governance framework.

As an interim measure, it would create a process for trafficking victims to access support.

In phase two, it would coordinate training and strengthen partnerships with Pacific countries to prevent child trafficking.

Citizens Advice Bureau wants an independent anti-slavery commissioner, saying volunteers were "genuinely horrified and shocked" when they discovered there was no support or protection for people in exploitative situations.

World.title: 'It made me so angry': Hipkins targets cost of living at Labour campaign launch
World.content:
Chris Hipkins is promising "plenty more fire" this election, as Labour promises to cut student debt if elected.

About 600 Labour supporters, volunteers and candidates packed into the Due Drop Events Centre in South Auckland for the party's election campaign launch.

The Pacific Youth Choir set the tone early, belting out classics like Mt Raskil Preservation Society's 'Bathe in the River' and Stan Walker's 'Aotearoa'.

Hipkins took to the stage in front of cheering supporters and immediately honed in on the cost of living as his focus for the election.

"Is there anyone Christopher Luxon hasn't talked down to?" he asked supporters.

"You can choose a prime minister who will fight to get your costs down or a prime minister whose response to rising prices was 'cry me a river'.

"Have you ever heard anything so out of touch?

"It made me so angry… it still does."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686469112

Hipkins also took aim at National - who had their own conference a couple hours earlier - for "bullshit" claims about Labour's tax policy.

"Christopher Luxon promised to fix the cost of living. He's had three years. He's failed.

"And ask yourself this - after three years of National, are you better off?" he said.

Hipkins said the election would be about the cost-of-living, making his pitch to parents, tradies, and small business owners: "This is middle New Zealand," he said.

"They get up, go to work, look after their families and do their best and right now, far too many of them are working harder than ever and still going backwards.

"I won't accept that as the future of New Zealand."

Hipkins announced Labour would write off 10 percent of eligible student loan balances, applying to current and future graduates who are New Zealand-based for tax purposes , did not benefit from the fees free scheme and still had a loan to pay back.

Loans of $2000 or less would be completely written off and the policy would cost $583.4 million over five years.

Speaking to media after the launch, Hipkins said his team was "fired up" for the election.

"We're out on the doorsteps every day at the moment, we're going to be fighting hard to win this election."

He said the party's student loan policy would give young people "more of a reason" to stay in New Zealand, rather than going abroad.

"We're seeing far too many New Zealanders giving up on this country. I want to give them more of a reason to stay."

He said National were telling "outright lies" about Labour's tax plans and he "calling them out on it".

"Christopher Luxon seems to stand for blame, excuses, slogans, no real answers, and New Zealand going backwards.

"At least I know that my whole team 100 percent backs me. He can't make the same claim, can he?" he said.

Asked how the upcoming election would be different to the 2023 election - where Labour lost much of the "red wave" vote they secured in 2020 - Hipkins accused media of "listening to National Party spin bullshit".

"I'd encourage you not to." he said.

Asked again, Hipkins said people would see "plenty more fire" over the election.

Chris Hipkins shakes hands with former Prime Minister Helen Clark during the Labour Party campaign launch at the Due Drop Centre in Manukau, Auckland, on 27 September 2026. Jo Moir / RNZ

The student loan announcement was met with cheers, as Hipkins declared "neo-liberal, trickledown economics does not work".

Responding to claims from the National Party about Labour, Hipkins was blunt: "It's bullshit."

"People aren't asking the prime minister to feel sorry for them. They're asking him to do his bloody job."

He also touched on Labour policies regarding supermarkets, public transport fare caps and free GP visits, before wrapping up his speech before a cheering crowd.

"You are how we win this," Hipkins told candidates and volunteers.

World.title: 'The job isn't done': Luxon launches National's election campaign in Auckland
World.content:
National's Auckland campaign launch has featured a significant focus on Labour, another pledge card rather than any new policy, and conspicuously empty seats.

At the International Convention Centre in Auckland, the event pitched to party faithful ran about half an hour behind schedule.

Large sections were roped off many of the seats in the back remained empty, a rough headcount putting number about 750 people - a surprise given parties typically pack such events to ensure a crowded, popular atmosphere for the evening news.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686469112

Leader Christopher Luxon launched a signed pledge card distributed after his speech making 10 promises:

Economic growth that delivers new jobs and higher wages

No new taxes so you keep more of what you earn

Compulsory KiwiSaver with higher contributions and a $1500 Baby Boost

Paid Parental Leave extension from 26 to 30 weeks

Better school results by replacing NCEA, regular assessment and teaching the basics brilliantly

Tougher consequences for criminals and more Police patrols

Faster healthcare and more medicines on top of 33 new cancer medicines already delivered

Better infrastructure with Roads of National Significance, new classrooms and new and upgraded hospitals

A better deal at the supermarket by driving competition

Books in surplus so we don't saddle our kids with new debt or more taxes.

The card was a follow-up to the eight-promise 2023 version launched to more than 1000 people at the Due Drop Centre in Manukau, where Labour would launch its own 2026 campaign just hours later.

The '23 edition included lower inflation and economic growth, tax cuts, infrastructure, law and order restored, higher school achievement, shorter health waiting times, support for seniors and "deliver Net Zero Carbon by 2050".

Entering to a standing ovation, Luxon gave the standard party plaudits before talking about his past, choking up when speaking about his mother.

"She went to university the same year I did... she taught me to walk across the room, find someone different from myself, and seek to understand before I'm understood."

But soon he was speaking about the elephant in the room: Labour.

"Labour lost the plot, and they borrowed more, and they taxed more, and they spent more, and through it all, they lost sight of what really matters: your business, your community, your family, and your safety."

He had taken the stage following a flashy television advert beginning with quotes from former Labour PM Jacinda Ardern against a backdrop of police sirens, and current leader Chris Hipkins over sad piano music.

That contrasted with a humanising pastiche of Luxon talking about letters sent by children, "Kiwi mums and dads", the "squeezed middle", tax relief and the party's already-announced election policies.

"National is the party of delivery, but friends, the job isn't done."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405686899112

Earlier speeches all devoted significant time to attacking Labour and other left-leaning parties.

Campaign chair Simeon Brown spent four minutes on thanks and greetings, four-and-a-half minutes talking about Labour and Chris Hipkins, and 60 seconds in call-and-response for "no new taxes" and "party vote National".

Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis also spent about as much time talking about Labour as everything else, taking less than two minutes to switch from talking up farmers, mums and dads to lambasting the "mess left to us by Labour and its mates".

"The last thing this country needs is nine new taxes."

The party's most popular leader in the modern era - Sir John Key - remains a prominent figure at National Party events and his speech highlighted the desire to see Luxon re-elected "unequivocally".

"We're here for one simple reason: to extend Chris Hipkins, Labour, and their band of lefty fellow travellers time in opposition, because even if we all had the net worth of Elon Musk, we can't afford those policies."

He also warned specifically against strategic voting.

"Don't try and do something that you think is clever or try some form of so-called strategic voting ... that is the opposite of clever."

Speaking to reporters later, Luxon was adamant National had more policy to unveil, and pushed back on multiple questions about the heavy focus on Labour.

"I'm really focused on making sure I make the choice really clear to all New Zealanders, and we have a positive plan. You know, we have a plan, not just a slogan; we have been executing our plan of fix the basics, build the future the last three years.

World.title: One dead after two-car crash on Massey road
World.content:
One person is dead after a serious two-car crash on Red Hills Road in Massey, Auckland.

Police were called to the crash about 11.30am Sunday.

One person died at the scene.

One other person was seriously hurt and taken to hospital. Four people suffered minor injuries.

World.title: Tornado smashes car windows, cuts woman's arm on Kapiti Coast
World.content:
A woman was cut by flying glass when an apparent tornado smashed through her car's rear window, sending stones and debris hurtling across a Kapiti Coast car park as witnesses scrambled for cover.

Mandy Butler was with her partner in the Paraparaumu car park when the tornado tore through at about 1pm, forcing them to duck for cover inside their car.

She said the tornado ripped through the area for about 10 seconds, pelting cars and people with debris.

She was cut on the arm by glass from her smashed rear window.

"[It] was so scary," she said.

The wind was so strong, said Butler, that she expected the damage to be worse.

Butler and her partner managed to cover the broken window with tarpaulins and duct tape before driving back to Wellington.

They made it home safely despite having to make the journey without a rear window, she said.

A local restaurateur who also witnessed the tornado said he saw seagulls being whipped around by the wind.

The car park was left strewn with debris and damaged vehicles.

World.title: More rain, snow forecast as severe weather system moves north
World.content:
Heavy rain has caused problems in Christchurch and Otago this afternoon.

Vehicles have had to drive around large pockets of surface flooding on State Highway 73 in the westbound lanes.

There has also been flooding on State Highway Six near Gibston in Central Otago.

State Highway Seven remains closed between Springs Junction and the turnoff to Hanmer Springs due to heavy snow.

The sections of State Highway 73, from Otira to Arthur's Pass, and Springfield to Castle Hill, are closed to towing vehicles and snow chains are required.

Snow ploughs have freed around 10 vehicles that became stuck in snow near Lake Pukaki in the Mackenzie Basin this morning.

The NZ Transport Agency said a truck and trailer unit became stranded on State Highway 8 near the intersection with Hayman Road causing the vehicles behind it to also get stuck.

Roading crews arrived and managed to clear snow from the road to allow the cars through, but the truck had to be towed.

Motorist Kyle Dinz said he was stuck near Lake Pukaki due to heavy snowfall while travelling on SH8 on Sunday 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

Kyle Dinz said he was caught in standstill traffic near Lake Pūkaki, behind several heavy trucks stuck on the road.

He eventually made it to Lake Tekapo, where he said the snow was even heavier.

Heavy snow blankets vehicles near Lake Tekapo on 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

NZTA also closed a section of road between Springfield and Castle Hill, including Porters Pass, to towing vehicles and advised drivers to use snow chains.

A driver told RNZ their car slid while crossing Porters Pass at about 9.30am because of the snow, forcing them to turn back.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405684778112

Orange warnings remain in place for heavy rain in the Tararua Range, heavy snow in Canterbury and severe winds across parts of the lower North Island.

The Tararua Range was expected to receive peak rainfall rates of 15 to 20mm an hour from late this morning.

MetService said streams and rivers could rise rapidly, with surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions possible.

In the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills south of Arthur's Pass, another 5 to 10cm of snow was expected to settle above 400 metres, with lesser amounts down to about 200 metres.

A severe weather system moving north over the country is bringing further heavy rain, snow and severe gales across central New Zealand on 27 September 2026. Screenshot / MetService

The snow was expected to ease from the south in the afternoon.

Severe west to northwest winds gusting up to 120km/h are forecast in exposed parts of Wairarapa, the Tararua District and Hawke's Bay south of Hastings.

Earlier today, the NZ Transport Agency said roading crews were helping vehicles stuck on SH8 near Lake Pūkaki because of heavy snow.

Snow falls on Porters Pass on Sunday morning, 27 September 2026. Supplied / Tracey Hunter

The Desert Road (SH1) is also under a snowfall warning from 7pm Sunday until 1am on Monday.

Several watches are in place across the country.

A Heavy Snow Watch remains in place for the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills about and north of Arthur's Pass, with rain expected to turn to snow above 200m and heavy snowfall possible above 400m.

Strong Wind Watches are in place for parts of Hawke's Bay, Horowhenua, the Kāpiti Coast, the Marlborough Sounds and the Chatham Islands.

The Heavy Snow Watch for Central Otago, the Queenstown Lakes District, inland Clutha and Southland north of Lumsden has been lifted after the threat of warning-level snowfall passed.

World.title: As it happened: Election campaign, 27 September
World.content:
Election 2026 coverage

Latest election news: Stay up to date with all the ins and outs on the campaign trail.RNZ policy guide: Our comprehensive guide to every policy announced by the parties vying for your vote.

World.title: Labour promises to write off 10% of some student loan balances
World.content:
Labour is promising to write off 10 percent of eligible student loan balances, as it launches its election campaign.

The policy would apply to current and future graduates who are New Zealand-based for tax purposes, did not benefit from the fees free scheme and still had a loan to pay back.

Loans with $2000 or less remaining would be written off entirely.

The policy was expected to cost $583.4 million over five years, the bulk of it in the first year when historical fees would be forgiven on 1 April 2027.

It would only apply to students who had completed their studies.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405688736112

Announcing the policy at the party's campaign launch at the Due Drop centre in Manukau on Sunday, leader Chris Hipkins said it will help open doors and encourage talented people to stay in the country.

"Student debt can follow people for years, making it harder to save for a home, start a family or simply get ahead," he said.

"This policy means more money to save for a home, start a family, build a business or just have a bit more breathing space."

Hipkins said Labour wanted to make it easier for graduates - whether they be nurses, healthcare workers, electricians or social workers - to stay and build a future.

Tertiary education spokesperson Shanan Halbert said graduates had done the hard work to get a qualification, and should not have to spend years watching their student loan barely move.

"Labour will cut that debt and give people a bit more freedom to get on with their lives."

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown said the policy was "yet another enormous bill on top of more than $18 billion in new spending promises".

"This policy simply shifts the debt onto taxpayers and means either higher taxes or more borrowing," he said.

"Tradies, farmers, truck drivers and other working Kiwis will be footing the bill so lawyers and other high earners with large student loans can benefit from another handout from Chris Hipkins."

ACT Party leader David Seymour said the policy was a bribe and Labour could not say how the bill would be paid.

"This policy reads like Chris Hipkins asked AI, 'what will make people like me?' What he needed to ask was, 'how will we balance the budget?'," he said.

World.title: Live: 12-man Newcastle through to grand final after Cleary's horrific leg break
World.content:
The Newcastle Knights are through to their first NRL grand final since 2001, defeating the Penrith Panthers 22-14 after Nathan Cleary suffered a catastrophic leg injury in the first half at Stadium Australia.

Cleary was in agony after going down in the tackle of Phoenix Crossland and Francis Manuleleua late in the first half, receiving immediate medical attention before being taken from the field on a medi-cab.

Cleary was then taken to hospital in an ambulance, accompanied by family members, while father Ivan has to continue coaching his team.

Crossland was sent off for his hip drop tackle on the star halfback, forcing the unfancied Knights to play the entirety of the second half a man down.

Follow all the action in our live blog below, check out all the stats in the full NRL and NRLW ScoreCentres, and tune in to our live radio coverage.

World.title: How the Lions claimed their moments to overcome a dominant Freo
World.content:
The footy season is a marathon, not a sprint.

Each game goes for about three hours, a long amount of time in our increasingly attention starved society. Multiply that by the 218 games over several months and the time starts to add up.

Especially if you are in one of the highest profile jobs in footy.

"The level of intensity that's required to be a senior coach, because it is a lifestyle, it never leaves you alone," premiership winning coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

"It's 365 days a year, seven days a week. It's just always in your head. You're always thinking about the club and what's next."

In the era of short form video and instant takes, being involved in football nearly forces you to do the opposite.

You don't scroll through football games, you absorb them.

But football games, especially important ones, aren't one continuous event. They are made up of a series of moments and contests that separate the winner from the loser.

The bigger the stakes, the more important those discrete moments are. It's also something that newly minted three-time premiership coach Fagan has previously attested to.

"Finals come down to moments," Fagan told afl.com.au in 2020.

It was a theme he has repeatedly come back to, year after year. Win enough of those moments at the right time and you might just win the premiership. It's a formula that the Lions have ridden to their spot as maybe the most successful side of the modern era.

The importance of moments is something that wasn't lost on his opposite number coming into the finals.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained earlier in September.

Those moments also turned the 2026 grand final into one of the greatest in recent history. It was in those moments that the two-time champion Lions became three-time champions.

By winning enough moments at the right time Brisbane was able to overcome the biggest lead in time-on in a final since at least 2001.

Much of the 2026 grand final played out the way that the 2026 season had progressed, with Fremantle in control. On paper, Fremantle not just dominated proceedings but played in a way that took away Brisbane's strengths.

"Fremantle deserved to win that game today. They were better," Fagan said.

"They were better than us for longer periods. They were killing us at clearance and contested possession, particularly in that third quarter and we couldn't get any territory. They had a lot of inside 50s. They had more shots."

On paper, Fremantle should have won the game and done so comfortably.

But Brisbane won the moments that mattered.

"It's a little bit like this group has become this team that seems to need to get themselves into a dire situation before they can actually produce their best," Fagan said.

This is how Brisbane won the 2026 grand final.

A tight first half

It wasn't just a late swing that made the game a classic. This year's grand final had twists and turns almost from the first bounce. The first half saw nine lead changes through the first two stanzas, with the two sides often trading goals.

Despite this, more things were breaking Fremantle's way than Brisbane's early.

In the first half Fremantle was able to control the game in ways that Brisbane usually thrive. The Dockers were able to effectively neutralise the Lions' usually strong clearance game through the first half, both gaining position and hitting the scoreboard.

While the Lions broke even at around the ground stoppages, the Dockers were able to dominate centre clearances and piled on three goals from the middle.

The Dockers were also able to effectively outmanoeuvre the Lions in the air. The Lions have traditionally had the best mark differential of any team, with Fremantle one of the few to seriously challenge them.

However Fremantle dominated the marking battle, with their tall timber taking the upper hand. Fremantle also seemed to find a way to isolate Brisbane's shaky defence, with Patrick Voss seemingly finding a weak spot in their defensive set up.

Even when the Lions were able to dominate field position — such as the ten minute or so burst in the middle of the second quarter — they were unable to pile on the points.

The only thing keeping the Lions in the game was their maniacal forward half pressure. The Lions managed nine first half tackles inside their own 50 to just two from the Dockers. Brisbane was also able to translate this into a four goal edge in front half intercept scoring in the half.

At the end of the first half, the margin was the same before a ball was kicked in anger. Instead of four quarters to decide the premier, there would be just two.

The back end

For much of the third quarter it looked like the control Fremantle were able to exert on the game was starting to pay off on the scoreboard. While the game still stayed within a couple of goals, Brisbane didn't look out of it.

That was until Fremantle piled on 14 points in around five minutes, seemingly creating enough of a barrier to preserve the Flagmantle dream.

Some things slowly started to turn Brisbane's way despite the Dockers looking like they were gaining an unassailable lead. The Lions were slowly able to gain ascendancy in the air, managing 15 marks on the lead in the second half to nil.

They were also slowly able to quell Caleb Serong's gigantic influence on the game, particularly at stoppage. After collecting 12 clearances in the first three quarters Serong managed just one in the final period.

Most importantly the Lions started to work out how to pierce the league's best defence absent its most important piece — captain Alex Pearce.

"We had to play a bit smaller and we missed his leadership across the back end of the game and clearly missed his leadership late. He gives us so much in that aspect of the game," Longmuir said after the game about Pearce's game-ending Achilles injury.

Before the injury Brisbane managed just one goal from set shots, with three coming after the injury. The Lions struggled to move the ball effectively up ground before his injury, but found the paths to goal over time. It's also easy to imagine how Pearce would have settled the ship once it started going down fast in the end.

Of course, those last four minutes are the things dreams — and nightmares — are made of. Will Ashcroft winning three straight centre clearances from the same spot, with every Lion rising around the young star.

The moments and the missed missed opportunities

In the end it's the moments that will resonate the longest after this magical grand final. We will remember how Ashcroft won the ball in the middle late, and how LOgan Morris kicked straight. We will remember Josh Dunkley's defensive prowess and Ryan Lester's last ditch effort to save a goal.

Brisbane didn't have any passengers, nor did Fremantle. That's what made the Norm Smith Medal so hard to choose this year, and so controversial.

Unfortunately the memories for Fremantle will be more bitter than sweet. If they had to map out what the perfect game would look like for them — scoring aside — it would have looked something like what played out in the end.

"Obviously for you know four quarters we played "Fremantle football" and it's the last two minutes we didn't take our moments," Norm Smith medallist Shai Bolton said after the game.

For now, it's Brisbane's day to celebrate yet again. Especially those four minutes and 18 seconds in the last quarter where Brisbane overcame Fremantle, a seventeen point deficit and, yes, Wharfie Time to cement their place as one of the greatest teams in football history.

World.title: Cyclist 'died eight times' before getting a new heart
World.content:
Wollongong cyclist Cameron Butcher likes to say he has nine lives.

After he had a pacemaker installed in his early 20s, he recorded the eight times it saved his life.

The first came at just age 22 when the device shocked his heart back into rhythm as he lay unconscious on the grass after picking up a frisbee.

Things became even more serious when he experienced four shocks in the space of 10 minutes.

Cameron in hospital after receiving his new heart. (Supplied)

"The heart kind of just gave out and I was put on the transplant list," Mr Butcher said.

" A week later I got the call to go in and get a new heart. "

Nearly two years on from his heart transplant, the 26-year-old elite cyclist is the fittest he's ever been and is competing in the Australian Transplant Games which kicked off in Launceston on Saturday.

The long road to a diagnosis

As a 20-year-old, Mr Butcher was mountain biking and road racing around Australia until he was struck down by severe fatigue.

He was initially misdiagnosed with poor liver function, but over time his symptoms continued to worsen.

"They found I was having three seconds between heartbeats and my left ventricle, which is the one that sends blood out to the rest of the body, had become really inflamed and enlarged and wasn't doing its job," he said.

Cameron Butcher got back on the bike just five weeks after his heart transplant. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Tests revealed Mr Butcher's heart was working at about a third of normal capacity.

A pacemaker was implanted but his heart began to fail.

Confronting his mortality at 24 was something he never expected.

"Getting that diagnosis of heart failure was probably the best thing that happened to me because for two and a half years I was trying to work out what was wrong," Mr Butcher said.

"I died eight times, so I always tell people I have nine lives."

Remarkable recovery

Less than five weeks after his transplant, Mr Butcher was back on the bike.

Cameron trains on Mount Keira in the Illawarra. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

"The first week [after the transplant] wasn't too pleasant," he said.

"But by the second week I was up [walking] and about doing 15 laps of the ward per day.

" I'm now the fittest I've ever been. "

Within six months, he won the mixed relay section of the 2025 Peoplecare Triathlon in Wollongong.

He also placed second at the 2025 Road Nationals in the transplant category, and won his age group in the 60-kilometre Willo Mountain Bike Race in March.

Celebration of life

The biennial transplant games is an Olympic-style sporting event for those who have undergone a transplant.

They were first organised by British transplant surgeon Dr Maurice Slapak in 1978 after he became inspired by a kidney recipient he ran with.

Chris Thomas, the CEO of Transplant Australia. (ABC Sport: Chris Taylor)

Chief executive of Transplant Australia Chris Thomas described the event as a celebration of life.

"Every participant owes their life to someone else," he said.

"They're people who were really once at death's door contemplating their future and then miraculously, someone has given them an organ to enable them to live.

"It's a really good opportunity to bring our community together to learn from one another."

Cameron Butcher with his mum post-heart transplant. (Supplied)

Mr Butcher will be competing in cycling, tennis, swimming and six-a-side soccer.

"I'm really competitive about the cycling stuff, but the other stuff's just a bit of fun and never been to Tassie before," he said.

The games will run until October 3.

World.title: 'Forever proud' fans cheer Dockers on team's return to Perth
World.content:
Still nursing the grief of their shock AFL Grand Final loss, the Fremantle Dockers touched down at Perth Airport this afternoon to cheers from supporters determined to give the team some love.

Shouting "we love you" and "forever Freo", a small group of fans cheered the players on as their buses left the airport. The team boarded the buses directly from the tarmac.

Another group of fans also waited for the team outside the Cockburn headquarters.

One mother brought her children to show their support.

Young fans welcomed the team back home. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

"It's not just about being there when it's good, it's also about riding the hard time," she said.

" We just want them to know we are still proud. "

The team boarded buses directly from the tarmac. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Fremantle fans were left heartbroken following the seven-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday's grand final.

But many said their disappointment was tempered by their pride in the club's efforts.

Despite the Dockers leading for most of the game, the Lions clawed back a 17-point deficit with just four minutes left in the final term.

Louise Austen says it was a delight to watch the Dockers all year. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Fan Louise Austen said: "I've actually been penning a letter this morning, in my head, just sort of want to write to the team to say how incredibly proud [we are].

" It was a delight to watch them all year. "

Another fan, Mike Rowe, was sharing an early coffee with friends and reflecting on how the match had brought people together.

Mike Rowe (second left) says the game brought everyone together. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"We were hugging, we were kissing, we were high-fiving, and then the stunned silence," he said.

"Everybody belongs, and it's a sense of belonging. It's fantastic," he said.

Meanwhile, WA Police confirmed 26 people were arrested in Fremantle yesterday, with 45 charges laid.

That included six who were taken into custody after a group assaulted two officers trying to arrest a 25-year-old man around half time.

Flight delays

Flight delays out of Melbourne due to poor weather were an additional let-down for many fans on the Dockers' way back to Perth.

As of 2:30pm, almost every flight arriving into Perth from Melbourne was listed as delayed. One Virgin flight to Perth was cancelled.

The quiet that descended on Fremantle on Sunday was a far cry from Saturday's festive atmosphere, when more than 40,000 people took over the Cappuccino Strip and sold out venues to watch the grand final.

Fans cheer Fremantle on Cappuccino Street on Saturday. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

The atmosphere was electric for the first three quarters — at one venue, fans were screaming and jumping on tables.

However, there was a noticeable shift as the minutes ticked away late in the game, with many fans visibly distressed as the Lions piled on late goals.

Fremantle fans knew their long wait would continue as Logan Morris sealed the game for the Lions. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

At the siren, collective moans of disappointment echoed throughout Fremantle's venues.

The Cappuccino Strip was cleared after the game. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

At one point, tension led to a physical altercation in the crowd, with multiple police and security trying to break up the fight.

One man was escorted away by police, with an ambulance called to attend to a woman seen on the ground.

Devastated fans

Fans were seen holding each other and crying.

It wasn't a happy end to the carnival atmosphere that saw huge crowds spill onto the streets of Fremantle to cheer their beloved Dockers on. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

One fan, Layla, said she felt sad but hopeful because of the fight the Dockers put up.

"I genuinely thought we had it," she said.

"And then in the last minute, my heart just broke."

Harry Thorn (right) says he's disappointed but stays faithful. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Harry Thorn was also in Fremantle to watch the game. He said it ran in his family to support the Dockers.

"I'm a little bit disappointed that we've never won a [grand] final, but we're gonna get there one year," he said.

Tayla Bowden was brought to tears when the final siren rang and said she was left devastated and shocked.

Tayla Bowden (left) says she was left shocked and Chelsea Bowden (right). (ABC News: Pip Waller)

She said being a Fremantle supporter was about a balance of hope and despair at the same time.

"We have stuck with them for 32 years, and we love them, no matter what. We haven't got a premiership yet; it's hard," she said.

"They're hard to love, and you can't help but love them at the same time."

Fremantle's Cappuccino Strip cleared quickly after the loss, with some devoted fans remaining in the city venues.

Fremantle Dockers's signs had been taken down. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Some of the Fremantle Dockers signs had been taken down with rubbish on the streets.

World.title: What is Wharfie Time and how did it backfire for heartbroken Dockers?
World.content:
As the bells tolled around the MCG on Saturday, Fremantle fans screamed in exhilaration.

This was finally their moment in the premiership sun after 31 long years of waiting.

Wharfie Time had arrived, and with four minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, there was surely no way that the Dockers could bottle this one — particularly with their viral celebration in full swing.

And then it all fell apart.

What is Wharfie Time?

You will no doubt have heard about it by now.

Before this year the phrase "Wharfie Time" would likely never have passed your ears, and now it's all the AFL world can talk about.

Wharfie Time is a viral celebration the Dockers have been using sparingly in close games at Perth Stadium during the 2026 season.

It's only ever used after a Fremantle goal, it's only ever used once in a game, and it's designed to get the crowd up and about to inspire the Fremantle players to see the game out as strongly as possible.

The lights in the stadium dim, leaving only an eerie glow of purple, as the bells from ACDC's song Hells Bells toll through the stadium and the words "Wharfie Time" appear on the big screen.

The Dockers have recently gone all-in on embracing ACDC, with former lead singer Bon Scott buried in the area due to his family emigrating there when he was young.

A guitarist at the top of the stadium starts every game playing Hells Bells, with the whole show being Fremantle's answer to the after goal songs that the Brisbane Lions do, or Port Adelaide fans singing INXS's Never Tear Us Apart before a game.

But what does the phrase 'Wharfie Time' even mean?

Great question.

It all goes back to former Dockers skipper and now Sydney Swans boss Matthew Pavlich using the phrase in a pre-match rev up in 2009.

Pavlich was mic'd up before the match and was caught telling his teammates "put on your Superman capes boys, it's Wharfie Time", as can be seen at the 39 second mark of the video below.

When it happened nobody really knew what the hell he was talking about. The "Wharfie" part was in reference to the dock workers and the club's mascot being the Dockers, but mixing it with Superman capes reference was a little … odd.

It went down in viral footy moments folklore, on par with Brett Kirk's infamous "Thanks Basil" speech.

The Dockers went on to embrace the quirkiness of it all and started the Wharfie Time celebration this year.

How did it backfire in the grand final?

In the lead-up to the match there had been a heap of talk around whether the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time at the MCG.

The Lions and the Cats had been allowed to use their goal celebrations in the 2025 grand final, with Charlie Cameron's Take Me Home, Country Roads celebration a particular fan favourite, often appearing to lift the Lions when they needed it most.

On the morning of the grand final, it was finally properly confirmed — the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time in the 2026 decider.

Just after confirmation, Brisbane football manager Danny Daly confirmed to ABC Sport's Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron that coach Chris Fagan had played the tolling bells to his Lions players in their Friday afternoon meeting. He didn't elaborate further.

We then witnessed one of the great grand finals in the history of the game.

After an incredible to-and-fro throughout, with 4 minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, Fremantle's Patrick Voss kicked a goal to put the Dockers up by 17 points.

The bells started to toll. Dockers fans went wild. It felt as if the end was nigh.

And the Lions came back from the dead.

Legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews has always said that he thinks the absolute limit of how many goals a team can kick in a particular amount of time is one goal per minute left.

Four minutes left. Four goals for the Lions. Heartbreak for the Dockers.

Several Lions players would go on to elaborate on Daly's earlier reveal to ABC Sport, saying Fagan had told them to use Wharfie Time against the Dockers, energising their own game instead.

"We talked about Wharfie Time and making that our energy [before the game]," Lions midfielder Josh Dunkley said.

"When I looked around at centre bounce and Wharfie Time came on, we all looked at each other, and connected, grew a leg and got it done.

"It's unbelievable."

Other players would say they felt the Dockers thought they had it won, and that you could feel the energy immediately rise in the Brisbane camp.

It was an inspired bit of coaching.

Will the Dockers use Wharfie Time again?

As ABC Sport writer Dean Bilton wrote in his analysis of the game, "it's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful".

The Dockers have not confirmed or denied, and we may have to wait until the first close clash at Perth Stadium next year to know if Wharfie Time has been finally laid to rest.

World.title: Darwin teen 'in shock' after being selected to play in FIFA under-15 World Cup
World.content:
Long before Mark O'Connor ever thought about donning the green-and-gold jersey, there was football in the streets of Darwin.

Back then, the now 15-year-old was just like any other kid playing kickabouts with his mates when his father signed him up to a local club.

He could not have imagined it would be the first step towards representing his country.

Mark has since played for local clubs Greater Palmerston United (GPU), Mindil Aces and Darwin Olympic and now is preparing to join Australia's U-15 FIFA World Cup squad in Baku, Azerbaijan next month.

Mark O'Connor says he never imagined he would be selected to represent Australia in soccer. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I'd say [I was] almost in shock, in disbelief, because I didn't expect any of this to happen," he says.

" And then I felt super excited, but also kind of in disbelief. "

For a Northern Territory teenager who never thought standing on the world stage was something that happened to kids from the Top End, the moment means everything.

"Ever since I was playing from a young age, this is the type of thing that I'd want to be selected for," he says.

Mark O'Connor has played for three local soccer clubs in Darwin including Darwin Olympic. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Raw Territory talent

Mark's success was built through Darwin's footballing community, with different clubs playing a crucial role in his development.

Darwin Olympic president Yianni Prouzos says Mark's selection is also recognition of the region's talent.

"Mark started off as a GPU player, then he had a few years at Mindil Aces, and he spent a fair bit of time at Darwin Olympic," he says.

"For the size of the population, I believe there is a lot of raw talent in the Northern Territory."

Yianni Prouzos says there is a lot of young talent in Darwin's local soccer scene. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Even so, Mr Prouzos says Mark stood out, and he still remembers the first time he saw the marauding midfielder whose inspiration is Premier League giant, Liverpool's Steven Gerrard, play the game.

"The first time he took the pitch, the way he moved with the ball, change of direction of the body, amazing scanning," he says.

"Very small body, a lot of people target him, [but] he gets up.

"His determination, he keeps on coming back and back."

Mark O'Connor has been praised for his skill and determination. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The underdog

Mark says playing football in the tropics, where travelling down south for tournaments often means arriving as the underdog, prepared him for the challenge ahead of facing some of the best young footballers in the world.

"The NT would never really, I'd say, do very well down south, so being the underdog a lot was quite challenging," he said.

"To play against some of the best junior players in the world, it's really special to me.

Mark O'Connor says his previous experience competing interstate has helped prepare him for the international games. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I can see the levels that they're at and see how I compare to them as well."

Darwin Olympic teammate Anthony Reichstein says Mark's selection gives other Territory players something to aspire to.

"I think it gives a lot of the boys and girls up here a chance to make it now because they're clearly looking at Darwin now and it gives everyone a lot of hope," he says.

Beyond Darwin

Football Australia selected players from all nine of its member federations, with young footballers from metropolitan and regional areas earning a place in the national squad.

Talent identification lead Michael Cooper says that representation is particularly important for regional players.

"When you're in these regional areas, you do need that role model," he said.

"You do need to know that pathway is alive for you."

Michael Cooper says the opportunity to play for Australia is particularly important for regional players and their families. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

For Mark, the message is one he knows from experience.

"I started out at the same level as everyone else, playing for the same clubs in the NT," he said.

"And you can really make it to any level you want through enough hard work and dedication."

World.title: 'Hope your tummy OK': Neale responds to Ginnivan's Instagram post
World.content:
Brisbane Lions star Lachie Neale has sent a tongue-in-cheek message to Hawks gun Jack Ginnivan on social media, after Neale was controversially allowed to play in the grand final despite hitting Ginnivan off the ball in the preliminary final.

Neale was initially handed a one-game suspension for the gut punch on Ginnivan, in line with nine other players who were cited for similar incidents throughout the year.

But during an appeals hearing on Thursday evening, it was decided Neale could play in the grand final under "compelling and exceptional circumstances", in that the Lions star had a clean suspension record from his 321 games.

Neale went on to play an important role in Brisbane's stunning come-from-behind victory over Fremantle in the grand final.

Lachie Neale responds to a comment from Jack Ginnivan on his Instagram. (Instagram: @lachieneale)

The dual Brownlow Medallist posted a photo of himself with Brisbane's three premiership cups on Instagram after the match, which Ginnivan replied to with a cherry emoji, signalling the cherry on top of a brilliant career at the Lions.

Neale then replied, "Hope your tummy OK my guy," to Ginnivan in reference to the gut punch.

Ginnivan was uninjured in the incident, however the AFL had been cracking down on strikes to the body off the ball throughout the 2026 season.

The grand final, widely considered one of the most entertaining in history, is likely to be Neale's final game with the Lions.

Having started his career at the Dockers, Neale has spent eight seasons in Brisbane, but looks likely to move to Collingwood next season as a free agent.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in. I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough," Neale said after the game.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life.

"I'm going to miss them very much."

World.title: Bloodied de Minaur scores stirring Laver Cup win over in-form Zverev
World.content:
Alex de Minaur may have ended up with a bloodied knee from a typically fearless diving volley but he was happy to draw blood for Team World by saving a match point en route to downing Alexander Zverev at the Laver Cup.

Helping drag Andre Agassi's side back into the three-day event at London's O2 Arena, the Australian, who simply thrives in team competition, maintained his 100 per cent singles win record against Europe in Laver Cup duels, fighting back to defeat double grand slam champ Zverev 2-6, 7-6 (7-5), 11-9.

"If you can notice, my blood is red as well," De Minaur said, smiling at how Team World's scarlet shirts had seemed to reflect his bloodied right leg, which he had hurt when making the spectacular tumbling Boris Becker-like volley on his way to winning a point in the match tie-breaker.

"It was a very tough match. A tough battle. I left it all out there and got fortunate in the end to get the job done and I'm happy to give some points for Team World."

It was de Minaur's fourth singles win in three editions of the Cup in which he's yet to be defeated in singles combat, and his second-straight victory over Zverev after defeating the German in San Francisco last year as Team World won the title.

"We were in the same position last year and it worked out pretty well for us. We know we can do some damage. We know we're the underdogs, but we also know that we can step out on this court and light it up," de Minaur said.

His victory on Sunday morning AEST put Team World into the lead after Europe's 3-1 overnight lead had evaporated when American Learner Tien outlasted Italy's Flavio Cobolli in a baseline slugfest to secure a 6-3, 2-6, 10-7 victory in the opener to the second day.

But de Minaur's victory was rather more unexpected, especially with Zverev being on a rare roll, unbeaten in nine matches and fresh from both his US Open triumph and two Davis Cup wins.

But de Minaur had looked in good shape on Davis Cup duty in Queensland too and he never gave up the ghost, even when Zverev was serving for the match.

"Check his oil," Agassi had told de Minaur, trying to get him to force Zverev into a wearying war of attrition.

Even then, Zverev missed his big chance, serving for the match and a straight-sets win at 5-4 in the second stanza only to cough up two double faults that allowed de Minaur to break and level the match on a tiebreak.

The next crisis point for de Minaur was when Zverev gained match point in the first-to-10-point match tiebreak, only to play a conservative point.

De Minaur then earned a match point of his own and capitalised on the world number two coming up with a weak smash, which he returned with an irretrievable sharp down-the-line backhand to seal his two-hour win.
